# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article discussing Meta's moderation bias problem suggest a similar impact on users compared to the TechCrunch article on Meta's proposed legislation for teen app downloads, with the former affecting Palestinian voices and the latter concerning parental oversight of teen social media usage?
context:
# Meta's Proposal: Parental Approval For App Downloads At The App Store

Meta wants to shift the burden of monitoring social media usage among teens back to the app stores — and to parents. In a blog post published November 15, 2023, Meta's global head of Safety, Antigone Davis, argued that parents should be responsible for approving their teens' app downloads, and staked Meta's position in supporting federal legislation that would require parental approval for app downloads for users under the age of 16.

The ground Meta offered is public opinion: it pointed to recent Pew research indicating that 81% of U.S. adults were in favor of requiring parental consent for teens to create social media accounts. TechCrunch's caveat is that while this may speak to popular opinion around parental sentiment, it does not mean that parents have thought through who should be responsible for preventing or allowing teens' access to social media, or how those apps should operate to protect teens.

The warrant tying the proposal to the app stores is one of existing capability: the app stores already have age guidelines, so it would seem to follow that they should also enforce them, if enforcement is to be regulated — or that seems to be Meta's thinking. TechCrunch also notes that a policy position like this is not something that would have been rushed out in a matter of days as a PR response to Bejar's claims, but something Meta has been stewing on for some time.



---


# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Meta's Under-13 Policy Versus Its Internal Growth Goals

An internal presentation called "2017 Teens Strategic Focus" appears to specifically target kids under 13, noting that children use tablets as early as 3 or 4, and that "Social identity is an Unmet need Ages 5-11." One stated goal, according to the lawsuit, was specifically to "grow [Monthly Active People], [Daily Active People] and time spent among U13 kids" — a growth objective aimed at the age group Meta's own account rules exclude.

TechCrunch flags an important boundary on what this does and does not show. While Meta does not permit accounts to be run by people under 13, there are plenty of ways it can lawfully and safely engage with that demographic: some kids just want to watch videos from SpongeBob Official, and that is fine. What the law requires is that Meta must verify parental consent, and the ways it can collect and use their data are limited. So targeting under-13s as an audience is not by itself unlawful; the legal question is consent and data use.



---


# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# Meta's Subscription Age Restriction And Teens

The subscription is only being offered to people aged 18 and up, which raises questions over how it will comply with requirements in the DSA and DMA not to process children's data for ad targeting, TechCrunch noted on 2023-10-30.

Meta's stated position on that gap: "We're continuing to explore how to provide teens with a useful and responsible ad experience given this evolving regulatory landscape."



---


# Common Sense Media's Teen Smartphone Study: Design And Scope

A study from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit group in San Francisco, California, researched phone usage among a diverse group of 203 kids aged 11 to 17, and the results were startling, experts say. The researchers found that smartphones have become a "constant companion" for young people, according to a news release, although results varied.

The method combined passive measurement with youth interpretation. In its report, Common Sense Media said it used "software to collect data from the smartphones of a diverse group of about 11- to 17-year-olds. We then interpreted this data with assistance from an advisory council of young people to understand the nuanced relationships that young people develop with their smartphones."

The study carries an explicit platform limitation: it was done with "Android phone users only, because Apple device tracking does not share with the research community the names of specific non-Apple apps that young people commonly use."



---


# The Republican State-Level TikTok Ban Push

Though opposition to TikTok has been bipartisan, the crusade to ban the platform over national security concerns is primarily led by Republicans at the state level, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02. The article treats that position as a likely contributor to the party's social media struggles with young voters.

The observation matters because it sets the party's legislative posture against its outreach problem: the same platform Republicans are campaigning to ban is the one where the youth vote concentrates.



---


# Discord's Graduated Warning System And Account Standing

Discord is introducing a new warning system for people who violate its policies: outside of incidents involving the most "extreme" violations, the company is moving away from permanent bans, doing so under the belief that most users will choose to be better online citizens given the chance and proper guidance.

In practice the system notifies a person when they have violated one or more of Discord's policies and details the restrictions on their account. It also links out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism. A new "Account Standing" tab within the settings menu lets users see all their current and past policy violations.

Discord frames the design as a model for the industry. "We think we've built the most nuanced and proportionate reporting system," Badalich told Engadget, adding that the company hopes other platforms will look to what Discord has created for inspiration in their own enforcement efforts. "We believe people, especially teens, have the capacity to grow."



---


# Pebble's Moderation-First Market Hypothesis

Pebble's founding hypothesis was that consumers were hungry for a Twitter alternative that prioritized trust, safety and moderation from the start. The company staffed for it: Pebble's founding team included co-founder Sarah Oh, Twitter's former human rights advisor.

What would falsify the proposition is a moderation-first Twitter alternative that consumers decline to adopt — which is the shape of the outcome TechCrunch is reporting on 2023-10-24, in a piece about Pebble shutting down.

qid: Are the concerns expressed by 'College football coaches' about the alleged sign-stealing as reported by 'The New York Times' aligned with the implications for the 'Wolverines (Michigan's football team)' as discussed in 'Sporting News' regarding the difficulty of erasing the scandal from the Big Ten record?
context:
# The Michigan Sign-Stealing Scandal In Outline

The Michigan sign-stealing scandal is an NCAA investigation into the Wolverines for in-person scouting and sign stealing, a saga that began in October 2023 and led to the resignation of staffer Connor Stalions on Nov. 3. The affair centred on an alleged illegal sign-stealing scheme run out of the football program, and it evolved by the hour, with one update after another adding a further wrinkle. On the field Michigan was in the midst of what could be a historic season; off it, the focus was rarely on the team's success.

The investigation produced conference discipline before it produced any NCAA finding. The Big Ten suspended coach Jim Harbaugh for three games on Friday while the team was on a plane en route to Penn State; Michigan had hoped to block the suspension but the Wolverines were left without their coach on the sidelines in Happy Valley. Under the Friday ruling Harbaugh was allowed to coach during the week but not to be on the sideline, and Michigan did not obtain a ruling on a temporary restraining order ahead of the showdown against No. 10 Penn State.

Michigan still won that game 24-15 under interim coach Sherrone Moore, but Sporting News judged that the fallout from the scandal would continue to have a far-reaching impact on the Big Ten, on Michigan and on college football beyond that year's College Football Playoff race.



---


# The NCAA Investigation Into Michigan's Scouting Scheme

The NCAA is investigating Michigan's football program amid allegations that the Wolverines used illegal in-person scouting and the recording of signals to steal signs this season, as reported by The New York Times on 3 November 2023.

The conference's involvement is dated. Ahead of the Michigan-Michigan State game on 21 October, the Big Ten approached MSU and said it was made aware of "credible evidence" regarding the sign-stealing allegations, and said it would monitor the NCAA's investigation into Michigan.

The timing problem is spelled out. The NCAA investigation is ongoing, a process that typically moves slowly, which makes it difficult to imagine it will reach a resolution by the time the postseason begins. The Big Ten does have the ability to act under its sportsmanship policy, but that doesn't mean it would want to act quickly or decisively before the NCAA completes its entire investigation and allows Michigan a chance to respond to its findings.



---


# Michigan's 2023 Team Culture And Expectations

Sporting News argued that the 2023 Wolverines were the most mature player-led Michigan football team on the field since 1997 — the year the program beat Ohio State 20-14 in a top-five showdown and split the national championship with Nebraska — and that the win over Ohio State showed a team that no longer merely hopes to win The Game but expects to. The grounds were the season's two parallel stories: an off-field one in which the team kept overcoming obstacles, self-inflicted and otherwise, and an on-field one described as a withering march through the Big Ten toward a third straight College Football Playoff berth.

The obstacle was Jim Harbaugh's three-game suspension from the Big Ten over the illegal in-person scouting and sign-stealing operation, which dominated headlines more than the Wolverines dominated opponents in the second half of the season. Staffer Connor Stalions and assistant coach Chris Partridge were gone, and Harbaugh was suspended; he addressed the team on Friday, and McCarthy listened closely. "The one thing he said that stuck out, the whole mantra, 'The Team, The Team, The Team,'" McCarthy said. "He said we are that team."

The warrant is the pattern of who blinks in high-magnitude games. Ohio State had not lost three in a row to Michigan since 1995-97, and since 1997 the Buckeyes had found a way in these games, with 2006 and 2016 the best examples; on a stage somewhere in between those classics, the Wolverines pointed the pressure the other way. Marvin Harrison Jr. had five catches for 118 yards and a touchdown, but Michigan then ran seven minutes off the clock and added a field goal — a further point of criticism for Ryan Day and defensive coordinator Jim Knowles.

The players' own framing matched. Just as the year before, McCarthy and Corum took turns repeating the famous Kobe Bryant mantra in the postgame press conference: "The job is not finished," McCarthy said. "We've been here before." Corum added, "We've been going through things all year, so we know how to stick together and play for each other and always have our brother's back." The previous two years had ended with Big Ten championship game victories followed by losses to Georgia and TCU in the CFP semifinals, and the story would now continue at least into the Big Ten championship game against No. 17 Iowa. The NCAA investigation would continue too, but Sporting News concluded that the Wolverines would play out the rest of the season on their terms — and that Harbaugh returned Monday.



---


# The CFP Committee's "Different Team" Justification For Florida State

The New York Times attacked the CFP committee's justification for omitting Florida State on 3 December 2023, arguing that CFP committee chair Boo Corrigan's statement — "Florida State is a different team. You look at who they are as a team without Jordan Travis — they are a different team" — is a well-informed opinion that is probably true, but is not a fact.

The premise under attack is that a team's quality without its injured starter can be reliably judged in advance. Choosing the best is entirely subjective and ultimately misleading given this is a sport that routinely features unpredictable results and unforeseen runs. The precedent cited is that the last time a team was relying on a third-string quarterback heading into the College Football Playoff — Ohio State in the inaugural season of the four-team field — it won the national title.

The rebuttal also concedes the disanalogy and then answers it. The difference between those Buckeyes and this Florida State team was that Ohio State won the Big Ten title game that year 59-0, while Florida State was in a close game with Louisville that was, quite frankly, not an enjoyable watch for people who love the excitement of big-time offense — perception, wrongly, became reality. Against that, one could make the case that Florida State is so good that it won a Power 5 conference championship game with a true freshman quarterback, and that in the CFP the Seminoles would have gotten second-string quarterback Tate Rodemaker back with a month to prepare for a semifinal game.



---


# Michigan State Hires Jonathan Smith Away From Oregon State

Michigan State hired Jonathan Smith as its next football coach, the school announcing the move on Saturday, as reported by CBS Sports on 2023-11-25. Smith, 44, had spent the past six seasons as coach at Oregon State, where he guided the Beavers to 18 wins over the past two seasons, including a 10-3 mark and a No. 17 finish in the AP Top 25 during a 2022 campaign that earned him Pac-12 Coach of the Year honors. He was among the initial pool of candidates linked to the Michigan State opening after the Spartans fired fourth-year coach Mel Tucker with cause midseason amid sexual harassment allegations, and he later emerged as the leading candidate to replace Tucker during the final week of the regular season — a week in which Oregon State suffered a 31-7 loss at rival Oregon.

Michigan State athletic director Alan Haller framed the hire around Smith's record: "Jonathan has a proven track record of success, building the Oregon State program from the ground up by implementing a plan resulting in sustained historic success for the Beavers. He's been a part of championship staffs, coached in the College Football Playoff, and understands what's required to be successful at the highest level, learning from some of the game's most successful coaches." Haller added that on the field Smith's teams are tough and physical yet innovative, that Oregon State that year had controlled the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball while ranking among the nation's leaders in both rushing offense and rushing defense, and that Smith has shown the ability both to recruit talented student-athletes who fit his system and to develop and maximize players once they're in the program. Smith, a former quarterback for the Beavers from 1998-2001, exited Oregon State with a 34-35 overall mark as coach, including a 1-1 record in bowl games, as he joined the Big Ten coaching ranks. In a statement posted to social media he thanked the players, coaches and colleagues of the last six years, said he would cherish the memories and friendships, and expressed his deepest gratitude to the people of OSU and Corvallis, noting that when he first arrived as a freshman college student he had no idea the opportunities and relationships the community would provide for him and his family.



---


# Everton Case Implications For Manchester City And Chelsea

Sean Dyche declined to comment on the implications of Everton's punishment for Manchester City and Chelsea, The Guardian reported on Nov. 24, 2023.

Manchester City had been charged with 115 financial breaches by the Premier League and deny any wrongdoing; Chelsea were also under investigation by the football authorities.

qid: Which company, recently discussed on both The Verge and TechCrunch, has the capability to address Android app distribution issues and uses specific criteria to rank local search results, while also being accused of harming news publishers' profits through its business practices?
context:
# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.

qid: Does 'The Verge' article suggest that Apple enforces uniform terms through its store and payment system in a similar way to how 'TechCrunch' claims Apple restricts browser selection on iPhones during setup?
context:
# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)



---


# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.



---


# Why iPhone Discounts Come From Carriers, Not Retailers

WIRED's Apple Black Friday guide of 25 November 2023 sets out a simple structure for how iPhone discounting works: you typically will not see many iPhone deals from retailers, because the sales that do exist usually come from carriers — AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile — and are attached to conditions rather than offered as straight price cuts.

The relation running through this model is conditional rather than promotional. Carrier iPhone offers carry several requirements, such as being on an unlimited plan or opening a new cell line, so the discount is granted in exchange for a service commitment rather than being available to any buyer at checkout. That is what distinguishes iPhone pricing from the rest of the Apple lineup covered in the same guide, where straightforward retailer discounts are the norm.

The range over which the model holds is narrow and stated: it applies to current iPhones during the November 2023 holiday sales, and WIRED notes the exceptions itself, having laid out a few deals on older unlocked iPhone models alongside some carrier promotions for readers in the market for a new phone.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

qid: Has the perspective on the US economy's risk of entering a recession as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald changed between the article published on October 1, 2023, and the one published on December 5, 2023?
context:
# Wall Street December 2023 Mixed Session

Most US stocks slipped in the overnight Wall Street session reported on 5 December 2023, though the market stayed near its highest level in 20 months after a mixed set of reports that kept alive questions about whether the world's largest economy can pull off a perfect landing in which it kills high inflation but avoids a recession. The S&P 500 edged down 0.1 per cent for its first back-to-back loss since October, the Dow Jones slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent.

Stocks fell more sharply in Asia amid worries about the health of China's economy, the world's second largest. US stocks and Treasury yields wavered after reports showed that US employers advertised far fewer jobs at the end of October than expected, while growth for services businesses accelerated more in the prior month than expected.

The underlying hope on Wall Street at the time was that the US economy was slowing from its recent hot pace by just the right amount: too much strength would give inflation more fuel, but too little would mean a recession. The Australian market's gains that day came after this mixed US session.



---


# The Wall Street September 2023 Selloff And Bond Yields

September 2023 brought a loss of 5.2 per cent so far for the S&P 500, putting it on track to be the worst month of the year by far, as the realisation set in that the Federal Reserve would indeed keep interest rates high for a long time. That growing understanding sent yields in the bond market to their highest levels in more than a decade, which in turn undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

Treasury yields rose again on Tuesday, 2023-09-26, following a mixed batch of reports on the economy: the yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.55 per cent from 4.54 per cent late on Monday and is near its highest level since 2007, up sharply from about 3.5 per cent in May and from 0.5 per cent about three years ago. One economic report that Tuesday showed confidence among consumers was weaker than economists expected — concerning because strong spending by US households has been a bulwark keeping the economy out of a long-predicted recession.



---


# The Middle East Conflict As A Market Risk In October 2023

Investors in October 2023 were treating the Middle East conflict as a conditional risk rather than an active one: with Israeli air strikes attacking Gaza on Tuesday and razing entire districts in the densely populated and impoverished enclave, markets were being sanguine, but the sanguine view was explicitly contingent on the fighting not spreading.

John Praveen, managing director and co-chief investment officer at Paleo Leon, set out the transmission both ways. "Everybody has one eye on the Middle East conflict and one eye on what's happening with bond yields. The decline in bond yields is the key driver today," he said. But that view could change if, for example, the fighting spread to other countries in the region: "If tensions escalate bond yields might decline further because they're a safe haven, but equities would sell off in that instance because of increased uncertainty and risk aversion." Other signals ran alongside. Billionaire investor Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC the current geopolitical environment was the "most threatening and challenging" he had ever seen following Hamas's attack on Israel over the weekend, and predicted the US will enter a recession early next year. The shekel regained its footing as the central bank duelled short sellers to contain the market fallout from Israel's conflict with Hamas. European gas prices jumped, with Finland on high alert as it suspects a gas pipeline leak in the Baltic Sea was caused by a deliberate act of destruction, fuelling concerns about the safety of Europe's energy infrastructure. And base metals sank amid fresh fears over property turmoil in China.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# An Australian Pandemic Account By Aisha Dow And Melissa Cunningham

Aisha Dow and Melissa Cunningham's account of how the pandemic affected Australia, published by Scribe at $35 on 3 October, is a timely publication coming only a few days after Daniel Andrews — "the man who approved probably the world's longest cumulative lockdown" — left office, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its defining feature is the treatment: while many people may not want to revisit those stressful years, the two journalists with Nine newspapers "manage to make this a riveting story of discovery, dismay, and recovery".

The reviewer places it against what was still to come: "Ahead of the government's impending inquiry, you might find some answers here."



---


# Australian Inflation Data And The RBA's Near-Certain November Rise

GSFM investment strategist Stephen Miller said the inflation data, taken with the October Reserve Bank board meeting minutes — which revealed the board had "low tolerance for a slower return of inflation to target than currently expected" — made the possibility of an interest rate rise from the central bank in November a "near certainty."

Commodity prices nonetheless supported mining companies, as iron ore prices increased 2.9 per cent overnight, bolstering Australia's iron ore giants. This came as Chinese President Xi Jinping stepped up support for the world's second-biggest economy and major commodity trading partner for Australia, issuing additional sovereign debt, raising the budget deficit ratio and even making an unprecedented visit to the central bank. On Wall Street, the benchmark S&P 500 index closed 0.7 per cent higher ahead of tech giants Microsoft and Alphabet reporting results after the close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.6 per cent and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 gained 0.9 per cent. Shares in Microsoft climbed 5 per cent in after-hours trading after the company said its sales jumped 13 per cent to $US56.5 billion ($88.9 billion) and profits climbed 27 per cent to $US22.3 billion in the three months through September.



---


# Wall Street November 2023 Relief Rally

Wall Street closed a strong week on the Friday before this 5 November 2023 report, with the S&P 500 climbing 40.56 points, or 0.9 per cent, to 4,358.3; the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 222.24, or 0.7 per cent, to 34,061.32; and the Nasdaq composite jumping 184.09, or 1.4 per cent, to 13,478.28. Stocks surged through the week on rising hopes that the Federal Reserve is finally done with its market-crunching interest rate hikes aimed at getting inflation under control, with a Friday report underscoring easing inflation pressure by showing employers hired fewer workers in October than economists expected.

The report described this as a stunning turnaround from just a week earlier, when Wall Street was reeling after the S&P 500 had fallen 10 per cent below its high point for the year, sending the index into what investors call a "correction". Since then, strong profit reports helped drive some stocks to towering gains: Generac, a maker of back-up generators, soared nearly 28 per cent for its best week since its stock began trading in 2010, and Expedia Group's stronger-than-forecast report sent its stock nearly 22 per cent higher for its best week since the market was surging out of the coronavirus crash in early 2020. Even so, it was interest rates, yields and inflation that were at the centre of all the wild movements for financial markets around the world.

Excitement about a potentially easier Fed was more than enough to offset a fall for Apple, Wall Street's most influential and most valuable US stock, which fell 0.5 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected; analysts said investors were likely disappointed with Apple's revenue forecast for the last three months of 2023.

qid: Who is the individual under 30 that was once the richest in the world, associated with the cryptocurrency platform FTX, and is facing allegations of fraud according to TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. # Betting The Other Majors And Team Golf Events

The US Open, PGA Championship and British Open — often referred to as The Open Championship — are among the four major championships in professional golf alongside the Masters, and each has unique course challenges and attributes that create many betting opportunities. The most popular markets for these events are to win; top 5, 10, 20 and so on; head-to-head matchups; nationality; first round leader; hole-in-one props; and top amateur.

Team golf events such as the Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup offer a thrilling twist to tournament viewing. # Moneyline Outcomes: Win, Loss, Draw And Push

A moneyline wager can end in several ways: the most straightforward outcomes are a win or a loss, determined by whether the team or individual you backed was victorious or defeated, and there is also the possibility of a draw if the event ends in a tie. Winning is simply a matter of picking the eventual winner — bet on Boxer B in a bout between Boxer A and Boxer B, and if Boxer B wins you are paid based on the odds at the time you placed the wager. A loss means the side you backed did not win: bet $100 on Team A in an NBA game and, if Team B wins, the bet on Team A loses.

Some sports price the draw as its own selection. In soccer especially, games can end in a draw and bettors can wager on that outcome, so a moneyline typically shows three sets of odds — one for each team to win and one for the draw. For a match between Team A and Team B, the odds might read Team A +150, Draw +220, Team B +180; a $100 wager on "Draw" that lands returns $220 in profit on top of the $100 stake, totaling $320, while a win by either team loses the $100.

A tie handled as a "push" is a different case, and the scope condition matters. When a push occurs bettors are refunded their original wager, with no money won or lost; but sports that typically allow a tie, like soccer, often offer the draw as a bet instead, and if the game ends in a draw and you did not bet that option, you lose. It is therefore essential to understand the specific rules of the sportsbook and the sport to know how ties are handled. Finally, in most sports and with most sportsbooks — including new betting sites — overtime or any extra time or tiebreakers do count toward a moneyline bet, though you should always check your sportsbook's specific rules.

# Prop Bet Examples By Sport

Every major sport with odds at the best sports betting apps will have prop bets, and the shape of those props follows each sport's statistics. The NBA offers a wide range, varying from player to team bets and leaning heavily on the statistical side of the game: how many points a player will score, the number of assists or three-pointers a player will have, which player will score the first basket. Team props are also available, such as whether a team will lead at the end of a certain quarter, or an over/under on the total number of points a team will score.

The NFL is the king of sports betting, and NFL betting sites have no qualms about showcasing every possible bet type. Bettors find many prop opportunities, especially for the Super Bowl; during the regular season one of the most popular options is the "anytime touchdown scorer" bet, where you wager on a player to score a touchdown at any point in the game, and other props focus on one team or both teams.

Baseball, hockey and soccer follow the same logic on their own stat lines. MLB props focus primarily on individual players and statistical achievements such as home runs, RBI and strikeouts — an over/under for a starting pitcher's strikeouts, or the number of bases a hitter will reach. NHL sites carry the props you would expect from a major North American league, such as player assists or a certain player scoring a goal, plus shots on goal, team goals in a game, and which team will score first. In Major League Soccer, where demand has increased as the sport's popularity grows nationwide, props often focus on individual accomplishments such as scoring a goal or collecting an assist, and also include how many cards the two teams will combine to draw or a team's total number of corner kicks.

# Totals Line Movement Drivers

The totals line can move, and Sporting News attributes that movement to four kinds of input: betting activity, injury updates, weather conditions, and other news and updates.

Betting activity is one of the most common reasons for line movement — a significant amount of money wagered on one side, either the over or the under, leads bookmakers to adjust the line to balance the action and protect themselves from potential losses. Injury updates work through the expected score: if a key player is injured or unable to play, that can influence the expected total score, leading bookmakers to adjust the line accordingly. Weather conditions matter in outdoor sports; heavy rain or snow in a football game might create expectations of a lower-scoring game, causing the line to move down. Finally, any other news that might affect team performance — changes in team strategy or recent performances — can influence totals lines.

# The Exorcist III

The Exorcist III, written and directed by William Peter Blatty — the original screenwriter of The Exorcist and author of the novel it was based on — is, in Polygon's judgment, the sequel that came closest to capturing the same lightning in a bottle as William Friedkin's original, which nearly 50 years after its theatrical release has withstood the test of time as one of the most terrifying and influential horror films in American cinema. It was the Oct. 31 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Prime Video and the Criterion Channel.

When a series of gruesome murders matching the modus operandi of an infamous serial killer begins to terrorize the city of Georgetown, Lt. William F. Kinderman, played by George C. Scott, investigates the psych ward of a local hospital in search of leads. Confronted with a suspect whose appearance matches that of his late friend Father Damien Karras, Kinderman is thrust into a battle for his very soul as he confronts an evil beyond his comprehension.

Polygon's Toussaint Egan calls the production history a tangled mess of false starts, studio interference, and thwarted artistic ambitions: it was originally conceived with Friedkin in mind to return as director, but he left over creative differences with Blatty; John Carpenter was at one time tapped to direct before he too stepped aside to let Blatty take the reins; and financier Morgan Creek Productions demanded Blatty reshoot the final act, which originally ended without an exorcism. Even so, Egan calls it a fascinating and terrifying film in its own right, with a hodgepodge of fascinating creative choices and literary dialogue that makes it feel like a sister piece to Blatty's The Ninth Configuration — maybe not the Exorcist sequel audiences at the time wanted, but still a damn fine picture.

# In The Mouth Of Madness: Carpenter's Apocalypse Trilogy Closer

In the Mouth of Madness is among the wildest movies John Carpenter has ever made — and Polygon notes that is saying something. Starring Sam Neill, Julie Carmen and Jurgen Prochnow, and watchable on YouTube, it follows insurance investigator John Trent (Neill), who is hired to find a missing famous horror novelist; things become increasingly unhinged as the plots of the author's books and the various monsters seem to invade the real world.

Its place in Carpenter's work is specific — this is the third film in his apocalypse trilogy, which also includes two other stone-cold classics, The Thing and Prince of Darkness, which are not on the list but which the reviewer recommends anyway.

# The Roland Doe Case and The Exorcist

Perhaps the most famous instance of purported demonic possession connected to Ouija board usage was the case of "Roland Doe", a young teenage boy from Maryland, who underwent numerous major exorcisms in 1949, said Fr. Dan Reehil.

Doe's story was adapted into the 1971 book "The Exorcist" by William Peter Blatty, which was then made into the 1973 movie starring Ellen Burstyn and Linda Blair.

# Five Nights at Freddy's Movie Development and Release

The possessed-animatronics horror video game Five Nights at Freddy's is less than a decade old, but a movie version had been in the works almost since the game launched — a protracted development process Polygon recounted on 2023-10-26.

Warner Bros. bought the movie rights in 2015, and the project moved over to Blumhouse a couple of years later. Game creator Scott Cawthon wrote and rewrote the script, while kid-horror filmmakers including Gil Kenan of Monster House and Chris Columbus of Gremlins and the first Harry Potter and Percy Jackson movies signed on and jumped off the project.

Finally, under director Emma Tammi, the film hit theaters simultaneously with a Peacock streaming debut. Polygon framed its accompanying Q&A as extremely spoiler-light and aimed at people other than the franchise's most hardcore fans, deliberately not digging into the considerable FNAF lore and focusing instead on who the film is for and what to expect.

# Scorsese's Maximalist, Improvisational Late Style

Where aging has meant settling for more routine and less challenging stories and shots on a tight production schedule for certain older filmmakers — Polygon names Clint Eastwood — Scorsese went in the other direction, into a maximalist, improvisational late style. The account is Polygon's, published 2023-10-26.

The Departed is the first case. From the outside it appears to be a cynical, domestic remake of a Hong Kong cops-and-robbers shootout, but Scorsese makes it his own and breathes bizarre life and energy into it: it contains the continuity errors, quick cutting, both rhythmic and arrhythmic needle bombs, and goofball humor his movies had not featured since Goodfellas. That earlier film essentially birthed an entire genre of filmic language, and The Departed goes a step beyond the original, being constantly rewritten and adjusted with the actors on the fly — exhilarating seat-of-the-pants filmmaking that Scorsese and his longtime creative partner, editor Thelma Schoonmaker, wrangled into a coherent film.

He brought the same cokey, maximalist energy to The Wolf of Wall Street, a pointed comedy as wildly, masterfully off the rails and improvisational as anything he has done, with Jonah Hill perhaps smuggling in a touch of Judd Apatow's "keep the camera rolling" ethos. Established-filmmaker confidence — and a touch of "eh, why not?" thinking — shows as DiCaprio's Ferrari changes color mid-narration during a highway blowjob, and when DiCaprio addresses the camera directly urging the audience not to worry about specific plot points. Polygon calls it a miracle that Scorsese and Schoonmaker produced a masterpiece out of the chaotic pieces of that production, again in post and with ample voice-over, with the shoot taking on something of a religious quality in the participants' retelling.

What grounds the style is the framing. Scorsese is telling a familiar story audiences have come to expect from him, about criminals and the pleasure they take in committing crimes and reaping the benefits; the brilliance is how he mines filmgoers' long relationship with his work, repurposing the style and tone of his gangster classics and inserting it into the world of finance. As he has done effectively since Casino, Scorsese weaponizes postmodernism, using viewers' presumed existing familiarity with his films as context — you do not get the full gale force of the film, its pleasures, or its overarching point without him reaching back to his past work and relying on viewers to recognize his voice in the storytelling.

# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.
