# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. ---

Temu, the Chinese e-commerce company, is Apple's most downloaded free app in the U.S. for 2023. Apple released an App Store feature on 12 December 2023 showcasing the top iPhone apps of the year, free and paid, as measured by app installs — its proxy for overall popularity. # Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# The Sherman Act Verdict As The First Major Tech Antitrust Win Since Microsoft

Tim Sweeney argued that the jury's finding for Epic showed "the Sherman Antitrust Act works in the new era of tech monopolies" — his grounds being that no major antitrust verdict against a tech company that meant change and benefits for everybody had landed since the 1990s and US v. Microsoft, back in the early days of the internet.

The warrant joining claim and grounds is his account of present-day harm: the industry, he said, is "being strangled by a few gatekeepers imposing insane amounts of control and extracting huge taxes," which not only raise prices for consumers but also make a lot of kinds of products simply unviable. If the statute can still reach that conduct after a three-decade gap, then it remains a working remedy, which is why he called the verdict "a great day for all developers" and "much needed by the industry." Sweeney was speaking about a trial four years in the making, tracing back to a September 2019 email produced in discovery about a plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust.



---


# Rogers Communications' Rebuttal On Information Access

Rogers Communications denied the sisters' premise that they were improperly cut off from information, saying the company took "reasonable steps" to protect company information from a competitor. Spokesperson Sarah Schmidt added that Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers could have resolved the matter by choosing a different lawyer, "and they chose not to do so" — putting the cause of their exclusion on their own choice rather than on any vendetta.

The company also disputed that the courtroom was the right venue and that the dispute was harming the business. "This matter should be resolved privately," Schmidt said by email. "We've demonstrated that we will not be distracted by these actions — we have significant momentum in the market, our merger is tracking ahead of plan, and we remain squarely focused on doing what's right for our customers and stakeholders."



---


# Lawsuit Redactions As Signal: The Amazon Precedent

TechCrunch reads heavy redaction as itself informative: you know it is bad news for the company when they request pages and pages of redactions.

The precedent it cites is recent. This recently happened with Amazon as well, and it turned out they were trying to hide the existence of a price-hiking algorithm that skimmed billions from consumers.

The comparison is used to rank severity rather than to equate the two: it is much worse, TechCrunch writes, when you are redacting COPPA complaints.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.



---


# The 2016 ISA Renegotiation And Its Revenue-Share Dispute

Eddy Cue testified that when Apple and Google renegotiated the ISA, Apple wanted a higher percentage of the revenue Google made from the Apple users it directed to the search engine, while Sundar Pichai wanted to keep the deal as it was; the two eventually compromised on some other number that was not disclosed in open court, and Google has been paying Apple that amount since.

Discussion of specific numbers was reserved for closed court sessions. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw asked Cue whether he would have walked away from the deal if the two sides couldn't agree on a revenue-share figure, and Cue said he had never really considered that an option: "I always felt like it was in Google's best interest, and our best interest, to get a deal done." Cue also argued that the deal was about more than economics, that Apple never seriously considered switching to another provider or building its own search product, and that "certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — adding that there still isn't one.

# YouTube's AI Music Incubator And Its Rightsholder Pledges

During its period of discussions with the majors, YouTube made a series of announcements aimed at the biggest issue for any rightsholder regarding AI-driven voice replication of artists: their ability to police it.

In August, YouTube and Universal Music Group jointly announced that the video platform was launching an "AI Music Incubator" — a program by which new tools and innovations would be developed at YouTube in close conjunction with artists and the music business; to progress the incubator, YouTube said it was working behind the scenes with a number of UMG-affiliated artists. Also in August, YouTube publicly committed to three principles or pledges behind its development of music-based generative AI tools. These pledges promised "appropriate protections… for music partners who decide to participate" in such tools, and promised "invest[ment] in the AI-powered technology" that, among other things, would help YouTube "protect our community of viewers, creators, artists and songwriters… [from] trademark and copyright abuse" — all of which seemed to hint at a desire to build a "Content ID"-style system on YouTube to control and police content made by cloning artists' voices. Then, earlier in November, YouTube announced it was developing a specific system for music partners allowing them to request the removal of content on its platform that "mimics an artist's unique singing or rapping voice."



---


# Sony Music's Absence From "Dream Track"

Dennis Kooker's public statements on AI arrived a week after MBW pointed out a notable lack of endorsement from Sony Music Entertainment, and its artists, of YouTube's experimental AI project "Dream Track," which lets creators clone the vocals of successful musicians.

The initial cohort of stars involved in the project included recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each of those two majors — but no Sony Music artists. In its earlier report MBW suggested that YouTube parent Google's recent submission to the United States Copyright Office, made in response to a request for written submissions as part of a study around copyright law and policy issues raised by AI systems, may have influenced Sony's absence from Dream Track.



---


# Thesis That Music Labels Are Headed for Irrelevance

The argument, common among music business observers from the world of tech, is that record labels could in the long term be headed for irrelevance. Its grounds are the arrival of digital platforms, including open ones like YouTube and SoundCloud, together with the proliferation of indie music distribution platforms such as DistroKid and TikTok's SoundOn.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is a claim about what labels are for: in a world where anyone can record music using a desktop audio workstation (DAW) and upload it directly to YouTube, or to Spotify via a distribution platform, labels have little left to do. Recording and distribution — the functions the label historically supplied — are available to any artist directly, so on this reasoning the label's remaining role shrinks toward nothing. Music Business Worldwide presented this as the speculation that tech-world observers "like to" make, and as the position Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl was answering at the Code Conference in September 2023.



---


# The UMG, Concord And ABKCO Lawsuit Against Anthropic Over Song Lyrics

Universal Music Group, Concord Music Group and ABKCO filed a lawsuit against AI developer Anthropic seeking potentially tens of millions of dollars for the alleged "systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics."

Music Business Worldwide noted on 2023-11-30 that the fair use argument Anthropic had advanced in its submission to the US Copyright Office could yet come into play in the company's legal battle with Universal.



---


# AI Copyright And Training Disputes

Universal Music Group's answer to generative AI trained on its catalogue rejects the premise that such training is a neutral technical act, recasting it as a choice of allegiance: "The training of generative AI using our artists' music . . . begs the question as to which side of history all stakeholders in the music ecosystem want to be on: the side of artists, fans and human creative expression, or on the side of deep fakes, fraud and denying artists their due compensation," the label said after a song using AI to imitate Drake and The Weeknd, two of its artists, went viral.

A second objection cuts against the label framing itself. These same conversations and contradictions are manifesting across creative industries, but artists themselves don't always have a seat at the table — so an industry-level statement of grievance is not the same thing as artists speaking for themselves. Independent artists in particular are learning that their voices resonate louder when coming together across disciplines to push back against what Holland describes as an "extraordinary spectrum of exploitation" that leverages their work.

The dispute is not confined to music. In a roundtable hosted by the FTC that same week, the agency brought together figures from across creative industries — from voice acting and science fiction to screenwriting, music, illustration and even fashion — to delve into how generative AI is affecting creatives. TechCrunch reported the exchange on 2023-10-06.



---


# The EU-US Asymmetry In Recorded Music Performance Rights

At the heart of the dispute is a difference in how the US and the EU pay artists for terrestrial (non-satellite) radio broadcasts of music and recorded music played in bars and restaurants.

In Europe, when recorded music is played over terrestrial radio or in venues, performance rights payments must be made to the artists and labels behind the recording, as well as to the songwriters and publishers who own the composition behind the recording. In the US, by contrast, performance rights payments are made only to the songwriters and publishers, and not to artists and labels.



---


# The Digital-First Artist Development Model

The success of "Si No Estás" illustrates how much artist development has changed: social media and digital music services have now become the number one source of music discovery, and Believe has developed an innovative, AI and data-driven expertise to develop tracks and artists that Alejandra Olea describes as unique in the music industry.

The model's components and their relations are stated together: the key to success is great partnerships with the artist and their label, and being able to combine strong AI data-driven expertise to maximise momentum for an artist and a track at the right time with the right tools and the right partnerships, supported by both local and global teams. Olea singles out the last element as particularly important and truly one of Believe's strengths, being able to mobilise teams multi-locally and globally to accompany audience development for artists. The forward-looking claim attached to the model is that this is only the beginning for Iñigo Quintero and that Believe anticipates many more successes like his in future.



---


# Reaction Content on YouTube

Reaction content is an umbrella term that applies to a content creator responding to or riffing on an existing piece of media, as Polygon defined it on 2023-10-25.

It has been controversial for a long time. In 2016 the Fine Brothers made an infamous attempt to copyright their "React" videos, which was met with near unanimous criticism.

The conversation reignited in August, when popular creators like Félix "xQc" Lengyel "reacted" to long-form content with very little — if any — original input or transformative commentary.



---


# TikTok Users' Music Discovery And Sharing Rates

The Luminate study found that the TikTok audience can be an effective marketing tool for artists, because TikTok users in particular are considerably more likely to discover and share music than overall social media and short video platform users.

In the UK, TikTok users were 108% more likely to discover and share music than other social media users; in Germany they were 100% more likely; and US TikTok users were 71% more likely. "In doing so, TikTok users help both emerging and established artists to reach new audiences," the Luminate report stated.



---


# Capitol's International-First, Direct-To-Fan Campaign Model

Capitol Music Group's changed approach to artist campaigns is to engage directly with international partners earlier than ever before, rather than unfairly relying on its ex-US affiliates within UMG to do the heavy lifting early on, since those affiliates have their own local repertoire to work on. The stated reason for the early emphasis on international is to start the process of building revenue streams as early as possible, specifically brand building and direct-to-fan monetization.

The model's range is illustrated by Ice Spice: she still has not released her debut album, yet is recognised around the world through commercials, syncs in video games, TV and film, a big soundtrack presence, and innovative products on her own store, with Michelle Jubelirer pointing to the Ice Spice American Flag and Chia Pet as examples. The case shows the mechanism working before the usual album milestone, which is the point of moving the international and commerce work earlier in a campaign.

qid: Does the article from Fortune suggest that the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes are unrelated to past conditions, such as booming home prices, while The Sydney Morning Herald article indicates that the Federal Reserve's future interest rate decisions will be based on incoming economic data?
context:
# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# US Treasury Yields And Fed Rate Expectations In October 2023

The mechanism linking data to yields to stocks ran in both directions during October 2023. On 4 October, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, the centrepiece of the bond market, pulled back from its highest level since 2007, down to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late on the Tuesday, with shorter- and longer-term yields also easing to allow more oxygen for the stock market. Yields fell following reports indicating a slowing US economy, the first suggesting that hiring by employers outside the government was much weaker than expected; on Wall Street that is currently good news because a cooling job market could mean less upward pressure on inflation, which in turn could convince the Federal Reserve to take it easier on interest rates. After already raising its main interest rate to the highest level since 2001, the Fed had indicated it may keep its overnight rate higher next year than earlier expected, and Treasury yields had correspondingly snapped higher as traders accept a new normal of high rates for longer; the Fed pays particular attention to the job market because too much strength there could drive wages much higher, which it fears could keep inflation well above its target of 2 per cent.

By 12 October the same mechanism was running the other way. The stock market has largely been taking its cue from the bond market recently, and weak results announced in the afternoon for an auction of 30-year Treasury bonds sent yields of all kinds higher; higher yields can knock down prices for stocks and slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive. Yields had already been rising in the morning after a report showing consumer-level inflation a touch higher than economists expected, raising worries about the Fed keeping its main interest rate high for a long time as it tries to undercut inflation by knocking down investment prices and slowing the economy. The report also had encouraging nuggets: after ignoring prices for food and fuel, which Fed officials see as a better predictor of where inflation is heading, prices consumers paid were in line with expectations and continued to decelerate from earlier months. A second report said slightly fewer US workers than expected applied for unemployment benefits, indicating a job market with few lay-offs and therefore strength for the overall economy, though it could also add fuel to upward pressure on inflation. After the reports the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.7 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Wednesday, and the two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks expectations for the Fed, climbed to 5.06 per cent from 4.99 per cent, with yields still down slightly for the week after regressing from more-than-decade highs following speeches that investors saw as hints the Fed may not raise its main overnight rate further. The big jump for the 10-year yield since the summer has pulled mortgage rates to their highest levels since the turn of the millennium, and such moves could slow the economy without requiring more Fed hikes; Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said nothing in Thursday's inflation report should sway the Fed one way or the other on what it will do on 1 November, calling the data "reassuringly uneventful".



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# US Home Prices Peaked In June 2022 And Returned To A Record High By July 2023

National U.S. home prices did not peak until June 2022 — even as mortgage rates soared and purchase applications plummeted amid the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hikes — and although prices fell more than 5% from that peak by January 2023, they returned to a record high in July 2023. This is the observation that has so far vindicated the majority of real estate veterans, who despite a widely bearish industry outlook avoided arguing that home prices would drop the way they did during the 2008 crash that kicked off the Global Financial Crisis.

The backdrop, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-06, is that housing market pessimists had been sounding the alarm for years about a pending crash in U.S. residential real estate. Even before the Fed began hiking interest rates to fight inflation in 2022 — pushing mortgage rates to a 23-year high in October 2023 — years of surging home prices had left some experts warning that the housing market was a massive bubble ready to pop.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article on the EU's warning to X (formerly Twitter) for illegal content and disinformation agree with the TechCrunch article on the EU's analysis of X's role in spreading disinformation regarding the European Union's stance on the platform's dissemination of false information?
context:
# The EU's Urgent Warning Letter To X

The European Union fired a public warning at Elon Musk-owned X (formerly Twitter) for failing to tackle illegal content circulating on the platform in the wake of Saturday's deadly attacks on Israel by Hamas terrorists based in the Gaza Strip — an "urgent" letter from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton that TechCrunch described as a very swift test of the bloc's newly updated content moderation rulebook. Breton shared the letter publicly, tweeting on October 10, 2023: "Following the terrorist attacks by Hamas against 🇮🇱, we have indications of X/Twitter being used to disseminate illegal content & disinformation in the EU. Urgent letter to @elonmusk on #DSA obligations". TechCrunch's later account places the letter on the Wednesday.

The letter's substance was twofold. Breton said the bloc had seen "indications" from "qualified sources" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded X of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted." Separately, the European Commission raised concerns about the spread of disinformation on X related to the terrorist attacks and their aftermath.

On the disinformation side Breton was specific about what had been reported and what he wanted done: "Public media and civil society organisations widely report instances of fake and manipulated images and facts circulating on your platform in the EU, such as repurposed old images of unrelated armed conflicts or military footage that actually originated from video games. This appears to be manifestly false or misleading information," he wrote. "I therefore invite you to urgently ensure that your systems are effective, and report on the crisis measures taken to my team."

TechCrunch's own characterisation of the platform at that moment was blunter than the letter's: rather than tackling the problem, it wrote, X "appears to be turning into an engine of disinformation" — one that had demonstrably enabled the very swift amplification of a smorgasbord of toxic fakes around the Israel-Hamas war, falsehoods that might be trying to manipulate opinion around the conflict, or otherwise exploit horrific events to drive engagement (clickbait) or for even more cynical and potentially harmful ends.



---


# X Found To Have The Worst Disinformation Ratio In EU Analysis

X, formerly Twitter, was called out in the European Union for having the worst ratio of disinformation and misinformation to posts not spreading falsehoods among mainstream social networks.

The finding came in a September 2023 speech by EU commissioner for values and transparency Vera Jourova, discussing the latest updates from platforms signed up to combat disinformation under a beefed-up EU Code of Practice linked to compliance with the bloc's legally binding Digital Services Act. X's poor performance was assessed during a pilot phase of testing of a new methodology developed by Code signatories. "A big novelty under the Code is now the publication of the first set of structural indicators such as how easy it is to find disinformation content, how much engagement such content receives or indicators about sources. These indicators — developed by the signatories — constitute an unprecedented and novel insight into disinformation on online platforms," she said. "Such insight is crucial to understand how effective platforms efforts are to fight this threat even more efficiently. This is a very valuable industry proposal that has great potential while it has to be still further developed. Here, signatories have decided to run a pilot phase in three Member States to evaluate the methodology on two of those indicators. X, former Twitter, who is not under the Code any more is the platform with the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts."

X was contacted for a response to the EU's analysis of the ratio of disinformation it is spreading, and replied with an automated email reading: "Busy now, please check back later." The finding fits a wider pattern: consistent moderation, fact-checking investment and researcher data access are areas where X under new owner Elon Musk has moved out of step with EU expectations on countering disinformation, suggesting that X — designated by the EU as a VLOP under the DSA back in April — continues to put itself squarely in the Commission's crosshairs, including over its priority issue of tackling Kremlin propaganda.



---


# The EU's First Formal DSA Proceeding, Against X

On 18 December 2023 the European Commission announced the opening of a "formal proceeding" against Elon Musk's X, making it the first confirmed investigation opened by the European Union under its rebooted digital rulebook, the Digital Services Act (DSA). The investigation will look at whether the social networking platform may have breached rules linked to risk management, content moderation, dark patterns, advertising transparency and data access for researchers.

The Commission set out the evidentiary basis for the step: "On the basis of the preliminary investigation conducted so far, including on the basis of an analysis of the risk assessment report submitted by X in September, X's Transparency report published on 3 November, and X's replies to a formal request for information, which, among others, concerned the dissemination of illegal content in the context of Hamas' terrorist attacks against Israel, the Commission has decided to open formal infringement proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act."

The EU added that "if proven, these failures would constitute infringements of Articles 34(1), 34(2) and 35(1), 16(5) and 16(6), 25(1), 39 and 40(12) of the DSA," and said it will now carry out an in-depth investigation "as a matter of priority." Internal market commissioner Thierry Breton announced the same day that the proceedings covered a suspected breach of obligations to counter illegal content and disinformation, a suspected breach of transparency obligations, and suspected deceptive design of the user interface.



---


# X As The Outlier Against Ofcom's Rules

X (formerly Twitter) is the one big outlier to Whitehead's generally encouraging read on industry cooperation, because its direction of travel runs against what the guidelines assume: Ofcom's guidelines specify that users should be able to easily block users, but Elon Musk has publicly stated his intentions to remove X's block feature.

The premise under attack is that the act's requirements can be met by platforms as they are currently evolving. The UK's efforts with the legislation long predate Musk's acquisition of Twitter, but it was passed as he fired large swaths of its trust and safety teams and presided over a loosening of moderation standards, which could put X at odds with regulators. Musk has clashed with the EU over similar rules and reportedly even considered pulling out of the European market to avoid them.

Ofcom would not be drawn on the specific case. Whitehead declined to comment when asked whether X had been cooperative in talks with Ofcom, but said the regulator had been "broadly encouraged" by the response from tech firms generally.



---


# Mozilla.social's Trust And Safety Moderation Stance

Mozilla's claim is that its instance will not be a neutral platform, and that neutrality is an excuse rather than a principle. "We are saying out the gate that this isn't a neutral platform," O'Hara stresses. "We think that that's often used as this crutch to allow, or even amplify, really toxic content in the name of engagement… In some cases, platforms aren't just brave enough to actually just take things down."

The commitments backing that stance are concrete. Its content policies indicate strict measures around hate speech, impersonation, self-harm, harassment, misinformation, violent and sexualized content and more, in addition to illegal content like CSAM (child sexual abuse material) and promotion of illegal goods. The instance, still in private testing, has a small team of moderators that will grow when it launches to the public in the coming months. "It's not just a commitment, it's beyond foundational for us — that is the thing that is going to be true about this instance," O'Hara says of Mozilla's plans to heavily moderate its space; though Mozilla will also rely on technology to do some of the work, it wants to make sure the human moderators "feel protected, supported and respected for their work."

The warrant that makes strict rules acceptable is the decentralized structure itself: exit is available. Mozilla has been leaning into its values around inclusion, dignity, security, agency and community for 25 years, O'Hara says, and those will guide its efforts in the fediverse. "We're going to have rules on how people can engage with one another…it's the fediverse, you have lots of other places to go if you don't want to abide by those rules," she adds.



---


# The EU AI Act's Training Data Disclosure Rule

The European Union's proposed AI Act contains a rule that would require AI developers to disclose whether their AI had been trained on copyrighted materials — going some, if not all, of the way toward the transparency regime the NMPA sought.

As of MBW's 2023-11-30 report the Act was still the subject of back-and-forth negotiations between the European Commission and the European Parliament, so the rule was proposed rather than in force. Transparency in the use of AI is also becoming a rule on social media sites where AI-generated content is likely to appear: both TikTok and YouTube have passed rules requiring AI-generated content to be labeled as such.

qid: Did TechCrunch fail to maintain consistency in its portrayal of Google's market behavior after reporting on October 31, 2023, that Google paid billions to secure its default search engine position, or after reporting again on December 15, 2023, citing AI's benefits to news publishers' bottom lines?
context:
# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."



---


# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.

qid: Does the Engadget article on the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 suggest that the act will not initiate reports on AI regulation and data sharing, while the other Engadget article on the executive order implies that the new reporting requirement will not impact existing AI models and AI companies due to a high threshold for enforcement?
context:
# The Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act Of 2023

Tuesday's Senate AI forum followed the recent introduction of new AI legislation dubbed the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 (S. 3050), co-sponsored by Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mike Rounds (R-SD), Charles Schumer (D-NY) and Todd Young (R-IN).

The bill proposes AI bug bounty programs and would require a vulnerability analysis study for AI-enabled military applications. Its passage into law would also launch a report into AI regulation in the financial services industry, as well as a second report on data sharing and coordination.

The financial-services provision lands on a problem the SEC's own chairman has been lamenting. "It's frankly a hard challenge," SEC Chairman Gary Gensler told The Financial Times recently, speaking on the challenges the financial industry faces in AI adoption and regulation. "It's a hard financial stability issue to address because most of our regulation is about individual institutions, individual banks, individual money market funds, individual brokers; it's just in the nature of what we do."



---


# The Biden AI Executive Order Of October 2023

The Biden Administration unveiled its next steps in addressing and regulating artificial intelligence development on Monday: an expansive executive order (EO) that seeks to establish further protections for the public as well as improve best practices for federal agencies and their contractors.

The order is framed as a whole-of-government instrument. "The President several months ago directed his team to pull every lever," a senior administration official told reporters on a recent press call. "That's what this order does, bringing the power of the federal government to bear in a wide range of areas to manage AI's risk and harness its benefits ... It stands up for consumers and workers, promotes innovation and competition, advances American leadership around the world and like all executive orders, this one has the force of law."

Its provisions are phased rather than immediate. The actions will be introduced over the next year, with smaller safety and security changes happening in around 90 days and more involved reporting and data transparency schemes requiring nine to 12 months to fully deploy. To keep that schedule, the administration is also creating an "AI council," chaired by White House Deputy Chief of Staff Bruce Reed, who will meet with federal agency heads to ensure the actions are being executed on time.



---


# The CPPA's Risk-Based Approach Versus The EU AI Act

The CPPA's approach to regulating ADMT is risk-based, per Soltani. That echoes another piece of in-train EU legislation, the AI Act — a dedicated risk-based framework for regulating applications of artificial intelligence which has been on the table in draft form since 2021 but is now at a delicate stage of co-legislation, with the bloc's lawmakers clashing over the not-so-tiny detail of how, or even whether, to regulate Big AI, among several other policy disputes on the file.

The relation TechCrunch draws between the two is one of comparative advantage under discord: given the disagreement around the EU's AI Act, as well as the ongoing failure of US lawmakers to pass a comprehensive federal privacy law — since there is only so much presidential Executive Orders can do — there is a plausible prospect of California ending up as one of the top global rulemakers on AI.

That relation holds only over a limited range. The impact of California's AI rules is likely to remain local, given its focus on affording protections and controls to state residents. In-scope companies might choose to go further, such as offering the same package of privacy protections to residents of other US states, but that is up to them; the bottom line is that the CPPA's reach and enforcement is tied to the California border.



---


# The EU AI Office And Its Scientific Advisory Panel

The AI Act will be implemented through a new AI Office set up within the EU's executive, which will coordinate with the Member State oversight bodies that will need to enforce the rules on AI firms and will oversee the most advanced AI models, including by contributing to fostering standards and testing practices — with a scientific panel of independent experts appointed to advise it about GPAI models.

Per internal market commissioner Thierry Breton, work to implement the agreement starts immediately with the set up of the AI Office. "We will welcome new colleagues… a lot of them," said Breton. "We will work — starting tomorrow — to get ready." The AI Office will play a key role in setting risk classification thresholds for GPAIs, but the Commission confirmed there is no budget nor headcount defined for the expert body as yet. Asked about resourcing, a Commission official said it will be decided in the future by the EU's executive taking "an appropriate and official decision," adding: "The idea is that we can create a dedicated budget line for the Office and that we will be able also to recruit the national experts from Member States if we wish to on top of contractual agents and on top of permanent staff. And some of these staff will also be deployed within the European Commission."

The scientific advisory panel, which the law will also establish, is meant to help the Office better understand the capabilities of advanced AI models for the purpose of regulating systemic risk. "We have identified an important role for a scientific panel to be set up where the scientific panel can effectively help the Artificial Intelligence Office in understanding whether there are new risks that have not been yet identified," the official noted. "And, for example, also flag some alerts about the models that are not captured by the FLOP threshold that for certain reasons could actually give rise to important risks that governments should should look at."



---


# Reaction To Biden's AI Order

Respondents to Biden's AI executive order attacked the premise that an executive order alone is a sufficient regulatory response, arguing that its breadth is real but its depth is not, and that the substantive work still requires Congress. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia said he was "impressed by the breadth" of the order, though, he implies, not the depth: "I am also happy to see a number of sections that closely align with my efforts around AI safety and security and federal government's use of AI," he said in a statement. "At the same time, many of these just scratch the surface – particularly in areas like health care and competition policy. While this is a good step forward, we need additional legislative measures, and I will continue to work diligently…" TechCrunch's own reading is that given the state of the legislature and the fact that an incredibly contentious election period is upcoming, it will be a miracle if any substantive law whatsoever is passed in the near future, let alone a potentially divisive and complex bill like AI rules.

Paul Barrett, deputy director of the NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights, acknowledged both sides of the issue and attacked the inference that direction of travel equals capacity to act. "President Biden is sending a valuable message that certain AI systems create immediate risks that demand immediate attention. The administration is moving in the right direction," he wrote. "But today is just the beginning of a regulatory process that will be long and arduous–and ultimately must require that the companies profiting from AI bear the burden of proving that their products are safe and effective, just as the manufacturers of pharmaceuticals or industrial chemicals or airplanes must demonstrate that their products are safe and effective. Without fresh resources provided by Congress, it's not clear that the federal government has the resources to assess the vastly complicated training process or the adequacy of red-teaming and other necessary testing."

A more favorable reading came from Sheila Gulati, co-founder of Tola Capital, who said the EO showed a "clear intention to walk the line of promoting innovation while protecting citizens." "It is most essential that we don't prevent agile innovation by startups. Putting AI explainability at the forefront, taking a risk-based approach with more focus on areas where harm or bias could be at play, and bringing security and privacy to the center of focus are all sensible steps," she told TechCrunch. "With this executive order and the standards implications through NIST, we would anticipate leadership from standards bodies versus legislators in the near term." It is worth mentioning as well that the federal government is a major customer of today's AI and tech products, and any company that intends to keep them as a customer will want to color inside the lines for the immediate future. Bob Cattanach, partner at legal mega-firm Dorsey and Whitney, added that the timing feels slightly off.



---


# AI Training Transparency And Recordkeeping Requirements

The NMPA argues for a new regulation requiring AI developers to keep records of what data their algorithms ingested: "Transparency and recordkeeping requirements are needed to disincentivize infringing activity and to support enforcement activities by copyright owners."

The grounds are an enforcement problem the submission makes repeatedly: enforcing copyright against AI algorithms could be exceedingly difficult for rights holders, because "reverse-engineering" an AI algorithm to prove it was trained on content the developer had no right to is no easy task — save for when the AI produces a work substantially similar to the original, as in the lawsuits currently pending against AI companies. The NMPA also specifies who should bear the duty: "The primary parties who should be required to maintain records under a transparency and recordkeeping scheme are developers of AI models, those who use existing AI models to develop new AI tools and those who broker datasets for use in AI training."
