qid: Has the stance of the Federal Reserve on interest rates as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald remained the same between the article published on October 1, 2023, suggesting smaller future rate cuts, and the one from November 5, 2023, indicating a continuation of rate increases?
context:
# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# US Treasury Yields And Fed Rate Expectations In October 2023

The mechanism linking data to yields to stocks ran in both directions during October 2023. On 4 October, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, the centrepiece of the bond market, pulled back from its highest level since 2007, down to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late on the Tuesday, with shorter- and longer-term yields also easing to allow more oxygen for the stock market. Yields fell following reports indicating a slowing US economy, the first suggesting that hiring by employers outside the government was much weaker than expected; on Wall Street that is currently good news because a cooling job market could mean less upward pressure on inflation, which in turn could convince the Federal Reserve to take it easier on interest rates. After already raising its main interest rate to the highest level since 2001, the Fed had indicated it may keep its overnight rate higher next year than earlier expected, and Treasury yields had correspondingly snapped higher as traders accept a new normal of high rates for longer; the Fed pays particular attention to the job market because too much strength there could drive wages much higher, which it fears could keep inflation well above its target of 2 per cent.

By 12 October the same mechanism was running the other way. The stock market has largely been taking its cue from the bond market recently, and weak results announced in the afternoon for an auction of 30-year Treasury bonds sent yields of all kinds higher; higher yields can knock down prices for stocks and slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive. Yields had already been rising in the morning after a report showing consumer-level inflation a touch higher than economists expected, raising worries about the Fed keeping its main interest rate high for a long time as it tries to undercut inflation by knocking down investment prices and slowing the economy. The report also had encouraging nuggets: after ignoring prices for food and fuel, which Fed officials see as a better predictor of where inflation is heading, prices consumers paid were in line with expectations and continued to decelerate from earlier months. A second report said slightly fewer US workers than expected applied for unemployment benefits, indicating a job market with few lay-offs and therefore strength for the overall economy, though it could also add fuel to upward pressure on inflation. After the reports the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.7 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Wednesday, and the two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks expectations for the Fed, climbed to 5.06 per cent from 4.99 per cent, with yields still down slightly for the week after regressing from more-than-decade highs following speeches that investors saw as hints the Fed may not raise its main overnight rate further. The big jump for the 10-year yield since the summer has pulled mortgage rates to their highest levels since the turn of the millennium, and such moves could slow the economy without requiring more Fed hikes; Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said nothing in Thursday's inflation report should sway the Fed one way or the other on what it will do on 1 November, calling the data "reassuringly uneventful".



---


# What Drove The ASX Rally On 10 October 2023

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark attributed the Australian sharemarket's strength to three things acting together: a calming bond market, a positive lead from Wall Street, and positive news out of China.

He set out how each fed through. "The bond market is retracing," he said. "There's also been strength in resource stocks amid rumours that the Chinese government might launch a substantial stimulus package." On the rates channel, Clark said interest-rate sensitive sectors climbed on increased probabilities of an easing in interest rates, because "Consumer discretionary and information technology companies are winners in lower-interest rate environments." Looking ahead, as more annual general meetings kicked off over the following weeks, Clark said he would be looking at trading updates, especially of companies that did not give solid guidance in their last update.

# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.



---


# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.



---


# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.



---


# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. # Sports Betting Terminology Glossary

CBS Sports set out the top Kentucky betting terms for new bettors on 13 October 2023, defining each bet type by what the bettor is actually wagering on and, in several cases, by a worked Kentucky example.

Against the spread means that instead of betting on an exact winner, the widely popular spread bet levels the playing field by letting you wager on how many points a team will win by: in basketball, if Kentucky is the 7.5-point favorite against Louisville then Kentucky covers by winning by 8 or more, while Louisville as the 7.5-point underdog covers by winning outright or losing by 7 or fewer. Money line is an elevated outright bet with odds adjusted to reflect a favored team and an underdog: if Kentucky is a -200 favorite against Florida you'd need to bet $200 to return $100, while Florida at +200 would return $200 on a $100 bet. An outright bet is the easiest wager to place and is perfect for horse racing, one of Kentucky's biggest sporting events — bettors choose one athlete, or thoroughbred, to win an entire event. An Over/Under has the sportsbook post an estimated total of both teams' final scores, with the bettor wagering on whether the actual final will be higher or lower: if the Over/Under for a Kentucky-Louisville basketball game is 125.5, you wager on the final total being Over 126 or Under 125. A player prop projects a player's stat at the end of a game and asks you to wager over or under that projection, with popular examples being how many touchdown passes a quarterback throws or how many three-pointers a basketball player hits; Kentucky is one of the 18 states that allows prop bets on collegiate athletes.

The remaining terms describe the market's participants and mechanics. The underdog is the team deemed less likely to win based on the odds, and a bet on one typically yields a larger return than a bet on the favorite; the favorite is deemed more likely to win, and bettors often pay a premium for backing one though they more often win outright. Consensus odds are generally defined as an average of all available betting markets, since different sportsbooks may price markets variably based on the action they've taken or their own interpretation of information. Futures markets encompass almost anything outside single-game bets — total regular-season wins, championship odds, MVP odds and more. A parlay requires two or more bets within a single wager, all of which must win: wagering $100 on a three-leg parlay at 6 to 1 odds could win $600 if all three legs win. Juice, also known as the vig or vigorish, is effectively the tax oddsmakers charge for handling a wager — if a book judges a game a virtual coinflip it may price both options at -110 to give itself a 10% rake on all the action. A push is a bet where neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins: if an over/under for total points is set at 44 and both teams combine for exactly 44, the result is a push and the principal is returned. Live or in-game betting allows bets on several different markets in real time — in basketball, on the outcome of a quarter, individual statistics and live-updated spreads and totals.

The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# Flexport Leadership Turmoil

Dave Clark, the former Amazon executive who was ousted as CEO of Flexport just a year into the job, fired back at the company's founder and board, calling recent reporting on the logistics company "deeply concerning."

Clark made the comments on Monday of the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, in a lengthy post on the social media site X. The post followed a CNBC report that had provided new information about his last days at Flexport. Flexport is described as a freight forwarding and customs brokerage startup valued at $8 billion.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.

# Thesis That Music Labels Are Headed for Irrelevance

The argument, common among music business observers from the world of tech, is that record labels could in the long term be headed for irrelevance. Its grounds are the arrival of digital platforms, including open ones like YouTube and SoundCloud, together with the proliferation of indie music distribution platforms such as DistroKid and TikTok's SoundOn.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is a claim about what labels are for: in a world where anyone can record music using a desktop audio workstation (DAW) and upload it directly to YouTube, or to Spotify via a distribution platform, labels have little left to do. Recording and distribution — the functions the label historically supplied — are available to any artist directly, so on this reasoning the label's remaining role shrinks toward nothing. Music Business Worldwide presented this as the speculation that tech-world observers "like to" make, and as the position Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl was answering at the Code Conference in September 2023.



---


# AI Day Of Action Campaign

In the week of 2023-10-06, digital rights organization Fight for the Future partnered with music industry labor group United Musicians and Allied Workers to launch #AIdayofaction, a campaign that calls on Congress to block corporations from obtaining copyrights on music and other art made with AI.

The mechanism the campaign is betting on is indirect. The idea is that by preventing industry behemoths like major record labels, for example, from copyrighting music made with the assistance of AI, those companies will be forced to keep looping humans into the creative process. Those same concerns — and the same potential strategies for pushing back against the onslaught of AI — exist across creative industries, which is why the launch was pitched beyond music.

The launch landed in a moment when creative industries were grappling with AI's explosion into every artistic medium at once, and separate calls from artists warning the world to take action before it's too late were starting to converge. From fake Drake songs to stylized Instagram profile pictures, art conjured with newly sophisticated AI tools was suddenly ubiquitous — and so were conversations about how to rein in the technology before it does irrevocable harm to creative communities.

By the following week, on 2023-10-13, TechCrunch characterized the effort as a campaign that targets potential corporate abuse of AI technology while remaining realistic about the ways that musicians and some other creatives could benefit on an individual level from automating parts of their work. The stated goal is that AI tools "become ways for individual humans to make more money, work less, and compete with the corporations that exploit them."

# Sony Music's Pipeline Of AI Startup Partnerships

Kooker said Sony Music has "roughly 200 active conversations taking place with startups and established players" right now about building new AI-related products and tools, and that some of these conversations "also include potential equity investments which would accelerate the development of these companies."

He framed this as the optimistic counterweight to the harms: despite the negative impacts of AI, including unauthorized clones and low-quality AI music, there are still "many positive and optimistic developments to highlight," and he highlighted legitimate AI startups and established firms "with music ideas that want to partner with the industry." The products under discussion range from tools for "creative or marketing assistance," to tools that "potentially give us the ability to better protect artist content or find it when used in an unauthorized fashion," as well as "brand new products that have never been launched before."

# Capitol Music Group's Turnaround Results In 2023

Two years into Michelle Jubelirer's tenure, CMG had returned to calmer waters with US market share year-to-date in the high-5% region, alongside glittering successes and a promising array of new talent being primed. Jubelirer said that year-over-year market share is up by 25 per cent and that the company has moved up a notch in the label rankings, while noting she is not one to rattle off a lot of statistics. On TikTok's 2023 wrap-up lists, Capitol was the top-performing label across both the global and US lists.

Asked what she is most proud of in the past 12 months, she called it an incredible year and said that calling it the biggest, the best or the strongest would all be accurate. Her summary claim, made in the interview published 7 December 2023, is that she does not think any label group has been able to turn things around as quickly as she and her team have done in less than two years.



---


# Why Spanish-Language Music Keeps Growing Globally

Asked what is driving the ability of Latin artists, particularly Latin American artists, to have global hits on distribution agreements without signing even licensing deals with major record labels, Alejandra Olea answers that Spanish-speaking music, from Spain and Latin America, just keeps getting bigger, and that Spanish and Latin artists have many more options to develop their audiences and monetize their music at each stage of their career.

The mechanism she gives has two linked parts. First, the world is one where music discovery and consumption are now primarily digital, artists have understood that, and they look for partners who get it too and whose expertise will allow them to leverage digital platforms to reach new and existing audiences wherever they are; artists like Iñigo Quintero and labels like Acqustic are prime examples of this profound shift within the Latin and the wider music industry. Second, the effect is strongest in Spanish-speaking markets, where music fans are among the most engaged audiences in the world, whether on digital platforms or on social media, and where music content is consumed with more frequency, in different formats, across multiple platforms and through different aspects related to the track.



---


# Digital Twins Deployed for Sustainability Goals

The first trend IoT Analytics highlights is that companies are deploying digital twins to meet sustainability goals, with the pursuit of those goals acting as a tailwind macro factor for the digital twin market. Sustainability was discussed in approximately 21% of recent CEO earnings calls and has remained a consistent topic throughout 2023.

The mechanism is that digital twins simulate real-world conditions and deliver real-time information, so organisations can optimise resource usage, reducing carbon emissions and improving supply and transportation networks. Survey evidence supports the link: according to Capgemini Research Institute's 2022 digital twins report, 57% of organisations agreed that one of the key drivers for their digital twin investments was improving their sustainability, and 51% agreed that digital twins would help achieve their organisation's environmental sustainability goals.

A former VP at an industrial automation vendor quoted in the report frames the scope over which the relation holds: "Digital solutions provide the visibility, analysis, and insight needed to address the challenges inherent in sustainability goals. A digital twin strategy as part of an overall digitalization plan can be a crucial capability for asset-intensive industries and needs to encompass the entire asset lifecycle, process, and value chain from design and operations through maintenance and strategic business planning." The worked example is Aden, a Chinese integrated facility service provider, which created a digital twin for one of its commercial centres in Chengdu, China, designed to help facility managers inspect, maintain and repair building assets; its 3D simulations assist managers in visualising, predicting and optimising energy consumption, with expected benefits including lower annual energy consumption, water usage and waste.



---


# TikTok's Claim To Be The Driving Force Behind Music Discovery

TikTok's argument, made by Global Head of Music Ole Obermann on the back of the Luminate findings, is that "TikTok is the driving force behind music discovery in the industry, and that TikTok users are active, engaged and highly valuable drivers of music industry revenues."

The stated motive for commissioning the research was to move beyond the anecdotal: "TikTok is already famous for being the launchpad for creating viral hits and breaking new artists, but we wanted to understand how TikTok and its users impact the music industry more broadly," Obermann said in a statement, adding that "Luminate's findings prove what we had long known." MBW places the study in a pattern: it is part of an ongoing effort by TikTok to highlight its growing role in the development of global music culture, and last year TikTok released a report asserting that 13 out of the 14 songs to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 2022 were driven by viral trends on TikTok.



---


# Sub-Saharan Africa Recorded Music Market Growth

Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) was the world's fastest-growing recorded music region in 2022, recording 34.7% year-on-year growth according to IFPI figures, and by the time of this October 2023 report the growth opportunity for subscription music streaming in the region was becoming significantly clearer.

Africa-focused music streaming service Mdundo illustrates the trend: it recently reported a 239% year-on-year jump in revenue from paid subscriptions and a 23.2% year-on-year increase in monthly active users. Geographically, Mdundo's focus is on five key SSA markets — Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Ghana and South Africa.

The connectivity base underpinning that opportunity is also expanding. According to a 2022 report from GSMA, 615 million people in sub-Saharan Africa are expected to sign up for mobile services by 2025, on top of the roughly 500 million already subscribed as of 2020.

Speculation that Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift were dating began in July 2023, when Kelce confessed that he had tried and failed to give Swift a friendship bracelet bearing his phone number at one of her Eras Tour concerts; he later invited her on his podcast to one of his games at Arrowhead Stadium, an invitation she famously accepted on 24 September 2023, and she had attended three more of his games by 25 November 2023.

# Travis Kelce's Friendship Bracelet Overtures To Taylor Swift

Travis Kelce's public overtures to Taylor Swift began with friendship bracelets in mid-2023, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023, which dates the sequence precisely.

# Taylor Swift And Joe Alwyn's Relationship And Breakup

In April 2023 it was revealed that Taylor Swift and British actor Joe Alwyn had broken up after six years of dating. The former couple were notoriously private: the Conversations with Friends star had previously said he did not want to discuss the relationship because doing so "feeds into a weird part of the culture."

# Marcus Corporation's Preparations For Eras Tour Screenings

Greg Marcus, chief executive and chair of the Marcus Corporation, headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, has been in the movie business for years but never expected to be urging moviegoers to take out their phones during a film — let alone crafting friendship bracelets in preparation for an opening weekend. # OpenAI's Founding And Its 2023 Board Crisis

The Rosewood hotel dinner led to the creation of a startup called OpenAI later that year; backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Elon Musk and other funders, the lab promised to protect the world from Larry Page's vision. Thanks to its ChatGPT chatbot, OpenAI has fundamentally changed the technology industry and introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence, and it is valued at more than $US80 billion, about $A123 billion, according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round. Musk and Sam Altman's partnership did not survive, and the two have since stopped speaking. Altman's own gloss on such splits: "There is disagreement, mistrust, egos. The closer people are to being pointed in the same direction, the more contentious the disagreements are. You see this in sects and religious orders. There are bitter fights between the closest people."

The month before the 9 December 2023 article, that infighting came to OpenAI's boardroom: rebel board members tried to force out Altman because they believed they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity, and over five chaotic days OpenAI looked as if it were going to fall apart until the board, pressured by giant investors and by employees who threatened to follow Altman out the door, backed down. The drama gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI, but years before the near meltdown there was a little-publicised but ferocious competition in Silicon Valley for control of the technology now quickly reshaping the world, from how children are taught to how wars are fought. That earlier story begins with DeepMind: five years before the Napa Valley party and two before the cat breakthrough on YouTube, Demis Hassabis, a 34-year-old neuroscientist, walked into a cocktail party at Peter Thiel's San Francisco town house and realised he had hit pay dirt, because there in Thiel's living room, overlooking the city's Palace of Fine Arts and a swan pond, was a chessboard; Hassabis had once been the second-best player in the world in the under-14 category, and said "I was preparing for that meeting for a year. I thought that would be my unique hook in: I knew that he loved chess."



---


# OpenAI's Nonprofit Governance And Capped-Profit Structure

OpenAI's for-profit subsidiary, OpenAI Global, LLC, is fully controlled by OpenAI's nonprofit: the subsidiary is permitted to commercialize its technology, but it is subject to the nonprofit's mission of attaining artificial general intelligence (AGI), which OpenAI defines as AI that can "outperform humans at most economically valuable work."

The discriminating feature of this structure is where the power over AGI sits. The nonprofit OpenAI's board has the power both to determine when the company has achieved AGI and to exclude that AGI from IP licenses and other commercial terms — including terms with Microsoft, one of OpenAI's biggest investors and a steadfast integrator of OpenAI's technologies. OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit in 2015 but restructured in 2019 as a "capped-profit" company in order to raise capital, an acknowledgement of the huge costs associated with training cutting-edge AI systems. Altman underlined the point in an interview with the Financial Times in the week of his firing, saying he "hoped" Microsoft would increase its investment to help pay for "huge" imminent model training costs.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.



---


# The Four Layers Of The GenAI Tech Stack

Rick Grinnell, founder and managing partner at Glasswing Ventures, categorizes the generative AI landscape into four distinct layers in the firm's proprietary view of the GenAI tech stack: foundation model providers, middle-tier companies, end-market or top-layer applications, and full stack or end-to-end vertical companies. He was answering, in TechCrunch's 13 October 2023 survey of AI investors, whether startups will build striated solutions for individual layers of the LLM stack — models, pre-training solutions and fine-tuning tools — or pursue a more vertical approach.

The relations between layers are stated as market-structure predictions. At the foundational layer, providers like Alphabet/Google's Bard, Microsoft/OpenAI's GPT-4, and Anthropic's Claude show that the more significant players possess inherent advantages regarding data accessibility, talent pool and computational resources; this layer is expected to settle into an oligopolistic structure like the cloud provider market, albeit with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption. Above the model itself lies the largest market opportunity: companies that introduce AI-powered APIs and operational layers for specific industries will create brand-new use cases and transform workflows, and by embracing this technology to revolutionize workflows, these companies stand to unlock substantial value. Within the stack, most of the opportunity lies in the application layer, where the best applications will harness their in-house expertise to build specialized middle-layer tooling and blend them with the appropriate foundational models, and where startups can use speed to their advantage as they work to "innovate, iterate and deploy solutions" to customers.

The range over which the model holds is explicitly limited by market immaturity. The market is still far from being crystallized; LLMs are still in their infancy, with adoption at large corporations and startups lacking full maturity and refinement, and robust tools and platforms are needed to enable broader utilization among businesses and individuals. Startups have the opportunity here to act quickly, find novel solutions to emerging problems, and define new categories. Even large tech companies recognize the gaps in their services and have begun investing heavily in startups alongside VCs — these companies apply AI to their internal processes and thus see the value startups bring to LLM deployment and integration, as with the recent investments from Microsoft, Nvidia, and Salesforce into companies like Inflection AI and Cohere.

A dissenting position within the same survey bears on how much weight the layer model should carry for strategy. Edward Tsai, a managing partner at Alumni Ventures, offered a potentially "controversial opinion that VCs and startups may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market."



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.
