# Super Mario Bros. Wonder: The Verdict

The review's verdict is that Super Mario Bros. Wonder is a marvelous game: its art and animations have a level of polish practically unmatched by rival titles, and the addition of Wonder Seeds subverts your expectations and keeps this 40-year franchise feeling new and innovative.

The grounds are a three-part answer to the problem the review poses — Mario has been stomping Goombas, smashing blocks and running from left to right for damn near 40 years, so how is Nintendo supposed to keep its classic side scroller feeling fresh? First, you shift the location to a brand new kingdom; next, you introduce a bunch of new enemies and power-ups; but what really pushes things over the top is the introduction of a new mechanic that turns everything you think you know about Mario games on its head. What you get is a game that dazzles and delights while living up to its name in a variety of ways.

The warrant is comparative: in a lot of ways Wonder reminds the reviewer of his favorite 2D Mario game, Super Mario World. The one reservation is about the wait — he wishes it had not taken more than 10 years for Nintendo to create a proper sequel to its last mainline platformer — but as he concludes, if that is what it takes to get a game like this, he is happy to sit and wonder what is next for Mario.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Super Mario Bros. Wonder, developed by Nintendo EPD for Nintendo Switch, is ranked 4 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31 — the first side-scrolling 2D platformer in the Super Mario Bros. line since New Super Mario Bros. U in 2012, and both a faithful rendition of the classic format and a complete reinvention of the series' irresistible formula.

When you activate the game's delightful whimsy via the aptly named Wonder Flower, it becomes more than a 2D platformer: a musical, a quiz show, a race, or a hidden object game, where pipes become inchworms, Piranha Plants burst into song, and Yoshi becomes a dragon. Critic N. Carpenter writes that each and every level finds some new way to delight and surprise, constantly introducing new ideas, enemies, and wrinkles only to pull back on them just when it is on the verge of becoming rote — like everything else in the Flower Kingdom, a few enemies shift and change in bizarre ways when the Wonder Flower is activated, such as Hoppo, the bouncy, round hippo equivalent that grows in size to create chaos. All of this weirdness, combined with Nintendo's platforming expertise, makes it an entrancing romp alone, with friends, or with strangers online, and the freshest Mario has felt in decades.

Polygon's 2023-10-20 couch co-op roundup adds the local multiplayer detail: Wonder brings together platforming shenanigans, silly power-ups, and lots of map secrets, and the best part is that four people can play local multiplayer, picking from classic characters including Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Princess Daisy, Toad, and Toadette.



---


# Wonder As A Return To 2D Mario Experimentation

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder shares the inventiveness of the earliest 2D Mario games and their disregard for what should and shouldn't be in a Mario game — making it, for middle-aged fans, a candidate for the first "true new Mario game" since Super Mario World in 1990. The grounds lie in a history the reviewer sets out: with each Super Mario Bros. on the NES and SNES, Nintendo's designers learned from the previous entry, cut what didn't work, made audacious additions (there was a time when adding a dinosaur named Yoshi felt like a gimmick), and gradually accumulated the pieces and tropes that would recur for the next thirty-plus years. Then, with Super Mario 64, 3D Mario games became the de facto labs for Nintendo's greatest experimentation — magical hats, water guns, galactic travel — while 2D Mario defaulted to a vessel for nostalgia, including the cheekily named New Super Mario Bros. series.

The warrant is that Wonder revives the old spirit specifically by letting the designers break their own machine. The traditional layer is intact — every level can be enjoyed as a loyal continuation of the plumber's work in the 2D platformer genre, which has kept a healthy cadence since the series debuted in 1985: dash from left to right, jump over pits, concuss enemies, collect the occasional power-up, and leap onto the flagpole that ends one level and unlocks the next. But the wonder of playing Super Mario Bros. in 1985 came from discovery, with Nintendo anticipating that players would climb outside the confines of the level and placing shortcuts in hidden crevices to reward the most rule-breaking players; badges now build on that freedom with skills that let you soar over towering enemies or use the Piranha Plant grappling hook to climb above the stage. "This is the most significant difference between 1985 and 2023," the reviewer writes: "Mario's creators have joined in the fun of breaking the machine." He imagines the game's origin as a notebook in which, since the '90s, every Nintendo developer wrote down each idea that "didn't fit the tone" or "wasn't Mario enough," until someone had the gall to say: "Let's turn this stuffed notebook of chaos into a game. Because why shouldn't Mario be an elephant? Why shouldn't Wigglers wear roller skates? And why shouldn't Luigi skydive?"



---


# Technology Dependence Creates Defense Blind Spots

Avner Barnea argues that relying on technology produces a specific cognitive failure: "When the thinking is that you don't need soldiers because there are monitors, you expect in advance that you will receive the warning about the threat via the technological means and no one imagines a situation in which the observation array would be neutralized. On the contrary, it is seen as invulnerable."

His grounds are that the enemy sees the same technology: "The problem begins when the enemy is also exposed to these means: RCWS are great, they are important and cost millions, but they are visible to everyone, and everyone knows where they are. Once you begin believing that the fence will stop all the relevant threats, you think even half a battalion on standby is enough. Technology greatly influences our way of thinking and is seen as the answer to everything — only no one ever asks themselves what the vulnerabilities are, and what is the backup plan for the doomsday scenario when the technology layer collapses." Barnea supports the pattern with a historical case, comparing Israel's sense of technological superiority with US activity during the Vietnam War between 1965 and 1968: "The Americans relied on massive aerial bombardment with precision bombs and napalm bombs that burned huge areas, and advocated the 'scorched earth' concept. They convinced themselves that the Vietcong could not withstand it. In practice, the North Vietnamese army studied the American activity. It dug tunnels, moved equipment and people between bombings, eventually enabling it to reach the important bases in the south of the country, and overwhelm the Americans. In fact, the US military so believed in the damage it was causing that they reported a far greater number of casualties on the other side than the actual number, which in turn created an illusion of victory. They told themselves, we have B-52 bombers, there's no way we can't win."



---


# Nostalgia-Driven Major Game Releases, 2023

TechCrunch cites three 2023 releases as evidence of gaming's turn to the familiar. This year's hit new Zelda game Tears of the Kingdom literally built a new game on top of the old one and remains a strong contender for Game of the Year.

Competition is stiff, more so now that Nintendo just casually dropped Super Mario Bros. Wonder, the first two-dimensional side-scrolling Mario game in more than a decade — another portal to the past given its departure from a long string of recent 3D Super Mario titles. Square Enix was so confident in its remake of the 1997 Japanese roleplaying mega-hit Final Fantasy VII that the reimagined version of the game comprises three standalone full-length games, each spaced a few years apart.



---


# AI21 Labs' Tel Aviv Office Lease

Less than a month before the war, Globes reported a huge deal in which Amnon Shashua's unicorn AI21 Labs announced it was leasing 7,000 square meters for NIS 15 million annually in Tel Aviv's Da Vinci project.

Writing on 3 December 2023, Globes notes that it will now be interesting to see when the next such big office-space deal is signed in Tel Aviv following the impact of the Israel-Hamas war. Sources in the income-producing property sector in Israel say that over the past few weeks there has been some interest in the sector, although mainly for smaller deals involving hundreds of square meters each.

qid: After the TechCrunch report on Google's antitrust case published on October 31, 2023, and the subsequent TechCrunch report on Epic Games' antitrust battle with Google that started on November 6, 2023, was there consistency in the portrayal of Google's alleged anticompetitive behavior?
context:
# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.



---


# Google One VPN

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

Engadget has not fully tested the Google One VPN yet, but says it will add it to the list if it feels it is warranted.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

qid: Does 'The Roar | Sports Writers Blog' suggest that 'The All Blacks' motivation for playing is the same as the Springboks' as per the first article, while also indicating that 'The All Blacks' handling was compromised by external factors in the second article, and does it confirm 'The All Blacks' losses to Argentina as stated in the third article?
context:
# The All Blacks' Final Moments In The 2023 World Cup Final

New Zealand's last chance in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final died in the 80th minute when Ardie Savea forced a ball out wide just as the men in black saw space and looked to open up the Springboks — a killer blow, in The Roar's phrase.

The wider failing was handling. The All Blacks had their chances, but their usual safe handling — a feature throughout the World Cup after their first-up loss to France — evaded them against the Springboks' blitz defence in the wet conditions, and all night their timing was off.

The end came at a set piece. Wayne Barnes, who was booed relentlessly, called a scrum reset as the seconds ticked by; moments later New Zealand hearts sank as the Springboks won the scrum and then hung onto the ball.



---


# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# Foster Rejects The Favourites Label Against Argentina

Although the All Blacks were 18-point favourites for the opening 2023 World Cup semi-final, Ian Foster rejected the premise that his side sees itself that way: "Firstly, you've never heard us say we're favourites."

His grounds for rejecting the label are recent results and a limit on what the past predicts. Argentina had knocked over the All Blacks the previous year in Christchurch, as well as inflicting a maiden defeat in 2020 in Sydney, and New Zealand had themselves suffered a shock semi-final loss to Eddie Jones' England in 2019. Foster also argued that familiarity does not transfer to this stage: "The past sets us up beautifully for both teams. We do know each other but we don't know each other in terms of a Rugby World Cup, so at this stage in the tournament it's new territory for us and as we've seen World Cups are very different."

He then converted the rejection into a demand on his own team: "We have learnt to greatly respect Argentina. They have a rich history of overachieving at the World Cup and have done a fantastic job to get here at the same level we are, so it is going to be a heck of a game." And: "We know these games are do or die. We're going to have to improve our performance. The stage gets bigger at this time in the tournament and you've got to grow your game. That's our strong focus. The best team on the night wins – Argentina has done that to us."



---


# Ireland: The Greatest Team Yet, Still Without A Knockout Win

This is the greatest Ireland team of all time, and may still even be the best team in the world — but on this day, the quarter-final curse, not to mention an inspired All Blacks side, ruled once more. The claim is that quality and knockout success have come apart: being the best team available is compatible with going out at the same stage as every Ireland side before them.

The consequence the argument draws is reputational. Instead of being feted as the heroes to finally overcome that insurmountable obstacle, the Ireland players will still have to answer endless questions about the heavy burden of previous knockout failures, and fans will endure at least four more years of choking jokes at their expense.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Coaching Record With Ireland And The All Blacks

Joe Schmidt took Ireland to the top of World Rugby's rankings while his Irish sides bombed out in successive World Cup quarter-finals under his leadership, and he later helped transform an All Blacks team that reached the 2023 World Cup final, as reported by The Roar on 11 December 2023.

His Ireland tenure is credited with more than results: Schmidt played an instrumental role in not just seeing them become one of the world's best teams but helped usher through transformational change off the field, as Ireland moved to a centralised system.

The New Zealander briefly exited the international coaching scene following the 2019 World Cup, citing a desire to move home to New Zealand to be closer to his family. After initially moving back into the coaching fray with the Blues in Super Rugby, he joined the All Blacks ahead of the previous year's Rugby Championship, as New Zealand Rugby shook up the All Blacks coaching team following their historic series loss to Andy Farrell's Irish. His expertise proved telling: he and Jason Ryan transformed the All Blacks and helped Ian Foster's side reach the final of that year's World Cup after stunning wins over Ireland and Argentina in the knockout stages.



---


# The 'Matildas Effect' And Its Limited Impact On Domestic Women's Sport

The Guardian argued on 26 October 2023 that the popularity of the Matildas' run to the Women's World Cup semi-finals has had only a limited impact on support for domestic women's sport, because the early spike did not persist.

The grounds come from the A-League Women, which launched that month with a first round highlighted by a crowd of more than 11,000 in Sydney — but more modest attendances in subsequent games, including two sub-2,000 crowds in Perth, follow it. The warrant is that a durable effect would show up beyond the opening round; a large first-round crowd followed by small ones is consistent with novelty rather than converted support.

Nicole Livingstone, the AFL's general manager of women's football, made the same point from the league side, saying the "green and gold fever" associated with the Women's World Cup was a one-off and that the AFL has plans in place for long-term growth: "We'll continue to keep building the base and keep building the foundations and have it not just strong at year seven, season eight, but strong for generations to come."



---


# How England And South Africa Reached The 2023 Semi-Final

England arrived at the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final as the only side still competing that had yet to lose a game, while South Africa had already beaten two of the tournament favourites. Dominant wins over Argentina, Japan and Chile sealed England's passage to the last eight, and after being given an almighty scare by Samoa in their final pool match, they overcame a Fijian fightback in Marseille to triumph 30-24 — outscored by three tries to two, but carried by captain Owen Farrell's 20 points at the expense of 2023's breakout stars.

The Springboks had done it tough. Comfortable defeats of Scotland, Romania and Tonga could not mask the disappointment of a 13-8 loss to Ireland, which consigned South Africa to second in Pool B. With Ireland then sent home by the All Blacks in the quarters, the Bokke showed their World Cup mettle to edge hosts France 29-28 at the Stade de France, sneaking past Les Bleus in one of the best games of rugby you're ever likely to see.

Both journeys had twists, turns and bumps in the road but left each side within 80 minutes of a Rugby World Cup final. England would be looking to echo the spirit of 2019, when they beat the All Blacks 19-7 to reach the final, but in South Africa they faced a side who had taken their game to new heights just to reach the semis.



---


# The NSW Waratahs' Licence Handover To Rugby Australia

The New South Wales Rugby Union was in the latter stages of handing over its licence to Rugby Australia, The Roar revealed in the week before Oct. 10, 2023 — a move by which the NSW Waratahs, who were on the brink of insolvency, handed over their commercial and high-performance property.

The practical effect is that all male and female Waratahs players, including coaches and high-performance staff, as well as all commercial and operations staff, will run out of RA's office. NSW Waratahs chief executive Paul Doorn informed stakeholders of the decision the previous week.

RA is cognisant that not every Super Rugby franchise will follow suit immediately, but the governing body is hopeful that now one of the two biggest states has agreed to hand over the keys, others will follow swiftly, with the Melbourne Rebels expected to be next. RA chief executive Phil Waugh says building trust back between the governing body and the states is essential to their plans.

qid: Which company, reported by both The Verge and TechCrunch, uses relevance, distance, and prominence to rank local search results, has spent billions to be the default search engine on multiple platforms, and has been accused of anticompetitive practices affecting news publishers' revenues?
context:
# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.



---


# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

The warrant tying them together is that each mechanism moves cost onto the user: platform ad incentives bury relevance, SEO gaming inflates the noise, and AI-generated content shifts verification work to the person searching.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. # Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. qid: Does the Fortune article suggest that Alameda Research's business practices with FTX were legal, in contrast to the TechCrunch article's focus on the valuation of Alameda Research's assets in FTT tokens?
context:
# Alameda Research

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.



---


# The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse](ftx_collapse_mechanism.md)
- [Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership](sbf_and_ellison_relationship_and_alameda_leadership.md)



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Letitia James' History of Investigating Trump

Letitia James, who campaigned for office as a Trump critic and watchdog, started scrutinising his business practices in March 2019, after his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth on financial statements provided to Deutsche Bank while trying to obtain financing to buy the NFL's Buffalo Bills.

Her office had previously sued Trump for misusing his own charitable foundation to further his political and business interests. Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to an array of charities as a fine, and the charity, the Trump Foundation, was shut down.



---


# Convoy's Digital Freight Shutdown

The digital freight broker Convoy told employees in the week before TechCrunch's 2023-10-22 report that it was shutting down, due to what executives described as a "massive freight recession." TechCrunch's takeaway: it turns out that disrupting the freight business is hard.

The abrupt closure wiped out investors, and comes about 18 months since the Seattle-based company raised $260 million in fresh funding that pushed its valuation to $3.8 billion.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that users are turning to Snapchat for information on a specific topic due to distrust in other platforms, while The Guardian article discusses legal actions against Snapchat for a completely different reason related to the platform's use?
context:
# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# Snapchat Design Features Alleged To Enable Drug Sales

The lawsuit against Snap claims that Snapchat's features facilitate practices like drug sales by connecting dealers to young customers while promising them safety from legal repercussions through anonymity.

Chief among those designs, according to Matthew Bergman, the lead attorney on the case, is the promise that a message will disappear not only for fellow users but also on the software's back end. That is the ground that turns a product feature into an enabler of crime: it prevents law enforcement officials from seeing the activity of a dealer even after the dealer has been identified.

The complaint names other features as problematic too: notifying individuals when another person screenshots their post, the ability to geolocate fellow users, and algorithms that suggest new connections based on demographics.



---


# Common Sense Media's Teen Smartphone Study: Design And Scope

A study from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit group in San Francisco, California, researched phone usage among a diverse group of 203 kids aged 11 to 17, and the results were startling, experts say. The researchers found that smartphones have become a "constant companion" for young people, according to a news release, although results varied.

The method combined passive measurement with youth interpretation. In its report, Common Sense Media said it used "software to collect data from the smartphones of a diverse group of about 11- to 17-year-olds. We then interpreted this data with assistance from an advisory council of young people to understand the nuanced relationships that young people develop with their smartphones."

The study carries an explicit platform limitation: it was done with "Android phone users only, because Apple device tracking does not share with the research community the names of specific non-Apple apps that young people commonly use."



---


# X's Revenue Decline And The Information-Network Decay Argument

Charging all users for access to X could be the final nail in the coffin of the platform as a real-time information network, because it risks triggering a further and final exodus of the remaining legacy users whose knowledge and engagement lent Twitter its original value.

The grounds are financial. Subscription revenues to the revamped Twitter Blue paid offering, now called X Premium, do not appear to have been substantial enough to plug the advertising gap, which may explain Musk's recent suggestion that he plans to charge all users a small fee. The warrant joining that to the conclusion is a claim about what makes an information network work: a bona fide information network depends on a critical mass of genuine users to pay attention and contribute value and vitality — its life-blood. Remove the paywall-averse legacy users and disinformation and spammers may rush in to fill the gap, generating a parody of activity; without the genuine users, X really will mark the spot of Twitter's demise.



---


# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Social Networks' Drift From Connection To Algorithmic Feeds

The claim is that social networks stopped being social. At some point they were no longer about connecting with your closest friends, keeping up with long-distance family members and feeling a special connection with people you love; TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, YouTube and X (formerly Twitter) are all slowly evolving to become the same infinite scrollable feed of algorithm-optimized short videos from top performers. TechCrunch's writer notes he had argued in a 2018 article that 2018 was "the year social networks were no longer social," and that while he is not sure 2018 was the turning point, the premise still holds up well.

The structural ground Mozilla offers is ownership and revenue: social networks are often run by large corporations — like Meta, Snap and Google — where advertisers pay the bills, which has created a world where modern social networks are profit-driven and consumer needs are not always at the forefront. The warrant is that when advertisers pay, the feed optimizes for them rather than for connection.

Mozilla dates the inflection point: this disconnect between what people want and what today's networks offer hit an inflection point in 2022, when billionaire Elon Musk bought Twitter, leading to a surge of interest in alternatives to centralized social networking including apps like Mastodon and Bluesky. Under Musk, Twitter — now called X — has prioritized "free speech" managed by crowdsourced-based moderation, and its policies have resulted in increased hate speech and toxic content on the platform, some studies have shown.



---


# The Republican State-Level TikTok Ban Push

Though opposition to TikTok has been bipartisan, the crusade to ban the platform over national security concerns is primarily led by Republicans at the state level, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02. The article treats that position as a likely contributor to the party's social media struggles with young voters.

The observation matters because it sets the party's legislative posture against its outreach problem: the same platform Republicans are campaigning to ban is the one where the youth vote concentrates.



---


# Elizabeth Warren's Criticism Of Apple Blocking Beeper

U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) rejected Apple's security rationale for cutting off Beeper Mini, attacking it as pretextual while the Beeper team scrambled for a fix. In a post on X, formerly Twitter, she wrote: "Green bubble texts are less secure. So why would Apple block a new app allowing Android users to chat with iPhone users on iMessage? Big Tech executives are protecting profits by squashing competitors. Chatting between different platforms should be easy and secure."

Her argument turns Apple's own premise against it: if the alternative to iMessage — green bubble texts — is less secure, then blocking an app that extends iMessage to Android cannot be explained by user security, leaving competitive self-interest as the explanation.



---


# Pebble's Moderation-First Market Hypothesis

Pebble's founding hypothesis was that consumers were hungry for a Twitter alternative that prioritized trust, safety and moderation from the start. The company staffed for it: Pebble's founding team included co-founder Sarah Oh, Twitter's former human rights advisor.

What would falsify the proposition is a moderation-first Twitter alternative that consumers decline to adopt — which is the shape of the outcome TechCrunch is reporting on 2023-10-24, in a piece about Pebble shutting down.

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith met when she auditioned for the role of his girlfriend on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air; she did not get the part, but the two hit it off — even though Smith was married to Sheree Zampino at the time, with whom he shares son Trey. Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in an interview with Parade, published 13 October 2023 and given while promoting her memoir Worthy, that she and Will Smith deliberately did not sign a prenuptial agreement before their 1997 wedding, because they had already decided divorce was not in the cards for them. # Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.

# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." qid: Does the article from The Verge suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried was aware of the financial discrepancies at FTX, while the TechCrunch article alleges that he knowingly committed fraud, or do both articles imply a level of awareness and intent by Sam Bankman-Fried regarding the financial issues at FTX?
