# Scorsese's Late Career Refutes Tarantino's Claim That Directors Do Not Get Better

Polygon's 2023-10-26 piece attacks the premise behind Quentin Tarantino's 2021 defense of his intention to make "just" 10 movies and retire: "I know film history, and from here on in, directors do not get better." The counter is that this view of both artistry and film is squarely at odds with Martin Scorsese's historic body of work.

The specific premise under attack is the claim of inevitable late-career decline. Scorsese had already made his 10th feature-length narrative film by 1986; he is now 80 years old, and his 27th, Killers of the Flower Moon, is a strong argument that directors are still capable of groundbreaking greatness late in life — and, in Scorsese's case, of continued exhilarating experimentation and discovery.

Polygon presses the point further: since the year 2000, Scorsese has curated a 23-year career within a career, and the quality and variety of his films have come not in spite of his age and experience but because of it. His movies have never been more relevant than in the past two decades, and with each subsequent release, as his career winds down, critical appreciation for him grows — Scorsese worship being the one remaining form of gerontocracy America is perfectly content with, and with good reason.

The mechanism the piece identifies is autonomy. This century Scorsese has zigged and zagged as always, but because he is following his own varied interests rather than moving from compromise to compromise as he once had to in order to keep working: an artist who spent the first 30 years of his career desperate for autonomy finally got it, and now takes full advantage — telling difficult stories, setting his own mega-budgets, and demanding every minute of run time he feels each picture demands. He has used that autonomy to revisit his work and revise the record, creating great new films and adding crucial addendums to past work while blazing new trails and adding layers to his style. Remarkably, the control that eluded him when he was younger has made his films more consistently collaborative and creative, more fluid and alive than he was often allowed to be before the 2000s, with the earned confidence of an artist who knows he will find something great in post. Polygon concludes that this should give Tarantino cause to reconsider, alongside any artist or critic who thinks the creative spark has an expiration date.

# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# White House "Army Of Influencers" Strategy

As an alternative to the politician-influencer, some campaigns are focusing on mobilizing creators who already have an engaged audience. As TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02, Biden is not on TikTok, but his digital strategy team is building an "army of influencers" to reach viewers who wouldn't typically keep up with the White House press corps. White House deputy chief of staff Jen O'Malley Dillon told Axios that the administration is trying to not only reach young people, but "people whose main way of getting information is digital."

Annie Wu Henry explained the logic of surrogates: "If you're not going to be directly on the platform, having surrogates — whether those be influencers, celebrities, normal people — do the messaging, that's likely going to be reaching people at a more personal level anyway," she said. "Everyone has a vested interest, for the most part, in what the president of the United States has to say, but if it's your friend, if it's this person you've followed for five years, you have a vested interest that's a little bit more personal. Usually that's more effective."



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Prior SEC And CFTC Actions Against Binance

The DOJ charges against Binance came over five months after the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission accused the exchange and Zhao of lying to regulators about its operations, filing 13 charges against the defendants in the federal case.

The SEC's theory concerned the relationship between Binance and its U.S. arm: Zhao and Binance were allegedly "intimately involved" in directing the trading entity's business operations and providing crypto-related services to the Binance.US platform, which claims it is an independent exchange in the SEC filing.

In late March 2023 the U.S. CFTC also filed a suit against Binance, Zhao and its Chief Compliance Officer Samuel Lim for allegedly breaking trading and derivatives rules.

Some computer scientists have criticized the focus on far-off risks — the existential dangers Altman called attention to — as distracting from the real-world limitations and harms of current AI products. The premise attacked is that future catastrophic risk is the most urgent thing to attend to.

Online signature company DocuSign (DOCU) was scheduled to release its Q3 results on Thursday of the week following Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 preview, after the closing bell, with Wall Street analysts cautious at a Hold rating and Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating system more optimistic at a Buy — the reverse of the usual split.

qid: Has the perspective on managing dementia in 'The Guardian' articles shown a change from the time Susan Saunders was reported to be caring for her mother with dementia (published at '2023-10-10') to the more recent report on new Alzheimer’s drugs (published at '2023-12-17')?
context:
# Joining The Dementia Research Register For Trial Participation

Health coach Susan Saunders' advice, reported by The Guardian on 10 October 2023, is a two-step procedure for anyone with a parent in the early stages of dementia: investigate all the available research trials, and start by joining Dementia Research, a nationwide register that matches volunteers to research programmes.

The precondition is stated explicitly — the advice is for a parent in the early stages of dementia, not later ones — and Saunders speaks from experience, having found herself "parenting" her mother, who had dementia, while her own daughters were babies.

The scope of the advice as given is limited to finding and entering trials through that register; the source does not extend it to any other treatment step.



---


# The First Drugs to Treat the Cause of Alzheimer's

The arrival of the first drugs that treat the actual cause of Alzheimer's — rather than merely helping patients manage symptoms, which is all doctors have been able to prescribe until now — has been welcomed as a justifiable cause for excitement, although experts warn their use should be treated with some caution.

"The new drugs slow down the development of Alzheimer's by six months to a year and are useful only for those in the early stages of the condition, so they are certainly not miracle medicines," said David Thomas, head of policy at Alzheimer's Research UK. "However, after decades of research, they are the first to improve patients' lives directly, and that is a justifiable cause for excitement. If nothing else, they suggest we are probably on the right road to tackling Alzheimer's." The point was backed by neurologist Cath Mummery, of the Dementia Research Centre at University College London: "It has been a very long, hard road, but finally we have something positive to look at. That is very welcome."



---


# Robin Williams' Lewy Body Dementia And 2014 Death

Robin Williams was unaware in the years before his death that he was dealing with Lewy body dementia; he died by suicide on 11 August 2014 and was diagnosed with the neurological disorder posthumously after an autopsy, FOX News Entertainment reported on 19 October 2023.

Before he died he reportedly appeared tired while on set and did not seem to be his usual self. Lewy body dementia is the second most common type of dementia after Alzheimer's, and the disease affects brain regions involved in thinking, memory and movement, according to the Mayo Clinic. The autopsy found no illegal drugs or traces of alcohol in Williams' system.

Comedian and friend Steven Pearl described the change during the Vice documentary: "The last time I saw Robin Williams, I hadn't seen him for a few months, and he was thin, and he didn't recognize my wife. He hardly said a word. It took him a second to recognize me. I go, 'Whoa, something's wrong here.' I didn't know what. Nobody would really tell me. And then I never saw him again after that."



---


# Alzheimer's Prevalence And The Value Of Early Detection

More than six million Americans of all ages have Alzheimer's, and every 67 seconds, someone in America develops the disease, according to the Alzheimer's Association.

Over the past several decades, there has been a steady increase in diagnoses of Alzheimer's disease, Antoun noted.

Detection timing changes what can be done about it. "However, when we are able to detect neurodegenerative conditions early, we can take positive steps that may slow the process and mitigate any major side effects of the disorder," he said.



---


# Alzheimer's: The Lecanemab And Aducanumab Approvals

Leqembi, lecanemab, developed by Eisai in collaboration with Biogen, was the first and only approved drug for Alzheimer's, approved in July 2023, coming after several failed attempts and one controversial false start in recent years. Alzheimer's disease is characterised by amyloid beta deposits on brain cells leading to shrinking and loss of cognitive abilities, and despite a clear marker of amyloid plaques and a target area to work on, pharma companies failed to address plaque removal or to show a statistical improvement in cognitive functioning after plaque removal until this approval; Pfizer, Eli Lilly, Merck and many others faced failure in the space, and the amyloid theory itself was in question.

Biogen's aducanumab had a peculiar start: the company itself stopped development in 2019 but surprisingly pursued a high-dose study into 2021, after which the FDA gave the high-dose version an accelerated approval that faced sharp criticism, with three advisers resigning over the approval of a drug that could have cost $56,000 per annum to administer. With a "traditional" approval for the Eisai-partnered lecanemab, compared with the accelerated approval for aducanumab, Biogen has the first approved treatment, putting aducanumab on the backburner. On the critical marker of cognitive function improvement, lecanemab delivers lower degeneration compared to placebo: the treatment reduced clinical decline by 27 per cent at 18 months on clinical dementia scoring and delivered a 37 per cent improvement compared to placebo on the daily living scale. The article's verdict is that the development is satisfactory but a lot more progress remains to be made on the Alzheimer's treatment curve.



---


# Whether Gastroparesis Persists After Stopping GLP-1 Drugs

For the cases of stomach paralysis in the study, the researchers could not assess whether the condition was temporary or permanent -- the data did not settle the question either way.

What exists beyond the study data is anecdotal and secondhand. "There are reports from other journalists where they have met patients whose symptoms have not gone away despite stopping the drugs," study co-author Dr. Mahyar Etminan, associate professor in the Departments of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences and Medicine at UBC, told Fox News Digital.

He added that there are medications that can be used to help with the condition.



---


# Diane Bazella's Switched-at-Birth Reunion

Diane Bazella, 64, of Minnetonka, Minnesota, gets to spend holiday time with her birth mother after a nearly 40-year search that revealed she may have been switched at birth — a reunion she described to Fox News Digital in a phone interview published on 15 December 2023.

"Merry Christmas" has a whole new meaning for her. "It means the world for me to be with my mom at the Christmas holiday," Bazella said. "It's all about love. My prayers have been answered, and my heart is full. We both hope we have many more Christmases to spend together." Enjoying Christmastime with her oldest child — and only daughter — has been a long time coming for Sherri Geerts, 81, of Sunnyvale, California. "It's a story with a good ending," Geerts told Fox News Digital.

The search itself was not an ordinary one but, as Bazella put it, an epic journey with numerous twists and turns; the process took grit and determination, research and genealogical skills, and most of all a deep-rooted desire to find out where she belonged. Bazella first found Geerts, her birth mother, in May 2021, and they met in person in 2022. It was only recently that she found the courage to share the story of her decades-long search. "I've spent a lot of time dealing with the healing part of it," Bazella said. "I think it kind of gives people hope that miracles are still going on, and the world needs to hear that right now. So that's part of the reason I've stepped out and told my story now."



---


# Robyn Davidson's Memoir, Published October 2023

Robyn Davidson's memoir, published by Bloomsbury at $34.99 on 3 October, tells the story of her life from childhood and beyond — largely avoiding the desert trip with her camels that made Tracks famous — The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its defining move is that omission: "You've read the book, you've seen the film – Tracks – but here is the story of Robyn Davidson's life from childhood, largely avoiding that trip across the desert with her camels, and beyond to a life of more travel, houses, lovers and family."

The book's centre is family, and particularly her mother, who took her own life at 46 and about whom Davidson has previously been unable to write to her own satisfaction. She is acutely aware that her version of the truth "can bury another's", but this one is hers.



---


# ASKP3's Forthcoming Guidelines For At-Home Ketamine Use

ASKP3 announced that it will soon publish guidelines for safe use of the drug.

The organization tied the decision directly to the Perry case and pre-committed to narrow conditions: "In the wake of Matthew Perry's autopsy report, we are committed to creating and publishing guidelines for at-home ketamine use, which should only be practiced with a very specific patient profile and only in the context of a close relationship with a physician and in-office follow-up," the organization said in a released statement.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Epic's Rebuttal Of Google's Leaked Email Summary

Pressed with the suggestion that the email Epic accused Google of leaking showed Epic was itself interested in a special deal, Tim Sweeney attacked the premise of the characterisation: Google did not leak the email, he said — it leaked "their ridiculously biased summary of it" to Abner Li at 9to5Google.

He supported the leak claim with trial testimony: Don Harrison testified that he didn't think Google leaked to the press, and was then presented with a document including Google's press team and Sameer Samat, head of all Android, summarising the articles that appeared as a result of Google's leaking of Epic's plans to the press. On the substance of the email, Sweeney said it is in evidence and is the same one he had already described: right before Christmas-ish 2019, with the new Marvel season and a lineup of Star Wars content planned, he asked Google's executives to let Fortnite come to the Google Play Store using Epic's own payment method and to open up the use of their own payment methods to all developers, not just Epic. The interviewer conceded the point, saying he had read that email in court and had not realised it was the same one, because it was so far off from what he had heard described as a "special billing exception."

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. # The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

# Discord's Graduated Warning System And Account Standing

Discord is introducing a new warning system for people who violate its policies: outside of incidents involving the most "extreme" violations, the company is moving away from permanent bans, doing so under the belief that most users will choose to be better online citizens given the chance and proper guidance.

In practice the system notifies a person when they have violated one or more of Discord's policies and details the restrictions on their account. It also links out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism. A new "Account Standing" tab within the settings menu lets users see all their current and past policy violations.

Discord frames the design as a model for the industry. "We think we've built the most nuanced and proportionate reporting system," Badalich told Engadget, adding that the company hopes other platforms will look to what Discord has created for inspiration in their own enforcement efforts. "We believe people, especially teens, have the capacity to grow."



---


# Ofcom's First Guidelines Under The UK Online Safety Act

After the Online Safety Act's arduous multiyear passage through the UK's lawmaking process, regulator Ofcom published its first guidelines for how tech firms can comply with the mammoth legislation — a proposal, part of a multiphase publication process, outlining how social media platforms, search engines, online and mobile games, and pornography sites should deal with illegal content like child sexual abuse material (CSAM), terrorism content, and fraud.

The defining feature of the regime is a duty of care rather than a fixed rulebook. "What this does for the first time is to put a duty of care on tech firms to have a responsibility for the safety of their users," Ofcom's online safety lead, Gill Whitehead, told The Verge. "When they become aware that there is illegal content on their platform, they have got to get it down, and they also need to conduct risk assessments to understand the specific risks that those services might carry."

The guidelines' status is a discriminating detail. They are released as proposals so Ofcom can gather feedback before the UK Parliament approves them toward the end of next year, and even then the specifics will be voluntary: tech firms can guarantee they are obeying the law by following the guidelines to the letter, but they can take their own approach so long as they demonstrate compliance with the act's overarching rules — and, presumably, are prepared to fight their case with Ofcom.

The aim is to require that sites be proactive to stop the spread of illegal content and not just play whack-a-mole after the fact. It is meant to encourage a switch from a reactive to a more proactive approach, says lawyer Claire Wiseman, who specializes in tech, media, telecoms, and data.



---


# OpenAI's Three-Tier AI Safety Team Structure

OpenAI divides safety work across three teams distinguished by how far along a model is. In-production models are governed by a "safety systems" team, which handles, for example, systematic abuses of ChatGPT that can be mitigated with API restrictions or tuning. Frontier models in development get the "preparedness" team, which tries to identify and quantify risks before the model is released. Finally there is the "superalignment" team, which is working on theoretical guide rails for "superintelligent" models — which, as TechCrunch notes, we may or may not be anywhere near.

The discriminating feature between the tiers is thus the model's lifecycle stage: shipped, in development, or hypothetical future superintelligence.



---


# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# Foundation Model Reporting And Red-Team Disclosure Under The EO

The executive order sets out a reporting procedure for the most capable AI systems: a company developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests — and that information must be shared prior to the model being made available to the public, which could help reduce the rate at which companies unleash half-baked and potentially deadly machine learning products. The legal instrument used to compel this is the Defense Production Act.

Alongside red-team results, the EO also requires disclosure of the system's training runs — essentially its iterative development history. The purpose officials gave for the sequencing is verification: "What that does is that creates a space prior to the release… to verify that the system is safe and secure." The EO more broadly directs the establishment of new standards for AI safety and security, including reporting requirements for developers whose foundation models might impact national or economic security, and those requirements also apply in developing AI tools to autonomously implement security fixes on critical software infrastructure.

The procedure has a deliberately narrow scope. Administration officials were quick to point out that the reporting requirement will not affect any AI models currently available on the market, nor independent or small- to medium-size AI companies going forward, because the threshold for enforcement is quite high. It is geared specifically at the next generation of systems that the likes of Google, Meta and OpenAI are already working on, with enforcement on models starting at 10^26 petaflops — a capacity currently beyond the limits of existing AI models. "This is not going to catch AI systems trained by graduate students, or even professors," the administration official said.

The order was cast as a step past voluntary measures. "In response to the President's leadership on the subject, 15 major American technology companies have begun their voluntary commitments to ensure that AI technology is safe, secure and trustworthy before releasing it to the public," the senior administration official said. "That is not enough."



---


# Handling Weak Signals Through Scenario Theory

Identifying strategic surprises is a human process that depends on analyzing what the intelligence community calls "weak signals," Barnea says — "pieces of relevant information that have been conveyed to the organization, but because they are low-key, or because of the information overload around them, the organization fails to identify and interpret them correctly" — and no amount of technological advancement in an army or intelligence gathering system removes that dependence.

The October 7 example: suspicious movement in Gaza convinced the Shin Bet head to send a special team to the southern border, but he was unable to convince the top IDF echelons to prepare accordingly. To handle weak signals, Giora Eiland says, one must use "scenario theory" — taking into account scenarios that have a low probability of occurring but devastating results should they occur, and the simple way to prepare for them. Eiland spells out the three questions in order: "You detect certain noises on Friday night, but conclude that the probability of an attack is low, let's say only 10%. Those who act only on the probability do not consider the question: if this attack happens – will you be able to live with yourself for eliminating this threat? There's also a third consideration, which is ease of effort: what is the effort required of me to prepare for this unlikely but dangerous scenario? It may be a relatively simple effort, like waking the troops up at 4:00 am, placing them position, and putting an aircraft in the air for a few hours. You don't even need pilots – unmanned aircraft operators are enough. There's no need to mobilize reserves or convene a cabinet. Every commander is allowed to give instructions to those under him – if that would have happened, everything would be different." The precondition is that the low-cost preparation be available without high-level authorisation. Eiland identifies the same omission fifty years earlier: "This is exactly the same type of failure that was at the basis of Israeli thinking at the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War. After information was gathered that indicated the intentions of the Egyptians and Syrians to launch an attack, they decided not to mobilize reserves because the cost was high. But why didn't they order the regular army to get ready? They thought the chance of war breaking out was low, they thought it was an exercise, but they didn't calculate the potential damage, they didn't imagine how serious the extreme scenario could be."



---


# Snapchat Design Features Alleged To Enable Drug Sales

The lawsuit against Snap claims that Snapchat's features facilitate practices like drug sales by connecting dealers to young customers while promising them safety from legal repercussions through anonymity.

Chief among those designs, according to Matthew Bergman, the lead attorney on the case, is the promise that a message will disappear not only for fellow users but also on the software's back end. That is the ground that turns a product feature into an enabler of crime: it prevents law enforcement officials from seeing the activity of a dealer even after the dealer has been identified.

The complaint names other features as problematic too: notifying individuals when another person screenshots their post, the ability to geolocate fellow users, and algorithms that suggest new connections based on demographics.

# War Duration and Scenarios Driving Israeli Growth Damage

Leo Leiderman's model of the war's economic damage has two drivers: duration and breadth. "First of all, the duration and character of the war will have a decisive impact on the depth of damage to the economy. Many studies, as well as past experience, indicate that the longer the war lasts, the broader will be the impact on the economy. It is also known that this connection between the length of the fighting and the economic damage might not be linear. And of course, the more the war widens to more fronts, the greater will be the economic damage."

He declined to quantify the effect. Asked on 12 October 2023 for a forecast of the consequences for growth, he said it was too early to make a quantitative estimate of the effects on the economy's growth in 2024 and 2025. Israel has a great deal of information about loss of growth and product in past episodes — the Yom Kippur War, the Lebanon War, two intifadas, various military operations, and the Covid pandemic — but in his view this is a completely different episode: "This is a new situation that has no precedent as far as the damage to the economy is concerned."

The range over which the model runs is therefore a spectrum of scenarios rather than a point estimate: "from a short war on the southern front only, to the nightmare scenario of a prolonged war with additional sectors involved." As of mid-October 2023, the Indian stock market's base case was that the Israel-Hamas hostilities would not escalate, and on that assumption the conflict was expected to have only a limited impact on markets. # Three Causes Of Psagot's Value Decline

A senior capital markets source told "Globes" that "Rani and Psagot suffered from a lot of bad luck, because sometimes it's all a matter of timing," and identified three significant things that happened since the acquisition and affected the company: rising interest rates, the government's judicial overhaul, and the war that broke out on October 7.

On 7 October 2023, Hamas carried out what Business Today described as the biggest coordinated attack in Israel, capturing some territory in southern Israel and taking control of some military bases and soldiers.

# Israel-Hamas War Context, October 2023

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)

---


# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.

Among games, the top free iPad titles were Roblox, Magic Tiles 3: Piano Game, Subway Surfers, Royal Match, Among Us!, Duet Cats: Cute Cat Games, Stumble Guys, MONOPOLY GO!, Bridge Race and Gardenscapes, while the top paid iPad games were Minecraft, Geometry Dash, Bloons TD 6, Stardew Valley, MONOPOLY, Five Nights at Freddy's, Red's First Flight, Poppy Playtime Chapter 1, Plague Inc. and Garten of Banban 2.

# Apple Store Credit And Gift Card Promotion, November 2023

Apple's November 2023 holiday promotion is not a discount at all: instead of cutting prices, Apple gives buyers of select items a gift card of Apple Store credit to spend later, running from the time of WIRED's 25 November 2023 guide through 27 November, with up to $200 in credit available.

The defining feature is the substitution of future store credit for an immediate price cut. WIRED's framing is that Apple notoriously does not run sales on its own storefront; what it usually does instead is throw in a gift card for Apple Store credit when you purchase select items. The amount of credit scales with the product bought: buying an iPhone 14 or iPhone SE earns up to $75 in store credit, while buying a MacBook Air earns up to $200, with the full list of qualifying items published by Apple.

A separate and distinct mechanism runs at another retailer: Amazon has a sale on Apple gift cards, where each card has its own unique corresponding coupon code. WIRED's example is a $100 Apple Gift Card bundled with a free $15 Amazon credit using the code APPLET5USAP, with many other cards to choose from. This second offer is a discount on the gift card itself rather than Apple's own purchase-triggered store credit, so the two should not be confused.

# Apple Price Adjustment Policy

Apple does not offer a price-matching policy: The Verge noted on October 25th, 2023 that while there have been some claims Apple will price-match up to 10 percent for products bought at certain major retailers, there is no official policy on the company's website.
