But at the same time, I think..." His brother, the Philadelphia Eagles player, finished the thought — "They're overdoing it" — and Kelce agreed: "They're overdoing it a little bit, for sure. Especially my situation. I think they're just trying to have fun with it." Commenters under the New Heights video echoed the complaint: "I agree the NFL needs to calm down. Pissing off football fans is not how you repay your boi [sic] for all he's done for the sport"; "Pity Taylor. All she ever wanted was to watch the football game. Now she's being blamed and hated left and right"; "The NFL needs to seriously tone it down and let Trav and Tay explore this beautiful thing they have going on in peace."



---


# NFL Figures React To The Swift-Kelce Romance

Coaches, players and owners around the NFL commented publicly on the Swift-Kelce story in late September 2023, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

On 25 September, New England Patriots head coach Bill Belichick — who does not always comment on situations that take place in the game — was fully ready with a sound bite: "Well I would say that Travis Kelce's had a lot of big catches in his career. This would be the biggest."

On 27 September, Patrick Mahomes confirmed he had met Swift. He had said he had not met her when asked in the postgame press conference, but he did meet her at the afterparty: "Yea I met her. She's really cool. Good people," Mahomes said, via KSHB 41 in Kansas City. "But like Trav said, imma let them have their privacy and just keep it moving."

Also on 27 September, Cowboys owner Jerry Jones commented on the Swift effect on 105.3FM The Fan in Dallas: "It is hard to move that needle dramatically on a great feeling, a great attraction in the NFL. We get a lot of eye balls. She blew it off the charts. It is amazing. It makes you smile. But it just shows the depth of her following, especially with her core constituency. We all, I think, felt the same way when she's sitting up there with [Travis Kelce's] mom and she's going nuts when he's playing and those hearts are popping out everywhere. How do you not get that? That's called images right there."



---


# Patrick Surtain II Broncos Midseason MVP

Yardbarker's Nov. 9, 2023 AFC midseason team MVP list named cornerback Patrick Surtain II the Denver Broncos' MVP, predicting it should be no surprise if he earned a second straight Pro Bowl nod.

The grounds are his eight-game production: the 23-year-old budding star had one interception and eight passes defended, tied for 11th in the NFL. The warrant is that top-tier coverage volume from a young corner at that rate is Pro Bowl form.



---


# Mayfield Against Zone Coverage And At All Four Levels

Per Next Gen Stats, Baker Mayfield did the brunt of his damage in the Buccaneers' 34-20 win over the Packers on Dec. 17, 2023 against zone coverage, going 20-of-24 for 361 yards and three touchdowns against it.

He whipped arrows beyond the Packers secondary time and time again. He also became the first player in seven years to complete a touchdown pass at all four levels of the field — the line of scrimmage, 1-10 yards, 11-20 yards, and 20-plus yards. Next Gen Stats noted it was the third time in Mayfield's career he had thrown a touchdown pass to all four levels, the most by any quarterback since 2016.

qid: What company spends billions to maintain its default search engine status on various platforms, influences local search rankings with specific criteria, and is accused by news publishers of anticompetitive practices that harm their revenue, according to articles from The Verge and TechCrunch?
context:
# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# Decentralization As A Free Market, Not An Anti-Capitalist Project

The Verge rejected the framing that decentralizing social media is a kumbaya anti-capitalist manifesto — "It's about openness and sharing, not capitalism, man!" — arguing that in practice it is the opposite: a truly free market approach to social networking.

The premise attacked is that decentralization is hostile to large commercial success. Mastodon may not be interested in becoming a trillion-dollar company, the argument concedes, but there's no reason there can't be plenty of trillion-dollar companies built on the fediverse. What changes is the winning strategy rather than the size of the prize: in a fediverse-dominated world, the way to win is not to achieve excellent lock-in and network effects — the only way to win is to build the best product.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article that discusses Sam Bankman-Fried's backing of a teens' startup present the same allegation of misconduct against Sam Bankman-Fried as the TechCrunch article covering the FTX collapse's courtroom updates, with both alleging fraud for personal gain?
context:
# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."

qid: Was Owen Teale's career impact discussed in The Sydney Morning Herald before Tate McRae's breakthrough performance on Saturday Night Live was reported by The Age?
context:
# Owen Teale's Missed Leading Man Opportunities

Owen Teale had several chances to become a leading man and each fell away — financing collapsed, an American star was demanded, and he chose family over Hollywood networking — The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

When The Fifteen Streets attracted a massive TV audience in Britain, Teale was offered a lead role in a movie playing a bare knuckle fighter, but the financing fell through and he signed up for a four-year stint with the Royal Shakespeare Company instead. Years later a producer offered him the lead in a big film being shot in Britain, but the money men demanded an American star and William Hurt got the gig. When Teale won a Tony Award in 1997 for his performance in Ibsen's A Doll's House, he was told he needed to spend time in Hollywood wooing producers and decided to fly home to his family in London instead: "My wife was about to give birth, so I said 'I'm off'. I'm sure part of it was I just didn't believe that I was going to waltz into leading man roles in Hollywood." Despite the plaudits, awards and steady offers of work, the piece observes, he has never been certain of his gifts — probably why he is so consistently good, since complacency is not in his nature.

He is far better at recognising brilliance in others, such as Toni Collette, with whom he worked on Dream Horse, a 2020 movie about an unlikely champion racehorse. "Toni just raised my game. That's a huge talent, huge," he says, shaking his head in wonder. "I recently received an award from BAFTA for the film and part of me thinks they should give it to Toni." He is happiest in a room full of actors working on a play, a film or a TV production: "What turns me on is the thought of collaborating with talented people. I'm very sociable with the rest of the company and fully intend to do that when I come to Melbourne."



---


# Tate McRae's Greedy TikTok Breakthrough

Tate McRae's song Greedy went viral in August 2023 after being used in a video by popular TikToker Tube Girl and then in countless hair-flip transition clips, eventually amassing over 320 million streams globally, topping charts internationally and becoming the 20-year-old's proper breakthrough, The Age reported on 30 November 2023.

Until then her career, the review says, had "a stench of desperation about it" — a wild thing to say about someone only 20, but the description of an artist trading explicitly in classic pop moves while failing to grab the popularity such expression necessitates. The Calgary-born musician had already had a journey: a professionally trained dancer since 6, at 13 she finished third on the US version of So You Think You Can Dance and attracted record label attention with songs uploaded to YouTube. In 2020 her weeper You Broke Me First had a chart moment, leading to her 2022 debut I Used To Think I Can Fly, an intriguing album of thrashy bangers and post-Billie Eilish sad-pop featuring production from pop titans Greg Kurstin (Adele) and Finneas (Eilish). It had at least one could've-been smash — the spiky What Would You Do? — but, fairly listless despite her swaggering delivery, it failed to ignite with either mainstream audiences or pop aesthetes.

Greedy also landed her a slot on Saturday Night Live, "that pop superstar rite-of-passage", and sold out shows for her Australian tour the following November. That it was the song to push her to the next level is somewhat confounding, the reviewer writes: it is not particularly memorable and her debut had better tracks that slipped listeners by, but its sassy sentiment — "I would want myself", particularly suited to clips of youthful coming-of-age expression — caught on with the TikTok crowd, "which is how pop stardom happens these days". In another popstar move, McRae channelled an alter ego, Tatiana, who is "ballsy, loud and obnoxious", for Greedy's vibrant music video, a fun throwback to choreographed Y2K-era aesthetics with McRae dancing all lustily on a Zamboni.



---


# Erin Phillips' AFLW Retirement

AFLW great Erin Phillips played her last game at Alberton Oval, with Port Adelaide saluting her with a huge 58-point win over Greater Western Sydney, 13.10 (88) to 4.6 (30), on the Saturday, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

The crowd — which included Phillips' father Greg and mother Julie, both in tears after the game, more family and friends, and Adelaide captain Chelsea Randall — erupted as the curtain came down on the three-time premiership player after eight seasons and 67 games. "It was an awesome game and four quarters of Port Adelaide footy … It was awesome to finish up like that," Phillips told Fox Footy after the win. The 38-year-old kicked a momentous goal from a set shot in the final quarter and was smothered by her jubilant teammates afterwards: "I don't think I've been as nervous to kick a goal in my life, to be honest," she joked. "But nah, it was awesome."

Earlier she told the ABC that she wanted her legacy to include doing everything she could to grow the game: "Hopefully I can be remembered as someone who took their opportunities, loved the game and was willing to do whatever it took to ensure the next generation was in a better position." On the same Saturday the competition said goodbye to a range of players including Western Bulldogs forward Richelle Cranston, who has battled stage five chronic kidney disease while playing that season and was chaired off the ground by teammates Isabelle Pritchard and Ellie Blackburn, and Hawthorn's Akec Makur Chuot, who played 40 games for three clubs.



---


# Craig McRae's "44 Sons" Shirt Collar Message

Collingwood coach Craig McRae had the message "44 sons" written under the collar of the shirt he wore through the 2023 grand final, to signify how he felt about each player in the Magpies squad during 2023 as they drove towards a premiership. He revealed the legacy theme when he spoke to players, coaches, past players, club employees, and their friends and family at Collingwood's official post-premiership celebrations, held at Centrepiece in Melbourne on the Saturday night.

McRae said each player on the list did the same, inscribing a personal message under the collar of their own jumper with words describing the legacy they wanted to leave as a person and a player in 2023. "All the players had inside their jumper something they want to be remembered for," McRae said. "It was an action. It was theirs ... when we created legacy, today players ideally lived theirs. In my shirt I had [written] 44 sons. I've got three beautiful daughters now, I don't have a son, but I consider all these guys in the squad my sons, so I wore that under my collar today."

The coach said on the Saturday night that he was yet to return to St Vincent's Hospital, where his wife Gabrielle gave birth to their daughter Maggie at 7.45am on grand final morning. Gabrielle went to the hospital with her sister at 10pm on the Friday night after going into labour, before ringing McRae at 6am to join them at the hospital to be with them when the baby was born. Collingwood president Jeff Browne praised McRae and the players for their character and for driving the change the club undertook when the new coach was appointed, calling the win "the ultimate satisfaction"; Browne was rapt to be there after a health scare put him in hospital briefly on the eve of the finals.



---


# An Australian Pandemic Account By Aisha Dow And Melissa Cunningham

Aisha Dow and Melissa Cunningham's account of how the pandemic affected Australia, published by Scribe at $35 on 3 October, is a timely publication coming only a few days after Daniel Andrews — "the man who approved probably the world's longest cumulative lockdown" — left office, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its defining feature is the treatment: while many people may not want to revisit those stressful years, the two journalists with Nine newspapers "manage to make this a riveting story of discovery, dismay, and recovery".

The reviewer places it against what was still to come: "Ahead of the government's impending inquiry, you might find some answers here."



---


# The Case For Schmidt Bringing Rugby Smarts To The Wallabies

Several sources told The Roar in December 2023 that Joe Schmidt is exactly the type of person the Wallabies need: the claim is that the highly detailed Schmidt would bring rugby smarts to the Australian program, and the warrant is that the Wallabies' detail and nous were clearly absent on the field over the previous year, which is precisely what his coaching supplies.

The evidence offered for that capability is what his Ireland teams demonstrably did: the manipulation and ability to play both sides of the ruck was clearly visible during his Irish tenure.

The argument also carries a political ground about acceptance within Australian rugby: should Rugby Australia move on him, Schmidt's backing would be largely supported by the Super Rugby franchises.

qid: Does the Queensland Rugby Union's stance on maintaining control over their high-performance model, as reported by The Roar | Sports Writers Blog, align with Rugby Australia's efforts to centralize high-performance programs across Super Rugby teams, or are their approaches different?
context:
# The QRU Refuses To Centralise Commercial Functions

The Queensland Rugby Union stopped short of wanting to hand over its commercial property, rejecting the step from high-performance centralisation to full centralisation: "While the QRU is very supportive of high-performance alignment, it will not agree to any proposal on centralising commercial or corporate functions."

The premise it attacks is that consolidating commercial operations under Rugby Australia would strengthen the game. The QRU's reason is local expertise: "The very strength of our State unions is the expertise they bring in their own markets. We are open to work on commercial initiatives together but will always retain our independence for the benefit of Queensland Rugby, its members and stakeholders."

It backed the position with its own financial and participation record. The letter cited a sustainable business model built through the elimination of legacy operating debt, four straight operating profits, and work in partnership with governments to deliver $31 million of improvements to Ballymore through the construction of the National Rugby Training Centre, home of the Wallaroos and Queensland Reds. It also pointed to 71,000 players across the state, including more than 16,000 female participants, 257 schools featuring rugby as part of their program, and the Hospital Cup and regional club competitions, as evidence the game was in good health in Queensland.



---


# The Rugby Australia High-Performance Director Role And Its Remit

The Rugby Australia director of high-performance is the position at the top of the governing body's high-performance structure, described by chief executive Phil Waugh in December 2023 as the biggest job on his leadership team in terms of its impact on the general sentiment around the game in Australia.

Three duties define the role as described. First, the director oversees all of Australia's men's and women's high-performance programs. Second, the holder is tasked with "integrating" those programs, as Rugby Australia tries to centralise all of Super Rugby's high-performance programs. Third — and perhaps most pressing at the time — the director must build a list of coaching candidates to take over from Eddie Jones, with Rugby Australia wanting the new Wallabies coach set in stone by the start of Super Rugby.

The scope conditions attached are timing and seniority. Rugby Australia always said it wanted the role filled by Christmas, and Waugh's framing sets the standard for the appointment: "It's a big job. It's the biggest job on my leadership team in terms of the impact it has on the general sentiment around the game."



---


# Jones Defends Leaving Cooper And Hooper Out Of The World Cup Squad

Against criticism of his squad selection, Eddie Jones said on Tuesday, Oct. 16, 2023 that he had no regrets about leaving experienced players such as Quade Cooper and Michael Hooper out of the side for the 2023 World Cup.

He conceded the critics' right to their view while rejecting its authority over his decision: "Everyone's got their own judgment and they're allowed to have that judgment."

His own reasoning rests on a longer horizon than the tournament just played: "My choice was that I decided to go with youth. And I stand by that because I think we've got a lot of good young players who are really going to benefit from that experience at the World Cup, and going forward to the 2027 World Cup."



---


# Samu Kerevi's Message On The State Of Australian Rugby

Asked by Wide World of Sports on 7 October 2023 to deliver a message to disillusioned Wallabies fans, Samu Kerevi argued that reports of rugby's death are contradicted by what the squad has seen overseas, and asked supporters to stick with a team that is working extremely hard.

His grounds were the crowds in France: "I think at home there's so many sports going on and some saying rugby's dying, but rugby's massive here overseas," he said. "Last week 45,000 fans (versus Portugal), last night (60,000 in Lyon). Rugby's such a small aspect in terms of Australians but our fans have turned up here, we've seen them and spoken to them and their unconditional love for us, the fact that they came 20,000km to get here and support us, has been awesome."

# Cheika's Underdog Framing Before The 2023 Semi-Final

Michael Cheika embraced underdog status before Argentina's 2023 World Cup semi-final while pointedly reminding the All Blacks who the favourites were: "The other team are heavy favourites, everyone is expecting a New Zealand and South Africa final. We just have to focus on what is required."

His grounds are a reading of what New Zealand demand of an opponent: "New Zealand has always been an example in rugby, a benchmark. # The All Blacks' Final Moments In The 2023 World Cup Final

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.

# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.

# Very Large Online Platform (VLOP)

## Definition

A Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) is a service designated by the European Commission under the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) as carrying obligations beyond the DSA's baseline, on the grounds of its scale. Designation is the discriminating feature: the DSA's general duties apply to digital services broadly, but a platform once designated a VLOP additionally must identify and mitigate the *systemic risks* its service poses — disinformation, threats to fundamental rights, and, for algorithmic services, the societal risks attached to their recommender systems. The parallel designation for search engines is the Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE).

## Context

In the corpus the term appears as the tier that triggers DSA enforcement against the largest platforms. The Commission designated Meta's Facebook and Instagram as VLOPs earlier in 2023, and designated X (formerly Twitter) a VLOP in April 2023; VLOP compliance obligations took effect over the summer of 2023. The Commission is the *sole enforcer* of the DSA over VLOPs, which is the basis on which it opened its own request for information and later a formal investigation into X, and weighed in on Meta's advertising consent model. Designation is also what obliges these platforms to mitigate the disinformation risks the EU raised around upcoming elections, and it is why the Commission treats the (voluntary) Code of Practice on Disinformation as underpinning the DSA, with its stated intention to transform the Code into a Code of Conduct forming part of a co-regulatory framework for addressing disinformation risks.

## Key Characteristics

- **Designation, not self-classification** — a service becomes a VLOP by a Commission decision, and only then carries the extra duties.
- **Systemic-risk duty** — beyond acting on illegal content, a VLOP must assess and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, even where the underlying content (e.g. disinformation) is not itself illegal in the EU.
- **Sole-enforcer model** — the European Commission, not national regulators, enforces the DSA against VLOPs directly.
- **Penalty exposure** — confirmed DSA breaches by a VLOP can draw fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover, with service blocking possible for repeated infringement.
- **Search-engine analogue** — VLOSEs are the equivalent designation for very large search engines, subject to the same systemic-risk logic.

## Background (external)

The corpus names VLOP designation but does not state the numeric threshold that triggers it. Per the European Commission, the DSA sets the bar at more than **45 million average monthly active users in the EU** (European Commission, *DSA: Very Large Online Platforms and Search Engines*, accessed 2026-09-02), and the first batch of VLOP/VLOSE designations was issued on **25 April 2023** (European Commission, *List of designated VLOPs and VLOSEs*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Innovation Is Disney's Real Legacy

Polygon argues that Disney's biggest legacy is not the princesses, the theme parks, or even Mickey Mouse, but the fact that all those elements started out as daring projects no one else was doing.

The grounds are a record of risk. Over the past 100 years Disney has taken big, risky swings and fumbled many times: the dark and dreary Black Cauldron almost bankrupted the studio in 1985, and the off-kilter adventure movies of the early 2000s flopped, with the studio's mold-breaking passion projects often turning into megaflops. Yet some of the company's most memorable movies stemmed from those same risks. The original 1940 Fantasia was one of Walt Disney's most ambitious passion projects turned box-office failures, but the Sorcerer Mickey short is as iconic as the mouse himself. Lilo & Stitch was so weird that the filmmakers basically hid it from the rest of the company, and it ended up making back more than three times its budget while turning Stitch into one of the studio's most memorable characters. Even The Little Mermaid, the film that kickstarted the Disney Renaissance, was a risk, since a big Broadway-style musical of its type had not been done in animation before. The warrant is Walt Disney himself, who famously pushed for progress and innovation in the studio's creative endeavors even when that meant poor financial decisions; what has made the studio special is how it looked forward, trying new things in the face of failure and taking chances other production houses could not afford or risk. Polygon's complaint is that Disney and its fans keep forgetting this, clinging to the past with such ardor that it does their idol's legacy a disservice.

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

---


# Google One VPN

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

Engadget has not fully tested the Google One VPN yet, but says it will add it to the list if it feels it is warranted.

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. # The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.
