# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# ASPI's Analysis Of TikTok Pixel Data Aggregation Risk

Researchers at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute argue that the danger of TikTok's tracking pixel lies less in the type of data collected — which resembles what US tech giants gather — than in how that data can be aggregated and in who can ultimately reach it.

Jocelinn Kang, a technical specialist at the institute, said data from a tracking pixel could be aggregated across websites, apps and social media platforms, and that pixel tracking could identify users through their "browser fingerprint," a combination of their IP address, browser and system details. The linking gets sharper as identifiers accumulate: "However, when more identifying data such as email and phone number is associated with a user, their web activity can be better linked," Kang said.

Strategic Policy Institute researcher Samantha Hoffman said the data collected by TikTok's pixel was similar to that of US-based tech giants Google and Meta, but that the difference was "the intent." Advertising data had "incredible propaganda value," she said, and the warrant joining that to the risk is state access: "If you think about that, plus the access that TikTok is required to give the Chinese government, that's the problem." She notes TikTok itself made that access explicit — in November 2022 the company changed its privacy policy to state clearly that user data can be accessed by some employees from across the world, including China. "They talk about how even data collected overseas can be used by the company and its partners, and would be kept private unless security organisations make demands of it," Hoffman said. China's national intelligence laws allow the government to pull data upon request from companies based there.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. # Alexa Kids Data Handling And The Echo Pop Kids Launch

Amazon says it is not training its LLM on kids' answers, and that "Explore with Alexa" and any future LLM-backed features will continue to follow the same data handling policies as "classic Alexa" — the non-AI Alexa. In practice that means the Alexa app will include a list of the questions asked by kids in the household, for those with a kids' profile, along with the response Alexa provided; that history can be stored or deleted either manually or automatically, depending on the account's settings. These statements were made by the company to TechCrunch and reported on 25 October 2023, alongside the launch of the feature.

The launch also brought hardware. The new Echo Pop Kids speakers became available for purchase at the same time, starting at $49.99 in the U.S., in two new designs — Marvel's Avengers and Disney Princess — that feature corresponding character themes, letting kids hear a greeting, fun fact or joke about an Avenger or Disney Princess in keeping with the theme. Both include six months of access to the Amazon Kids+ subscription service, which, beyond "Explore with Alexa," also offers a range of kid-friendly games, apps, books, videos and more, including custom Alexa themes. Buying a Kids device is not a precondition for the feature, however: "Explore with Alexa" works on any device set to kids mode, or any communal family device, if parents have set up their kids' voice ID.

Two scope limits attach to the launch as described. The experience is available in English only at first, with internationalization further down the road. And the offline arrangement is framed as a stage rather than an endpoint — Amazon eventually wants the generative AI experience integrated at runtime for both kids and adults, while knowing it needs to proceed carefully, especially with kids: "We do want to integrate an LLM in runtime in a more protected way than we would integrate it for adults…However, this approach lets us iterate and figure out the right ways to get both safe and delightful content outputted from the LLM for kids," says Venkataswamy. On the adult side, he says Amazon was preparing to launch an AI-powered "Let's Chat" Alexa experience later that same year.



---


# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

# TikTok Pixel Pre-Consent Data Collection Test

Testing by The Age found that personal information typed into Australian websites was sent back to TikTok often before the user clicked "I consent" to the website's privacy policy.

The test was run by installing a browser extension and then visiting websites such as Sportsbet, Kmart, Beyond Blue and many others. On each site the testers went to sign up for an account, entering personal information including their full name, email address and phone number. Using Omnibug, they could see in real time that information being sent back to TikTok — and, crucially, that this often happened before consent to the site's privacy policy had been given.

The mechanism named in the report is a TikTok tool called "automatic advanced matching," which sees when a user enters text into a form field or a search box and, if it looks like an email address or phone number, scrapes that data.



---


# TikTok Bans And ByteDance Data Concerns

One remaining and major potential pitfall for TikTok is the rise in tensions between China and Western countries: amid concerns that parent company ByteDance may be sharing TikTok user data with the Chinese government, numerous governments — from the US to the European Union to Australia — have banned the app from government-issued devices.

A small number of jurisdictions have banned or are attempting to ban TikTok altogether, including Montana and, most recently, Nepal.

# Dak Prescott As A Week 6 2023 Sit At The Chargers

CBS Sports listed Dak Prescott under "Sit Him" for Week 6 of the 2023 season at the Los Angeles Chargers: the claim is that trusting Prescott is a tall task even in what looks like a favourable matchup, and the warrant is that his collapsed throwing depth, a compromised offensive line and a former coach who knows his tendencies leave the favourable matchup unable to produce fantasy points.

The core grounds are Prescott's depth-of-target profile. His completion rate this season is fine at 69.4% and his off-target rate is low at 8.1%, but his average depth of target is 6.5, ranking 28th among 33 qualifying quarterbacks, and he is second-to-last in pass attempts of 10-plus air yards, with only Daniel Jones throwing fewer. The scary part, the column notes, is that his average depth of target had been over a yard lower at 5.4 going into the previous week's game, so the Cowboys tried to let him air it out and the plan completely backfired: he got aggressive on downfield throws early and missed until hitting KaVontae Turpin for a 26-yard touchdown, then had to throw deep to climb back and got sloppy on two interceptions, with a third bouncing off Michael Gallup's hands; he did not play the last 12 minutes and Dallas was blown out. The offensive line is offered as the underlying cause — injuries dating back to Week 2 plus declining play from Tyler Biadasz and Terence Steele may be why Prescott, not wanting to get hit, gets the ball out as fast as he can; even against the 49ers he sped up his motion and overshot targets, and the offense isn't adjusting well enough. The breakdown lists Dallas at the Chargers, the Cowboys favoured by 2.5, an over/under of 51, an opponent ranked 21st versus quarterbacks, 18.9 projected points, a 15th quarterback ranking, and year-to-date totals of 1,061 passing yards, 45 rushing yards, five touchdowns, four interceptions and 13.8 fantasy points per game.

The matchup evidence cuts both ways, which is what makes the sit a judgement call rather than a projection. The Chargers traditionally play a good amount of zone but have used more man this season, including against Miami in Week 1, and despite headliners in the front seven and 16 sacks in their past three games they rank fourth-worst in pass-rush pressure rate at 29.5% while blitzing at about the league average — in theory not a difficult matchup for Prescott. Every quarterback except Raiders rookie Aidan O'Connell has taken at least 22 fantasy points off the Chargers. Against that, the column raises Kellen Moore, Prescott's quarterback coach and playcaller for the prior five seasons, who will be coaching the Chargers offense on Sunday and is sure to have spilled the beans on Prescott's tendencies — offensive coordinators come back to wreck their old teams all the time. It also expects Dallas to pivot to a slower approach with Tony Pollard handling the run game more than he has recently, which could take pressure off Prescott without meaning he will unload statistically. # North Texas Mean Green 2023 Profile

North Texas' 2023 team was carried by junior quarterback Chandler Jones and undermined by the worst defense in the country. Until two of his passes were picked off in a 38-20 defeat to UTSA the previous Saturday, Jones had thrown 262 passes through seven games with 19 touchdowns and no interceptions. The defense was another story. Since allowing 681 total yards to Cal in the opener, its past three opponents had rung up 1,460 total yards and 15 touchdowns, and its yield of 479 yards per game was the worst in the country — a line Sporting News, writing on Nov. 7, 2023, imagined SMU super sophomore quarterback Preston Stone licking his chops over.

Most of Apple's current-generation devices went on sale for Black Friday 2023, and most of those deals looked like they would carry over through the weekend and into Cyber Monday, Engadget reported on 2023-11-24 — meaning shoppers otherwise occupied on Friday could still save on iPads, Apple Watches, MacBooks, AirPods and more. This 32-inch display has built-in apps and lets you access streaming services just as you would on a smart TV. It can also act as a smart home hub, showing your smart camera feeds and more.

# The Verge Staff Favorites Black Friday Roundup

Black Friday and Cyber Monday may be in the past, but some sales are still hanging around — although maybe not for long — and The Verge points readers to the rest of the Cyber Monday deals still available for more leftovers across all categories.

Much of the gear is still discounted from Cyber Monday.

# Mozilla's Rationale For Investing In The Fediverse

Mozilla believes there is a better way forward for social networking and, more importantly, that now is exactly the right time to invest in that path. Its structural claim about why it can pursue that path: as a wholly owned subsidiary of a nonprofit, the company says it is not motivated by generating earnings for shareholders or returning a VC investment, allowing it to progress with a collaborative approach where it takes in input from a lot of different voices.

The grounds, per Mozilla Senior Director of Content Carolyn O'Hara, are a decade of observed behavior by incumbents: Mozilla's involvement came about because the company looked at the history of social media over the past decade and did not like what it saw. "I think that it's a pretty poor track record by existing companies that are only model motivated by profit and just insane user growth, and are willing to tolerate and amplify really toxic content because it looks like engagement," she says. "[They] aren't just putting forward the kind of standards that are good for people, but are just good for their bottom lines." The timing claim rests on a change in consumers: they are now becoming aware of this, which is new. "Consumers feel that the vibes are off a little bit…these platforms aren't necessarily working in their best interests, or satisfying them," O'Hara points out.

For Mozilla, that discontent presented an opportunity to enter the social networking space and compete for consumers' attention — but with a broader goal of helping the fediverse itself gain traction, not just its own Mastodon server. "We're not seeking to get, like 2 billion users on our instance. We want people to have choice and agency," says O'Hara, adding that choice is in line with Mozilla's values. As TechCrunch characterizes it, Meta's updated offer to EU users is either hand over your privacy or hand over your hard earned cash. # Pebble's Moderation-First Market Hypothesis

# Black Friday 2023 Headphone Deals Overview

Black Friday is often a boon for deals on headphones and earbuds, and 2023 was no different, Engadget reported on 2023-11-24: the shopping holiday brought a plethora of deals on all kinds of headphones, including several top picks from its guides to the best wireless headphones, wireless earbuds, budget wireless earbuds and gaming headsets.

# TikTok's Ad-Free Subscription Tier Test

qid: Who is the individual that, according to reports from The Verge and TechCrunch, faced challenges managing the growth of FTX and Alameda Research, allegedly used FTX customer funds to buy out Binance, was informed about a financial discrepancy after a judge's intervention, and is accused by the prosecution of committing fraud for personal gain?
context:
# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

qid: Which company, reported by TechCrunch, has both invested $26.3 billion to maintain its default search engine status across devices and platforms in 2021, and has been accused in a class action lawsuit of harming news publishers' revenues and readership through anticompetitive practices?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Alphabet Q3 2023 Earnings Preview

Alphabet was set to announce its Q3 results during Tuesday 24 October 2023's post-market session, with the search-engine giant having outperformed the broader market index at a 55% growth rate that year, surpassing the S&P 500's 12%.

Following the company's upbeat Q2 results, investment firm Bank of America said it was expecting "favorable" headlines, due in part to strength in YouTube, search and artificial intelligence. Just a few days before the earnings report, Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating system changed its view from Strong Buy to Hold, while Wall Street analysts maintained a bullish view with a Strong Buy rating.

Consensus EPS estimates were $1.45 and consensus revenue estimates $75.73B. On the earnings insight, Google had topped EPS expectations in 4 of the past 8 quarters, beating revenue estimates in 5 of those reports.



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."

In an interview with WSJ Magazine published on 20 November 2023, Travis Kelce described how much he admires Taylor Swift's skills as a musician and said he was not letting media attention affect the relationship.

"I've never been a man of words. Being around her, seeing how smart Taylor is, has been f***ing mind-blowing. I'm learning every day," he explained. When she acts like that I better not be the one acting all strange."

# Shadowbanning

## Definition

Shadowbanning, as TechCrunch describes it, is when a platform "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of" a user's content without the platform notifying the user that anything has been restricted, so the user only discovers it by noticing a drop in views or reach.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the central accusation in the October 2023 controversy over Meta's handling of Palestine-related content: Instagram users accused Meta of shadowbanning their Stories about Palestine, and TechCrunch frames the belief that Meta "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of," such content as longstanding rather than new to that month.
The same allegation is cited beyond Meta's own platforms as a driver of platform choice: users turned to Snapchat's Snap Map for firsthand Gaza content specifically because accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content on Instagram and Facebook had eroded their trust in those platforms.
Meta's official response did not deny that reach had dropped; it denied the mechanism, attributing the reduced Story reach specifically to a global, content-neutral bug in Stories that re-shared Reels or Feed posts, and separately attributed a different global bug — one that had prevented some users from going live — to technical error rather than deliberate suppression tied to subject matter.

## Key Characteristics

- **Covert, not disclosed** — the defining feature reporters and users pointed to is that visibility drops silently, with no notification to the affected account; Bella Hadid described being "immediately shadowbanned" and her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million" with no explanation from the platform.
- **Detected by comparison, not confirmation** — users inferred shadowbanning by comparing engagement across their own posts (e.g., a user whose Stories fell from "100s of views to zero or a handful" and rebounded only after posting unrelated content like a cat photo), since the platform provided no direct evidence of restriction.
- **Contested mechanism** — Meta disputed that the effect was shadowbanning-by-design, attributing the reduced Story reach to a bug that "affected accounts equally around the globe" and "had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content," rather than confirming intentional visibility limits.
- **Trust-eroding beyond the platform itself** — the accusation pushed users toward alternative platforms (Snap Map) even though the accused conduct occurred on Instagram and Facebook, showing shadowbanning claims can shift audience behavior across platforms, not just within one.

# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# Theory: Copyright Liability Over OpenAI's Training Data

The proposition is that the board acted over mounting accusations that OpenAI's product was built on a dataset including thousands or millions of copyrighted works, with the CEO systematically downplaying the potential liability. TechCrunch's reporter notes that Altman told him at OpenAI's Dev Day earlier that month that the company does not want to incur any copyright problems by using datasets of pirated books, but that a lot of research he had been reading contradicts that, as does pretty much every AI data scientist he talks to. The framing of the hypothesis is a question about the board's likely reaction: if you were the board and facing those accusations, and your CEO had systematically downplayed the potential liability, how would you feel? "I'd feel very hurt."

What works against it is again the succession. If copyright liability was the reason, it seems unlikely that the board would promote the CTO; presumably OpenAI's Chief Science Officer Ilya Sutskever would also have been in the know, and he is still on the board.

# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

A longtime NFL executive challenged the analytics-driven push toward aggressive play-calling on 16 October 2023, asking whether coaches have "come too far with coaches wanting to 'win' the game instead of sometimes being more traditional" after the Eagles threw a killer interception on third-and-9 from their own 46-yard line while protecting a 14-12 lead against the Jets with two minutes left in the fourth quarter.

The premise attacked is not that aggression is generally wrong. Most would agree teams have gotten smarter in their handling of fourth-down situations, going for it when it makes sense instead of punting almost out of habit; making the aggressive play to win can absolutely be the smart play regardless of results, and it is progress when teams seriously wrestle with these questions, not just on fourth down but in all aspects of strategy. What the exec disputes is the automatic application of that reasoning to a particular game state: Philadelphia could have run the ball on third-and-9, then punted from around midfield, leaving the Jets with barely more than a minute remaining, no timeouts and Zach Wilson behind center facing a ferocious Eagles pass rush. "Are coaches not willing to go against the slight statistical benefit that WPA (win probability added) provides?" he asked. "Is it no longer OK to let your defense win the game when it clearly has a huge talent/performance advantage? This Eagles game was 14-12, not 37-35."

The inference the counter-argument targets is the neglect of situation-specific factors. In that game the Jets' offense had netted 19 yards on its previous three possessions, producing one field goal on a drive that gained 16 of those yards; the Eagles had already suffered three turnovers, and they knew Wilson would be taking over deep in his territory with very little time remaining. "To me, these are exactly the type of factors that a coach needs to consider when deciding," the exec said. "I think they were ignored here." A veteran coach added an incentive-based explanation — critics attuned to the trend toward aggressiveness pounce when teams pass up chances to go for the kill, coaches know team owners tend to be fans rather than football strategists and listen to those criticisms, which creates an incentive to go down swinging: "Everybody thinks they are playing Brady, Manning or Rodgers in two-minute. If before the game someone offered Philly to put its defense against Zach Wilson on a need-field-goal drive starting inside his own 15 with no timeouts and a minute left, you think they would have taken it?" The base rate is thin: the situation Philly faced was the seventh time since 2000 that a team leading by 1-2 points in the final two minutes faced third down with 7-10 yards to go from the minus-40 yard line to midfield with the opponent holding no timeouts; three of the seven passed, resulting in one first down, one sack and Hurts' interception, and of those three only the Eagles lost the game.



---


# NFL Week 11 Power Rankings, 25-32

At the bottom of Sporting News' Week 11 rankings on Nov. 13, 2023, the Green Bay Packers were 25th at 3-6 (previous week: 25), showing improved work from Jordan Love and his young weapons spreading the ball well in the passing game, but with run-defense woes and key holes in coverage that had all but doomed their playoff hopes. The Los Angeles Rams were 26th at 3-6 (26), hoping to find answers during a bye as Sean McVay's good early-season coaching job went by the wayside with key offensive injuries, needing Matthew Stafford to save face or the season would look a lot like 2022. The Tennessee Titans were 27th at 3-6 (27), with Will Levis going through rookie lumps after a dazzling debut as brutal offensive line woes exacerbated by injuries got to him and the whole offense — though the Titans still needed to keep starting him, since they could not overcome those systemic problems or those in overall pass defense.

The Chicago Bears were 28th at 3-7 (29): they do not care how they win, and should have been pleased their running game and defense bailed out a limited passing game with Tyson Bagent to secure another Week 10 win, hoping to finish strong with Justin Fields soon. The Arizona Cardinals jumped to 29th at 2-8 (32) after an immediate offensive spark with Kyler Murray and James Conner back, looking invigorated for Jonathan Gannon on defense and special teams and likely to finish strong and play a lot of spoiler. The New England Patriots were 30th at 2-8 (28), having tried to win by hiding Mac Jones and their quarterbacks in general and nearly pulling it off with a dominant running game and short-handed defense making plays, but without results in Germany ahead of a tough bye for Bill Belichick.

The New York Giants were 31st at 2-8 (30) and could flush away the season without Daniel Jones and Tyrod Taylor, with early and relentless injuries to the offense and a defense now falling apart too — the question being whether Brian Daboll would get a massive mulligan after his rookie playoff leadership. The Carolina Panthers were last at 1-8 (31), finding better defense and special teams to stay in the game in Chicago, but with Bryce Young still unable to unlock a limited passing game and an offensive line and running game that had not helped nearly enough.



---


# NFL Week 11 2023: Three Starting Quarterbacks Hurt, All Three Stayed Or Returned

In Week 11 of the 2023 NFL season, as reported by CBS Sports on 2023-11-19, three starting quarterbacks took injury scares and none of them ended the day sidelined for good. C.J. Stroud of the Texans left for a single play against the Cardinals after absorbing a hard hit, with backup Davis Mills entering in relief; Stroud did not receive an injury designation and returned after a quick check-in from trainers. Sam Howell of the Commanders received medical attention on the sidelines after enduring several hard hits to the upper body on a touchdown run against the Giants, was quickly cleared of a potential concussion and remained in the game, with veteran journeyman Jacoby Brissett listed as Washington's backup.

The most consequential case was Geno Smith of the Seahawks, who suffered an injury to his throwing arm after guiding a 16-7 lead over the Rams, showing frustration while trying to stretch the arm after a hit from Aaron Donald. Seattle quickly ruled him questionable to return with an elbow issue, and backup Drew Lock took over under center with 18 seconds left in the third quarter. Smith did return for the final drive of the game, in a losing effort. Head coach Pete Carroll said Smith will "make it back," and when asked whether that meant for Thursday's matchup against San Francisco, the coach said, "I would think so." The wider Week 11 context given by the same roundup: the week provided plenty of drama, from the Bears hanging with the Lions to the Giants getting a rebound from emergency quarterback Tommy DeVito, alongside another wave of unfortunate injuries.
