qid: Has the portrayal of Google's market practices in reports by The Age before October 22, 2023, remained consistent with the depiction in The Verge's coverage of the Epic v. Google case, and with TechCrunch's report on the class action antitrust suit filed against Google?
context:
# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Google One VPN

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

Engadget has not fully tested the Google One VPN yet, but says it will add it to the list if it feels it is warranted.

qid: Between the report by FOX News - Health on 'People engaging in virtual interactions' due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the article by Polygon on the 'Dungeons & Dragons campaign' moving to virtual online play, is the trend of virtual engagement for activities typically done in person consistent or inconsistent?
context:
# The Pandemic Shift To Videoconferencing

With the COVID-19 pandemic, Zoom and other videoconferencing platforms "exploded in popularity," said Dr. Carl Nassar, PhD, a professional counselor based in Denver, Colorado.

The shift covered nearly every kind of relationship at once. "We all found ourselves at home looking at the people we worked with, the people we went out for drinks with and the people in our extended family on a computer screen," he told Fox News Digital. "Our work went virtual, our social life went virtual, our doctors' appointments went virtual, and even our intimate relationships sometimes went virtual," he said. "And this meant a lot of time looking at each other on-screen instead of in person."

Long after the pandemic, many of these habits have persisted.



---


# Fortnite's Battle Royale Live-Service Model

Fortnite is a battle royale-style third-person shooter where 100 players swarm a massive but shrinking virtual island with the goal of being the last man standing. In the process they generally engage in myriad well-animated virtual antics as the game has become wackier and more elaborate over time, all while dressed in custom skins you earn by playing or purchase in Epic's lucrative virtual swag shop.

What makes it a live-service game is its release cadence: like other live service online games, Fortnite releases new content every three-ish months, refreshing the destinations scattered across its cartoony island locale, changing the rules of physics and generally adding additional mayhem, often in the form of weapons. Epic's hit game has both imported and exported popular culture since its launch in 2017, and those seasons are punctuated by flashy concerts and pop culture tie-ins, like a psychedelic Ariana Grande show, an in-game lightsaber fight with Darth Vader or the appearance of Dragon Ball Z's Goku as an in-game skin. The massive online shop for skins and other character customizations betrays Epic's loftier aspirations of building an interconnected virtual online world — a kind of metaverse, if you will.



---


# The Third Place

The third place is a sociological term that refers to a physical space that isn't work or home, where people can socialize without the obligations of productivity. The membership test is simple: if you can hang out there, it's a third place.

The category has boundary cases in both directions. During the pandemic, virtual communities served as ad hoc third places in lieu of coffee shops, bookstores and gyms, and Twitch, which saw exponential growth during the pandemic, was one of them. In the other direction, a place can be plentiful and still fail the role: last year's San Diego-based TwitchCon, for all of its faults, took place in a walkable city abundant with nearby places to hang out, allowing attendees to bond, network and interact outside of the convention center, while there's no shortage of third places in Las Vegas — but for many TwitchCon attendees, nightclubs and casinos aren't accessible alternatives to San Diego's more casual venues.



---


# Dungeons & Dragons In 2023

Two Polygon contributors describe their 2023 with Dungeons & Dragons, and both accounts are about how the game is actually played rather than about its rules.

Mike Haracz, corporate R&D chef and host of Heroes' Feast, is in the seventh year of a homebrew campaign played with friends locally in the Chicagoland area. The campaign is called The Heartsguard Saga and is based on Deven Rue's map of a place called Euphoros; his players are around level 15, and he frequently gives them amazing and unique gear he has dreamed up, which they go on to forget they have and never use. The group used to play in person but since the pandemic he runs it virtually from his house, with a camera hovering over his gaming mat and a labeled grid so players call out moves like "Move me from A5 to B10," and during important rolls he makes players face their camera toward their dice for added suspense. Petrana Radulovic, entertainment reporter, had wanted to play since high school but never knew how to get in; in the doldrums of 2020 someone she knew knew someone who knew someone interested in running a game, which kicked off her D&D career, but 2023 was the year everything clicked and it went from a hobby she enjoyed to one she spends every free minute thinking about. She credits reliable groups — after some initial shuffling of members she had two separate groups in 2023, both with enthusiastic members committed to at least trying to meet regularly — and also Baldur's Gate 3, which helped her understand some of the more complicated D&D mechanics and made her excited about combat in a way she never was before. She has still yet to play in person, since her groups are spread across North America, and hopes to manifest an in-person session soon.



---


# Platform Culture As A Model Of Political Engagement

The model TechCrunch sets out on 2023-10-02 is that to engage with users online, politicians must understand the culture of the platform — the relation between cultural fit and engagement outcome holds regardless of a politician's reach or resources. Two structural elements do the work: borrowed audiences and format-native behaviour.

On the audience side, the streamers who appeared on Ocasio-Cortez's stream brought their own fans, who may not have been politically engaged at all before their favorite creator introduced it to them. On the behaviour side, Ocasio-Cortez is a regular gamer herself and is up to date on the most popular games on Twitch: in 2020 it was "Among Us," while in her most recent stream she played the cooperative puzzle game "Pico Park." Gaetz, on the other hand, fumbled his launch by treating his stream like a podcast recording, limiting the back-and-forth banter with viewers that makes Twitch so engaging. Annie Wu Henry states the general relation: "The amount of media and content that we consume, political and cultural, where people get their information … It's getting more and more intertwined," she said. "To be effective ideologically, when it comes to campaigns and these wins that we want, we have to understand how these ecosystems work, and be strategically using them or else we risk being left behind."



---


# Digital Engagement Protects The Ageing Brain

The Guardian's 10 October 2023 piece sets out a model in which grappling with technology — not being rescued from it — protects the ageing brain, because novel and difficult tasks force the brain to work in new ways.

The structure has three linked parts. First, the difficulty itself is the active ingredient: a recent study from the University of Texas involving more than 200 elderly adults found that those who engaged with technology had better cognition and memory than their non-engaging peers, and the study authors concluded that digital engagement — whatever the device — protects the brain; even the stress experienced while battling with a computer can be helpful, sharpening mental acuity. These findings reflect earlier studies that found older people who made active use of technology were less likely to get dementia. The implication is that the well-meaning helpfulness of children who "delight in parenting" their parents on all things digital "might not be as beneficial as we think".

Second, novelty generalises beyond devices. Dr Eamon Laird, researcher in health and ageing at Limerick university, agrees that older parents should be encouraged to try new things, and the further out of their comfort zone they feel, the better: "It's always good to keep the mind active and fresh. New challenges can help build and maintain new brain connections and can be good for brain and overall health." Third, sociability compounds the effect: if older people use technology to keep in touch with extended family and friends, "that's a double whammy" — when the author's 84-year-old mother recently joined Instagram she both expanded her grey matter and found an effective means of staying in touch with her grandchildren. Being social, says Laird, is as important as trying new things: "Research shows that those who are more social are also more resilient to chronic conditions and often have a stronger immune system."



---


# The Social And Developmental Costs Of Heavy Phone Use

Licensed clinical social worker Jennifer Kelman argues that heavy phone use costs children the capacities that only in-person life builds: face-to-face connection, problem-solving skills, and confidence.

Kelman, who is based in Boca Raton, Florida, provides expert advice on the Justanswer platform and was not involved in the study. "They lose the ability to have face-to-face interactions, and to converse and connect with others," she said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "The phones and all the apps aren't real-life interactions, and there is beauty in connecting with others face-to-face that is lost," Kelman went on.

Kids also lose out on developing problem-solving skills, since they aren't typically tasked with negotiating "tough spaces" or navigating human challenges, the expert added. "The more apps we use, the more likely it is that we lose parts of ourselves, our confidence and self-esteem," said Kelman.

Her warrant is that the substitute does not deliver what the original does: "People feel good and are enhanced by interactions with others, and those feelings cannot be replicated by connecting through a phone."

qid: Between the report from The Verge on Apple's defense of its Google Search deal published on September 26, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on the class action antitrust suit against Google published on December 15, 2023, was there a change in the portrayal of Google's market influence and competitive practices?

# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---


# Deft's Competitive Landscape: Search Incumbents

Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

In September 2023, Amazon updated its visual search feature that lets users snap a photo of a product and search for similar items on the platform. Google released its multi-search feature in 2022, letting users fuse images and text — the same combination Deft offers.

Separately, Deft will also face competition from other startups like Objective, a Matrix Partners-backed startup building an API platform for multimodal search.



---

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.

## Definition

In the corpus, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is never defined on its own — it appears only as one item in a longer list of security practices that a source recommends or claims to already follow, alongside things like passwords, encryption, and security audits.

## Key Characteristics

# Johansson's Rebuttals To The Case Against The CSAM Scanning Proposal

Against opponents who characterise her CSAM-scanning proposal as mass surveillance, as a slippery slope, and as a law written around two vendors' technology, Ylva Johansson argued to MEPs that each of those premises is wrong: the proposal names no technology, would scan less than happens today, and forbids using detection for anything other than child sexual abuse. TechCrunch reported her answers on 25 October 2023, from her appearance before the committee.

The opposition she was answering had been aired earlier that week. A seminar organized by the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), an advisory body to the Commission on data protection law, heard from more than 20 speakers across civil society, academia and industry expressing deep misgivings about the Commission's approach — including a warning from the EDPS himself that the EU could be at a tipping point for freedom and democracy if it does not turn back from the plan to do non-targeted scanning of private messages. Johansson had been invited to participate in the seminar but declined to attend, and she did not offer a direct response to the EDPS' concerns at the hearing, instead countering a number of the arguments heard at the session.

Her first counter attacks the premise that the proposal is built around particular vendors. She denied that only Thorn and Microsoft have technology "that is necessary for the scanning", calling that claim "absolutely not true". "There are no specific technologies mentioned [in the proposal] and I think this is an important part. So there's no specific technology that's been favoured in this proposal," she told the committee, adding: "So many technologies are being developed all the time — while we are speaking — and they will continue to develop. So I think it's important that the legislation has to be technology neutral."

Her second counter attacks the inference from the proposal to mass surveillance. "My proposal would not mean that all communication will be scanned. Compared to the situation today it will be much more limited," she claimed, referencing the temporary ePrivacy derogation that currently gives messaging firms a legal basis to scan non-encrypted content for CSAM — a derogation intended to be replaced by the proposed regulation which, critics contend, will force platforms to scan end-to-end encrypted content too. "Today companies are allowed to scan if they search for child sexual abuse material. That's why we receive these 5.2 million videos and pictures and grooming attempts — 70% from private communication. If my proposal is adopted, this will be limited."

The warrant she offered for that comparison is the proposal's ordering of obligations: in-scope platforms are first required to deploy prevention measures to try to stop the spread of CSAM and/or prevent abuse of their tools by people intent on abusing children. "First comes prevention. Only if prevention is not enough, then you might be allowed to do detection — but only after a court decision," she said. "So only those that really cannot deal with the problem with mitigating measures… and only after a court decision and only during a specific period they will be allowed to do the detection. We will also limit the reporting so that we will also receive fewer but hopefully better reports."

Her third counter attacks the overreach and slippery-slope premises by pointing outside the proposal, to other EU laws acting as balancing checks on the scope of possible CSAM-scanning. "It's also important that we continue to comply with all relevant legislation. For example the GDPR and other requirements, there are no derogation from that in my proposal," she said. "It's also important — and I know that's been part of the debate — that it should not be a slippery slope. Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. # Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. # Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# What SEO Is, And Why People Hate It

Search engine optimization is the practice of telling the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results, leveraging Google's supposed objectivity to lure people in and then, usually, show them some kind of advertising — a business model. It is less straightforward than buying the advertising space labeled "Sponsored" above organic search results; it is more like the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority.

The discriminating feature is that SEO borrows credibility from a system users believe is neutral. Over time SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up "sneaker" in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike ("footwear that allows you to just do it!"). Perhaps this is why nearly everyone hates SEO and the people who do it for a living: the practice seems to have successfully destroyed the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff.

The reputational context in 2023 is a broad unhappiness with finding information online, which for almost everyone means the quality of Google Search results. Users call the links that come back "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Some blame Google itself, asserting that an all-powerful, all-seeing, trillion-dollar corporation with a 90 percent market share for online search is corrupting our access to the truth; others blame the SEO practitioners.

The stereotype of the practitioner is a hustler: a content goblin willing to eschew rules, morals, and good taste in exchange for eyeballs and mountains of cash — a nihilist in it for the thrills, a prankster gleeful about getting away with something. "This is modern-day pirate shit, as close as you can get," explained Cade Lee, who has over a decade working in SEO. What Lee said he has noticed most at SEO conferences and networking events is a certain arrogance: "There's definitely an ego among all of them. You succeed, and now you're a genius. Now you've outdone Google." The writer's own admitted starting position was that a bunch of megalomaniacal jerks were degrading our collective sense of reality because they wanted to buy Lamborghinis and prove they could vanquish the almighty algorithm — which, technically, constitutes many algorithms, but we think of as a single force.

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Lawsuit Redactions As Signal: The Amazon Precedent

TechCrunch reads heavy redaction as itself informative: you know it is bad news for the company when they request pages and pages of redactions.

The precedent it cites is recent. This recently happened with Amazon as well, and it turned out they were trying to hide the existence of a price-hiking algorithm that skimmed billions from consumers.

The comparison is used to rank severity rather than to equate the two: it is much worse, TechCrunch writes, when you are redacting COPPA complaints.

# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# Meta Enforcement Volume

Meta reported removing or marking as disturbing more than 795,000 pieces of content in Hebrew and Arabic in the three days following October 7, for violating the policies described in its Israel-Hamas war response. The figure appears in the company blog post covered by TechCrunch on 13 October 2023.

Meta also gave a rate comparison for one specific policy: "As compared to the two months prior, in the three days following October 7, we have removed seven times as many pieces of content on a daily basis for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy in Hebrew and Arabic alone." Both the 795,000 total and the sevenfold daily increase are scoped to Hebrew and Arabic content, not to the platform as a whole.



---


# BEUC And 18 Member Groups File A CPC Complaint Against Meta

A coalition of almost 20 consumer protection organizations filed a complaint against Meta's pay-or-consent model with the network of consumer protection authorities (CPC) on November 30, 2023, taking the united view that Meta's switch to railroading users into agreeing to being tracked and profiled so it can keep profiting from microtargeting them is "unfair" and "illegal," breaching EU consumer protection law "on several counts." The filing came days after a privacy complaint was lodged against Meta in the European Union over its latest controversial shift of legal basis claimed for processing people's data for ads.

The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) led the complaint, saying in a press release: "This is an unfair choice for users, which runs afoul of EU consumer law on several counts and must be stopped." BEUC was joined by 18 of its member organizations, consumer advocacy groups located in Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain and Sweden.

The groups object both to how Meta has gone about implementing the "pay-or-consent model" — using what they assess as "unfair, deceptive and aggressive practices" — and to the model itself, which they dub "illegal." They have also raised data protection concerns which are already the focus of the complaint sent to the Austrian data protection authority earlier that week by the privacy rights not-for-profit noyb. Ursula Pachl, deputy director general of BEUC, said in a statement: "The choice the tech giant is currently providing to consumers is unfair and illegal — the millions of European users of Facebook and Instagram deserve far better than this. Meta is breaching EU consumer law by using unfair, deceptive and aggressive practices, including partially blocking consumers from using the services to force them to take a decision quickly, and providing misleading and incomplete information in the process. Consumer protection authorities in the EU must now spring into action and force the tech giant to stop this practice."



---


# Arturo Bejar's Critique Of Meta's Teen Safety Self-Regulation

In the absence of a legislative decision, Meta began regulating itself, adding new defaults and features that would restrict teens' access to content on its apps, protect their privacy and limit ad targeting to teens, as well as introducing parental controls. The premise under attack is that this self-regulation was sufficient.

In the weeks before November 15, 2023, a second Meta whistleblower, Arturo Bejar, came forward to express concerns that Instagram's approach to protecting teens was not working to keep them safe from sexual predators and unwanted sexual advances and harassment. Bejar had been hired as a consultant on the matter and eventually blew the whistle on Meta after seeing issues remain unresolved following years of work.

His argument essentially was that the improvements and safety features Meta was implementing were not enough and not effective — so the attack is on efficacy rather than on whether Meta acted at all, and its evidentiary weight comes from his having worked on the problem from inside for years.



---


# Irish DPC's Assessment Of Meta's Consent Model

Meta's lead regulator in the EU for the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), told TechCrunch: "Meta notified the DPC on July 27 of its intention to implement an alternative, consent-based model in which users would be given a choice between ads-funded versions of its platforms, and subscription versions in which, in return for payment of monthly fee, it is said that users will not receive targeted advertising."

The regulator also set out the timing and its cause: "While February 2024 was initially identified by Meta as the earliest date by which its consent model would be operational, it agreed to bring forward that date to November 2023 at the direction of the DPC, the DPC having been concerned to ensure that changes would be implemented to the platforms as soon as practicable in light of earlier findings to the effect that Meta had failed to demonstrate its entitlement to rely on the legal bases on which it was then relying when processing users' data for behavioural advertising purposes. These included findings made by the Court of Justice of the European Union when delivering judgment on July 4, 2023 in a case in which the Court examined the legal bases on which Meta's processing of users' data for behavioural advertising purposes is grounded." On the review itself: "Acting in consultation with its fellow European supervisory authorities, the DPC has been engaged in a detailed regulatory assessment of the consent-based model since it was first proposed by Meta in July. That exercise is being led by the DPC, reflecting its position as Lead Supervisory Authority for Facebook and Instagram in Europe. The exercise has not yet concluded, and no findings have been made to date. It is due to be completed shortly, at which point the DPC will notify Meta if it considers that the manner in which its new user offerings are to be implemented is compatible with Meta's obligations under GDPR." So Meta's move hasn't been signed off by data protection authorities as yet, and further regulatory interventions could follow — Norway's DPA, which has a local ban order on Meta's tracking ads, told TechCrunch it's concerned about the subscription plan, saying it has doubts as to whether it would constitute valid consent.

qid: Does 'The New York Times' article suggest that Lamar Jackson's effectiveness is enhanced when regulated to pocket passing, while 'Sporting News' indicates that Arthur Smith has found success with Bijan Robinson's playing style for the Atlanta Falcons?
context:
# The Baltimore Ravens' Pass-Oriented Offense Shift

The New York Times questioned on 16 October 2023 whether Baltimore's shift toward a more conventional pass offense will make the Ravens tougher to defend, noting they have never scored fewer points or amassed less offensive EPA through the first six games of a season with Lamar Jackson in the lineup.

The grounds are Jackson's changed rushing profile. He has one rush longer than 20 yards, where he had four or five by that point in previous seasons, and he is gaining at least eight yards on 15 percent of carries, half his previous rate. The schedule and injuries have played roles in the scoring decline, but the open question is whether the explosive quarterback runs are mostly in the past — and the writer is not expecting a consistent precision passing game to suddenly materialise.

An executive pressed the argument further, holding that the change subtracts more than it adds: "The defense keeps them in it, but I don't necessarily think this offensive change is going to make them any better when it counts. Lamar Jackson does not appear as dynamic as a runner, but in this offense, he does not need to be. He is regulated to pass from the pocket, but you are taking away the biggest weapon the offense had when you do that. Odell (Beckham) is not that guy anymore. Who are you truly afraid of on that offense? Nobody but Lamar, and if you are not using Lamar in a certain capacity, he becomes just like the rest of these quarterbacks around the league — hit or miss."



---


# Jonnu Smith As A Week 5 2023 Sneaky Sleeper At Tight End

CBS Sports listed Jonnu Smith as a "Sneaky Sleeper" for Week 5 of the 2023 season against Houston: the claim is that Smith is doing what Kyle Pitts is supposed to do — get open and make plays after the catch — and the warrant is that Houston's heavy zone coverage leaves open the short middle of the field, which is exactly where Smith operates.

The role grounds compare the two Atlanta tight ends directly. Week 4 was the second time in three weeks Smith outproduced Pitts, and the first time it was so lopsided; the difference in snaps played and routes run is marginal, with Pitts doing more of both, but Smith is taking advantage of shorter routes with a quarterback who doesn't like to challenge downfield much. Smith averaged more yards per catch not only in Week 4 but also in Week 2, and was behind Pitts by less than a yard in Week 3 when both had at least eight targets. On film Smith is running shorter routes and getting open faster than Pitts, which has earned him targets from Desmond Ridder, who seemed to have better timing with Smith; Smith is not drawing tight coverage like Pitts, mostly because he stays closer to the line of scrimmage, and after the catch he has been a handful, breaking three tackles in Week 4 alone and picking up extra yards — not fast, but faster than Pitts, and for at least Week 4 and Week 2 that changed the calculus for how Atlanta divvied up targets. He certainly hasn't done anything to lose his role.

The matchup grounds are Houston's tight end problem. The Texans have had a bundle of troubles with tight ends, giving up an 84% catch rate and 6.76 yards after catch per reception to the position, both bottom-six in the league; that includes allowing an 89% catch rate on 18 total targets to Colts and Jaguars tight ends in Weeks 2 and 3, for 9.9 yards per catch and 7.2 yards after catch per reception. Those numbers were a byproduct of the amount of zone coverage Houston played against both teams, leaving the short middle of the field open, and Houston has played the third-most zone coverage of any team this year and should do so again. The breakdown lists Atlanta at home versus Houston, the Falcons favoured by 2, an over/under of 41.5, an opponent ranked 18th versus tight ends, 5.2 projected points, a 24th tight end ranking, and year-to-date totals of 15 receptions on 20 targets for 179 yards, no touchdowns and 8.2 fantasy points per game. The recommendation is bounded twice: the hope depends on the game staying competitive, as most Falcons games tend to be, and while the author doesn't mind chancing it with Smith as a streaming tight end, he doesn't have the conviction to start him over Pitts.



---


# Brock Purdy Leads Lamar Jackson In The 2023 MVP Odds

According to oddschecker, as cited by Yardbarker on 2023-12-24, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy was listed as the heavy favorite to be named league MVP at -230, while Baltimore signal-caller Lamar Jackson held the second-shortest odds at +525.

Purdy, the final pick of the 2022 NFL Draft, had seen his career unfold as if it were a fairy tale that just keeps getting more remarkable: the 23-year-old ranked first in the NFL in QBR at 76 and in touchdown passes with 29, while ranking third in passing yards with 3,795 — all especially impressive considering he was coming off offseason elbow surgery. Jackson might not have been posting the ridiculous numbers of his 2019 MVP campaign, but the adjustment in his play style in his first season under offensive coordinator Todd Monken had led to sustainable, winning football. Nevertheless, Baltimore needed an upset win for Jackson to capture another MVP Award; he had thrown for 3,105 yards and 17 touchdowns while adding 741 yards on the ground with five scores that season.



---


# Lamar Jackson Ravens Midseason MVP

Yardbarker's Nov. 9, 2023 AFC midseason team MVP list named quarterback Lamar Jackson the Baltimore Ravens' MVP, concluding that he was the reason, once again, that Baltimore was a Super Bowl contender.

The grounds are his production and its timing: Jackson had inserted himself into the league MVP conversation during his team's four-game win streak, and the 2019 NFL MVP had thrown for 1,954 yards and nine touchdowns while posting 440 yards and five touchdowns rushing. The warrant is that dual-threat production concentrated in a winning run is what converts individual numbers into team contention.



---


# Logan Thomas As A Week 6 2023 Start At Atlanta

CBS Sports listed Logan Thomas under "Start Him" for Week 6 of the 2023 season at Atlanta: the claim is that streaming Thomas is worth the risk considering how the Falcons have let up numbers to tight ends, and the warrant is that Washington values the position heavily, Thomas sees the most throws from Sam Howell, and Atlanta's expected heavy zone coverage should produce a bunch of underneath throws for him to take in.

The opponent grounds come first. The Falcons see the third-most targets per game to tight ends, 9.0, which has made them bottom-five in raw stats like total catches and yards allowed, though they float around league average in catch rate allowed (77.8%, below league average) and yards per catch (8.9, better than league average); however, no team has allowed more first-down receptions to tight ends, 17. The column adds the scope caveat that this defense hasn't seen tight ends better than Evan Engram, Sam LaPorta or Dalton Schultz. On coverage, Atlanta usually plays a lot of zone early and sticks with it for the whole game if it works, as in Week 5; in Weeks 3 and 4 against the Lions and Jaguars they played much more man, especially when they needed a fourth-quarter turnover — and because Howell is much less explosive against zone looks, the author expects the Falcons to stick with zone much more this week.

The usage grounds carry a health caveat. Washington throws to its tight ends on 26.3% of its throws, fourth-most in football, but that hasn't always meant a huge target share for Thomas: in Weeks 1 and 5 he saw at least 22.9% of Howell's targets, but he left Week 2 after suffering a concussion, was absent in Week 3, and was not much part of the game plan in Week 4, with a 7.7% target share against Philadelphia — perhaps all health related, and perhaps his Week 5 volume will stick. That Week 5 volume also came with a game-script asterisk: Thomas was a big-time beneficiary of Washington chasing points against Chicago's heavy zone, seeing 10 of his 11 targets once the Bears built a 17-point lead in the first half, with a 24-yard catch on the final play of the half against prevent defense not hurting either. The breakdown lists Washington at Atlanta, the Falcons favoured by 2.5, an over/under of 42.5, an opponent ranked 31st versus tight ends, 8.4 projected points, an 11th tight end ranking, and year-to-date totals of 18 receptions on 25 targets for 183 yards, two touchdowns and 11.6 fantasy points per game. The stated hope is at least seven targets, which is possible; the verdict gives Thomas the nod over Jake Ferguson, Dalton Schultz and Tyler Conklin, and calls it close in full PPR over Kyle Pitts.

qid: Who is the individual who has been a notable figure in generative AI technology, was considered a prodigy in Silicon Valley from a young age, and is at the center of controversy over allegations of not being fully truthful with the board, according to articles from both Fortune and TechCrunch?
context:
# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Second Senate AI Insight Forum, October 2023

Senator Charles Schumer (D-NY) hosted Silicon Valley's AI leaders on Tuesday as the US Senate reconvened its AI Insight Forum for a second time, and on leaving the meeting Schumer told the assembled press that "it is clear that American leadership on AI can't be done on the cheap," reporting that almost all of the experts in the forum called for robust, sustained federal investment in the private and public sectors to achieve American-led transformative and sustainable innovation in AI.

The guest list for this second session included manifesto enthusiast Marc Andreessen and venture capitalist John Doerr, along with Max Tegmark of the Future of Life Institute and NAACP CEO Derrick Johnson. According to a release from Schumer's office, the agenda covered "the transformational innovation that pushes the boundaries of medicine, energy, and science, and the sustainable innovation necessary to drive advancements in security, accountability, and transparency in AI."

On cost, National Security AI Commission estimates put the required federal investment at around $32 billion a year. Schumer believes those funding challenges can be addressed by "leveraging the private sector by employing new and innovative funding mechanisms — like the Grand Challenges prize idea." He framed the goal as a balance: "We must prioritize transformational innovation, to help create new vistas, unlock new cures, improve education, reinforce national security, protect the global food supply, and more," but in doing so "we must act sustainably in order to minimize harms to workers, civil society and the environment." As he put it, "We need to strike a balance between transformational and sustainable innovation. Finding this balance will be key to our success."

Schumer closed by saying the participants would leave "with a deeper understanding of how to approach American-led AI innovation," and that the conversation would continue "in weeks and months to come — in more forums like this and committee hearings in Congress — as we work to develop comprehensive, bipartisan AI legislation."



---


# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.



---


# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."



---


# ChatGPT's First Year Overview

Over the course of two months from its debut in November 2022, ChatGPT exploded in popularity, from niche online curio to 100 million monthly active users — the fastest user base growth in the history of the Internet. In less than a year, it has earned the backing of Silicon Valley's biggest firms, and been shoehorned into myriad applications from academia and the arts to marketing, medicine, gaming and government.

In short, ChatGPT is just about everywhere, and few industries have remained untouched by the viral adoption of the generative AI's tools. Engadget published this retrospective on 2023-11-30, the first anniversary of its release.



---


# USD Funds In China Turn To Overseas Deals

On a weekday afternoon at Red Rock Coffee, the café known for spotting venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, one is likely to overhear a few conversations in Mandarin. With China reopening its borders in spring 2023 following three years of COVID-19 restrictions, managers of U.S. funds in the country have been flocking to the Bay Area.

The trips themselves are not new; their purpose is. While these trips were routine before the pandemic, they have now taken on a fresh purpose of discovering deals beyond China.

As China's domestic investment appeal wanes, some investors start to look for opportunities beyond its borders. Rather than a complete departure, they are merely following the footsteps of Chinese talent who have already embarked on global expansion.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.

qid: Do the TechCrunch and Seeking Alpha articles agree on the trend of companies' spending on cybersecurity, or do they present differing views on this matter?
context:
# Cybersecurity Spending Resilience And Breach Costs

Security continues to be a huge priority for enterprises and smaller businesses, and it is one area where companies have returned to spending even when other IT categories have remained frozen or constrained.

The cost trend is the driver. A McKinsey report from the previous year notes that breaches are on track to collectively cost $10.5 trillion annually by 2025, a 300% increase on 2015 figures. While a lot of companies clamped down on spending and IT budgets over the previous couple of years, security budgets came back. "For end customers, security is still a big business risk, so budgets are back in action and we're seeing sales picking up in Q3 and Q4," one source told TechCrunch. "Security companies will want to tap into this opportunity aggressively."



---


# Cybercrime Cost Growth Drives Cybersecurity Demand

The financial damage from cybercrimes will reach an astronomical $10.5 trillion by 2025 — a figure that, as global economies go, would rank third behind only the US and China. Global cybercrime damage costs are expected to increase 15% annually over the following two years, according to Cybersecurity Ventures.

Seeking Alpha framed this on 18 November 2023 as bad for global conglomerates and the average person but an opportunity for cybersecurity firms like Check Point Software. The demand signal holds even as rivals such as Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet cite an uncertain macroeconomic environment for weak billings forecasts.

Check Point President Rupal Shah Hollenbeck put it this way in a Zoom interview that week: "There's never been a better time to be in cyber. It's fortunate in that organizations are understanding the business value of cybersecurity in a really big way. Unfortunately, it's because there are more hacks out there than ever before."



---


# AI Market Spending Forecasts Reported In October 2023

# Drawbacks Of Prop Bets

Against the case for props, Sporting News presses three objections: props are difficult to research, they can tie up your bankroll, and exotic props are a guessing game. The first attacks the assumption that a bet's specificity makes it tractable. Prop bets are so specific you would think they would be easier to research than other bet types, but sports are extremely volatile and you can never truly predict how an athlete or a team will perform, which makes smart props very hard to nail down — you might bet a player to score "over" a point threshold and lose because he had an off-night, even though he would have won that bet easily in other recent games.

The bankroll objection targets the role props should play in a strategy. Sporting News would not recommend using prop bets as your main bet type: use most of your budget on more stable bet types such as moneylines, spreads or totals, and focus only a small percentage of your bankroll on props.
