# Sports Betting Terminology Glossary

CBS Sports set out the top Kentucky betting terms for new bettors on 13 October 2023, defining each bet type by what the bettor is actually wagering on and, in several cases, by a worked Kentucky example.

Against the spread means that instead of betting on an exact winner, the widely popular spread bet levels the playing field by letting you wager on how many points a team will win by: in basketball, if Kentucky is the 7.5-point favorite against Louisville then Kentucky covers by winning by 8 or more, while Louisville as the 7.5-point underdog covers by winning outright or losing by 7 or fewer. Money line is an elevated outright bet with odds adjusted to reflect a favored team and an underdog: if Kentucky is a -200 favorite against Florida you'd need to bet $200 to return $100, while Florida at +200 would return $200 on a $100 bet. An outright bet is the easiest wager to place and is perfect for horse racing, one of Kentucky's biggest sporting events — bettors choose one athlete, or thoroughbred, to win an entire event. An Over/Under has the sportsbook post an estimated total of both teams' final scores, with the bettor wagering on whether the actual final will be higher or lower: if the Over/Under for a Kentucky-Louisville basketball game is 125.5, you wager on the final total being Over 126 or Under 125. A player prop projects a player's stat at the end of a game and asks you to wager over or under that projection, with popular examples being how many touchdown passes a quarterback throws or how many three-pointers a basketball player hits; Kentucky is one of the 18 states that allows prop bets on collegiate athletes.

The remaining terms describe the market's participants and mechanics. The underdog is the team deemed less likely to win based on the odds, and a bet on one typically yields a larger return than a bet on the favorite; the favorite is deemed more likely to win, and bettors often pay a premium for backing one though they more often win outright. Consensus odds are generally defined as an average of all available betting markets, since different sportsbooks may price markets variably based on the action they've taken or their own interpretation of information. Futures markets encompass almost anything outside single-game bets — total regular-season wins, championship odds, MVP odds and more. A parlay requires two or more bets within a single wager, all of which must win: wagering $100 on a three-leg parlay at 6 to 1 odds could win $600 if all three legs win. Juice, also known as the vig or vigorish, is effectively the tax oddsmakers charge for handling a wager — if a book judges a game a virtual coinflip it may price both options at -110 to give itself a 10% rake on all the action. A push is a bet where neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins: if an over/under for total points is set at 44 and both teams combine for exactly 44, the result is a push and the principal is returned. Live or in-game betting allows bets on several different markets in real time — in basketball, on the outcome of a quarter, individual statistics and live-updated spreads and totals.



---


# Favorites And Underdogs In Moneyline Odds

The favorite is the participant — team or individual — expected to win the event or matchup, and the underdog is the participant deemed less likely to win compared to the opponent. The distinction is a judgment about relative chances, and it is what the sign on a moneyline price encodes.

In moneyline odds, especially in the American odds format, the favorite is usually represented with a minus (-) sign: if Team A is a favorite listed at -150, a bettor would need to wager $150 to win $100. Underdogs, again particularly in the American format, are usually represented with a plus (+) sign: if Team B is an underdog at +130, a bettor would win $130 for every $100 staked, should Team B win.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.

# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."

# Bankman-Fried's Defense Strategy And Appeal Groundwork

Bankman-Fried's defense can itself introduce risks for people who dealt with him, because his lawyers have several simultaneous objectives: first and foremost proving their client not guilty, but also — just in case they don't get the outcome they want — laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments.

The consequence is procedural: any piece of evidence they want to introduce for those two purposes has to come into play during the trial. Christopher LaVigne notes that Bankman-Fried's lawyers are already marking arguments that his constitutional rights are being violated by his pretrial incarceration because, among other things, his internet connection wasn't good enough for him to plan his defense — which could be grounds for an appeal.

# Wang's Cooperation Agreement With Prosecutors

Gary Wang testified under a six-page cooperation agreement with the government that requires him to meet with prosecutors, answer their questions truthfully and turn over evidence; he faces up to 50 years in prison when he goes before a judge for sentencing following the trial.

Wang said he returned to the U.S. and met with prosecutors the next day. For months Bankman-Fried has known that Wang and Ellison, integral members of his personal and professional inner circles, had turned on him: both pleaded guilty in December and have since been cooperating with the U.S. attorney's office in Manhattan. Wang's testimony, which stretched into Friday, was given under that cooperation agreement, and Ellison was expected to take the stand under a similar arrangement. U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided.

# Cohen's Cross-Examination Of Caroline Ellison

Mark Cohen's cross-examination of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 aimed at the premise that her direct testimony was reliable — she had recounted many conversations held in person or on auto-deleting messaging platforms, and she had an incentive to flip on Bankman-Fried in the form of possible leniency at sentencing — but The Verge's reporter judged that the defense absolutely biffed it. In Cohen's disorganized cross-examination he mostly bored the jury; at one point two different jurors appeared to be asleep, and midway through the morning the reporter began wondering whether there was a mercy rule for cross-examinations.

The lines of attack were opened and dropped. Cohen established that Bankman-Fried had a much larger appetite for risk than Ellison, that the two reacted differently to stress, and that they took different approaches to media — Ellison avoided it while Bankman-Fried sought it out — without building on any of it. He drew out that Alameda had one accountant in 2021 and hired two more junior accountants in 2022, and had a problem retaining accountants, then dropped that too. He appeared to be trying to suggest the government had coerced Ellison's testimony by getting her to plead guilty to defrauding investors, conduct she could not have been involved in since she did not prepare materials for them; unfortunately she said she had had conversations with investors as part of their due diligence, and Alameda was in any case taking on losses from FTX to keep FTX's balance sheet pristine. Cohen also pressed the hedge he had blamed her for not taking out in his opening — hedging being long crypto by selling Nasdaq futures — which raised the question of whether the defense was that she should have taken more customer funds, or taken them sooner.

Small failures accumulated. Cohen asked Ellison to define what "buy on the way down" meant as though it were a term of art, which seemed to puzzle her, and at other times he seemed to forget what she had testified to and brought up things she had not said; like FTX employee Adam Yedidia before her, Ellison was fastidious about making sure a question was clear and her answer precise. She appeared at one point to be toying with him: having testified on direct about the token Luna, she noted when Cohen asked about Terra/Luna that she had only spoken about Luna, leaving him to fumble the relationship between the two. There were many sidebars, enough that several jurors looked entertained when one occurred, and in one the day before the prosecution complained that Bankman-Fried was visibly scoffing at Ellison's answers, per the court transcript. What Cohen was up against was strong direct evidence: fake balance sheets, one sent to crypto lender Genesis, after which a Genesis representative texted Ellison to say he had spoken to Bankman-Fried — strongly suggesting Bankman-Fried knew the contents of the fake balance sheet. Afterwards, the defendant's mother Barbara Fried engaged Christian Everdell in an animated conversation, gesticulating and clearly holding a strong opinion; Everdell walked off and Cohen talked to her for a bit.

# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

qid: Do the articles from The Roar | Sports Writers Blog discussing The All Blacks' actions in the Rugby World Cup final and their previous encounters with Argentina both present The All Blacks as having effortlessly dominated in their gameplay, or do they portray different situations regarding The All Blacks' performance?
context:
# The All Blacks' Final Moments In The 2023 World Cup Final

New Zealand's last chance in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final died in the 80th minute when Ardie Savea forced a ball out wide just as the men in black saw space and looked to open up the Springboks — a killer blow, in The Roar's phrase.

The wider failing was handling. The All Blacks had their chances, but their usual safe handling — a feature throughout the World Cup after their first-up loss to France — evaded them against the Springboks' blitz defence in the wet conditions, and all night their timing was off.

The end came at a set piece. Wayne Barnes, who was booed relentlessly, called a scrum reset as the seconds ticked by; moments later New Zealand hearts sank as the Springboks won the scrum and then hung onto the ball.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Coaching Record With Ireland And The All Blacks

Joe Schmidt took Ireland to the top of World Rugby's rankings while his Irish sides bombed out in successive World Cup quarter-finals under his leadership, and he later helped transform an All Blacks team that reached the 2023 World Cup final, as reported by The Roar on 11 December 2023.

His Ireland tenure is credited with more than results: Schmidt played an instrumental role in not just seeing them become one of the world's best teams but helped usher through transformational change off the field, as Ireland moved to a centralised system.

The New Zealander briefly exited the international coaching scene following the 2019 World Cup, citing a desire to move home to New Zealand to be closer to his family. After initially moving back into the coaching fray with the Blues in Super Rugby, he joined the All Blacks ahead of the previous year's Rugby Championship, as New Zealand Rugby shook up the All Blacks coaching team following their historic series loss to Andy Farrell's Irish. His expertise proved telling: he and Jason Ryan transformed the All Blacks and helped Ian Foster's side reach the final of that year's World Cup after stunning wins over Ireland and Argentina in the knockout stages.



---


# Foster Rejects The Favourites Label Against Argentina

Although the All Blacks were 18-point favourites for the opening 2023 World Cup semi-final, Ian Foster rejected the premise that his side sees itself that way: "Firstly, you've never heard us say we're favourites."

His grounds for rejecting the label are recent results and a limit on what the past predicts. Argentina had knocked over the All Blacks the previous year in Christchurch, as well as inflicting a maiden defeat in 2020 in Sydney, and New Zealand had themselves suffered a shock semi-final loss to Eddie Jones' England in 2019. Foster also argued that familiarity does not transfer to this stage: "The past sets us up beautifully for both teams. We do know each other but we don't know each other in terms of a Rugby World Cup, so at this stage in the tournament it's new territory for us and as we've seen World Cups are very different."

He then converted the rejection into a demand on his own team: "We have learnt to greatly respect Argentina. They have a rich history of overachieving at the World Cup and have done a fantastic job to get here at the same level we are, so it is going to be a heck of a game." And: "We know these games are do or die. We're going to have to improve our performance. The stage gets bigger at this time in the tournament and you've got to grow your game. That's our strong focus. The best team on the night wins – Argentina has done that to us."



---


# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# Ireland: The Greatest Team Yet, Still Without A Knockout Win

This is the greatest Ireland team of all time, and may still even be the best team in the world — but on this day, the quarter-final curse, not to mention an inspired All Blacks side, ruled once more. The claim is that quality and knockout success have come apart: being the best team available is compatible with going out at the same stage as every Ireland side before them.

The consequence the argument draws is reputational. Instead of being feted as the heroes to finally overcome that insurmountable obstacle, the Ireland players will still have to answer endless questions about the heavy burden of previous knockout failures, and fans will endure at least four more years of choking jokes at their expense.



---


# How England And South Africa Reached The 2023 Semi-Final

England arrived at the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final as the only side still competing that had yet to lose a game, while South Africa had already beaten two of the tournament favourites. Dominant wins over Argentina, Japan and Chile sealed England's passage to the last eight, and after being given an almighty scare by Samoa in their final pool match, they overcame a Fijian fightback in Marseille to triumph 30-24 — outscored by three tries to two, but carried by captain Owen Farrell's 20 points at the expense of 2023's breakout stars.

The Springboks had done it tough. Comfortable defeats of Scotland, Romania and Tonga could not mask the disappointment of a 13-8 loss to Ireland, which consigned South Africa to second in Pool B. With Ireland then sent home by the All Blacks in the quarters, the Bokke showed their World Cup mettle to edge hosts France 29-28 at the Stade de France, sneaking past Les Bleus in one of the best games of rugby you're ever likely to see.

Both journeys had twists, turns and bumps in the road but left each side within 80 minutes of a Rugby World Cup final. England would be looking to echo the spirit of 2019, when they beat the All Blacks 19-7 to reach the final, but in South Africa they faced a side who had taken their game to new heights just to reach the semis.



---


# Kieran Crowley Criticises The Italian Rugby Federation

Kieran Crowley pushed back on 6 October 2023 against the idea that Italy's World Cup should be judged on its two heavy defeats, arguing instead that the players deserve better treatment off the field from the Italian Rugby Federation — and that this, not the results, is the real problem.

His tenure ended in profound disappointment, though the crushing defeats by the All Blacks and now the hosts were offset by victories against Namibia and Uruguay. Crowley had wanted to continue: "I've said before, I'd like to take this team forward. I think the next World Cup is our cycle … we'll get to the next tournament, and a lot of these players will have 60, 70 caps. But that wasn't my decision."

The premise he attacks is that the last two games are a fair measure of the group. "What needs to happen is that these players need to be treated with a bit of respect off the field … They [the Italian Rugby Federation] need to get some of that stuff sorted. Quite honestly, I don't know if I'd want to be involved unless that gets sorted. I respect these guys, these players and staff. They've gone way beyond … and yet people will judge us on these last two games. It's disappointing."



---


# England vs South Africa: 2023 Rugby World Cup Semi-Final

England faced defending champions South Africa in the Rugby World Cup semi-final in Paris from 8:00pm on 21 October 2023, having secured victory over Fiji in the quarter-finals, with talkSPORT carrying updates from all the action.

Victory would take England into their second consecutive Rugby World Cup final. Owen Farrell would be looking to inspire England to victory against the Springboks. The fixture formed one half of a double crunch point for England against South Africa on the same day, as they also met in the ODI Cricket World Cup — talkSPORT framed it as crunch time for England in the World Cups.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article claim that "Microsoft's investment in OpenAI" is unspecified, while The Age article focuses on the "founding of OpenAI" without specifying financial figures?
context:
# OpenAI's Nonprofit Governance And Capped-Profit Structure

OpenAI's for-profit subsidiary, OpenAI Global, LLC, is fully controlled by OpenAI's nonprofit: the subsidiary is permitted to commercialize its technology, but it is subject to the nonprofit's mission of attaining artificial general intelligence (AGI), which OpenAI defines as AI that can "outperform humans at most economically valuable work."

The discriminating feature of this structure is where the power over AGI sits. The nonprofit OpenAI's board has the power both to determine when the company has achieved AGI and to exclude that AGI from IP licenses and other commercial terms — including terms with Microsoft, one of OpenAI's biggest investors and a steadfast integrator of OpenAI's technologies. OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit in 2015 but restructured in 2019 as a "capped-profit" company in order to raise capital, an acknowledgement of the huge costs associated with training cutting-edge AI systems. Altman underlined the point in an interview with the Financial Times in the week of his firing, saying he "hoped" Microsoft would increase its investment to help pay for "huge" imminent model training costs.



---


# OpenAI's Partnerships With Microsoft And The Associated Press

OpenAI's key business partner is Microsoft, which has invested billions of dollars into the startup and helped provide the computing power to run its AI systems. Microsoft said the leadership transition would not affect its relationship: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers," an emailed Microsoft statement said.

A second, narrower arrangement is with a news organization: The Associated Press and OpenAI have a licensing and technology agreement allowing OpenAI access to part of the AP's text archives.



---


# Microsoft's OpenAI Investment And Early Capability Tests

The first look at the disruptive potential that generative AI offers came when ChatGPT managed to pass a series of law school exams — albeit by the skin of its digital teeth, Engadget notes.

Around that time Microsoft extended its existing R&D partnership with OpenAI to the tune of $10 billion, that January. Engadget's aside on the figure: that number is impressively large and likely why Altman still has his job.



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.



---


# Theory: A Financial Mismatch At OpenAI

The proposition is that some major mismatch in the financial department was the cause for dismissal. Could OpenAI be losing even more money than Altman admitted or projected? It seems impossible, TechCrunch writes, but the costs of running this operation have no precedent, nor really does the operation itself.

A variant, offered as purely speculative: what if Altman had been secretly pursuing an internal project, perhaps at significant cost, against the advice of the board and without the necessary safety measures that probably should accompany such research? It sounds a little wild, but firing your CEO like this is also a little wild.

What weighs against the family of financial theories is the difficulty of concealment: it is hard to imagine what Altman could have kept from the board and CTO that would be so damning. A separate possibility is that Altman was making personal investments in a way the board disagreed with — with OpenAI poised to be a kingmaker in the field, he would certainly be in a position of power. One would think that, as an ideologically driven person already rich beyond belief and at the head of the world's leading AI company, Altman would have risen beyond having to do this kind of side deal, or at the very least that scrutiny on him and those close to him would prevent them. But one can never be sure.



---


# OpenAI Board's Merger Approach To Anthropic

During the leadership crisis, OpenAI's board of directors approached Dario Amodei, the co-founder and CEO of rival large-language model developer Anthropic, about a potential merger of the two companies, according to a report by The Information.

The approach was part of an effort by OpenAI to persuade Amodei to replace Altman as CEO. Amodei quickly turned down the CEO offer.



---


# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# OpenAI Chip Rumors And Nvidia's Position

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-13 that rumors were swirling that OpenAI may be considering developing its own AI chips, and set that against Nvidia's position: Nvidia's ongoing stock market rally is likely driven by the current boom in AI, so an in-house OpenAI chip would make things interesting.

Two further figures anchor the week. ChatGPT's mobile app hit a record $4.6 million in revenue in the previous month, but growth is slowing. And the newsletter argues there is no need to shed tears for Nvidia quite yet, pointing to Brian's piece breaking down how Nvidia became a major player in robotics — that is, Nvidia's exposure is not confined to supplying the AI boom.

The surrounding context that week was AI coverage generally. TechCrunch's most-read stories consistently continue to be about AI, the AI hype cycle continues apace, and that week brought a batch of stories about what the newsletter calls the seedy underbelly of AI, including how humans are part of the problem, continuing to trick AI systems into generating boobs and 9/11 memes. TechCrunch spoke with investors to figure out whether the future of AI has hope beyond daft memes, and reports that it does. The OpenAI chip item is explicitly a rumor as of that date, not a confirmed plan.

context:
# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.



---


# The Competitive Response To ChatGPT Across The AI Industry

ChatGPT became priority number one at OpenAI — not simply a one-off product but a development platform to build upon — and, as often happens in a competition-driven marketplace, it shifted the focus at other AI firms and research labs too.

Google scrambled to launch a response to ChatGPT, eventually releasing Bard, a more or less comparable AI chatbot, in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives have arrived to market since, most recently Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. And DeepMind, Google's premier AI research lab, is expected to debut a next-gen chatbot, Gemini, before the end of 2023.



---


# ChatGPT Competitors And Alternatives

There are multiple AI-powered chatbot competitors to ChatGPT — Together, Google's Bard and Anthropic's Claude among them — and developers are creating open source alternatives, though the latter are harder, if not impossible, to run today.

Bard is the closest comparison. Much like ChatGPT, Bard is a chatbot that answers questions in natural language; Google announced at its 2023 I/O event that it would soon add multimodal content to Bard, meaning it can deliver answers in more than just text, with rich visuals — pictures for now, and later possibly maps, charts and other items. The discriminating advantage claimed for ChatGPT is time in the field: its generative AI has had a longer lifespan and thus has been "learning" for a longer period than Bard.

Two further challengers were in development. The Google-owned research lab DeepMind claimed that its next LLM would rival, or even best, ChatGPT; DeepMind is using techniques from AlphaGo — its AI system that was the first to defeat a professional human player at the board game Go — to make a ChatGPT-rivaling chatbot called Gemini. Apple is developing AI tools to challenge OpenAI, Google and others, and has created a chatbot that some engineers internally refer to as "Apple GPT," although Apple has yet to determine a strategy for releasing the AI to consumers.



---


# ChatGPT's Mid-2023 Usage Decline

By June, a little bit of ChatGPT's shine had started to wear off: Congress reportedly limited Capitol Hill staffers from using the application over data handling concerns, and user numbers had declined nearly 10 percent month-over-month.

Even so, ChatGPT was already well on its way to ubiquity, and a March update enabling the AI to comprehend and generate Python code in response to natural language queries only increased its utility.



---


# Imagine With Meta AI, Meta's Image Generator

Not to be outdone by Google's Gemini launch, Meta rolled out a new, stand-alone generative AI experience on the web in the week of 9 December 2023: Imagine with Meta AI, which allows users to create images by describing them in natural language.

Similar to OpenAI's DALL-E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion, Imagine with Meta AI creates high-resolution images from text prompts, and is powered by Meta's existing Emu image-generation model.



---


# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating.
