qid: Do the articles from The Roar | Sports Writers Blog discussing The All Blacks' actions in the Rugby World Cup final and their previous encounters with Argentina both present The All Blacks as having faced challenges in their gameplay, or do they portray different situations regarding The All Blacks' performance?
context:
# The All Blacks' Final Moments In The 2023 World Cup Final

New Zealand's last chance in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final died in the 80th minute when Ardie Savea forced a ball out wide just as the men in black saw space and looked to open up the Springboks — a killer blow, in The Roar's phrase.

The wider failing was handling. The All Blacks had their chances, but their usual safe handling — a feature throughout the World Cup after their first-up loss to France — evaded them against the Springboks' blitz defence in the wet conditions, and all night their timing was off.

The end came at a set piece. Wayne Barnes, who was booed relentlessly, called a scrum reset as the seconds ticked by; moments later New Zealand hearts sank as the Springboks won the scrum and then hung onto the ball.



---


# Foster Rejects The Favourites Label Against Argentina

Although the All Blacks were 18-point favourites for the opening 2023 World Cup semi-final, Ian Foster rejected the premise that his side sees itself that way: "Firstly, you've never heard us say we're favourites."

His grounds for rejecting the label are recent results and a limit on what the past predicts. Argentina had knocked over the All Blacks the previous year in Christchurch, as well as inflicting a maiden defeat in 2020 in Sydney, and New Zealand had themselves suffered a shock semi-final loss to Eddie Jones' England in 2019. Foster also argued that familiarity does not transfer to this stage: "The past sets us up beautifully for both teams. We do know each other but we don't know each other in terms of a Rugby World Cup, so at this stage in the tournament it's new territory for us and as we've seen World Cups are very different."

He then converted the rejection into a demand on his own team: "We have learnt to greatly respect Argentina. They have a rich history of overachieving at the World Cup and have done a fantastic job to get here at the same level we are, so it is going to be a heck of a game." And: "We know these games are do or die. We're going to have to improve our performance. The stage gets bigger at this time in the tournament and you've got to grow your game. That's our strong focus. The best team on the night wins – Argentina has done that to us."



---


# Joe Schmidt's Coaching Record With Ireland And The All Blacks

Joe Schmidt took Ireland to the top of World Rugby's rankings while his Irish sides bombed out in successive World Cup quarter-finals under his leadership, and he later helped transform an All Blacks team that reached the 2023 World Cup final, as reported by The Roar on 11 December 2023.

His Ireland tenure is credited with more than results: Schmidt played an instrumental role in not just seeing them become one of the world's best teams but helped usher through transformational change off the field, as Ireland moved to a centralised system.

The New Zealander briefly exited the international coaching scene following the 2019 World Cup, citing a desire to move home to New Zealand to be closer to his family. After initially moving back into the coaching fray with the Blues in Super Rugby, he joined the All Blacks ahead of the previous year's Rugby Championship, as New Zealand Rugby shook up the All Blacks coaching team following their historic series loss to Andy Farrell's Irish. His expertise proved telling: he and Jason Ryan transformed the All Blacks and helped Ian Foster's side reach the final of that year's World Cup after stunning wins over Ireland and Argentina in the knockout stages.



---


# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# Ireland: The Greatest Team Yet, Still Without A Knockout Win

This is the greatest Ireland team of all time, and may still even be the best team in the world — but on this day, the quarter-final curse, not to mention an inspired All Blacks side, ruled once more. The claim is that quality and knockout success have come apart: being the best team available is compatible with going out at the same stage as every Ireland side before them.

The consequence the argument draws is reputational. Instead of being feted as the heroes to finally overcome that insurmountable obstacle, the Ireland players will still have to answer endless questions about the heavy burden of previous knockout failures, and fans will endure at least four more years of choking jokes at their expense.



---


# Kieran Crowley Criticises The Italian Rugby Federation

Kieran Crowley pushed back on 6 October 2023 against the idea that Italy's World Cup should be judged on its two heavy defeats, arguing instead that the players deserve better treatment off the field from the Italian Rugby Federation — and that this, not the results, is the real problem.

His tenure ended in profound disappointment, though the crushing defeats by the All Blacks and now the hosts were offset by victories against Namibia and Uruguay. Crowley had wanted to continue: "I've said before, I'd like to take this team forward. I think the next World Cup is our cycle … we'll get to the next tournament, and a lot of these players will have 60, 70 caps. But that wasn't my decision."

The premise he attacks is that the last two games are a fair measure of the group. "What needs to happen is that these players need to be treated with a bit of respect off the field … They [the Italian Rugby Federation] need to get some of that stuff sorted. Quite honestly, I don't know if I'd want to be involved unless that gets sorted. I respect these guys, these players and staff. They've gone way beyond … and yet people will judge us on these last two games. It's disappointing."



---


# How England And South Africa Reached The 2023 Semi-Final

England arrived at the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final as the only side still competing that had yet to lose a game, while South Africa had already beaten two of the tournament favourites. Dominant wins over Argentina, Japan and Chile sealed England's passage to the last eight, and after being given an almighty scare by Samoa in their final pool match, they overcame a Fijian fightback in Marseille to triumph 30-24 — outscored by three tries to two, but carried by captain Owen Farrell's 20 points at the expense of 2023's breakout stars.

The Springboks had done it tough. Comfortable defeats of Scotland, Romania and Tonga could not mask the disappointment of a 13-8 loss to Ireland, which consigned South Africa to second in Pool B. With Ireland then sent home by the All Blacks in the quarters, the Bokke showed their World Cup mettle to edge hosts France 29-28 at the Stade de France, sneaking past Les Bleus in one of the best games of rugby you're ever likely to see.

Both journeys had twists, turns and bumps in the road but left each side within 80 minutes of a Rugby World Cup final. England would be looking to echo the spirit of 2019, when they beat the All Blacks 19-7 to reach the final, but in South Africa they faced a side who had taken their game to new heights just to reach the semis.



---


# England vs South Africa: 2023 Rugby World Cup Semi-Final

England faced defending champions South Africa in the Rugby World Cup semi-final in Paris from 8:00pm on 21 October 2023, having secured victory over Fiji in the quarter-finals, with talkSPORT carrying updates from all the action.

Victory would take England into their second consecutive Rugby World Cup final. Owen Farrell would be looking to inspire England to victory against the Springboks. The fixture formed one half of a double crunch point for England against South Africa on the same day, as they also met in the ODI Cricket World Cup — talkSPORT framed it as crunch time for England in the World Cups.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article reporting on the EU's investigation into X over alleged disinformation disagree with the TechCrunch article warning Elon Musk's X (formerly Twitter) about illegal content and disinformation in terms of the type of content being circulated, with both mentioning the circulation of false information and manipulated content?
context:
# The EU's Urgent Warning Letter To X

The European Union fired a public warning at Elon Musk-owned X (formerly Twitter) for failing to tackle illegal content circulating on the platform in the wake of Saturday's deadly attacks on Israel by Hamas terrorists based in the Gaza Strip — an "urgent" letter from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton that TechCrunch described as a very swift test of the bloc's newly updated content moderation rulebook. Breton shared the letter publicly, tweeting on October 10, 2023: "Following the terrorist attacks by Hamas against 🇮🇱, we have indications of X/Twitter being used to disseminate illegal content & disinformation in the EU. Urgent letter to @elonmusk on #DSA obligations". TechCrunch's later account places the letter on the Wednesday.

The letter's substance was twofold. Breton said the bloc had seen "indications" from "qualified sources" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded X of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted." Separately, the European Commission raised concerns about the spread of disinformation on X related to the terrorist attacks and their aftermath.

On the disinformation side Breton was specific about what had been reported and what he wanted done: "Public media and civil society organisations widely report instances of fake and manipulated images and facts circulating on your platform in the EU, such as repurposed old images of unrelated armed conflicts or military footage that actually originated from video games. This appears to be manifestly false or misleading information," he wrote. "I therefore invite you to urgently ensure that your systems are effective, and report on the crisis measures taken to my team."

TechCrunch's own characterisation of the platform at that moment was blunter than the letter's: rather than tackling the problem, it wrote, X "appears to be turning into an engine of disinformation" — one that had demonstrably enabled the very swift amplification of a smorgasbord of toxic fakes around the Israel-Hamas war, falsehoods that might be trying to manipulate opinion around the conflict, or otherwise exploit horrific events to drive engagement (clickbait) or for even more cynical and potentially harmful ends.



---


# X Found To Have The Worst Disinformation Ratio In EU Analysis

X, formerly Twitter, was called out in the European Union for having the worst ratio of disinformation and misinformation to posts not spreading falsehoods among mainstream social networks.

The finding came in a September 2023 speech by EU commissioner for values and transparency Vera Jourova, discussing the latest updates from platforms signed up to combat disinformation under a beefed-up EU Code of Practice linked to compliance with the bloc's legally binding Digital Services Act. X's poor performance was assessed during a pilot phase of testing of a new methodology developed by Code signatories. "A big novelty under the Code is now the publication of the first set of structural indicators such as how easy it is to find disinformation content, how much engagement such content receives or indicators about sources. These indicators — developed by the signatories — constitute an unprecedented and novel insight into disinformation on online platforms," she said. "Such insight is crucial to understand how effective platforms efforts are to fight this threat even more efficiently. This is a very valuable industry proposal that has great potential while it has to be still further developed. Here, signatories have decided to run a pilot phase in three Member States to evaluate the methodology on two of those indicators. X, former Twitter, who is not under the Code any more is the platform with the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts."

X was contacted for a response to the EU's analysis of the ratio of disinformation it is spreading, and replied with an automated email reading: "Busy now, please check back later." The finding fits a wider pattern: consistent moderation, fact-checking investment and researcher data access are areas where X under new owner Elon Musk has moved out of step with EU expectations on countering disinformation, suggesting that X — designated by the EU as a VLOP under the DSA back in April — continues to put itself squarely in the Commission's crosshairs, including over its priority issue of tackling Kremlin propaganda.



---


# The EU's First Formal DSA Proceeding, Against X

On 18 December 2023 the European Commission announced the opening of a "formal proceeding" against Elon Musk's X, making it the first confirmed investigation opened by the European Union under its rebooted digital rulebook, the Digital Services Act (DSA). The investigation will look at whether the social networking platform may have breached rules linked to risk management, content moderation, dark patterns, advertising transparency and data access for researchers.

The Commission set out the evidentiary basis for the step: "On the basis of the preliminary investigation conducted so far, including on the basis of an analysis of the risk assessment report submitted by X in September, X's Transparency report published on 3 November, and X's replies to a formal request for information, which, among others, concerned the dissemination of illegal content in the context of Hamas' terrorist attacks against Israel, the Commission has decided to open formal infringement proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act."

The EU added that "if proven, these failures would constitute infringements of Articles 34(1), 34(2) and 35(1), 16(5) and 16(6), 25(1), 39 and 40(12) of the DSA," and said it will now carry out an in-depth investigation "as a matter of priority." Internal market commissioner Thierry Breton announced the same day that the proceedings covered a suspected breach of obligations to counter illegal content and disinformation, a suspected breach of transparency obligations, and suspected deceptive design of the user interface.



---


# X As The Outlier Against Ofcom's Rules

X (formerly Twitter) is the one big outlier to Whitehead's generally encouraging read on industry cooperation, because its direction of travel runs against what the guidelines assume: Ofcom's guidelines specify that users should be able to easily block users, but Elon Musk has publicly stated his intentions to remove X's block feature.

The premise under attack is that the act's requirements can be met by platforms as they are currently evolving. The UK's efforts with the legislation long predate Musk's acquisition of Twitter, but it was passed as he fired large swaths of its trust and safety teams and presided over a loosening of moderation standards, which could put X at odds with regulators. Musk has clashed with the EU over similar rules and reportedly even considered pulling out of the European market to avoid them.

Ofcom would not be drawn on the specific case. Whitehead declined to comment when asked whether X had been cooperative in talks with Ofcom, but said the regulator had been "broadly encouraged" by the response from tech firms generally.



---


# X Post-Volume Discrepancy

X CEO Linda Yaccarino's post-volume figure contradicts Elon Musk's: speaking at an event in the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, she claimed X was seeing 500 million posts per day on the platform, whereas in September Musk had said X users were creating 100 million to 200 million posts every day, excluding retweets.

The contradiction attacks the reliability of the platform's own content-volume claims rather than any single argument built on them: two of X's most senior figures, weeks apart, gave figures that differ by a factor of roughly two to five. TechCrunch does not adjudicate between them, closing the item with "So who's right? Beats us." The item also does not state whether Yaccarino's 500 million figure excludes retweets, as Musk's explicitly did — so part of the gap may be definitional and part may not.



---


# The Contested Evidence On Social Media Harm

Buck records a reasonable counter-discussion about how many of our problems can really be laid at the feet of social media: the research on the impacts of social media on political dysfunction, mental health, and society writ large does not paint a neat portrait.

The objection attacks the causal premise rather than the description of the media ecology. Scholars have argued that putting too much emphasis on the platforms can be too simplistic and reeks of technological determinism, and have also pointed out that cultures like the United States' and the legacy media have a long history with post-truth.

That literature sits alongside a substantial body of work outlining the contours and dynamics of the current media ecology and what it does: Siva Vaidhyanathan's Antisocial Media, Safiya U. Noble's Algorithms of Oppression, Geert Lovink's Sad by Design, Shoshana Zuboff's Surveillance Capitalism, Richard Seymour's The Twittering Machine, Tim Hwang's Subprime Attention Crisis, Tressie McMillan Cottom's writing on how to understand the social relations of Internet technologies through racial capitalism, and many more. Buck's own position concedes the uncertainty without abandoning the concern: there are certainly dynamics going on that we did not anticipate, and we do not seem quite sure what to do with them, even with multiple areas of scholarship in communication, disinformation, and social media and democracy working on these inquiries for years.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article claim that Google's anticompetitive behavior specifically harms news publishers' revenue, while The Age article suggests a general acceptance of foul play by Google without specifying the impact on revenue?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."

qid: Who is the individual accused of using a colleague as a front for unauthorized access to customer funds, persuading a former coworker to join his trading and development ventures, and making an executive decision to use a substantial amount of customer money to settle with a competitor, all while facing allegations of committing fraud for personal gain, as reported by Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch?
context:
# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

qid: Was the policy on price matching for customers at HP inconsistent according to The Verge before Polygon reported on the ineligibility for price matching on purchases?
context:
# HP Price Match Policy

According to HP's website, the company will match the current pre-tax price for new comparable PCs and for identical HP printer, display, and accessory model numbers from nationally recognized online retailers such as Dell, Amazon, Newegg, and Best Buy. For computers the specs have to be the same, but the product model number does not need to be identical. The claim must be made at the time of purchase by calling 1-800-888-0229 — you cannot request a price match via email or chat.

The policy does not extend to items bought during promotional periods, and it does not apply to membership stores like Costco and Sam's Club.

There is a separate post-purchase route: if you find a comparable product at a lower price during the return period, you can email HP at myhpsales@hp.com. That applies only to branded HP products and not to products purchased during certain promotional events, including Green Monday and products on sale during the week of Thanksgiving and the week after. The Verge published this summary on October 25th, 2023, illustrating it with HP's Spectre x360 14.



---


# Holiday Price Matching Policies, 2023

Some major retailers ensured price protection on purchases during the 2023 holiday season, but the terms differ sharply by retailer, so whether you get price matching depends on where and when you shop.

Amazon does not price match, which Polygon calls annoying but tolerable since it often has the lowest prices of all retailers anyway; Amazon only protects the price on pre-orders carrying its "Pre-order Price Guarantee," which ensures you pay the lowest amount a product sells for before it launches. Best Buy not only matches prices from "qualified competitors" but says on its site that most products bought between the article's publication and December 30 can be price-matched through January 13, 2024. Walmart's policy says it will not price match with competitors, nor does it price match for products purchased online that later decrease in price. Target says purchases made between October 22 and December 24 can be price-adjusted if the cost falls within that span and you show proof of purchase; eligibility exists, but the rules for submitting documentation vary depending on whether you shop online or in store.



---


# Seller Complaints About Amazon's Fees And Pricing Policies

Many sellers have zeroed in on Amazon's pricing policies and rising fees as rightful areas of concern in the FTC's lawsuit.

Molson Hart, whose company Viahart sells toys on Amazon, has been a longtime critic of Amazon's pricing policies: he complained about how Amazon's seller fees impact pricing in a 2019 Medium post and later that year testified about his experience before a House committee. Hart said Amazon sales comprise about 90% of his business, meaning any hit those sales take on Amazon has a considerable impact. He recalled "24 anxious hours" in September 2022 when a third-party seller of his popular construction toy Brain Flakes listed the toy for a lower price on Target than it was offered on Amazon.



---


# Thanksgiving 2023 Retail Closure Policy

Because Thanksgiving Day is a federal holiday in the US, some stores shut down completely on the holiday — and for the two largest chains this is now a standing policy rather than a one-off: both Target and Walmart announced permanent closures on the holiday in 2020, with the policy remaining in place ever since.

The origin of that policy was the pandemic. The outbreak had initially pushed these chains to close their doors on Thanksgiving in order to limit crowding and spread out the shopping season.

The closure is not universal, and it is short. Not all grocery stores remain closed on Thanksgiving Day — there are some retailers that shoppers could visit on the morning of the holiday, in preparation for the annual feast — and once Thanksgiving Day comes to a close, many stores reopen on the Friday, operating during their earlier or usual business hours in preparation for some of the biggest sales of the year.



---


# Polygon's Weekend Deals Roundup, December 9 2023

Coming up for air from its coverage of The Game Awards, Polygon published its weekend deals roundup on 2023-12-09, pointing readers to discounts on a variety of 2023 Game Awards-winning titles on Steam.

Other highlights it flagged that weekend were a sitewide sale on Blu-Rays from The Criterion Collection, and the Xbox Series X matching its Black Friday price at Walmart and Amazon. Polygon notes the format is a standing one: as it does every weekend, it rounded up a collection of favourite deals from the worlds of gaming and entertainment, along with some of the best-selling products that had recently appeared on its site.



---


# Thanksgiving Observance Outside the United States

Thanksgiving is not observed only in America: while it is one of the most important cultural holidays in the United States, Canada also has its own Thanksgiving Day, held on the second Monday in October, and Liberia celebrates Thanksgiving on the first Thursday of November.

The distinguishing feature between these observances is therefore the date rather than the existence of the holiday — the American fourth-Thursday-in-November timing is one national convention among several.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Models And Pricing

Valve kept Steam Deck pricing the same as the original line while increasing storage at every tier, and set the Steam Deck OLED on sale from November 16, 2023 through the Steam storefront.

The three models are $649 for the 1 TB OLED, up from 512 GB at that price; $529 for the 512 GB OLED, up from 256 GB; and $399 for a 256 GB non-OLED Steam Deck, up from 64 GB. For a limited time the company also offered a special edition 1 TB Steam Deck OLED with a translucent shell for $679, sold only in the U.S. and Canada — a limited run Polygon's reviewer predicted would sell like hotcakes, prompting Valve to reconsider the definition of "limited supply." Polygon discloses that the hardware was reviewed with a unit provided by Valve, and that Vox Media has affiliate partnerships which do not influence editorial content though the company may earn commissions on products purchased via affiliate links.



---


# Discogs' 2023 Seller Fee Increase

Discogs raised its seller fee from 8 to 9 percent on May 22nd, 2023 and — crucially — started charging that same fee on shipping costs for the first time, which matters given how international the record market is. The Verge's reporter noted that one of the beauties of Discogs had previously been finding and purchasing rarities from sellers in Japan or Germany, citing his own most expensive purchase, a copy of Cannonball Adderley's debut album from a seller in Switzerland; the site now takes considerably larger slices of those kinds of sales. Discogs declined to comment for the story.

To make up for the lost revenue, Discogs suggested sellers use a tool it had created to raise the prices of all of their inventory by a percentage, and another Discogs email to sellers suggested they offer free shipping to avoid the fee — without accounting for the fact that the seller would then be either covering that cost out of pocket or integrating it into the price of the record, which would result in the same amount of money going to Discogs. Sellers were essentially told to raise their prices and/or offer free shipping, two options that threaten their bottom lines. "Their communication, too — it's like, 'I said what I said, and we're done,'" says Doug Martin. "Well, you're really not, because we all have to live with this and so do you."

The tension between Discogs' old-internet charm and its attempts at growth came to a head earlier in the summer around a since-deleted viral Twitter thread by artist and label head Mike Simonetti lamenting "the fall of discogs," which sounded the alarm about increasing fees and subsequently increasing prices, a growing influx of scammers, rising shipping costs, and the dysfunction of the website itself, among other issues. "We had kind of thought Discogs was on our side as sellers," says Gene Melkisethian, who runs Joint Custody, a record store in Washington, DC, and sells on Discogs. "But when they started charging fees on shipping, it just felt really punitive." The Connecticut seller put it more bluntly: "In their communication, it was beyond insulting the way they framed it. Like, 'Oh, you can just not charge for shipping.' The sudden fee increase was a huge, huge blow to a lot of people."



---


# NFL Thanksgiving Day Games 2023 Viewership

The NFL's Thanksgiving Day games in the 2023 season made history, Essentially Sports reported on Dec. 25, 2023: across all three games the NFL recorded an average viewership of 34.1 million, surpassing the previous year's record of 33.6 million.

Furthermore, the combined unduplicated audience for all three games reached 133 million, marking the second-highest total audience on Thanksgiving, surpassed only by the previous year's numbers. Despite the impressive viewership numbers of the NBA's Christmas Day games, the NFL's Thanksgiving figures eclipse them by a considerable margin.



---


# Kia EV9 Reservations

Kia has started taking reservations for its EV9 full-sized SUV, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22. Reservations are $750 and can be applied to the purchase of the company.

This is one of the first vehicles Kia has allowed customers to reserve in advance.

qid: After the report by Business Today | Latest Stock Market And Economy News India on October 7, 2023, regarding a surprise attack on Israel, and the subsequent report by Fortune on October 13, 2023, concerning the blockade of Gaza and the warning issued to residents, is the sequence of events reported by both news sources regarding Israel's security and humanitarian situation consistent?
context:
# Hamas October 7 2023 Surprise Attack on Israel

On 7 October 2023, Hamas carried out what Business Today described as the biggest coordinated attack in Israel, capturing some territory in southern Israel and taking control of some military bases and soldiers.

The reaction the report documents was directed at Israel's famed intelligence agency, Mossad, which is known for its intelligence-gathering capability. For some observers, the belief that Mossad was among the best in the spying world was shattered that day. The report is explicit that it was not the fact of an attack that surprised people, but the scale at which Hamas operated.



---


# Israel-Hamas War Context, October 2023

As of TechCrunch's 2023-10-14 report, Israel is retaliating militarily against the attacks on its people, on its soil, and the hostages subsequently taken by Hamas — the ruling organization in Gaza that kidnapped at least 150 people and took them into Gaza during brutal attacks on Israel last weekend that killed 1,300 people. That strategy has seen Israel pummeling the "Gaza Strip" with bombs to eradicate it of Hamas and to get its hostages back, and over 1,500 people in Palestine so far have been killed as a result.

The tech industry in Israel — the country's biggest export and its biggest single contributor to GDP — is also taking a big knock, but inevitably the impact on the smaller and more fragile ecosystem in Gaza has been significantly more serious, and the physical, economic and societal destruction resulting from that leaves any future for the tech industry there in doubt: quite simply, there is no escaping the consequences of the war for anyone, let alone tech workers. Israel has now amassed soldiers near the north of Gaza ahead of an expected ground offensive into the densely populated enclave, and about 1.1 million people living in northern areas have been told to leave in the next day. The UN has warned of "devastating humanitarian consequences" from these latest moves, and a total blockade on the territory is being enforced with fuel, food and water running out; Israel says it won't lift the restrictions unless Hamas frees all hostages. TechCrunch notes the piece was later edited to include relevant information about the attacks by Hamas.



---


# The October 2023 Cutoff Of Supplies To Gaza

Israel stopped allowing deliveries of food, fuel and other supplies to Gaza's 2.3 million residents on Oct. 10, 2023, and was reportedly preparing for a ground invasion; on Oct. 12, 2023 it warned 1.1 million Gaza residents in the northern section of the enclave to leave for the southern region in advance of that potential invasion. International aid groups warned that they could not deliver food and other basic services to people in the Gaza Strip and that a "dire" humanitarian crisis was set to worsen. Those groups provide food and other means of support to about 63% of people in Gaza.

What changed in October is the scope of the restriction rather than its existence. International aid groups now face the same problem in Gaza that local businesses and residents have encountered for about 16 years: a blockade that prevents civilians and items, like medicine, from easily moving into or out of the enclosed area, roughly 25 miles long. That 16-year blockade did not apply to the food and fuel that groups brought into Gaza. Now it does.



---


# Egypt's Strategic Value To Europe: Gas And Security

The war "underscores the important role Egypt has always played vis-a-vis security in and around Gaza," said Robert Satloff, executive director at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy — a role that is not lost on European governments.

Those governments woke up to Egypt's importance as a regional gas producer after Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. European officials visited to assess Egypt's potential as a gas supplier — with Israel's help — to supplant at least some Russian supplies.



---


# Easing Escalation Concerns Around Israel-Gaza In Late October 2023

Concerns about the conflict spreading more broadly have eased amid growing calls within Israel to rethink a ground invasion of Gaza, because of fears about the fate of some 200 hostages held there, the danger of retaliation by Hezbollah and the risk of Israeli military casualties.

The same 2023-10-24 wrap carried the quote of the day from Magellan chairman Andrew Formica, speaking as the group's chief executive stepped down abruptly amid the company's efforts to turn around its performance: "I think when you get to those decisions, you can then sit on them for a while… or you can say let's just deal with it [and] that's what we have done today."



---


# Disinformation On X After The Hamas Attacks On Israel

In the days after Saturday's Hamas attacks on Israel, posts identified as false circulated widely on X, including footage repurposed from a video game and clips entirely unrelated to the conflict. TechCrunch reported the pattern in two articles, on 10 and 13 October 2023, drawing on fact-checkers, public media, civil society organisations and X's own safety account.

The observed content fell into several kinds. Graphic videos apparently showing terrorist attacks on civilians circulated on X from Saturday onward. Alongside them were posts purporting to show footage from the attacks inside Israel, or from Israel's subsequent retaliation on targets in the Gaza Strip, which fact-checkers identified as false. A number of videos posted since the attacks were identified as entirely unrelated to the conflict — including footage filmed the previous month in Egypt, and a clip from the video game Arma 3 posted with the false claim that it showed Hamas missile attacks on Israel. Shayan Sardarizadeh (@Shayan86) flagged the Arma 3 clip on October 9, 2023: "This video certainly doesn't show a new air assault on Israel by Hamas militants, because it's actually from the video game Arma 3."

The volume was substantial. In remarks via X's safety account, the company reported more than 50 million posts globally over the past two days that referenced the weekend's terrorist attack, underlining the scope of content generated.

Two conditions shaped the environment. First, the attacks themselves: Hamas militants inside Gaza got past border fences and mounted a series of surprise attacks on Israeli civilians and tourists, after which Israel's prime minister declared "we are at war" and its military retaliated by firing scores of missiles into the Gaza Strip. By Thursday afternoon, per TechCrunch's 13 October report, Hamas' attack had killed more than 1,200 people according to the Israeli Military, and at least 1,537 people had been killed in Gaza by Israel's retaliatory strikes according to the Gaza Ministry of Health. Second, amplification on the platform itself: Eliot Higgins (@EliotHiggins) wrote on October 10, 2023 that "a totally false claim about Israel bombing a church in Gaza" had gone viral "thanks to multiple blue tick accounts repeating an unverified claim that had no evidence to back it up", adding that "Musk has created a fundamental issue with Twitter's credibility in moments of crisis."

X's owner was himself part of the observed pattern: at one point Musk recommended that people follow accounts that had posted antisemitic comments and false information in the past, though he subsequently deleted the tweet in which he made the suggestion. A Wired report published the day before TechCrunch's 10 October article summed up the situation on the platform under the headline "The Israel-Hamas War Is Drowning X in Disinformation."



---


# The Gaza Conflict's Information Environment, Late 2023

Israel has retaliated against Hamas' October 7 attack with unprecedented force against the Palestinian territory, claiming over 9,000 Palestinian lives according to Gaza Health Ministry numbers reported by the Associated Press, as of November 3, 2023.

Reporting capacity in the territory has been degraded on two fronts. The Committee to Protect Journalists reports that at least 30 journalists have been killed since Israel's bombardment and total blockade of the region began, and journalists in Gaza say that without consistent access to food, water and power it is becoming "impossible" to continue reporting.

At the same time, misinformation about the escalating violence is rampant on social media — so the shortfall in professional reporting coincides with an unreliable information supply.



---


# Hostile Interview Questions Put To Israeli Spokespeople

Asked whether he is asked many questions that smack of antisemitism or a lack of understanding and support for Israel's position, Eylon Levy answers "how long have you got" and lists examples from his interviews. The BBC asked him in a radio interview whether there is CCTV evidence that the hostages are in Shifa Hospital and what medical treatment they were receiving. Sky News asked why Yahya Sinwar was releasing hostages even though Israel is bombing Gaza, and he had to explain that it was because Israel is bombing Gaza.

He was asked twice, in Ireland and by the Voice of America, why Hamas had been begging for five weeks to return hostages and Israel was only now bowing to US pressure to take back its children. He was also interviewed by Piers Morgan in London, whom he describes as very confrontational, who spoke about pictures from Gaza and said "this is the most shocking thing I have ever seen"; Levy told him that "the most shocking thing we have seen in our lives was the slaughter on October 7", and Morgan answered "you are right".

qid: Which company spent $26.3 billion to ensure its position as the default search engine, while being accused of manipulating search results to maximize ad revenue and siphoning off content and ad revenue from news publishers, as reported by TechCrunch and The Age?
context:
# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." # Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).
