Engadget says there are frankly too many deals to list them all, but highlights for PlayStation and Xbox owners include Assassin's Creed Mirage and the dramatic action-RPG Final Fantasy XVI for $40 each, God of War Ragnarök for $35, Gran Turismo 7 for $30, the rhythm action game Hi-Fi Rush for $22, Marvel's Spider-Man: Miles Morales and Horizon Forbidden West for $20 each, and Halo: The Master Chief Collection for $10 — many of which make Engadget's lists of the best PS5 games and best Xbox games. On the Switch side, the turn-based strategy game Mario + Rabbids Sparks of Hope was on sale for $15, Xenoblade Chronicles 3 and Luigi's Mansion 3 were each down to $40, and the excellent 2D platformer Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze was down to a new low of $30, with plenty more games on sale beyond those and more PC game deals expected over the course of the week.



---


# Roblox's PlayStation And Cross-Platform Expansion

At Roblox's annual developer conference in San Francisco two weeks before the Code Conference interview published on October 12th, 2023, the biggest crowd reaction in the opening keynote was for PlayStation support. Asked what took so long, CEO David Baszucki said the company had put enormous focus on mobile quality over the last couple of years because mobile is its hugest market: Roblox started as a PC product, went to Mac, and always held the vision of connecting people around the world on every platform. With mobile in really good shape and Xbox in good shape, it started rolling out new platforms. The creator community loves PlayStation because all of their existing creations will work there, so for creators making a living and building new businesses it is an immediate expansion of their business.

Asked whether anything was unique about PlayStation from an economics or business partnership perspective, or whether the delay was all technical, Baszucki said nothing too unique: every platform has been very thoughtful about when to start allowing social cross-platform everywhere, and five or 10 years ago, when Roblox started this notion, Xbox and PlayStation were arguably a little more walled garden-ish. The vision of connecting and communicating in a 3D space no matter where you are, with the best user interface, the best camera, and the best motion — whether on a phone or a console — has, he said, really come to bear right now.

# Mario + Rabbids Kingdom Battle

Mario + Rabbids Kingdom Battle is a silly collaboration between Nintendo and Ubisoft that became one of the sleeper hits of its release year. It appears in Polygon's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

The squad tactics game pairs Mario and friends with their own doppelganger Rabbids against a veritable sea of evil Rabbids.

Polygon flags a scope limit on the co-op: local play is limited to five specific challenges, so the outlet would not recommend buying the game specifically for co-op alone — but those levels are especially fun, since working together changes the tactical dynamics.



---


# Lil Gator Game

Lil Gator Game, developed by MegaWobble for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X, is ranked 35 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31.

Critic Chris Grant acknowledges that in an unprecedented year for game releases, readers may be surprised to see it this high on the list — and says he was just as surprised to find, in a moment of introspection, that it was one of his own favorite games of 2023.

At the risk of diminishing its accomplishments, he offers a comparison that should cut to the quick for interested parties: this is the most A Short Hike-alike he has discovered yet, a singular high he has been chasing for years. His recommendation is for a lazy weekend afternoon spent playing — not gaming, but playing, in the joyous, unstructured sense of a day in the park.



---


# Amazon Prime Free Games And DLC

Amazon offers freebies for Prime members round the calendar year, not just during the holiday months, and Polygon reports that Amazon's suite of giveaways has improved over time.

The catalog is not fixed: offerings expire over time and new ones are added. As a sample of what was up for grabs as of the article's November 2023 publication, Polygon named Rage 2, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and Doom 3, and said it collects the latest free games and DLC on an ongoing page.



---


# Console Subscription And Store Gift Cards For Gamers

If you're not sure which type of games your giftee prefers, The Verge suggests an Xbox, PlayStation, or Nintendo subscription: these memberships grant access to free digital titles and come with perks such as online multiplayer and cloud-based saves.

For a PlayStation 4 or PlayStation 5 owner, PlayStation Plus grants access to free titles and discounts every month, online play, and cloud-based backups; memberships start at $9.99 a month, and you can subscribe directly via PlayStation or buy a three-month subscription with a PlayStation Plus gift card, available at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target for $30. Nintendo Switch lovers might enjoy an annual Nintendo Switch Online subscription starting at $19.99 a year (Amazon, Best Buy, and GameStop), which lets them play more than 70 retro games from the NES, SNES, and original Game Boy eras, play online with friends, and use cloud saves. Spending more buys the annual Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack, which adds Game Boy Advance, Sega Genesis, and Nintendo 64 games plus DLC content for some titles: individual plans cost $49.99 (Amazon, Walmart), while a family plan covering up to eight accounts is currently available via gift card at Amazon and Walmart for $71.89, $8 off. Alternatively, a gift card to a store like GameStop (Amazon, GameStop) is useful if you don't know which console your giftee prefers or want to give them the option of buying accessories and games.



---


# Classic Nintendo Franchise Picks For The Switch

Polygon's advice for a first-time Switch owner is to start with the modern-day Zelda, Mario, and Animal Crossing games, on the grounds that Nintendo is home to some of the most iconic gaming franchises.

The selection is explicitly a narrowing: it is hard to pick just a handful from this wealth of options, to say nothing of other iconic Nintendo series, so Polygon says it has narrowed the field to some of the platform's absolute best.



---


# Roblox As An Online Game Platform

Roblox is a widely popular online game platform that "lets you play, create, and be anything you can imagine," according to its description on the Microsoft Store. Its defining features are that players customise characters and play minigames within the game, and that while the platform is free to download on a number of platforms — including Android and iOS smartphones, Xbox game consoles and Windows computers — players can also spend money on in-game items and customisations.

Its user base is young. According to TechCrunch, Roblox's millions of users range between the ages of eight and 18, with its key demographic between nine and 15 years old — the fact that makes parental controls and spending safeguards the recurring point of contention around the platform.

# The Surprise Vampire Trope

The surprise vampire is a story that is not a vampire story but that turns out to have vampires in it — a device Polygon rates cooler than a vampire story proper.

It is a rich tradition, unfolding across many different media intended for all kinds of audiences. Sometimes the surprise vampire is a prominent part of a story that is made richer for the unexpected presence of a bloodsucker. Sometimes it is subtle, an easily missable detail that rewards only the most observant. In the best version, Polygon says, the vampires are always there, in the background, waiting for you to discover them — just like in real life.

# Season of Blood's Real Draw Is Quality of Life, Not Vampire Powers

Polygon's claim, published 2023-10-04, is that although Diablo 4's Season of Blood brings some cool new vampire powers into the fold, the real star of the second season is its sweeping quality-of-life changes.

The grounds are what those changes do for ordinary play: players will now have an easier time leveling up, gaining quality loot, and just navigating the open world of Sanctuary.

The warrant is that these improvements touch the activities every player performs constantly, which is why they outweigh a headline feature. The reporting basis is a roundtable interview game director Joe Shely and associate game director Joe Piepiora gave to Polygon and other outlets ahead of Blizzard's Oct. 4 livestream, in which they gave additional context on Nightmare Dungeon changes, Renown, and more.

# Laurell K. Hamilton: Vampire Verdict

Polygon's verdict on Laurell K. Hamilton, author of the Anita Blake: Vampire Hunter series (1993-present), is: not a vampire.

Her books are described as the final evolution of an undead Pokémon. Where Anne Rice made vampires sexy but still took pains to remind readers they were fundamentally the stuff of nightmares, Hamilton's Anita Blake series is more like the merrily obscene aesthetic of a 1970s grindhouse flick: her characters bash, slaughter, and jump one another's bones, animated or otherwise, but it is all in good fun, so the sexy and violent vampire has reached a Looney Tunes stage of madcap romp that audiences cannot get enough of. That is exactly why Polygon acquits her. Nothing serves the vampire cause less than undermining the air of looming menace vampires have been cultivating since the 15th century — Vlad the Impaler worked for that nickname, and the last thing they need is an airport novel making a stake through the heart look fun. So Hamilton is not among the denizens of the undead; she is the one thing they have come to fear this millennium: a good punchline.

# Diablo 4 Season 2 Vampiric Powers

Season 2 of Diablo 4 adds Vampiric Powers, which allow players to slot five additional abilities into their character to gain new effects.

There are 22 total Vampiric Powers.

Each is class agnostic, meaning no power is unique to any one class. Polygon states this identically in both its Sorcerer build guide of 2023-10-18 and its Barbarian build guide of 2023-10-19.



---


# Vampire Survivors

Vampire Survivors is a deceptively simple roguelike bullet-hell in which players min-max various buffs to avoid waves of mob attacks, and Polygon's writer says they have donated hours and hours of their life to it. It appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Multiplayer changes everything: having more reinforcements to fight waves of attacks means each player can try out unique combinations of weapons and buffs.

The constraint to plan around is that you and your teammates must stay on the same screen, because there is no split screen.



---


# Dracula 2000 (Dimension Films)

Dracula 2000 is Patrick Lussier's turn-of-the-millennium vampire film starring Gerard Butler, and Polygon argues that with the scars of nu-metal healed and Olivia Rodrigo's Paramore-infused pop tracks having gone full "vampire," now is the time to give Butler's half-bare-chest take on Dracula the respect it is due. It was the Oct. 6 pick in the 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Max.

Called maybe the most Dimension Films movie to ever bear the Dimension Films studio logo — with The Faculty a close second — the film follows a group of thieves, including of-the-moment faces like Omar Epps, Jennifer Esposito, and Shane West, transporting a stolen silver coffin from London to New Orleans in the belief there is treasure inside. When they find Dracula instead, they unleash overacted, canted-angled, seven-string-guitar-plucking hell. As Dracula hunts down local college student Mary Van Helsing, played by Justine Waddell, with whom he already shares a psychic connection, Mary's dad's new vampire-hunter assistant Simon, played by a young Jonny Lee Miller, is on his tail.

Critic Matt Patches writes that Butler, never more a heartthrob, plays Dracula in a mesmerizing, baroque manner — think Nicolas Cage doing Dracula if this year's Renfield was emo turn-of-the-millennium trash — and constantly bites unsuspecting B-list actors to add to his army of hot people, who fight the heroes in multiple obligatory scenes of wire-fu. Lussier cuts it all up like it is the video for "Freak on a Leash," which makes it objectively quite unlike most horror movies available today; enjoyment may vary depending on tolerance for Hot Topic goofs, but without it you cannot enjoy Lussier's sequel Dracula II: Ascension, starring Jason Scott Lee as a martial-arts-fighting priest.



---


# Author Endorsements In Book Publishing

Book blurbs have become a central part of the publishing industry, on the reasoning that there is no better endorser of a book than other authors and thought leaders. The distinguishing feature of the form is therefore the identity of the recommender: an endorsement carries weight because it comes from someone who writes or thinks professionally in the field.

TechCrunch applied that same spirit editorially for the 2023 holiday season, asking several writers to recommend books that its readers may want to gift.



---


# Let The Right One In: A Kaleidoscopic Swedish Vampire Friendship

Let the Right One In, directed by Tomas Alfredson and starring Kåre Hedebrant, Lina Leandersson and Per Ragnar, is available on Hulu, Prime Video, Roku Channel, Crackle, Hoopla and Kanopy. A 12-year-old Swedish boy finds a friend in a vampire who looks roughly his age but is actually an old vampire permanently trapped in the body of a young child.

The defining quality Polygon's reviewer identifies is that the film is kaleidoscopic, each viewing revealing something different than the last. He offers his own readings as evidence: the first time he saw it, as a pessimistic college student, he read the central relationship as a warning about the parasitic nature of love; after college, the children's bond reminded him of the impermanence of youth and why growing up is a mixed blessing; this past year he was far more focused on the girl's relationship with her caretaker, an older man who sacrifices everything for her existence.

The film was adapted from John Ajvide Lindqvist's 2004 novel of the same name, which inspired not just this Swedish film but a 2010 American adaptation, a comic-book prequel, and two stage plays. The plays have their own legacy — one was adapted by the National Theater of Scotland and eventually had a run at St. Ann's Warehouse in 2015 — which leads the reviewer to say he is recommending the book just as much as the film.



---


# Custom Character Versus Origin Character In Baldur's Gate 3

An Origin character in Baldur's Gate 3 is one of the NPCs from your party that you can simply choose and play as right from the start, whereas a custom character is one you build yourself by picking a race and background.

The discriminating feature is the trade between setup effort and narrative freedom. Playing an Origin character is a perfectly fine way to play if you would rather not go through the process of picking a race and background, but you are then limited to that character's predetermined story. A custom character is a bit more work at the beginning, yet gives you far more freedom to experience the entire story of Baldur's Gate 3. Polygon presents this as the decision to settle before moving on to the class rankings themselves.



---


# Polygon's Weekend Streaming Roundup, November 3 2023

Polygon's new-releases roundup for the weekend of 2023-11-03 named Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, then streaming on Netflix, as the week's biggest debut.

Netflix also took Insidious: The Red Door, the fifth installment in the Insidious horror franchise, and Jawan, one of the biggest Indian action movies of the year. Elsewhere, A Haunting in Venice arrived on Hulu, the Italian superhero movie Freaks vs. the Reich landed on Prime Video, and The Kill Room and Outlaw Johnny Black, from director-star Michael Jai White, premiered on VOD.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

qid: Who is the individual facing a criminal trial as reported by TechCrunch, persuaded a former colleague from Jane Street to join his ventures as noted by Fortune, communicated his intentions regarding FTX's governance structure to Paradigm according to Cnbc | World Business News Leader, and is accused by the prosecution of committing fraud for personal gain as covered by TechCrunch?
context:
# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."

Speculation that Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift were dating began in July 2023, when Kelce confessed that he had tried and failed to give Swift a friendship bracelet bearing his phone number at one of her Eras Tour concerts; he later invited her on his podcast to one of his games at Arrowhead Stadium, an invitation she famously accepted on 24 September 2023, and she had attended three more of his games by 25 November 2023.

In August 2023 Travis Kelce hinted on the New Heights podcast that Taylor Swift would like his moustache — a clear suggestion he had made contact with her — and shortly afterwards took a week off training to visit New York City while Swift was re-recording her 1989 tracks there, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

The counter-position to the Swift-Kelce media wave attacks its premise that the story is genuine and welcome, and it comes from within the fanbase and from commentators. Travis Kelce, 34, made remarks about starting a family during a February 2023 episode of New Heights, the podcast he hosts with his brother Jason, that resurfaced in October 2023 amid his romance with Taylor Swift — after a source claimed to Yahoo Entertainment that the couple "have talked about kids" within the next year.
