# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The M3 MacBook Pro Lineup And Its Configurations](m3_macbook_pro_lineup_and_configurations.md)
- [Counterarguments On Uber's Assault Rate And Duty Of Care](surveillance_privacy_tradeoff.md)



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Platform Owners Should Treat Developers As Partners

Tim Sweeney argued that any tech company, Apple and Google included, would be much better off in the long term if it viewed developers as awesome partners and did everything it could to support and empower them rather than get in their way financially — and said the opposite behavior at Apple and Google is what has disappointed him most.

His grounds are a comparison and a diagnosis. The comparison is Microsoft: even at the peak of the antitrust trial against Microsoft, he said, Microsoft was awesome to developers — always respectful, giving developers a great deal and treating them as partners — so that even as Microsoft was crushing corporate competitors, the developer experience was excellent. The Verge appended an editor's note that Netscape might feel differently. The diagnosis is that Google and Apple both treat developers as adversaries, trying to attack developer revenue streams and prevent them from competing with the platforms' own products, and have built massive self-preferencing schemes around excluding developers and disadvantaging third parties — which Sweeney calls very shortsighted. The warrant is that a platform's own long-term position improves when its developers thrive, and Sweeney offers Epic's own conduct as the demonstration: this has been Epic's philosophy with Unreal Engine and the Epic Games Store, where Epic wants to be "a cool partner that helps other companies succeed the way we do." He suspected such a philosophy change at Apple and Google may only come with a generational change in the companies' management.



---


# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

# The 2023-24 MLB Offseason Market After The Winter Meetings

As of Sporting News' Dec. 23, 2023 free agency tracker, the 2023-24 MLB offseason was a market whose two biggest names were already settled but whose bulk was still unresolved: Shohei Ohtani and Juan Soto had already found new homes, while much of the offseason had yet to play out.

The defining features of the remaining market were a marquee international free agent, a set of unsigned veterans, and a trade market waiting on them. Japanese pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto was the focus of many teams as he prepared to sign a massive deal, while Blake Snell, Cody Bellinger and Jordan Montgomery remained on the market. The trade market was also expected to be active once more dominoes fell, with Dylan Cease, Corbin Burnes and Tyler Glasnow among the starters who could be moved that winter. The boundary condition on the calendar was that the Winter Meetings were over, but because of the timeline of the major decisions by Ohtani and Yamamoto, there could be a flurry of activity leading up to the end of the year.



---


# NASCAR 2024 Offseason Preparation Window

The NASCAR offseason, as characterized by CBSSports.com on Dec. 7, 2023, is the wintertime respite from what is otherwise a demanding, year-long grind of racing — welcome but very short, and decisive out of proportion to its length.

What distinguishes it is what gets settled in it: come 2024 the grind would soon begin again, and exactly what it looked like would be based in large part on these months, when driver lineups, crew lineups and rules packages are set. With much activity going on within the confines of race shops across NASCAR, the piece rounded up the major storylines for the week of Dec. 4 as the offseason continued.



---


# MLB 2023-24 Offseason Trade Market Landscape

As of Yardbarker's Nov. 13, 2023 rundown of the top 25 MLB offseason trade candidates, trade season had not yet arrived: the offseason had gotten rolling, but the Tigers' acquisition of Mark Canha from Milwaukee was the biggest swap of the first couple of weeks, and the GM Meetings simply served to set the stage for future transactions.

Notable trades were surely coming, but unlike at the summer deadline, projecting which players would change hands was difficult at that stage of the offseason. Aside from the A's, no team was clearly in rebuild mode; clubs like the Rockies, Royals, White Sox, Nationals and Angels faced uphill paths to contention, yet none had indicated it was prepared to punt on the 2024 season entirely. The Padres, Twins, Rays, Brewers and Guardians were all aiming to contend but had questions about their payroll — standard operating procedure for Tampa Bay, Milwaukee and Cleveland, while San Diego and, to a lesser extent, Minnesota had shown a willingness to spend in recent years but were scaling back, in both cases likely tied to their uncertain local television rights contracts.

That informed a trade landscape headlined by a few stars deep into their arbitration windows. Without many clear rebuilders, it was possible the winter would see more swaps of big leaguers at positions of need between teams that expected to compete.



---


# What The MLB Winter Meetings Are And Why The 2023 Edition Mattered

MLB's winter meetings are the window in which many of the top executives, players and agents all come together at the same spot, which makes them always a prime time for moves to happen, per Sporting News' 2023 tracker published Dec. 3, 2023.

The discriminating feature is the concentration of decision-makers and the chain reactions it produces. The previous year's winter meetings wound up being explosive: Aaron Judge, Justin Verlander, Trea Turner and Xander Bogaerts all came away with new contracts. The 2023 edition could wind up being similarly busy — there was a growing sense Shohei Ohtani could sign during the winter meetings, and a move of that magnitude could kick off the next wave of moves; there was also a number of top players on the trade market, including star Padres outfielder Juan Soto.

The 2023 meetings ran starting Sunday, Dec. 3 through Wednesday, Dec. 6, and were held in Nashville, with MLB's offseason expected to really kick into high gear over that span. Sporting News tracked all the latest news and rumors, following any signings and trades from Nashville.



---


# An Early Ohtani Signing Would Reshape The Offseason

Reporting from Alden Gonzalez of ESPN on Nov. 11, 2023 raised the possibility that Shohei Ohtani could sign before the Winter Meetings, and Sporting News argued that pretty much everyone in baseball would love that to happen — because an early resolution benefits both the signing team and every other club.

For the signing team, the gains are commercial and competitive: it will kick the Ohtani hype machine into gear as soon as possible, with merchandise to sell, and the front office will use the signing to help lure other potential free agents, maybe even for a "play with Ohtani" discount. For the other teams, the warrant is opportunity cost — knowing Ohtani is off the board relatively soon into the offseason would allow them to shift to other priorities, like trading for Juan Soto or deciding which free-agent pitchers to pursue with the money that might otherwise have been earmarked for Ohtani.



---


# The Toronto Reports And Denials Of Dec. 8, 2023

On Friday, Dec. 8, 2023, a cascade of conflicting reports had Ohtani picking the Blue Jays and flying to Toronto, only for other reporters to place him at his home in Southern California with no decision made.

The sequence began with Dodgers Nation's J.P. Hoornstra reporting that Ohtani had selected the Blue Jays, who had reportedly won the sweepstakes; official details were not reported, though the report indicated the deal would shatter Mike Trout's record 12-year, $426.5 million contract. Sportsnet's Ben Nicholson-Smith countered that Ohtani had not yet made his decision and that there was no timeline, while noting Toronto was a finalist. MLB Network's Jon Morosi then reported that Ohtani, while not having officially picked a team, was headed to Toronto, after previous reports that he had picked the Blue Jays had since been denied. Hours after Morosi's report that the two-way star was headed to Toronto for a Friday meeting, USA Today's Nightengale and Sportsnet's Nicholson-Smith reported that Ohtani was at his home in Southern California; the Blue Jays remained finalists but his landing spot was not official. Morosi also reported that Ohtani was expected to make his decision soon, possibly as early as that Friday — coincidentally, Ohtani had made his original decision to sign with the Angels on Dec. 8, 2017, six years to the day.



---


# The Angels' 2023 Offseason: Ohtani And Trout Availability

The Los Angeles Angels faced the impending exit of their star two-way player Shohei Ohtani after a heartbreaking 2023 season, and were also open to trading nine-time Silver Slugger hitter Mike Trout should he request it, as reported by Essentially Sports on 18 November 2023.

The report frames this as a huge miss: a team that couldn't do well even with two of the league's biggest talents on its roster may lose those stars at the same time, leaving open the question of whether they will choose to stay in Los Angeles.

It also sets up the Dodgers angle. The Halos' cross-town rivals, the Los Angeles Dodgers, have been eyeing the dynamic Troutani duo for a long time; however, despite fans' expectations, the Dodgers' Ohtani-Trout conquest might not take place — and for good reasons.



---


# MLB Props And Futures: World Series, MVP, Home Run Leader And Win Totals

MLB props and futures let you bet on team and player performance irrespective of individual game outcomes. Popular examples include the World Series, where you bet on which team will become the next champion — futures odds appear nearly as soon as the previous World Series ends and change based on offseason moves, team news, team performance and more.

The other named markets are MVP, where you wager on the player you believe will take home the Most Valuable Player award for the season, described as a fun way to keep tabs on certain players all year; home run leader, on which player will crank out the most homers during the regular season; and regular-season win totals, an over/under wager on whether a team will finish over or under the number of wins a sportsbook sets for them.

Every sportsbook offers its own selection of futures and props bets, so shop around to find the books that best fit your needs.

# The Zincophilic and Iodophilic Hydrogel Mechanism

The anode and cathode sides of the hydrogel carry different functional groups that make it zincophilic (with an affinity for zinc) and iodophilic (with an affinity for iodine) respectively, and this asymmetry is what lets one electrolyte fix problems at both electrodes.

On the anode side, the design repels dissolved polyiodides — negatively charged ions composed entirely of iodine atoms — allowing the zinc to be deposited uniformly and protecting the anode from iodine-caused corrosion. Ensuring that zinc accumulates evenly on the anode side is the purpose of the hydrogel modification, Hongjin Fan explained, and it mitigates the diffusion back and forth of polysulfide between anode and cathode, the so-called "shuttle effect," which can cause poor cycling stability and severe anode corrosion in batteries. On the cathode side, the polyiodides are immobilized, and redox reactions — in which iodine is both stripped of electrons (oxidation) and granted electrons (reduction) — are sped up thanks to the synchronized rapid transport of ions and electrons, so the hydrogel electrolyte also accelerates the iodine conversion reaction. Finally, the solid nature of the hydrogel electrolyte limits the growth of dendrites through its mechanical strength, acting as a physical barrier not present in liquid electrolytes.



---


# Record Salt Loading Hydrogel Results

The gels soaked up more and more saltwater over time, and the top absorber got about three times saltier than previous hydrogels, caching 20 grams (0.7 ounce) of salt per gram of gel — and it absorbed more moisture than previous gels too.

To test moisture uptake, the researchers dried their gels and placed them in environments with different levels of humidity; even in relatively dry air, such as that found in deserts, the best-performing hydrogel absorbed 15 percent more water than previous hydrogels. The team reported its findings on May 18 in Advanced Materials. "We did this in a very simple and low-cost way, which makes it even more exciting," says Díaz-Marín, whose team still needs to test how to get all that water out of the gels afterward. "I am impressed by their results," says Swee Ching Tan, a materials scientist at the National University of Singapore who works with hydrogels but did not take part in the study. "This could be a new world record." The new work, he says, could help with the water crisis by producing safe drinking water in places that lack it.



---


# Practical Limitations of MXene Carbon Capture

Against the enthusiasm for MXenes as carbon absorbers, the article notes that because they are still fairly new, MXenes today are only used in research, and scientists have to iron out several kinks before they will be ready for real-world use — which will take several years at least.

The specific weaknesses attack different premises of the case. Chemically, MXenes can break down and transform into other solids called oxides in the presence of oxygen, so water and oxygen make MXenes less reactive, though scientists think they can overcome this by tweaking MXenes' structure — capping the materials' edges with bulky salts, for instance, could shield them from damage by oxygen. In manufacturing, it is hard right now to make large amounts: in the lab, researchers can make only several kilograms in a single batch, and several companies are working out how to boost batch sizes. Anupma Thakur points out one irony: making MXenes for carbon capture can have a big carbon footprint, because it takes a lot of electricity to get the heat needed to make them and much of that electricity is made using CO2-spewing fossil fuels, so it is important to make sure the energy used does not spew more CO2 than the MXenes can later sop up — otherwise their use in carbon capture is defeated. MXenes also cost a lot to make, and that high cost would matter less if they could withstand thousands of CO2 capture-and-release cycles so that new material need not keep being made; so far no one has tested MXenes' durability for stored CO2 removal and reuse, though it helps that they are mechanically rugged, with research showing certain types can be as strong as steel.



---


# Advances in Deep-Sea Sensory Ecology

Sensory ecology has been an area of many interesting papers over the past five years, Jon Copley says: researchers are finding out a lot more about how deep sea animals interact with each other and their environment.

That work concerns how animals perceive their environment, how they respond to it, and how they avoid being seen by predators, and Copley says it was nice to bring some of those findings together in a couple of chapters of his new book.



---


# Reactions to the Quantum Dot Nobel

Researchers welcomed the award: "They're the ones who built the foundation," said Warren Chan, a biomedical engineer and chemist at the University of Toronto in Canada, calling the prize well-deserved. "I'm really happy that the field is getting credit for really changing the world."

Chan and his colleagues found one of the first uses for quantum dots in the 1990s, using them to tag cells in lab experiments. He notes that the Nobel committee does not just look at past impacts of a discovery but also considers the effects it may have in the future, and quantum dots could have a whole medley of uses not yet explored; his own team is now using quantum dots to detect infections such as flu and HIV. "I was absolutely thrilled to see this," said Judith Giordan, president of the American Chemical Society. "We have three people recognized who brought this technology from a dream, a hope, a theoretical construct … all the way through synthesis and manufacture."



---


# Sample Size Critique of the Jellyfish Learning Result

Björn Brembs, who studies the nervous systems of animals at the University of Regensburg in Germany, views the results more cautiously, pointing to the small number of jellyfish tested — attacking the inference from a handful of animals to a general claim that jellyfish learn.

"I want this to be true, as it would be so very cool," he says of the results. But it will take tests with more jellyfish to convince him that the animals really do learn.



---


# CRISPR-Based Antibacterial Therapy

CRISPR can be turned into an antibacterial by using it to shred bacterial cells' own DNA — an idea inspired by the observation that CRISPR-Cas occasionally, rather than attacking phages, goes after the bacterial cell's own DNA and triggers a lethal autoimmune reaction, which prompted Chase Beisel and his colleagues to explore the approach deliberately.

Its defining property is sequence specificity. "The real draw of it is that it is a sequence-specific tool," meaning it targets only the DNA you tell it to, and not sequences present in other bacteria, Beisel told Live Science; once administered to a patient, "the CRISPR machinery gets into a set of cells, but only those that have the sequence or sequences you picked will be attacked and killed." Delivery is the open problem: various research groups are testing different delivery methods, but at present the best strategy seems to be loading CRISPR machinery into a phage that infects the target bacterium, Beisel said. Beisel is a co-founder and scientific adviser of Locus Biosciences, a biotech company currently testing a CRISPR-enhanced phage therapy in a midstage, roughly 800-person trial; that approach couples the bacteria-killing prowess of phages with the ability of CRISPR-Cas to destroy essential bacterial genes. As with CRISPR-less phage therapies, clinical trials are needed to determine the treatment's safety profile and appropriate dosing. "I can see these [treatments] coming about in the five- to 10-year time frame," Beisel said.



---


# Origin of the Cavefish Ketogenic Diet Collaboration

Believing that cavefish might be useful for the study of autism, Masato Yoshizawa approached his colleague Ryan Lee, a physician working with autism patients at Shriners Hospital for Children Honolulu: "When I showed him the video of the cavefish he immediately said, 'yes, that is very similar to what I observe in my patients'," Yoshizawa recounted.

Lee, who has experimented with ketogenic diets to improve autism symptoms with some success, suggested they try it with the fish. In humans, not all patients receiving the ketogenic diet improve, but some do; if it worked with the fish, the researchers might then be able to figure out how the diet affects behaviour and improve the effectiveness of the treatment for humans. # Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

In September 2023 the Justice Department charged Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.) and his wife Nadine with accepting bribes and allegedly using his Senate seat to improperly aid the Egyptian government; Menendez pleaded not guilty.

A raid of Menendez's house turned up $100,000 in gold bars and bundles of cash stuffed into jacket pockets. # Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

Sydney, winless in their debut season the previous year, secured eighth spot and their first AFLW finals berth in 2023 by storming home with three unanswered goals against Fremantle, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

The game's played at both ends and you need to find a rhythm to generate some natural enthusiasm, and we haven't been able to do that for good stretches."

# Melbourne United Beat Illawarra 96-84 In Round 5

Chris Goulding fired off a season-high seven three-pointers — more than any other player in a game that season — to steer NBL ladder leaders Melbourne United to a 96-84 win over the Illawarra Hawks at John Cain Arena, finishing with 33 points.

Melbourne operated without injured guards Ian Clark (hamstring) and Matthew Dellavedova (concussion), and suffered a first-half scare when Luke Travers was forced off after a knock to his left knee as visiting Illawarra surged as much as 10 points clear in a high-scoring first half. Goulding's hot hand kept United in the contest with 21 first-half points including five three-pointers, and the team's tough defence in the second half carried them home. Shea Ili (17 points) and Tanner Krebs (14) also reached double figures. The result extended United's winning streak to six games for an 8-1 record on top of the ladder.

Import forward Gary Clark (24 points) and Justin Robinson (20) tried to lift Illawarra, but Tyler Harvey managed just 10 points three days after his clutch three-pointer sealed a thrilling win over Cairns. In a sloppy start United committed five turnovers in the first period and trailed at quarter-time for the first time that season, with Clark's eight points on perfect shooting leading Illawarra to a 29-24 advantage; his tally swelled to 16 by the main break and the Hawks' lead reached double figures soon after United temporarily lost Travers, before Goulding caught fire to give United a 52-51 lead at halftime.

Defence was key in the second half as both sides tightened up, with Melbourne holding the visitors to just 15 points in the final period. Travers returned after halftime to finish with six points and a game-high 11 rebounds, while Ariel Hukporti retained his spot in Melbourne's starting five ahead of Jo Lual-Acuil Jr and impressed with seven points and 10 rebounds, four of them on the offensive end.



---


# UK Support Organisations For Older Adults

The Guardian's 10 October 2023 piece lists five organisations older adults and their families can turn to, each defined by a distinct function.

Age UK has a database of social activities and groups for older folk. The Walking Football Association keeps keen amateur footballers playing long into their 50s and 60s. Action for Elders offers social and exercise programmes.

The Centre for Ageing Better provides information on working and living as an older person, and u3a, a charity collective, provides local opportunities for people no longer in work to acquire new skills and knowledge.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest the absence of a legislative remedy for AI risks and abuses, while the Music Business Worldwide article indicates that the National Music Publishers Association is advocating for regulations in AI development?
context:
# The US Copyright Office's 2023 Study Of AI And Copyright

The US Copyright Office is spearheading one of the key US efforts to address AI and copyright: in the summer of 2023 it issued a call for submissions on the issue of AI and copyright, with the goal of putting together a study to "help assess whether legislative or regulatory steps in this area are warranted."

The call for submissions came as legislators and regulators around the world grappled with the many issues that had emerged since AI technology "went mainstream" about a year earlier. Numerous businesses involved in AI, and those with substantial copyright holdings, submitted their thoughts on the issue — including Universal Music Group and AI developer Anthropic.



---


# Sony Music's Generative AI Principles For Congress

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, asked Congress at the November 29, 2023 AI Insight Forum to embrace a set of five principles around generative AI, on the argument that "if copyrights are protected and enforced appropriately, we are at the beginning of a multi-decade marathon that will change the creative and commercial landscape for music."

The framing condition Kooker set is that "Music is a tremendous driver for AI technology, and AI technology presents a tremendous opportunity for the creative development of music. But these opportunities must be grounded by the human creators' vision with the machine assisting, not with the machine replacing the human creator." The principles are: Assure Consent, Compensation, and Credit — "New products and businesses built with music must be developed with the consent of the owner and appropriate compensation and credit. It is essential to understand why the training of AI models is being done, what products will be developed as a result, and what the business model is that will monetize the use of the artist's work. Congress and the agencies should assure that creators' rights are recognized and respected." Confirm That Copying Music to Train AI Models is Not Fair Use — "Even worse are those that argue that copyrighted content should automatically be considered fair use so that protected works are never compensated for usage and creators have no say in the products or business models that are developed around them and their work. Congress should assure and agencies should presume that reproducing music to train AI models, in itself, is not a fair use." Prevent the Cloning of Artists' Voices and Likenesses Without Express Permission — "We cannot allow an artist's voice or likeness to be cloned for use without the express permission of the artist. This is a very personal decision for the artist. Congress should pass into law effective federal protections for name, image, and likeness." Incentivize Accurate Recordkeeping — "Correct attribution will be a critical element to artists being paid fairly and correctly for new works that are created. In addition, rights can only be enforced around the training of AI when there are accurate records about what is being copied. Otherwise, the inability to enforce rights in the AI marketplace equates to a lack of rights at all, producing a dangerous imbalance that prevents a thriving ecosystem. This requires strong and accurate record keeping by the generative AI platforms, a requirement that urgently needs legislative support to ensure incentives are in place so that it happens consistently and correctly." And Assure Transparency for Consumers and Artists — "Transparency is necessary to clearly distinguish human-created works from AI-created works. The public should know, when they are listening to music, whether that music was created by a human being or a machine." MBW summarised the intended effect: "The principles will ensure that intellectual property businesses can succeed in this new world alongside tech partners, further advancing investment and expanding economic opportunities."



---


# Fair Use, Explained Plainly

"Fair use" is, as it sounds, the argument that there are cases where copyrighted material can be used and even replicated that are fair enough.

Music Business Worldwide's 2023-11-23 piece offers a deliberately clumsy example: I read a great book, then I meet you for breakfast, where I tell you about the story and quote a couple of my favorite passages to you. To suggest that this is copyright infringement would not only be silly — it would mean that copyright protections were getting in the way of the commercial furtherment of the author or rightsholder, since you might go and buy the book on the recommendation.



---


# Kyncl Prediction: Music Is the First Industry to Feel AI's Impact

Robert Kyncl's proposition, put at the Code Conference in September 2023, is that the music business will be out ahead of other industries in exploiting the potential of AI, and — out of necessity — also ahead on the question of how to regulate and monetise the use of AI by non-rights-holders. He attached a date to it: asked when that sea change would occur, he said "I would say within the next year you will see lots of evolution around AI… What you will likely see is increasing quality at a very fast pace."

His reasoning is structural rather than accidental. "Music – because it's so broadly distributed and it's so well aligned with the internet, because it's short format, it lends itself to recommendations, it's on all platforms – is generally first in most transformations and most innovations. So it digitizes first." He generalises from the previous cycle: "Whatever happened to the music industry 20 years ago is starting to happen in the movies and TV shows now. In the meantime, music emerged out of [digitization] better and stronger and more resilient. So, I would imagine the same will happen here, which is we'll likely be first."

The hypothesis is falsifiable on two fronts as stated. It fails if other industries, rather than music, lead on both exploiting and regulating AI; and it fails on its own timetable if the year following September 2023 does not bring the predicted rapid evolution and fast-rising quality in AI. Because the argument rests on music's broad distribution, short format and recommendation-friendliness, an AI transformation that arrives first in a long-format medium would also count against the mechanism he proposes.



---


# The AI Legislation Gap Behind Biden's Executive Order

Biden's AI executive order can only be a stopgap, because there is no legislative remedy to potential AI risks and abuses outside of those that can be applied to tech companies in general — and many have argued over the years that those general remedies are also inadequate. The order therefore props up the "voluntary" practices many companies are already choosing to implement, and the limits on what a president can do with a wave of their hand mean it amounts to a lot of sharing results, developing best practices and providing clear guidance.

The grounds for that reading are the state of federal action and the state of prospective law. Federal action on social media and de facto monopolies like Amazon and Google has been sporadic, though a hawkish new FTC may change that trend. Meanwhile, a comprehensive law defining and limiting the use of AI seems as far off now as it was years ago: the industry and technology have evolved so quickly that any rule would likely be outdated by the time it was passed, and it is not even really clear what ought to be legislatively limited as opposed to being left to state law or expert agencies.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is that executive authority cannot substitute for the institutional machinery a durable regime would need. Perhaps the wisest approach is to set up a new federal agency dedicated to regulating AI and technology, but this cannot be accomplished by fiat. In the meantime, the EO at least instructs several AI-focused groups, like one in the Department of Health and Human Services dedicated to handling and assessing reports of AI-related harms in healthcare.



---


# The EU-US Asymmetry In Recorded Music Performance Rights

At the heart of the dispute is a difference in how the US and the EU pay artists for terrestrial (non-satellite) radio broadcasts of music and recorded music played in bars and restaurants.

In Europe, when recorded music is played over terrestrial radio or in venues, performance rights payments must be made to the artists and labels behind the recording, as well as to the songwriters and publishers who own the composition behind the recording. In the US, by contrast, performance rights payments are made only to the songwriters and publishers, and not to artists and labels.



---


# EU AI Act Scope Exclusions For National Security And Research

The AI Act does not apply to areas outside the scope of EU law, and the Council's press release on the deal emphasizes that the provisional agreement "clarifies that the regulation does not apply to areas outside the scope of EU law and should not, in any case, affect member states' competences in national security or any entity entrusted with tasks in this area."

The Council also confirmed that the AI Act will not apply to systems exclusively for military or defence purposes. A further exclusion covers early-stage and non-commercial use: "Similarly, the agreement provides that the regulation would not apply to AI systems used for the sole purpose of research and innovation, or for people using AI for non-professional reasons," the Council added.



---


# The AI Development Moratorium Open Letter

Not everybody was enthusiastic about the pace at which generative AI was being adopted. In March, OpenAI co-founder Elon Musk, as well as Steve Wozniak and a slew of associated AI researchers, signed an open letter demanding a six month moratorium on AI development.

The letter attacks the premise underlying the industry's integration wave — that faster deployment is straightforwardly good — by asking for development itself to be paused rather than merely regulated.

qid: Which national rugby team, highlighted in articles from 'The Independent - Sports' and 'The Roar | Sports Writers Blog', suffered defeats in their home country as well as in Sydney and Christchurch, against opponents including Ireland, South Africa, and Argentina?
context:
# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# Cheika's Underdog Framing Before The 2023 Semi-Final

Michael Cheika embraced underdog status before Argentina's 2023 World Cup semi-final while pointedly reminding the All Blacks who the favourites were: "The other team are heavy favourites, everyone is expecting a New Zealand and South Africa final. We just have to focus on what is required."

His grounds are a reading of what New Zealand demand of an opponent: "New Zealand has always been an example in rugby, a benchmark. They make you think of high-level skills in a really open game but there are always threats in the lineout, mauls and rucks. You have to take the moments you are in the game and see them coming at you at different times." Cheika, whose Wallabies lost the 2015 final, was readying for another clash against the All Blacks and a second semi-final.

He also refused to over-read Argentina's 2020 win as evidence: "In the game in 2020 there were things you could pinpoint. You can't say that one game means we can do it as there are a lot of games where we haven't. That moment has to be just a part of it. What we have done since then, all the success and failures [matters in our preparation]." The same week he said he hoped Los Pumas "inspired" Argentina "not by our results but by our ambition".



---


# How England And South Africa Reached The 2023 Semi-Final

England arrived at the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final as the only side still competing that had yet to lose a game, while South Africa had already beaten two of the tournament favourites. Dominant wins over Argentina, Japan and Chile sealed England's passage to the last eight, and after being given an almighty scare by Samoa in their final pool match, they overcame a Fijian fightback in Marseille to triumph 30-24 — outscored by three tries to two, but carried by captain Owen Farrell's 20 points at the expense of 2023's breakout stars.

The Springboks had done it tough. Comfortable defeats of Scotland, Romania and Tonga could not mask the disappointment of a 13-8 loss to Ireland, which consigned South Africa to second in Pool B. With Ireland then sent home by the All Blacks in the quarters, the Bokke showed their World Cup mettle to edge hosts France 29-28 at the Stade de France, sneaking past Les Bleus in one of the best games of rugby you're ever likely to see.

Both journeys had twists, turns and bumps in the road but left each side within 80 minutes of a Rugby World Cup final. England would be looking to echo the spirit of 2019, when they beat the All Blacks 19-7 to reach the final, but in South Africa they faced a side who had taken their game to new heights just to reach the semis.



---


# Erasmus And Nienaber Depart After The Springboks' 2023 Title

The 2023 World Cup final victory was the perfect sign-off for the Springboks' management, with director of rugby Rassie Erasmus set to follow head coach Jacques Nienaber out — a duo The Roar says will go down as the greatest coaching pair in rugby history, having led South Africa to back-to-back World Cup triumphs.

Nienaber framed the win as the endpoint of a long plan and thanked the country: "We came a long way with the players. We always planned for this World Cup, since 2018. Massive credit to our fans. They were special from South Africa, 62 million people, the videos we had to play from them. It was unbelievable."

The departures were not only from the coaching box: veteran back-rower Duane Vermeulen would also call time on his illustrious career.



---


# Peter Horne's Appointment As Rugby Australia High-Performance Director

Rugby Australia was moving closer to naming World Rugby's director of high-performance Peter Horne as its new director of high-performance, a move The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 could also help land highly-regarded coach Joe Schmidt for the vacant Wallabies job.

The Roar had reported the previous week that Horne emerged as the leading candidate, and it is believed he edged out former Sydney University, Australian Sevens and Harlequins director of rugby Billy Millard for the role. The finer points of the negotiations were being worked out, with an announcement likely over the following week once Horne wrapped up a crucial series of meetings with World Rugby — he was leading World Rugby meetings with tier-two nations that week in Sydney, with former Fiji coach Simon Raiwalui in attendance before officially joining World Rugby. His appointment reflects Rugby Australia's desire to go down an administrative path rather than choose a former coach of any standing, as Millard would have offered, and Horne will sit at the top of the high-performance tree with the next Wallabies coach reporting into him.

His background is given in some detail. Horne joined World Rugby in 2015 as a general manager of high-performance before moving into his current role, and during that tenure the Sydneysider played an important role in setting up competitions, high-performance structures and pathways across developing countries. He also played a role in helping Super Rugby integrate Fiji Drua and Moana Pasifika into the competition. Those successes played out at the recent Rugby World Cup, with Chile, Fiji, Georgia and Portugal delivering encouraging performances that positively reflected World Rugby's desire to spread and build the game. He briefly worked at Saracens as a general manager.



---


# Ireland's Rugby World Cup Quarter-Final Curse

Ireland's "quarter-final curse" is the pattern by which the team has never won a Rugby World Cup knockout match: on quarter-final weekend, for the eighth time in 10 Rugby World Cups, Ireland headed home defeated, and the wait for a first-ever knockout win goes on. This time was supposed to be different — this Ireland team were different, are different — but come the end, the result was the same.

The boundary of the pattern is how rarely Ireland have even threatened to break it. Since 1991, when Michael Lynagh's late try handed Australia victory, Ireland had not come close to ending their last-eight hoodoo; never mind winning one, they had not led a World Cup quarter-final since the first half of the 1995 defeat to France, a mammoth 10,353 days earlier.

The 2023 defeat will hurt more than any other, because here they had a legitimate chance to reverse the curse. Multiple times they got within a point of the All Blacks, only for their opponents to agonisingly pull away once more — and then there were those 37 phases, the most painful finish in Irish rugby history.



---


# England's 2023 Cricket World Cup Qualification Crisis

England's Cricket World Cup hopes hung by a thread after a shock defeat to Afghanistan, leaving their chances of finishing in the top four and progressing to the semi-finals looking dubious as they prepared to face South Africa in Mumbai from 9:30am on 21 October 2023, talkSPORT reported.

Having also lost to New Zealand in their opener, victory for England could scarcely be more crucial. They were boosted by the news that Ben Stokes was fit for the match after picking up a hip injury five days before the tournament.

There was one encouraging sign in the opposition's form: South Africa, despite winning their first two games, suffered a shock defeat to the Netherlands in their most recent match — an indication for England that the Proteas can be beaten. talkSPORT would bring updates from the game in India.

qid: Who is the individual under 30, formerly associated with FTX and Alameda Research, who was described by 'Fortune' as using a front for secret access to customer funds, by 'The Verge' as overwhelmed by the growth of his company to manage it alongside another, and by 'TechCrunch' as both the richest person in his age group with altruistic spending intentions and as someone accused of committing fraud for personal gain?
context:
# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."

qid: Between the Sporting News report on Lionel Messi's involvement with Inter Miami published on October 7, 2023, and the Sporting News report on Lionel Messi's contribution to Argentina's youth movement in the forward line published on October 12, 2023, was there no change in the focus of Messi's football activities as reported by the same news source?

# Shaqiri Before Facing Inter Miami: Preparation Unchanged, And Team Messi

Ahead of the Chicago Fire's Oct. 4, 2023 match with Inter Miami, Xherdan Shaqiri said the Fire's preparation would not change regardless of whether Lionel Messi played. Speaking in his pre-match availability on the Monday, and reported 90 minutes before kickoff, Shaqiri said: "The preparation is not going to change, we're going to prepare as normal as always. Everybody is excited to play against Inter Miami. If Messi is injured or not, personally I am not thinking too much about this. Of course Inter Miami is a different team when Messi is playing or not playing, you see that in the last games when Messi is in the team they are better, but we prepare like normal for every game." Sporting News noted that many teams had indicated their preparation for Inter Miami varied wildly depending on Messi's availability, while Shaqiri played his cards close to his chest.

Shaqiri also framed the stakes of the match itself: "These are the best games to play all the time. As a player, you want these kinds of final games and to play for something. We put ourselves in this position, and we have a chance to do it, so now we have to perform."

Asked "Messi or Ronaldo?", Shaqiri confirmed he was Team Messi: "I'm always a big Messi admirer, if I have to choose now I will go with Messi. He won the WC which was the only thing he missed. So for sure Messi." He also said: "For me it's clear, Messi and Ronaldo are the best players in the world… these guys are among the best athletes in the history of sport, along with Michael Jordan and Tom Brady."



---


# Against Messi's MLS MVP And Newcomer Nominations: The League Minutes Do Not Support Them

Sporting News argued on Oct. 7, 2023 that Lionel Messi's nominations for both 2023 MLS Newcomer of the Year and 2023 MLS MVP were unwarranted, attacking the premise that his impact had come in the league at all. Reported 75 minutes before kickoff, the nominations were called a blatant PR move that "laughable doesn't even begin to describe."

The grounds for the objection are the split between competitions: most of the damage Messi had done for Inter Miami came in Cup competitions, and in actual MLS competition he had one goal and two assists in 247 minutes of play. The conclusion drawn was that Messi had been fun, but that the league should not make a mockery of itself by actually giving him either honor.



---


# Argentina's Squad And Starting XI Against Paraguay, October 2023

Lionel Scaloni's Argentina started 4-3-3 against Paraguay on Oct. 12, 2023: E. Martinez (GK) — Molina, Romero, Otamendi, Tagliafico — De Paul, Mac Allister, E. Fernandez — J. Alvarez, L. Martinez, N. Gonzalez.

Scaloni had named a bloated 36-man squad for that month's matches against Paraguay and Peru, but Angel Di Maria, Paulo Dybala and Juan Foyth were forced to withdraw through injury, and Lisandro Martinez was also unavailable after undergoing another foot operation. Nicolas Tagliafico, who started both September matches, retained his starting spot even though Marcos Acuna was back with the team following an injury. Lionel Messi's club teammate Facundo Farias was included on the roster, but it would have been surprising had he seen the field.

The absences sharpened a generational shift. Messi was helping usher in a youth movement up front, with Julian Alvarez and Alejandro Garnacho considered the future of the forward line, and with Di Maria not fit for duty that month those two were even more in the spotlight against Paraguay and in the follow-up in Peru.



---


# The Cancelled China Tour And The NYCFC Noche d'Or Replacement

Inter Miami's planned two-match tour of China in early November 2023 was cancelled for "commercial and bureaucratic" reasons, and was replaced by a hastily arranged friendly against NYCFC at DRV PNK Stadium on November 10 dubbed the "Noche d'Or" or "Night of Gold" in honor of Lionel Messi's most recent Ballon d'Or.

The tour existed because of the club's elimination from 2023 MLS playoff contention, which left Messi facing nearly a full month off from competitive fixtures before taking the field for Argentina against Uruguay and Brazil in CONMEBOL World Cup qualifying. Likely with the sole intent of keeping Messi fit in that time off, and the added bonus of raking in significant cash, Inter Miami scheduled the China trip after their regular season concluded, expecting to visit two Chinese Super League sides — Qingdao Hainiu on November 5 and Chengdu Rongcheng three days later.

# Messi's Fitness And Inter Miami's Offseason, October 2023

Lionel Messi's club Inter Miami were eliminated from MLS playoff contention by a 1-0 loss to FC Cincinnati the weekend before Argentina's Oct. 12, 2023 qualifier against Paraguay — and that elimination changed the calculus around his minutes for Argentina.

Messi had missed the previous four matches, including Argentina's fixture against Bolivia, but returned for the final 30 minutes against Cincinnati and was powerless to turn the tide after Inter Miami missed so many gilt-edged chances in the first half. Had Inter Miami still been in the playoff hunt with a postseason run on the horizon, Argentina might have played it a bit safer with Messi in this international window; with his long offseason break confirmed, he could be more aggressive with his minutes, knowing that after Inter Miami's final two meaningless regular-season matches he would only have international breaks to keep him sharp until February. With Messi starting on the bench, reports also indicated Nicolas Otamendi would wear the captain's armband until Messi entered.

A rumour that Messi could head to Barcelona on loan to cover the gap left by Inter Miami's failure to qualify never made much sense and was squashed on numerous fronts. Inter Miami coach Gerardo Martino made light of it in his post-match press conference after the Cincinnati defeat, saying he would only go to Spain "for fun" — "Is he going for fun? Maybe he's going to visit Barcelona. Other than that, I don't know anything else about it" — while Fabrizio Romano shot it down from a journalistic standpoint. There is not enough of a break for Messi to reasonably integrate with Barcelona, and at 36 years old he is sure to welcome the extended time off.

# Jean-Claude Blanc and the United Chief Executive Challenge

The question The Guardian posed on 25 December 2023 is whether any chief executive can make Manchester United a best-in-class elite club again — and the candidate in frame is Jean-Claude Blanc, billed as the "Lionel Messi of business" by Nice's chief executive, Fabrice Bocquet.

Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.
