# Patent Litigation

## Definition

In the corpus, patent litigation is the set of formal legal proceedings companies use to fight over patent rights — a patent holder's lawsuit in federal district court and, in parallel, a case before the US International Trade Commission (ITC) — with remedies that can include a monetary verdict or an ITC import ban, and with the accused party able to counter-sue or get the asserted patents ruled invalid or unenforceable.

## Context

The corpus documents two concrete disputes that illustrate the mechanics of patent litigation. Sonos sued Google and won a $32.5 million verdict over patent infringement, but a federal judge later threw out that win after finding Sonos' patents "unenforceable and invalid" — showing that a litigation win is not final until it survives post-trial and appellate review. Separately, Masimo sued Apple in the US District Court for the Central District of California in 2020 for trade-secret theft and infringement of 10 patents related to pulse-oximetry (SpO2) sensing technology, and when that case dragged on, Masimo additionally filed a parallel case with the US International Trade Commission (ITC) in 2021; Apple counter-sued Masimo the following year. The ITC route matters because, unlike a district court, it can issue an import ban that blocks the accused product (the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2) from entering the US market, and any such ban is then subject to a 60-day presidential review period during which the President or US Trade Representative may veto it.

## Key Characteristics

- **Dual venues** — patent disputes can run in federal district court (damages, injunctions) and, in parallel, before the ITC (import bans), as in the Apple-Masimo dispute where Masimo pursued both.
- **Invalidity/unenforceability as a defense** — a defendant can defeat an infringement verdict after the fact by getting the asserted patents ruled unenforceable and invalid, as happened to Sonos' win against Google.
- **Countersuits** — litigation can escalate into cross-litigation, as when Apple sued Masimo back, alleging Masimo's own watch cloned Apple's design.
- **ITC import-ban remedy plus presidential review** — an ITC finding of infringement can trigger a ban on importing the infringing product, but the ban is not final until a 60-day presidential/USTR review period lapses without a veto.
- **Long timelines** — the Apple-Masimo dispute originated roughly a decade before the resulting Apple Watch import ban took effect, illustrating how a single patent dispute can span years across multiple proceedings.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, patent litigation is generally described as the process of enforcing patent rights, and it is decided exclusively by federal (not state) courts in the US.

Remedies available in such litigation typically include a permanent or preliminary injunction ordering the infringing act to stop, and a damages award such as a reasonable royalty.

A defendant can raise defenses including that the patent has expired, that it holds a license, or that the patent is invalid or unenforceable, and disputes may also end in a settlement that includes a licensing agreement.

Source: Wikipedia, "Patent infringement," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement.

# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

# X's Competitive Position In October 2023

X was facing more competition than ever before at the time it introduced its bot-countering fee, and its own numbers were going the other way: a report published that week by market intelligence firm Similarweb found that X's web traffic and monthly active users on mobile had declined post-acquisition. TechCrunch reported this on 18 October 2023, noting that as Musk's chaotic product and policy changes took root, some X users abandoned the platform for rivals or decreased their posting.

The competitive field had widened on two fronts. Twitter-like startups and tech companies gave users far more options for microblogging and public discourse — Spill, Bluesky, Pebble, Countersocial, Spoutible, Hive, and the open source platform Mastodon — and tech giants had entered too, with Meta's new app Threads. On pricing, X was close to alone: few of the other social apps currently charge a fee, unless it's for premium features, as some third-party Mastodon apps do.

One scope condition limits how far the fee comparison can be pushed. X's charge was at that point only an experiment, and TechCrunch noted it was not clear the $1 fee would be a permanent requirement when the new subscription policy rolled out more broadly to other markets.

# The Reaction To Francesca Scorsese's Slang Video

Francesca Scorsese's TikTok of her father guessing popular slang terms had been viewed one million times by the time The Independent reported on it on 10 October 2023, days after its Thursday posting. Commenters were shocked both to see the legendary director on their screens and that he managed to guess many of the terms correctly.

"Can't believe we live in a world where I get to watch Martin Scorsese become familiar with the term sneaky link. Blessings," read one comment. "I cannot believe I exist in a timeline where I can watch Martin Scorsese film TikToks," said another. A third wrote: "I can't believe I'm watching one of the greatest filmmakers of our lifetime be quizzed by his daughter about teen slang lol," while someone else said: "Gonna describe sneaky links as personal picadillos from now on." It was not Scorsese's first appearance in one of his daughter's TikToks: in April 2021 Francesca went viral asking him to identify "feminine products" such as an eyelash curler, bobby pins, a hair donut and nipple pasties.

# Scorsese's Late Career Refutes Tarantino's Claim That Directors Do Not Get Better

Polygon's 2023-10-26 piece attacks the premise behind Quentin Tarantino's 2021 defense of his intention to make "just" 10 movies and retire: "I know film history, and from here on in, directors do not get better." The counter is that this view of both artistry and film is squarely at odds with Martin Scorsese's historic body of work.

The specific premise under attack is the claim of inevitable late-career decline. Scorsese had already made his 10th feature-length narrative film by 1986; he is now 80 years old, and his 27th, Killers of the Flower Moon, is a strong argument that directors are still capable of groundbreaking greatness late in life — and, in Scorsese's case, of continued exhilarating experimentation and discovery.

Polygon presses the point further: since the year 2000, Scorsese has curated a 23-year career within a career, and the quality and variety of his films have come not in spite of his age and experience but because of it. His movies have never been more relevant than in the past two decades, and with each subsequent release, as his career winds down, critical appreciation for him grows — Scorsese worship being the one remaining form of gerontocracy America is perfectly content with, and with good reason.

The mechanism the piece identifies is autonomy. This century Scorsese has zigged and zagged as always, but because he is following his own varied interests rather than moving from compromise to compromise as he once had to in order to keep working: an artist who spent the first 30 years of his career desperate for autonomy finally got it, and now takes full advantage — telling difficult stories, setting his own mega-budgets, and demanding every minute of run time he feels each picture demands. He has used that autonomy to revisit his work and revise the record, creating great new films and adding crucial addendums to past work while blazing new trails and adding layers to his style. Remarkably, the control that eluded him when he was younger has made his films more consistently collaborative and creative, more fluid and alive than he was often allowed to be before the 2000s, with the earned confidence of an artist who knows he will find something great in post. Polygon concludes that this should give Tarantino cause to reconsider, alongside any artist or critic who thinks the creative spark has an expiration date.

# Murder By Contract (1958)

Irving Lerner's Murder by Contract is a lean, mean noir that had a big influence on Martin Scorsese, who has listed it among his guilty pleasure movies and called it the film that influenced him the most, especially in Taxi Driver. It streams free with ads on Tubi.

Scorsese's stated reason is economy: "The film puts us all to shame with its economy of style," he wrote, adding that "Murder By Contract was a favorite of neighborhood guys who didn't know anything about movies. They just liked the film because they recognized something unique about it." In the film, Vince Edwards plays a methodical hitman asked to kill a witness in a high-profile case; when he finds out his target is a woman he bucks — not on moral grounds, but because women are harder to kill, being in his view unpredictable. Polygon's Pete Volk credits Lerner with directing masterfully on a minimal budget: a tight 81 minutes, aided by Edwards' fantastic lead performance and a great all-guitar score from Perry Botkin.

# Sam Reich's Advice To Creators: Find A Better Business Model

Asked what five years of Dropout has taught him for creators, producers or fans looking to get away from algorithmically powered viral demand, Sam Reich's answer is blunt: "My advice is find a better business model." His claim is that sustainability requires something to offer off the algorithmic platforms — "for you to make this sustainable you need to have something to offer that's off of those platforms."

His grounds are an account of how platforms shape content. "I think we live in an era of online content right now that is being defined and shaped by algorithms. And that's true no matter the platform." Different platforms shape content in different ways, which he finds exciting as a creator — "Which of these sports am I most excited to play?" — and he gives a concrete example: TikTok has lately been prioritising videos longer than a minute because it is trying to encourage watch time, while YouTube Shorts still doesn't allow anything longer than a minute. Platforms compete with each other and themselves and yield these kind of Frankenstein products. He is careful not to write the platforms off — he is regularly inspired by what he sees, loves hanging out on them, and thinks some creators are getting really creative.

The warrant is that off-platform offerings restore independence, and he names several routes: creating a subscription offering like Patreon and driving people to it; leveraging an online presence into opportunities in traditional Hollywood; or, for people who aren't content creators first and foremost, using it to market their music or physical products, which is working out well for them. For Dropout itself, "the heart and the soul of what we do is on Dropout. We are very lucky, very lucky, that social media has turned out to be such a good way for us to market this platform. And we are also gleefully no longer beholden to it." The context for the question was something Reich told NPR earlier in the year: that Dropout found success not by going broad for the viral video but by going for "something that feels special to a small group of people."



---


# Eli Roth's Horror Filmography And Acting Roles

Eli Roth has helmed over 20 films as a director, more than double that as a producer, and has also appeared onscreen — notably as Sgt. Donny "The Bear Jew" Donowitz in Quentin Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds (2009) and, most recently, in 2023's comically maligned The Idol, where he played a wracked Live Nation rep, The Age reported on 15 November 2023.

He has been horror's most provocative maestro for decades, a filmmaker who finds sinister glee in pushing the envelope; it was his film Hostel (2005) that spawned the term "torture porn". Of returning to the slasher form he says: "Every time I make a horror movie, it's like a badge of honour for me. It's like, this is my chance to make a slasher film, you know? I grew up with Freddie, Jason, Michael Myers, Chucky – I loved those movies so much – and in the '90s, we had Ghostface and other slashers that were overlooked, like Mute Witness (1995) which is one of my favourites. I just thought, well, it's time for a new slasher. I want a new killer in town, so let's create another one." Recalling a Q&A screening for his feature debut Cabin Fever (2002) at Glebe's now defunct Valhalla cinema about 20 years earlier, Roth remembers "a kid coming up to me after, with his friend Angus, and we talked for half an hour about how much he loved the movie. And I was doing Angus' radio show the next day and that kid came up to me again and he's like, 'Yeah, I made a short film called Saw.' It was Leigh Whannell."

Although he was not involved in The Idol's troubled first incarnation, Roth says he enjoyed his experience on creator Sam Levinson's set — "You saw this negative stuff come up [in the press] and I'd be thinking, 'What are people talking about?'" He completed The Idol right before directing Thanksgiving and credits the experience with "switching up my brain to use another side of my creativity". "I think that's why I really am an actor's director and why actors like working with me, is that they know I understand what they go through," he says. "In the rehearsal process with the cast, or getting ready to do a scare scene, I want to give them the room to go off-script a bit until we find something interesting, and that's all from my personal experience as an actor."

# The NCAA Investigation Into Michigan's Scouting Scheme

The NCAA is investigating Michigan's football program amid allegations that the Wolverines used illegal in-person scouting and the recording of signals to steal signs this season, as reported by The New York Times on 3 November 2023.

The conference's involvement is dated. Ahead of the Michigan-Michigan State game on 21 October, the Big Ten approached MSU and said it was made aware of "credible evidence" regarding the sign-stealing allegations, and said it would monitor the NCAA's investigation into Michigan.

The timing problem is spelled out. The NCAA investigation is ongoing, a process that typically moves slowly, which makes it difficult to imagine it will reach a resolution by the time the postseason begins. The Big Ten does have the ability to act under its sportsmanship policy, but that doesn't mean it would want to act quickly or decisively before the NCAA completes its entire investigation and allows Michigan a chance to respond to its findings.



---


# Michigan's Counterclaim That Rivals Shared Its Signs

Michigan's counter to the sign-stealing case is that it is hardly alone in trying to decipher opponents' signals, and it has shared evidence with the Big Ten and the NCAA showing that staff members at Ohio State, Purdue and Rutgers exchanged intelligence on the Wolverines' signals before the previous year's Michigan-Purdue Big Ten Championship Game. The Athletic reported that documents breaking down Michigan's signals for numerous plays were compiled by Purdue staffers ahead of that game based on information provided by Ohio State and Rutgers football personnel. The person who supplied the documents told The Athletic that he spent 10 to 12 hours per week trying to decode signals from game video, and that sharing decoded signals with other schools is a common practice.

The counterclaim does not dispose of the charge, because it attacks the wrong premise. The primary difference, per the same reporting, is that Michigan is accused of using in-person scouting — prohibited under NCAA rules for nearly 30 years — to acquire its information, rather than decoding from video.

Ohio State denied the allegation outright. Asked about the claim that Ohio State had given information about Michigan's signs to Purdue before the 2022 Big Ten championship game, coach Ryan Day said, per the Columbus Dispatch: "I can tell you this right now that nobody here did any of that. We went through and made sure we asked all the questions and got our compliance people involved. None of that came back at all. I can answer very strongly that that did not happen." Separately, Yahoo Sports reported that Day and his family have no connection to the Big Ten and NCAA investigations into Michigan; a weekend report had suggested Day may have had some involvement in the probe into the Buckeyes' arch-rivals, but the NCAA told the Big Ten there are no ties that it knows of between the Ohio State coach and the investigation.

At the LIBE committee hearing the journalist Apostolis Fotiadis testified that documents he and his colleagues obtained showed email threads granting a CSAM-scanning "key stakeholder" privileged access inside Johansson's department, and, under pressure from MEPs, the commissioner read out a list of her meetings with technology companies and child safety organizations. TechCrunch reported the session on 25 October 2023.

Fotiadis, one of the journalists involved in the investigation the committee was examining, had also been invited by the committee to participate in the exchange of views, and he took the opportunity to defend their reporting from direct public attacks by Johansson. In a blog post ahead of the hearing — which deploys a crisis-PR-esque headline claim of "setting the record straight" — she criticized the article as "a series of insinuations looking for a home", claiming it paired an outline of "a selection of meetings I had, of events I attended, or conferences I addressed" with "a conspiratorial tone" in an attempt "to create the impression of financial influence where there is none".

Asked by the LIBE committee about the accusation that the journalists had, essentially, been spreading disinformation — and specifically whether he believed Johansson and the Commission's response to it amounted to a restriction on media freedom — Fotiadis responded by saying he did not think that was the case. He went on to express surprise at how the Commission had reacted to the scrutiny, and at its instinct to deploy "spin-doctor" tactics to try to discredit the article rather than engaging with the substance of the concerns being raised. The Commission risks straying close to making attacks on journalists by using such tactics, Fotiadis warned, adding: "You cannot just dismiss everything by calling fake news" — before also noting that Johansson's office had declined multiple interview requests ahead of publication of the article.

On the substance of the reporting, Fotiadis said documents obtained by the journalists included email threads between Commission officials in Johansson's department, DG-Home, and a "key stakeholder" advocating for the use of technology for CSAM-scanning, which indicated what he described as "privileged access" that "speaks directly to cooperation" and goes "way beyond" mere consultation or exchange of views on the proposal.

He gave the committee the shape of that access. "It's an official chain discussing invitation, how the stakeholder would be able to allocate experts that would speak in workshops — first attended by representatives of the Member States, and then afterwards actually by ministers in the Council in a meeting chaired by commissioner Johansson. So when we say facilitate, it's obvious that the EU officials discuss what kind of experts will be available from this particular stakeholder to attend these meetings and to present the point of view, which seems to be a privileged access," he explained. "Also in the same email thread there's mention of EU officials being allocated to specifically attend the cooperation between the stakeholder and DG-Home on the proposal, which to our understanding is something that goes way beyond the level of consultations or exchange of views or exchange of opinions on the proposal and speaks directly to cooperation."

The committee then pressed Johansson about her contacts with companies and other lobbyists during the drafting of the CSAM proposal, with MEPs saying they wanted clear answers to the allegations of commercial interest and heavy lobbying when the Commission was setting up and drafting the proposal. In the event MEPs got some bare bones detail. Asked for a list of these contacts, the commissioner responded that she had met with Google six times; Microsoft, Meta and TikTok three times each; twice with Twitter (X); and once apiece with Apple and Amazon. She also said she had met with the child safety organizations Thorn (twice) and Brave Movement (twice), and with Tech Alliance and ICANN once apiece.

In wider responses related to concerns about how much commercial interest had influenced the Commission, Johansson highlighted her decision for the CSAM-scanning proposal to be "technology neutral" — meaning the draft regulation does not support any specific tech solution — with the suggestion being that EU lawmakers had resisted lobbying by companies for a law that would explicitly favor their existing tech tools.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. # FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. The fallout was still settling, but it might empower competitors such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, or help other AI startups get attention and funding as the industry watched OpenAI implode and put itself back together. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. GPT-4, which can write more naturally and fluently than previous models, remained largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, although it could be accessed for free through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Safari web browsers. Beyond GPT-4 and the OpenAI DevDay announcements, OpenAI had recently connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users, and with the integration of DALL-E 3, users could generate both text and images right inside ChatGPT.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.



---


# The Four Layers Of The GenAI Tech Stack

Rick Grinnell, founder and managing partner at Glasswing Ventures, categorizes the generative AI landscape into four distinct layers in the firm's proprietary view of the GenAI tech stack: foundation model providers, middle-tier companies, end-market or top-layer applications, and full stack or end-to-end vertical companies. He was answering, in TechCrunch's 13 October 2023 survey of AI investors, whether startups will build striated solutions for individual layers of the LLM stack — models, pre-training solutions and fine-tuning tools — or pursue a more vertical approach.

The relations between layers are stated as market-structure predictions. At the foundational layer, providers like Alphabet/Google's Bard, Microsoft/OpenAI's GPT-4, and Anthropic's Claude show that the more significant players possess inherent advantages regarding data accessibility, talent pool and computational resources; this layer is expected to settle into an oligopolistic structure like the cloud provider market, albeit with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption. Above the model itself lies the largest market opportunity: companies that introduce AI-powered APIs and operational layers for specific industries will create brand-new use cases and transform workflows, and by embracing this technology to revolutionize workflows, these companies stand to unlock substantial value. Within the stack, most of the opportunity lies in the application layer, where the best applications will harness their in-house expertise to build specialized middle-layer tooling and blend them with the appropriate foundational models, and where startups can use speed to their advantage as they work to "innovate, iterate and deploy solutions" to customers.

The range over which the model holds is explicitly limited by market immaturity. The market is still far from being crystallized; LLMs are still in their infancy, with adoption at large corporations and startups lacking full maturity and refinement, and robust tools and platforms are needed to enable broader utilization among businesses and individuals. Startups have the opportunity here to act quickly, find novel solutions to emerging problems, and define new categories. Even large tech companies recognize the gaps in their services and have begun investing heavily in startups alongside VCs — these companies apply AI to their internal processes and thus see the value startups bring to LLM deployment and integration, as with the recent investments from Microsoft, Nvidia, and Salesforce into companies like Inflection AI and Cohere.

A dissenting position within the same survey bears on how much weight the layer model should carry for strategy. Edward Tsai, a managing partner at Alumni Ventures, offered a potentially "controversial opinion that VCs and startups may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market."



---


# ChatGPT Misuse Fears Versus Observed Abuse

The premise under attack is the set of dire predictions made about ChatGPT's misuse: interestingly — and fortunately — some of them did not come to pass. Some researchers feared the chatbot would be used to generate disinformation on a massive scale, while others sounded the alarm over ChatGPT's phishing email-, spam- and malware-generating potential.

Those concerns had real effects: they pushed policymakers in Europe to mandate security assessments for any products using generative AI systems like ChatGPT, and led over 20,000 signatories — including Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak — to sign an open letter calling for the immediate pause of large-scale AI experiments like ChatGPT.

The counter-evidence is observational, and TechCrunch attaches an explicit time limit to it: examples of ChatGPT abuse in the wild have been few and far between — so far.

# Israel-Hamas War Context, October 2023

As of TechCrunch's 2023-10-14 report, Israel is retaliating militarily against the attacks on its people, on its soil, and the hostages subsequently taken by Hamas — the ruling organization in Gaza that kidnapped at least 150 people and took them into Gaza during brutal attacks on Israel last weekend that killed 1,300 people. That strategy has seen Israel pummeling the "Gaza Strip" with bombs to eradicate it of Hamas and to get its hostages back, and over 1,500 people in Palestine so far have been killed as a result.

The tech industry in Israel — the country's biggest export and its biggest single contributor to GDP — is also taking a big knock, but inevitably the impact on the smaller and more fragile ecosystem in Gaza has been significantly more serious, and the physical, economic and societal destruction resulting from that leaves any future for the tech industry there in doubt: quite simply, there is no escaping the consequences of the war for anyone, let alone tech workers. Israel has now amassed soldiers near the north of Gaza ahead of an expected ground offensive into the densely populated enclave, and about 1.1 million people living in northern areas have been told to leave in the next day. The UN has warned of "devastating humanitarian consequences" from these latest moves, and a total blockade on the territory is being enforced with fuel, food and water running out; Israel says it won't lift the restrictions unless Hamas frees all hostages. TechCrunch notes the piece was later edited to include relevant information about the attacks by Hamas.



---


# The Scale Of Israel's Technology Sector In 2022

Technology is, without question, a giant part of Israel's economy: in 2022 it contributed more than 18% of the country's GDP, the most of any single sector, according to the latest annual report from the Israel Innovation Authority at the time of writing in October 2023. A total of 14% of Israeli citizens work in high tech, which in a country of just 9.2 million people works out to about 1.3 million.

The startup base is correspondingly large. The active number of startups in the country is 9,000, third-highest in the world after the Bay Area and NYC, and over the last five years those startups collectively brought $95 billion into the country by way of venture capital. Combining the business development of startups with the larger tech companies operating in Israel — Intel, Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and many others have operations there — they collectively exported $71 billion in the prior year, 48.3% of the total amount exported across all industries.

These figures are the pre-war baseline, and the article's own caveat is that all of them are going to be significantly lower this year, not least because the disruptions of the war are coming directly on the heels of a major protest movement.

The context for that qualification is that the world was still coming to terms with Hamas' deadly attacks on Israelis the previous weekend, and with everything that had unfolded in the aftermath, including the barrage of retaliation strikes on Gaza. TechCrunch was explicit that the ramifications for the technology ecosystem pale in comparison to the human toll the fighting is taking on both sides, and that the industry is worth considering only because it bears on how the wider region will weather the destruction and one day recover. In such a small country, just about everyone knows someone who was directly affected by the attacks, or someone involved in the subsequent defense and retaliation — and often all three.



---


# Israel-Hamas Conflict: The Limited-Market-Impact Base Case

As of mid-October 2023, the Indian stock market's base case was that the Israel-Hamas hostilities would not escalate, and on that assumption the conflict was expected to have only a limited impact on markets. The grounds are threefold. First, the world can ill-afford another full-fledged war while economies are already battling high inflation and interest rates, an ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and a slowing China, which is precisely why many countries are trying to restrict any escalation; the market movement in the week before 14 October 2023 indicated that non-escalation was the presumed base case. Second, the US treasury secretary stated that the current conflict is not likely to significantly impact the global economic outlook. Third, history supports the same conclusion: a study of past conflicts between Israel and Hamas found that they tend to have limited impact on global financial markets, across crude oil, US 10-year yields, US equities and market volatility.

The warrant joining the evidence to the claim is that market impact tracks escalation, not the mere existence of hostilities: because the incentives of major countries point towards containment and because previous Israel-Hamas episodes transmitted little into the four channels that matter (oil, yields, equities, volatility), the priced-in outcome is a contained conflict. The argument is explicitly conditional on the non-escalation premise holding.



---


# Visual Intelligence Versus Human Sources

Technological sophistication and massive investment in intelligence means have greatly increased the IDF's visual intelligence gathering capabilities, according to former IDF Intelligence Directorate head General (ret.) Aharon Ze'evi-Farkash — but visual collection and human sources play different roles, and only the latter supplies interpretation.

"I'm sure it doesn't come at the expense of human sources, but as time goes by, gathering visual intelligence is easier than human sources and they bring better results," Ze'evi-Farkash said. "It's hard to bring in a Palestinian 'Ashraf Marwan,' the agent who passed the information to Israel before the Egyptian attack in 1973. It's a problem because the human source is essential to provide an interpretation of the rest of the information that's received, and to make decisions. Golda knew who Marwan was and expected to hear what he would say about the Egyptian deployment in the south." Two further gaps sit alongside that structural point: according to "The New York Times," a year before the attack the IDF stopped monitoring Hamas's radio communications, and the US had put stock in Israeli intelligence regarding Hamas in recent years and had not monitored it independently.



---


# Israeli Economy in the First Week of the Gaza War

As the first week of fighting in the war in Israel's south drew to a close, the main index on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the Tel Aviv 35, had fallen 6.4% over the week, with financial markets trying to gauge the damage the Israeli economy would sustain. Globes reported on 12 October 2023 that this was clearly a very significant event, but that the fog of war made it hard to estimate its full consequences.

The assessment came from Prof. Leo Leiderman, chief economic adviser at Bank Hapoalim and a professor of economics at Tel Aviv University, who set out for Globes his proposals for rehabilitating the economy and repairing the damage the war would cause. Asked what had been going through his mind in those first days, Leiderman said: "What most preoccupies me is not the economy but concern for the families of the soldiers, the wounded, and the captives, and solidarity with them. I have four relatives from Kibbutz Nir Oz who are still missing, and we have no information about them. I find it hard to understand how a war like this landed on us in a country as powerful as Israel. But we have no choice but to win."



---


# AI21 Labs' Tel Aviv Office Lease

Less than a month before the war, Globes reported a huge deal in which Amnon Shashua's unicorn AI21 Labs announced it was leasing 7,000 square meters for NIS 15 million annually in Tel Aviv's Da Vinci project.

Writing on 3 December 2023, Globes notes that it will now be interesting to see when the next such big office-space deal is signed in Tel Aviv following the impact of the Israel-Hamas war. Sources in the income-producing property sector in Israel say that over the past few weeks there has been some interest in the sector, although mainly for smaller deals involving hundreds of square meters each.



---


# Check Point Business Continuity During the Israel War

Like many companies in Israel, Tel Aviv-based Check Point has been impacted by the war: President Rupal Shah Hollenbeck said in November 2023 that some of its employees have been killed and others have been called to serve.

She stressed, however, that operations are normal and business is continuing as usual. Check Point has levels of redundancy around the world and research and development happening in several locations. In addition, the company's supply chain is 100% outside of Israel, and its tech support centres and data centres are found around the world. "We have the right level of redundancies and business continuity plans in place around the world," Hollenbeck said. "So we're okay."

# Walmart Cyber Monday 2023 Over-Ear Headphone Deals

WIRED's Walmart Cyber Monday roundup of 27 November 2023 recommended six discounted over-ear headphones: Sony's WH-1000XM5 and WH-1000XM4, Bose's QuietComfort Ultra, Sennheiser's HD 660S2, a cheaper pair of Sony noise cancellers and Soundcore's Life Q30.

As Sony's priciest wireless headphones, the WH-1000XM5 had a lot to live up to after the remarkably popular WH-1000XM4, but WIRED says they deliver with upgraded noise cancelling, a posh new design and a more refined sound signature — especially on sale. Bose's QuietComfort Ultra (9/10, WIRED Recommends) arrived in October 2023 with only one notable problem, their very high price; the discount makes it easier to get their class-leading noise cancelling, great sound and luxuriously comfy, feature-loaded design. Sony's older WH-1000XM4 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) have been a stalwart for years, offering excellent noise cancelling, warm and detailed sound and a ton of modern features in a comfy design that puts them among the best travel headphones you can buy.

WIRED's only complaints about Sennheiser's HD 660S2 (7/10, WIRED Review) — bass-enriched audiophile headphones — were the high price and stiff clamping force, and at this price it can live with the tighter fit given gloriously clear and richly detailed sound. Sony's "working-class" noise cancellers offer solid performance, clear sound and impressive battery life at a much more reasonable price than the brand's top offerings, and with this sale WIRED calls them some of the best value in their class from one of the top names in the business. Soundcore's Life Q30 are already impressive at full price thanks to noise cancelling that punches well above its class, so the deal makes them something of a steal, with accessible and adjustable sound quality, good features and great battery life.

# Sony WH-1000XM5 Black Friday Deal

The Sony WH-1000XM5 came down to $328 at Amazon, B&H and other retailers for Black Friday 2023 — a $72 drop from its $400 list price. Engadget's headphone roundup calls that a tie with the lowest price it has seen; the wider Black Friday roundup describes it as not an all-time low but about $70 off Sony's list price and $20 lower than the headphones' usual recurring sale price.

The XM5 is the top recommendation in Engadget's guide to the best wireless headphones and earned a review score of 95 last year. Its active noise cancellation is among the better options tested, its design is comfortable to wear over extended periods, its call quality is crisp and its battery lasts a solid 30 or so hours per charge. By default its sound goes heavy on the bass, which should please fans of hip-hop, EDM and pop, though the EQ curve can be customized through Sony's app, and like many Sony headphones it comes with useful bonus features such as "Speak-to-Chat," which automatically pauses your music when you start speaking.



---


# Bose QuietComfort 45 Headphones Deal Prices

The Bose QuietComfort 45 over-ear headphones fell to $229-$230 for October Prime Day 2023 and then to a record-low $199 in Amazon's Cyber Monday sale, according to Engadget and Mashable roundups across the season.

Mashable's Cyber Monday post of 27 November 2023 said there is "only one pair of Bose over-ear headphones you can grab for just under $200, and that's the QuietComfort 45s at a record-low price of $199", crediting the classic pair with top-of-the-line ANC, 20 hours of battery life and all-day comfort "for less than half of the AirPods Max's sale price". Engadget's 10 October 2023 Prime Day roundup put them at $230, about $80 cheaper than their usual selling price, and said they earned a spot in its best wireless headphone guide thanks to their comfortable if a little dated design, excellent ANC and balanced audio.

Engadget's headphone-specific Prime Day list, also 10 October 2023, listed them at $229 against a $329 list price (save $100), noting that $229 is $30 more than the lowest price it had tracked but still $80 below their average street price. That piece adds that this is another noise-cancelling set Bose recently replaced, but the differences between the QC 45 and the new QuietComfort Headphones appear small, so the older model is worth a look when discounted; Engadget gave the QC 45 a review score of 86 in 2021 and still likes its lightweight design, upper-tier ANC and easygoing sound. The caveats: you cannot manually adjust ANC intensity, unlike the newer model, and Sony's XM5 and XM4 provide longer battery life and a more versatile feature set for those willing to pay up.



---


# Sony Headphone And Earbud Deals During Prime Big Deal Day

Sony's headphones and earbuds were discounted at Best Buy during the anti-Prime Big Deal Day sales, led by the flagship WF-1000XM5 earbuds at $280, down from $300 — 7% off.

The over-ear Sony WH-1000XM4 was $250, down from $350 — 29% off; they can last up to 30 hours on a single charge and provide a comfortable listening experience thanks to their plush ear pads. The WF-1000XM5 earbuds improve upon the previous model with richer sound quality, slightly more powerful ANC, and vastly improved comfort thanks to their reduced size and weight. Sony's LinkBuds, which normally retail for $179.99, were $129.99 at Best Buy; the wireless earbuds work great for making calls and offer a unique "open-style" donut-shaped design that keeps the wearer aware of their environment. The Sony LinkBuds S were also on sale for $129.99, $70 off, at Best Buy; unlike the LinkBuds, these offer active noise cancellation, support for the LDAC lossless audio codec, and a slightly more conventional design. Sony's WH-CH720N were down to $99.99, $50 off, at Best Buy; the over-ear headphones may not offer all the bells and whistles of Sony's premium noise-canceling headphones, but they offer decent ANC and up to 35 hours of battery life.



---


# Sony LinkBuds Open-Ear Earbuds Deal Listings

Sony's standard LinkBuds appear in The Verge's December roundup at around $138 from Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Sony directly, against a normal $179.99, and in WIRED's Prime Day roundup (8/10, WIRED Recommends).

The Verge calls them a clear departure from conventional earbuds, using an "open-style" donut-shaped design instead of typical silicone ear tips, which allows better spatial awareness and, for some, a more comfortable fit; they provide crisp sound quality and excellent voice call performance, though as a result of that design they aren't very practical in louder environments. Possibly their coolest feature is the controls, which let you tap the side of your head rather than the earbud itself — "certainly very Sony." WIRED likes them for the same open-ear design that lets you hear what's going on around you, calling them a great option if you do a lot of city walking or use earbuds somewhere it's important to be aware of your surroundings, "like while feeding lions at the zoo."



---


# The Verge Staff Favorites Black Friday Roundup

Black Friday and Cyber Monday may be in the past, but some sales are still hanging around — although maybe not for long — and The Verge points readers to the rest of the Cyber Monday deals still available for more leftovers across all categories.

The roundup's premise is a recurring feature: every month or so The Verge asks its staff about their favorite stuff — pet toys, travel aids, kitchen gadgets, or straightforward tech — and the results are usually very different, very interesting, and a lot of fun.

In celebration of the annual post-Thanksgiving sales, the staff looked through recent "favorites" articles and found deals on a lot of the tech, kitchen tools, travel aids, and pet toys they like — listed in case readers had previously thought "well, that sort of sounds good, but it's a bit pricey," or "that's pretty cheap, but maybe I'll wait until the price goes down some more." Much of the gear is still discounted from Cyber Monday.



---


# WIRED's Pre-Black Friday 2023 Deal Window

WIRED's October 19, 2023 roundup covers the lull between sales events: with the latest Amazon-created Prime-themed sale day behind us and Black Friday slowly approaching, the deals world feels a bit like Pippin waiting on the edge of battle.

The point of the list is that the lull is not empty — there are still sales to score while waiting for winter to come — and its scope is the best deals right now on TVs, gaming gear, and other electronics.

qid: What company, recently discussed in TechCrunch articles, is not only facing criticism for its new generative AI model's architecture compared to GPT-4 but is also under scrutiny for its content practices on YouTube and accused of anticompetitive behavior that harms news publishers' revenue?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Theory: Copyright Liability Over OpenAI's Training Data

The proposition is that the board acted over mounting accusations that OpenAI's product was built on a dataset including thousands or millions of copyrighted works, with the CEO systematically downplaying the potential liability. TechCrunch's reporter notes that Altman told him at OpenAI's Dev Day earlier that month that the company does not want to incur any copyright problems by using datasets of pirated books, but that a lot of research he had been reading contradicts that, as does pretty much every AI data scientist he talks to. It is exceedingly hard to imagine that OpenAI built GPT-3 with the copyrighted books database, as seems to be the case, but not GPT-4 or succeeding models.

The framing of the hypothesis is a question about the board's likely reaction: if you were the board and facing those accusations, and your CEO had systematically downplayed the potential liability, how would you feel? "I'd feel very hurt."

What works against it is again the succession. If copyright liability was the reason, it seems unlikely that the board would promote the CTO; presumably OpenAI's Chief Science Officer Ilya Sutskever would also have been in the know, and he is still on the board.



---


# Google's Copyright Filing Against YouTube's Music Reassurances

MBW's counter to the idea that YouTube's rightsholder assurances settle the matter is that Google's take on copyright "harvesting" by generative AI models sits in odd contrast to the copyright-related reassurances YouTube was careful to make to the music industry during the pre-development, development, and trial launch of "Dream Track."

The premise attacked is that the platform relationship and the parent company's legal position can be read separately. MBW's sources close to Sony Music were keen to point out that the company's general ongoing relationship with YouTube and YouTube Music is a harmonious one — YouTube is now the second largest commercial partner of the major record companies, with a stated ambition to catch up with Spotify in the years ahead, and says it paid out over USD $6 billion to music rightsholders in the year to end of June 2022, with around $2 billion of that coming just from ads on user-generated content. However, the October US Copyright Office filing from Google has definitely put the cat amongst the pigeons at Sony Music HQ, as MBW is sure it has at the other two major record companies, because of its position that "Any prohibition or limitation on the use of copyrighted materials for purposes of AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the many opportunities that come with this technology." As well as part-explaining Sony Music's refusal to be included in Dream Track thus far, Google's USCO filing also perhaps explains the careful words selected by Robert Kyncl and especially Sir Lucian Grainge in their respective comments endorsing YouTube's AI experiment — Grainge's statement, after all, began: "We have a fundamental responsibility to our artists to ensure the digital ecosystem evolves to protect them and their work against unauthorized exploitation, including by generative AI platforms…"



---


# Prediction: AI-Generated Content Will Overwhelm Search

Daron Babin's proposition is that Google results will soon be even worse, dominated entirely by AI-generated crap designed to please the algorithms, produced and published at volumes far beyond anything humans could create — far beyond anything we had ever seen before.

The mechanism he gives is cost collapse at the bottom of the market: "All the assholes that are out there paying shitty link-building companies to build shitty articles now they can go and use the free version of GPT."

The prediction's strong form is that the volume is unstoppable: "They're not gonna be able to stop the onslaught of it," he said, then laughed and laughed, thinking about how puny and irrelevant Google seemed in comparison to the next generation of automated SEO. "You can't stop it!" What would falsify it is exactly that — Google proving able to stop the onslaught, so that results are not dominated by machine-produced content.



---


# Mozilla's Open Letter On AI Openness

The letter's claim is that openness makes AI safer, against the counter-position that proprietary control does. In an open letter published by Mozilla a few weeks before November 21, 2023, Meta's chief AI scientist Yann LeCun joined some 70 other signatories in calling for more openness in AI development, and the letter has since garnered more than 1,700 signatures. The backdrop is that Big Tech companies such as OpenAI and Google's DeepMind have called for more regulation, warning of catastrophic consequences if the AI levers were to meet the wrong hands — in other words, arguing that proprietary AI is safer than open source.

LeCun and his co-signatories disagree, and concede the risk before turning it around: "Yes, openly available models come with risks and vulnerabilities — AI models can be abused by malicious actors or deployed by ill-equipped developers. However, we have seen time and time again that the same holds true for proprietary technologies — and that increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous. The idea that tight and proprietary control of foundational AI models is the only path to protecting us from society-scale harm is naive at best, dangerous at worst." The warrant is that scrutiny, not secrecy, is what makes technology safe.

On a personal level, LeCun has accused the big-name AI players of trying to secure "regulatory capture of the AI industry" by lobbying against open AI R&D — an argument about motive rather than safety. And on a company level, Meta is doing all it can to encourage collaboration and "openness," recently partnering with Hugging Face to launch a new startup accelerator designed to spur adoption of open source AI models.



---


# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.



---


# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.

qid: Who is the individual associated with FTX and Alameda Research that was reported by The Verge as being overwhelmed by their growth, convinced a former Jane Street trader to join him as per Fortune, and is accused of committing fraud for personal gain according to TechCrunch?
context:
# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. # Sports Betting Terminology Glossary

CBS Sports set out the top Kentucky betting terms for new bettors on 13 October 2023, defining each bet type by what the bettor is actually wagering on and, in several cases, by a worked Kentucky example.

Against the spread means that instead of betting on an exact winner, the widely popular spread bet levels the playing field by letting you wager on how many points a team will win by: in basketball, if Kentucky is the 7.5-point favorite against Louisville then Kentucky covers by winning by 8 or more, while Louisville as the 7.5-point underdog covers by winning outright or losing by 7 or fewer. Money line is an elevated outright bet with odds adjusted to reflect a favored team and an underdog: if Kentucky is a -200 favorite against Florida you'd need to bet $200 to return $100, while Florida at +200 would return $200 on a $100 bet. An outright bet is the easiest wager to place and is perfect for horse racing, one of Kentucky's biggest sporting events — bettors choose one athlete, or thoroughbred, to win an entire event. An Over/Under has the sportsbook post an estimated total of both teams' final scores, with the bettor wagering on whether the actual final will be higher or lower: if the Over/Under for a Kentucky-Louisville basketball game is 125.5, you wager on the final total being Over 126 or Under 125. A player prop projects a player's stat at the end of a game and asks you to wager over or under that projection, with popular examples being how many touchdown passes a quarterback throws or how many three-pointers a basketball player hits; Kentucky is one of the 18 states that allows prop bets on collegiate athletes.

The remaining terms describe the market's participants and mechanics. The underdog is the team deemed less likely to win based on the odds, and a bet on one typically yields a larger return than a bet on the favorite; the favorite is deemed more likely to win, and bettors often pay a premium for backing one though they more often win outright. Consensus odds are generally defined as an average of all available betting markets, since different sportsbooks may price markets variably based on the action they've taken or their own interpretation of information. Futures markets encompass almost anything outside single-game bets — total regular-season wins, championship odds, MVP odds and more. A parlay requires two or more bets within a single wager, all of which must win: wagering $100 on a three-leg parlay at 6 to 1 odds could win $600 if all three legs win. Juice, also known as the vig or vigorish, is effectively the tax oddsmakers charge for handling a wager — if a book judges a game a virtual coinflip it may price both options at -110 to give itself a 10% rake on all the action. A push is a bet where neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins: if an over/under for total points is set at 44 and both teams combine for exactly 44, the result is a push and the principal is returned.
