qid: What company is at the center of antitrust discussions due to its default search engine deals with various tech companies, impact on the internet's appearance, potential legal outcomes regarding phones and app stores, and allegations of harming news publishers' revenue as reported by The Verge and TechCrunch?
context:
# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# The Sherman Act Verdict As The First Major Tech Antitrust Win Since Microsoft

Tim Sweeney argued that the jury's finding for Epic showed "the Sherman Antitrust Act works in the new era of tech monopolies" — his grounds being that no major antitrust verdict against a tech company that meant change and benefits for everybody had landed since the 1990s and US v. Microsoft, back in the early days of the internet.

The warrant joining claim and grounds is his account of present-day harm: the industry, he said, is "being strangled by a few gatekeepers imposing insane amounts of control and extracting huge taxes," which not only raise prices for consumers but also make a lot of kinds of products simply unviable. If the statute can still reach that conduct after a three-decade gap, then it remains a working remedy, which is why he called the verdict "a great day for all developers" and "much needed by the industry." Sweeney was speaking about a trial four years in the making, tracing back to a September 2019 email produced in discovery about a plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust.



---


# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# US Tech Giants' 2023 App Download Rankings

Meta and Google both lost ground in Apple's 2023 U.S. iPhone download rankings. Meta, which last year held the No. 3, No. 4 and No. 9 spots with WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook respectively, showed up in the top 10 this year with a slightly different mix: Facebook is gone from the charts, while Meta's new app Instagram Threads was the No. 3 app by U.S. downloads, with Instagram and WhatsApp following at No. 6 and No. 9, both slipping from their ranking last year.

Google had dominated last year's list with the No. 2 app YouTube, just behind TikTok, as well as No. 5 Google Maps, No. 6 Google Search and No. 7 Gmail. In 2023, however, Google's only two apps in the top 10 by downloads were No. 7 Google Search and No. 8 YouTube, both also slipping in ranking from last year.

The only other top app in the list not from Meta, Google or a Chinese firm was Max, formerly HBO Max, which showed up as the No. 3 app by downloads in the U.S.



---


# The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.

qid: Did the article from The Verge suggest that law enforcement adequately assessed the harassment threat towards Janani Umamaheswar and Alex Sinha, while the article from CBSSports.com considers Otto Wallin a greater threat to Anthony Joshua than Joseph Parker is to Deontay Wilder?
context:
# Otto Wallin Fighter Profile

Otto Wallin, as characterized by CBSSports.com on Dec. 23, 2023, is a 33-year-old native of Sweden considered much more a live dog than Joseph Parker — that is, a genuinely plausible upset threat rather than a safe opponent.

His discriminating features are size and stance: standing only half an inch shorter than Joshua's 6-foot-6 frame, Wallin is a southpaw. His reputation was extremely bolstered in 2019, when he lost a title shot against Tyson Fury despite opening up a cut that required 47 stitches above Fury's eye and coming close to giving Wallin a stoppage win.



---


# The Cyberstalker's Twitter Campaign Against Asian Academics

When Janani Umamaheswar looked up the Twitter account her former colleague had flagged in March 2022, she found thousands of tweets posted under S.'s name — most of them racist, sexual, vulgar, and violent, and little of the ranting coherent. The user tweeted at all hours, sometimes nearly a hundred times a day, and the tweets focused solely on three people: Umamaheswar, her husband Alex Sinha, and the Vassar professor Catherine Tan who had alerted them. The account had started posting in October of 2021 — seven months of tweets before they knew it existed. It featured an image of a white woman's face that Umamaheswar recognized as the student she once taught.

The targeting spread by association rather than contact. Sinha had never met or taught S., had never been employed on the same campus as his wife, and by then they lived over six hours away from her; Tan had likewise never taught or met S. and did not know her personally, but had published papers with Umamaheswar, and the account's author had linked Tan back to her, likely through that academic work and their benign social media interactions. Anyone Umamaheswar collaborated with professionally or even interacted with online had become a potential target. The tweets frequently denigrated all three for being Asian, using racial slurs against Umamaheswar and Sinha, alleging Sinha was abusive to his wife, and including lines such as "Live in hell bitch" and "I have super detailed deaths I like to think about them experiencing."

The threats escalated over time and across accounts. Sinha decided he needed to monitor the account closely, screenshot everything, and head off any potential danger; Umamaheswar did not want to keep looking. The graphic nature and racist sentiments sent a wave of fear and anger through Sinha, coming in a year when a white man had murdered six Asian women in three Atlanta-area spas and anti-Asian hate crimes had increased by over 300 percent. "There was this moment of 'wow, this has been happening all this time?'" Sinha said. "We moved to another state. We've been living our lives. We've been raising our kids." The tweets kept coming almost every week except during periods when S. was suspended by Twitter before restarting under a new account, reaching at least 40,000 tweets and counting by Sinha's estimate. They included racist slurs casting Sinha as a "dirty Indian hacker" and a terrorist; a tweet from April 16th, 2022 calling for someone to "get rid of" him; a post a month later pairing an image of a grisly murder in Game of Thrones with a farewell to Alex; and "I would like for these professors to die." As Sinha put it: "She calls for people to murder us. She says that she wants me raped. She would pay money to watch us bleed to death." Other tweets described wanting the three of them hanging off a cliff so she could step on their hands and watch them fall, and ended: "I want them to suffer." While Sinha captured the images, Umamaheswar began writing letters to her current administration and to Vassar on behalf of Tan, alerting them to her history with S.



---


# Joseph Parker's Upset Win Over Deontay Wilder

Kiwi heavyweight Joseph Parker, a big underdog according to FanDuel Sportsbook, beat former champion Deontay Wilder in Riyadh on the card reported by The Roar on 23 December 2023, ruining Wilder's chances of facing Anthony Joshua.

The 31-year-old Parker looked the better fighter throughout while the 38-year-old Wilder looked his age in a match-up of former heavyweight champions. Parker, moving to 34-3-0, dominated from the start, landing powerful punches with his right hand while keeping Wilder on his heels with a smart and methodical approach; there was only one round in which Wilder got the better of him.

Parker described the plan afterwards: "Dangerous fight, tough fight, we trained very hard for this. We had great momentum coming into this fight. The strategy was to stay calm, stay relaxed, stay focused … every minute of every round. This is a great finish to the year." Wilder's account was that "My timing was off a little bit. He did a great job of avoiding a lot of my punches. I did feel like I had the upper hand, but things happen. We move on to the next step."



---


# Musk's Position On Disinformation

Musk's answer to the EU's warning did not dispute the regulator's authority so much as the premise underneath it: that "disinformation" is a category anyone can independently arbitrate. Replying on X to journalist Glenn Greenwald — who had attacked the DSA as a "censorship law" that he claimed would be used to "punish X" — Musk avoided expressing the same trenchant criticism of the EU's approach and instead invited relativism, writing: "Let the public hear exactly what this disinformation consists of and decide for themselves."

That reply attacks the EU's inferential step rather than its legal one. The bloc's demand that X be "effective" against disinformation presupposes that false content can be identified as such by some competent party, so that a platform's failure to act on it is a measurable compliance gap. Musk's move was to sow doubt that disinformation is something that can be independently arbitrated at all, implying that fact-checking is merely a convenient exercise for targeting different opinions — essentially echoing Greenwald's position — by claiming that "many times" the "official fact-checker" has been found making false statements, before adding, for plausible deniability, the rhetorically empty offer that "Maybe this is the case here, maybe not". If no arbiter is trustworthy, the adjudication the EU's obligation depends on cannot be performed, and the public becomes the only judge.

TechCrunch treats this as of a piece with a wider mismatch. A rule of law clash between Musk and the EU had looked increasingly inevitable in recent months, and had indeed been predicted by some industry watchers since rumours of the billionaire's plan to take over Twitter emerged the previous year; asking Musk to be "effective" against disinformation, the publication wrote, is a bit like asking the sea to stop moving. Musk's extremely iterative — or just plain erratic and arbitrary — management style is so far from the responsive and responsible qualities the EU's rulebook demands of digital leaders that TechCrunch found it hard to see how the clash could end well for either side. But this is how the regulatory dance must go, and after the dance comes the denouement: if a DSA breach is confirmed, enforcement follows, and actual penalties might be a bit harder for Musk to troll.

A second exchange illustrates the practical cost of the position. Musk chipped into a conversation in which an X user had commented on a screengrab of an apparent exchange of threats between Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Khamenei, and an official Israeli government account in relation to the war, writing: "Amazing to see this exchange!" The irony, TechCrunch notes, is that Musk's destruction of Twitter's legacy verification of notable accounts means you can't, at a glance, be sure whether the exchange really happened — so the "decide for themselves" standard is being applied on a platform whose own authenticity signals he removed.



---


# SBF's Defense Counsel

Bankman-Fried will be represented by the firm Cohen & Gresser, with Mark Cohen — a high-profile defense attorney and former federal prosecutor — as lead attorney. That was the state of play in TechCrunch's "where we are today" account of the case on 2023-10-01.

Cohen's name was already familiar from another trial: he also represented Ghislaine Maxwell in her sex trafficking trial related to Jeffrey Epstein. He requested an early release for Bankman-Fried, but was denied.



---


# IPVM's Rebuttal Of Hikvision's Human Rights Record

Experts on the surveillance tools used in the repression of Uyghurs reject Hikvision's compliance defence on the ground that the company's own history shows it has not followed through on previous commitments to preserve human rights — attacking the premise that its assurances can be taken at face value.

The specific rebuttal comes from Conor Healy, director of government research at the surveillance research publication Internet Protocol Video Market (IPVM), in a statement to the Guardian.

"Hikvision's critical role in surveilling and oppressing Muslims in Xinjiang and the company's failure to take accountability shows that the company is not serious about ethics or protecting human rights," Healy said.

# AI21 Labs' Tel Aviv Office Lease

Less than a month before the war, Globes reported a huge deal in which Amnon Shashua's unicorn AI21 Labs announced it was leasing 7,000 square meters for NIS 15 million annually in Tel Aviv's Da Vinci project.

# Israeli Economy in the First Week of the Gaza War

As the first week of fighting in the war in Israel's south drew to a close, the main index on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the Tel Aviv 35, had fallen 6.4% over the week, with financial markets trying to gauge the damage the Israeli economy would sustain. Globes reported on 12 October 2023 that this was clearly a very significant event, but that the fog of war made it hard to estimate its full consequences.

The assessment came from Prof. Leo Leiderman, chief economic adviser at Bank Hapoalim and a professor of economics at Tel Aviv University, who set out for Globes his proposals for rehabilitating the economy and repairing the damage the war would cause. Asked what had been going through his mind in those first days, Leiderman said: "What most preoccupies me is not the economy but concern for the families of the soldiers, the wounded, and the captives, and solidarity with them. I have four relatives from Kibbutz Nir Oz who are still missing, and we have no information about them. I find it hard to understand how a war like this landed on us in a country as powerful as Israel. But we have no choice but to win."



---


# The Surge In Terror Financing Reports After October 7

Before October 7, IMPA received about 100 reports a day dealing with terror financing; that number jumped to about 1,000 — a 900% increase.

"Overnight, we started receiving hundreds of reports about unusual activity by customers of financial institutions in the State of Israel," Ostrovitch-Levi says. "There is a 900% increase in reports on terror financing, and we don't waste time, everything happens very, very quickly. As we receive the information, we simultaneously pass it on to the operational professionals who locate the money pipelines, and block them. Some information will not necessarily lead to terror financing, but we don't have time to waste. Bank CEOs call and draw our attention to the information they convey to us that warrants special attention." Asked whether information from banks and financial institutions has led to blocking a money pipeline for terrorism, she said: "There was very high-quality intelligence that we passed on to the security agencies. # Visual Intelligence Versus Human Sources

Technological sophistication and massive investment in intelligence means have greatly increased the IDF's visual intelligence gathering capabilities, according to former IDF Intelligence Directorate head General (ret.) Aharon Ze'evi-Farkash — but visual collection and human sources play different roles, and only the latter supplies interpretation.

"I'm sure it doesn't come at the expense of human sources, but as time goes by, gathering visual intelligence is easier than human sources and they bring better results," Ze'evi-Farkash said. "It's hard to bring in a Palestinian 'Ashraf Marwan,' the agent who passed the information to Israel before the Egyptian attack in 1973. It's a problem because the human source is essential to provide an interpretation of the rest of the information that's received, and to make decisions. Golda knew who Marwan was and expected to hear what he would say about the Egyptian deployment in the south." Two further gaps sit alongside that structural point: according to "The New York Times," a year before the attack the IDF stopped monitoring Hamas's radio communications, and the US had put stock in Israeli intelligence regarding Hamas in recent years and had not monitored it independently.

In 2022-23, Israel's share in exports from India stood at 1.87 per cent, with India shipping goods worth around $8 billion to Israel; petroleum products accounted for 65 per cent of those exports, followed by gems and jewellery at 15 per cent and electrical machinery at 3 per cent. Two disruption conditions are attached to the observation. Trade can be adversely impacted if operations at the Israeli ports are disrupted. Separately, fertiliser movement from Israel's Port of Ashdod accounts for 3 per cent of global potash supply, and any disruption on that front will also be a dampener.



---


# Check Point Business Continuity During the Israel War

Like many companies in Israel, Tel Aviv-based Check Point has been impacted by the war: President Rupal Shah Hollenbeck said in November 2023 that some of its employees have been killed and others have been called to serve.

She stressed, however, that operations are normal and business is continuing as usual. Check Point has levels of redundancy around the world and research and development happening in several locations. In addition, the company's supply chain is 100% outside of Israel, and its tech support centres and data centres are found around the world. "We have the right level of redundancies and business continuity plans in place around the world," Hollenbeck said. "So we're okay."



---


# The Scale Of Israel's Technology Sector In 2022

Technology is, without question, a giant part of Israel's economy: in 2022 it contributed more than 18% of the country's GDP, the most of any single sector, according to the latest annual report from the Israel Innovation Authority at the time of writing in October 2023. A total of 14% of Israeli citizens work in high tech, which in a country of just 9.2 million people works out to about 1.3 million.

The startup base is correspondingly large. The active number of startups in the country is 9,000, third-highest in the world after the Bay Area and NYC, and over the last five years those startups collectively brought $95 billion into the country by way of venture capital. Combining the business development of startups with the larger tech companies operating in Israel — Intel, Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and many others have operations there — they collectively exported $71 billion in the prior year, 48.3% of the total amount exported across all industries.

These figures are the pre-war baseline, and the article's own caveat is that all of them are going to be significantly lower this year, not least because the disruptions of the war are coming directly on the heels of a major protest movement.

The context for that qualification is that the world was still coming to terms with Hamas' deadly attacks on Israelis the previous weekend, and with everything that had unfolded in the aftermath, including the barrage of retaliation strikes on Gaza. TechCrunch was explicit that the ramifications for the technology ecosystem pale in comparison to the human toll the fighting is taking on both sides, and that the industry is worth considering only because it bears on how the wider region will weather the destruction and one day recover. In such a small country, just about everyone knows someone who was directly affected by the attacks, or someone involved in the subsequent defense and retaliation — and often all three.

qid: Does the 'Fortune' article suggest that the foundation of FTX's success is the same as the 'TechCrunch' articles' implication that Sam Bankman-Fried's actions were based on fraudulent intentions?
context:
# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

# The Swans' Matchday Experience Model For Local Attendance

The Sydney Swans' attendance strategy, described on 26 October 2023 by executive GM of marketing Loretta Johns, has two linked components: target local communities, and make match days compelling for fans on and off the field.

The off-field half is delivered through food, entertainment and promotion. At North Sydney Oval that means quince paste and hand-picked grapes, cheddar cheese and biscuits in a little box with beautiful wrapping — "they've really thought about what they're doing and made it an experience."

# Sydney Swans' First AFLW Finals Berth

Sydney, winless in their debut season the previous year, secured eighth spot and their first AFLW finals berth in 2023 by storming home with three unanswered goals against Fremantle, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

"Any club that's able to go from winless one year to a finals berth, it's incredible," Sydney co-captain Chloe Molloy told Fox Footy after the match. "You can see the emotion on the girls' faces. Coming into the season, the odds were against us. Just to get into the eight, we've managed to do that. We're stoked. It's pretty special for the club." Missing star ruck Ally Morphett to a season-ending wrist injury, Laura Gardiner stood tallest in the midfield — the 20-year-old off-season recruit from Geelong had the ball on a string with a game-high 33 disposals and 18 contested possessions — while Molloy (two goals), Montana Ham, Rebecca Privitelli and Brooke Lochland hit the scoreboard.

The Swans' rise had been signalled earlier in the season by a record-breaking win over the Western Bulldogs, propelled by a Chloe Molloy masterclass: after a five-goal second term that included a four-minute burst of three majors, Sydney had already brought up their largest score in an AFLW game by half-time, and while the Bulldogs held their own in the last quarter the damage was done. The total was also the biggest the Dogs had conceded in their history, topping the 83 Melbourne kicked against them in round three. Molloy, the Swans' star off-season recruit and a former Collingwood ace, was a class above, kicking 3.4 from her 28 possessions and playing a crucial role in setting up numerous other Sydney goals. "She was itching to get in there [in the midfield]," Swans coach Scott Gowans said. "We kept her forward deliberately. It was important Chloe played a good block of time forward so we could have a look at it." # Pochettino And Arteta's Friendship From PSG

Mauricio Pochettino calls Mikel Arteta "family" because the two joined Paris Saint-Germain at the same time in early 2001 — Pochettino then 28, Arteta 18 — and hit it off immediately, with Pochettino wowed by Arteta's charisma and his reading of the game. "Already, he was a coach," Pochettino said.

The relationship explains Pochettino's tolerance of what some perceive as Arteta's histrionic touchline behaviour, about which he has no qualms. "It's how you are and about your character," Pochettino said. "He feels football. I am 51 and still sometimes I feel that decisions are no good or unfair. You are competitive. Like with Mikel or myself or other coaches that played football, in our minds, we still believe we can play. Still, we have the animal instinct. We cannot be thinkers."

The boundary Pochettino draws is not suppression but direction: for him it must be about channeling the emotion in the right way rather than stifling it. # UK Support Organisations For Older Adults

The Guardian's 10 October 2023 piece lists five organisations older adults and their families can turn to, each defined by a distinct function.

Age UK has a database of social activities and groups for older folk. The Walking Football Association keeps keen amateur footballers playing long into their 50s and 60s. Action for Elders offers social and exercise programmes.

# Mary Jane's Mission Pacing And The Verdict On Spider-Man 2

Essentially Sports argued on 1 November 2023 that the best thing about Mary Jane's quests in Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is that they never try to overpower the ongoing story: the claim is that restraint improves them, and the warrant is that keeping her sequences within limits lets each character shine without her missions overlapping Peter's or Miles' stories.

The grounds are about proportion. The game's narrative remains intact no matter what, and there never occurs a feeling of the developers trying too hard to make her missions stretch beyond their boundaries; although they are designed well this time, the article commends Insomniac's team for keeping a limit on not making MJ's gameplay moments seem forced or going beyond a certain point. At times it may feel like her playable sequences should have been extended, but the article treats the decision not to as correct — sometimes less is more and fine. Despite Spider-Man 2 being more of Peter's story in its entirety, MJ's role has been given equal significance, with visible growth in her arc especially considering her profession as a journalist; she is Peter's love interest, but that's not everything she's there for, and players can easily see it happening throughout the game's duration.

The verdict concedes a limit on the claim before stating it. It's obvious to expect that a lot of fans who didn't like MJ's missions in the first installment won't like her this time either, but considering how she was before and how she is in Spider-Man 2, the overall change is quite praiseworthy. Her missions now have actual meaning attached to them rather than acting like fillers; players who want a few interesting moments aside from the main quests featuring Miles and Peter can get a sense of finishing well-designed stealth quests, and Mary's gameplay missions end up increasing the overall quality of Spider-Man 2 — so it is great to see Insomniac improving on this aspect instead of removing it completely.

# Age Appropriateness of the Five Nights at Freddy's Movie

Polygon's conclusion, published 2023-10-26, is that the PG-13 rating's 12-or-13 age cutoff is probably about right for the Five Nights at Freddy's movie — though, as with any such judgment, every kid is different.

The question arises because, for an ostensible horror franchise built on nostalgia for and subversion of animatronic characters dating to the 1980s, the FNAF games have a surprising number of young fans. Their kid appeal echoes a time when playgrounds were alight with elementary school kids describing the antics of Freddy and/or Jason, whether witnessed firsthand or pieced together from rumors. Unlike A Nightmare on Elm Street or Friday the 13th, however, Freddy's is rated PG-13 rather than R.

The grounds for leniency are that the movie is far from an unrelenting thrill ride: it is not as intense as fellow PG-13 horror movies The Ring or Drag Me to Hell, the most ghoulish aspects of the Freddy's backstory are kept off screen or entirely unmentioned, none of its set-pieces seem like pure nightmare fuel, and several of the titular five nights pass without much incident at all.

The grounds for caution are that there are plentiful cheap music-sting jump scares and a few gruesome bits of junior-level gore. Violence-wise this is a harder PG-13 than the average superhero movie — something Polygon expects will only entice its younger YouTube-versed fans more.

Against that optimism, President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. told members of the US-ASEAN Business Council who visited Malacañang, in remarks reported by ABS-CBN on 9 August 2023: "We worry about our debt-to-GDP ratio in the Philippines, as it stands at about 63% and that's a little high for us and it is not ideal."



---


# Philippine Inflation In 2023 And The Government Response

In his second State of the Nation Address, President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. singled out inflation as the country's most pressing problem. In the first nine months of 2023, inflation averaged 6.6%, far above the upper end of the 2-4% target range set by the BSP. If left unchecked, inflation could undermine growth: it not only increases costs to organizations but sets in motion second-round effects as workers start demanding higher wages, consequently increasing business costs and discouraging investments.

Inflation is partly driven by supply-side issues, and the government is allocating more resources to the agriculture sector to boost production. Marcos mentioned that the National Government had distributed 28,000 new tools and machinery to farmers, and that an additional 600 km of farm-to-market roads were laid down to support the 14 million hectares of farmland, enhancing farmer access to markets. He also signed Executive Order No. 28 in May, forming the Inter-Agency Committee on Inflation and Market Outlook, tasked with keeping inflation within government targets and boosting the economy.

# Fiscal Cost Channels of the Israel-Gaza War

Leo Leiderman set out the war's cost to the Israeli budget as a set of direct and indirect channels: "As with any war, the current war has and will have direct and indirect impacts."

On the spending side, the war will substantially raise defence spending in the coming years for procurement of equipment, ammunition and advanced systems in accordance with the new needs. A second direct expense is payment for the reserve duty days of those mobilised. A third channel runs through financing costs: given current interest rate levels around the world, the cost of servicing public debt as a proportion of GDP will rise.

On the revenue side, he expects a decline in state revenues from taxation. The combined result of these channels is a rise in the fiscal deficit.

# Global Rate Shock Risk to Emerging Market Debt

Rajan Jain, Head of Credit Research at SBI Caps, framed the open question in a note: whether the yield curve dynamics mean the US is moving to a structurally higher-rate economy versus the post-GFC normal remains moot, with important implications for investment demand and system risk.

The transmission he describes runs outward from US rates. These movements have had a cascading effect on global economies, which have seen routs in their respective bond markets besides a fresh round of currency depreciation.

The vulnerable case is specific: emerging market economies with large volumes of USD-denominated debt, which could be caught in a vicious circle where their external debt in local currency terms balloons due to a strong DXY while their servicing ability is impaired by tepid economic activity owing to high rates. The stress is not confined to them — even advanced economies have felt the heat, and the ECB and others have maintained a hawkish narrative, Jain said.

# Australian Inflation Data And The RBA's Near-Certain November Rise

GSFM investment strategist Stephen Miller said the inflation data, taken with the October Reserve Bank board meeting minutes — which revealed the board had "low tolerance for a slower return of inflation to target than currently expected" — made the possibility of an interest rate rise from the central bank in November a "near certainty."

Commodity prices nonetheless supported mining companies, as iron ore prices increased 2.9 per cent overnight, bolstering Australia's iron ore giants. This came as Chinese President Xi Jinping stepped up support for the world's second-biggest economy and major commodity trading partner for Australia, issuing additional sovereign debt, raising the budget deficit ratio and even making an unprecedented visit to the central bank. On Wall Street, the benchmark S&P 500 index closed 0.7 per cent higher ahead of tech giants Microsoft and Alphabet reporting results after the close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.6 per cent and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 gained 0.9 per cent. Shares in Microsoft climbed 5 per cent in after-hours trading after the company said its sales jumped 13 per cent to $US56.5 billion ($88.9 billion) and profits climbed 27 per cent to $US22.3 billion in the three months through September.



---


# Powell's Rejection Of Monetary-Fiscal Coordination

Fed Chair Jerome Powell, sitting to Christine Lagarde's right at the panel discussion, signaled he wasn't ready to rely on the kind of cooperation between monetary and fiscal policy she described as sometimes helpful.

His stated ground rejects the premise that the central bank's mandate is contingent on what fiscal authorities do: "Our assignment is to deliver price stability kind of regardless of the stance of fiscal policy."



---


# FAPE And PEAC: History And Programs

FAPE, the Fund for Assistance to Private Education, was part of the Special Fund for Education set aside by the American government in 1963 from the surplus funds authorized by the War Damage Act of 1962, and was organized under Executive Order 156 issued by President Ferdinand Marcos on 5 November 1968. From initial seed money of $6,154,000, or P215 million based on the 1968 peso-to-dollar exchange rate, the FAPE fund had in 55 years barely grown to P277 million; in contrast, the trustees managing the fund expanded their services, basically as a service provider to the DepEd, and as a consequence it was spun off as a separate organization, the Private Education Assistance Committee, PEAC.

Over the years PEAC has evolved into co-implementing externally funded programs, namely the DepEd's Education Service Contracting, Teachers' Salary Subsidy, the SHS Voucher Program, In-Service Training, and Bayanihan for Basic Education, as well as implementing internally funded programs of assistance for private education in the areas of training, school quality assurance, school improvement programs, and grants programs. In sum, PEAC has been an effective instrument to operationalize "complementarity" between private and public schools as provided in the Philippine Constitution, and an incorruptible partner of the education agencies in efficiently co-implementing national subsidy programs for students and teachers in private schools.

# Growth In India's High-Net-Worth Investor Population

According to recent wealth reports cited by Business Line on 28 October 2023, the population of Indian high-net-worth individuals holding assets worth $1 million or more, which was 7.9 lakh in 2022, will rise to 16.5 lakh, a 107 per cent increase in five years.

The observation is offered as the consequence of a cause: India's remarkable economic growth has resulted in a notable increase in the country's high-net-worth investors. # Adobe Analytics And Salesforce Measurement Methodology

The two sources of holiday e-commerce figures rest on different measurement bases: Adobe Analytics' figures are based, it says, on 1 trillion visits to U.S. retail sites, 100 million SKUs and 18 product categories, while Salesforce says it taps data from 1.5 billion consumers in its research.

qid: What is the name of the leading AI development company that is not only the creator behind ChatGPT and is planning to release GPT-4 with vision alongside GPT-4 Turbo API, but is also anticipated to champion an "app store for AI" as a key platform for AI tools and toys, as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# GPT Model Releases From GPT-3.5 To GPT-4

ChatGPT first launched to the public as OpenAI quietly released GPT-3.5: the model broke cover with ChatGPT, a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that is essentially a general-purpose chatbot able to engage with a range of topics including programming, TV scripts and scientific concepts.

Writers everywhere rolled their eyes at the new technology, much as artists did with OpenAI's DALL-E model, but the chat-style iteration seemingly broadened its appeal and audience. GPT-4 followed on March 14: a powerful image- and text-understanding AI model, released to paying ChatGPT Plus users and through a public API, with developers able to sign up on a waitlist to access the API.



---


# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.



---


# ChatGPT Plus And The Plugin Platform

March saw more of the same, with OpenAI announcing a new subscription-based service — ChatGPT Plus — which offers users the chance to skip to the head of the queue during peak usage hours and adds features not found in the free version. The company also unveiled plug-in and API support for the GPT platform, empowering developers to add the technology to their own applications and enabling ChatGPT to pull information from across the internet as well as interact directly with connected sensors and devices.

ChatGPT also notched 100 million users per day in March, 30 times higher than two months prior, and companies from Slack and Discord to GM announced plans to incorporate GPT and generative AI technologies into their products.



---


# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.



---


# The Four Layers Of The GenAI Tech Stack

Rick Grinnell, founder and managing partner at Glasswing Ventures, categorizes the generative AI landscape into four distinct layers in the firm's proprietary view of the GenAI tech stack: foundation model providers, middle-tier companies, end-market or top-layer applications, and full stack or end-to-end vertical companies. He was answering, in TechCrunch's 13 October 2023 survey of AI investors, whether startups will build striated solutions for individual layers of the LLM stack — models, pre-training solutions and fine-tuning tools — or pursue a more vertical approach.

The relations between layers are stated as market-structure predictions. At the foundational layer, providers like Alphabet/Google's Bard, Microsoft/OpenAI's GPT-4, and Anthropic's Claude show that the more significant players possess inherent advantages regarding data accessibility, talent pool and computational resources; this layer is expected to settle into an oligopolistic structure like the cloud provider market, albeit with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption. Above the model itself lies the largest market opportunity: companies that introduce AI-powered APIs and operational layers for specific industries will create brand-new use cases and transform workflows, and by embracing this technology to revolutionize workflows, these companies stand to unlock substantial value. Within the stack, most of the opportunity lies in the application layer, where the best applications will harness their in-house expertise to build specialized middle-layer tooling and blend them with the appropriate foundational models, and where startups can use speed to their advantage as they work to "innovate, iterate and deploy solutions" to customers.

The range over which the model holds is explicitly limited by market immaturity. The market is still far from being crystallized; LLMs are still in their infancy, with adoption at large corporations and startups lacking full maturity and refinement, and robust tools and platforms are needed to enable broader utilization among businesses and individuals. Startups have the opportunity here to act quickly, find novel solutions to emerging problems, and define new categories. Even large tech companies recognize the gaps in their services and have begun investing heavily in startups alongside VCs — these companies apply AI to their internal processes and thus see the value startups bring to LLM deployment and integration, as with the recent investments from Microsoft, Nvidia, and Salesforce into companies like Inflection AI and Cohere.

A dissenting position within the same survey bears on how much weight the layer model should carry for strategy. Edward Tsai, a managing partner at Alumni Ventures, offered a potentially "controversial opinion that VCs and startups may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market."

# Shai Hope's Anchor Innings In The T20 Decider

Shai Hope's 43 off 43 balls steered West Indies to their target in the deciding T20I, an exemplary anchoring innings that the live blog identified as the wicket England really needed.

At 16 overs West Indies were 112-4 with Hope on 29, and he opened the face to steer Rehan Ahmed for his first boundary; Rehan had struggled as the series progressed, and later in the over Powell muscled him over long-on for six, leaving West Indies 21 runs from a hat-trick of T20 series wins that year — South Africa away, India and England at home. # Andre Russell's Comeback In The First T20I

Andre Russell was named Player of the Match in the first T20I against England, taking 3-29 and smashing 29 not out off just 14 deliveries in his first T20I in over two years.

He seemed very pleased to be back in maroon, saying: "Life is so funny. Since when I got selected for the West Indies two weeks ago I've been dreaming of being man of the match." # India vs Australia At The 1983 World Cup

India met Australia for the very first time at a World Cup in 1983 and lost that match by 162 runs. Australia posted a target of 321 runs courtesy of a brilliant 110 runs off 131 balls by Trevor Chappell, with Kapil Dev taking a fifer in that innings; India crumbled within 158 runs, with Ken MacLeay picking up six wickets for Australia.

India got their revenge in the very same World Cup, defeating the Australian side by 118 runs. India set a target of 248 runs after being bowled out in 55.5 overs, with Yashpal Sharma scoring 40 off 40 and Jeff Thompson and Rodney Hogg picking up three wickets each for Australia. Samu Kerevi said he did not perform at the 2023 Rugby World Cup where he wanted to, after injuries conspired to limit his potential in France, Wide World Of Sports reported on 7 October 2023.

Kerevi was photographed holding his face in disbelief in one of the defining images of the World Cup, after the Wallabies were pumped 40-6 by Wales in Lyon. # Australia Women's White-Ball Reset Before The 2024 T20 World Cup

Australia have spoken about shifting their mindset in white-ball cricket after the losses in England, pursuing a more attacking approach, and the three ODIs against India in the following week plus three ensuing T20s will be the first showing of that, with the hosts also a rising force in the white-ball game, as reported by The Roar on 24 December 2023.

Alyssa Healy framed the six matches as both a proving ground and a staging post. "Within our group we're really comfortable with where we're at, and the progression we're on," she said. "Ultimately there's a big T20 World Cup in Bangladesh towards the end of next year, that is a real carrot for us. These are the sort of big trophies that we're wanting to win. # India's 1983 World Cup Semi-Final Against England

India beat England by six wickets with 5.2 overs to spare in the semi-final at Manchester on 22 June 1983, storming into a World Cup final for the first time. India had lost in the first round of the 1975 and 1979 World Cups and were underdogs in the third World Cup, which was being held in England for the third consecutive time, but in that tournament India wronged many of their critics by reaching the semi-finals and playing the mighty hosts.

With the ball, skipper Kapil Dev struck three wickets while Roger Binny and Man-of-the-Match Mohinder Amarnath took two each as India restricted England to 213 all out in 60 overs. # The First ODI Cricket World Cup, 1975

England hosted the inaugural ODI World Cup in 1975 and held the event the following three times too, with the West Indies winning the first tournament.

The playing conditions were unlike the modern game: initially the game was played in cricket whites and with a red ball instead of a white ball. Eight teams took part in that inaugural tournament — India, Pakistan, England, Australia, West Indies, New Zealand and a composite team from East Africa and Sri Lanka. Current cricketing powerhouse South Africa was banned at the time from international sport due to its policy of racial segregation under the Apartheid system, and so did not take part in the first ODI World Cup.

The early honours went to two teams. The West Indies won the first tournament and defended the title in the second World Cup in 1979, while India's first taste of glory came when they clinched the trophy in 1983 by defeating the West Indies by 43 runs in the final.

context:
# Bankman-Fried's Defense Strategy And Appeal Groundwork

Bankman-Fried's defense can itself introduce risks for people who dealt with him, because his lawyers have several simultaneous objectives: first and foremost proving their client not guilty, but also — just in case they don't get the outcome they want — laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments.

The consequence is procedural: any piece of evidence they want to introduce for those two purposes has to come into play during the trial. Christopher LaVigne notes that Bankman-Fried's lawyers are already marking arguments that his constitutional rights are being violated by his pretrial incarceration because, among other things, his internet connection wasn't good enough for him to plan his defense — which could be grounds for an appeal.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.
