# TikTok Bans And ByteDance Data Concerns

One remaining and major potential pitfall for TikTok is the rise in tensions between China and Western countries: amid concerns that parent company ByteDance may be sharing TikTok user data with the Chinese government, numerous governments — from the US to the European Union to Australia — have banned the app from government-issued devices.

A small number of jurisdictions have banned or are attempting to ban TikTok altogether, including Montana and, most recently, Nepal.

qid: Which company, covered by both The Verge and TechCrunch, has influenced internet navigation and local search ranking, while also spending billions to be the default search engine and facing antitrust allegations for affecting news publishers' revenues?
context:
# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# Lawsuit Redactions As Signal: The Amazon Precedent

TechCrunch reads heavy redaction as itself informative: you know it is bad news for the company when they request pages and pages of redactions.

The precedent it cites is recent. This recently happened with Amazon as well, and it turned out they were trying to hide the existence of a price-hiking algorithm that skimmed billions from consumers.

The comparison is used to rank severity rather than to equate the two: it is much worse, TechCrunch writes, when you are redacting COPPA complaints.

qid: Who is the individual that, before the FTX collapse, was portrayed as a reliable figure in the cryptocurrency sector, and is now facing allegations of directing a multi-billion dollar misappropriation of customer funds and committing fraud for personal gain, with these accusations being discussed in courtroom updates and analyses by both TechCrunch and The Verge?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article on Meta's GDPR compliance concerns suggest the same legal issue as the TechCrunch article on Meta's responsibility for teen social media monitoring, and does it also differ from the TechCrunch article on Meta's moderation bias affecting Palestinian voices?
context:
# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# The GDPR Track Running Alongside The Consumer Complaint

As of November 30, 2023 the data protection question about Meta's pay-or-consent offer was unresolved and running on a separate track from the consumer complaint. "The company's approach also raises concerns regarding the GDPR," BEUC's Ursula Pachl noted, and a spokesman for BEUC told TechCrunch it might, at a later stage, file a complaint about Meta's data protection compliance with the relevant privacy authority once it has completed its own assessment of the issues — though he emphasized it was too early to say whether or not it would take that step.

Meta's lead data protection authority in the EU, Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), had for several months been assessing its pay-or-consent offer but had yet to communicate a conclusion. In the meanwhile, Meta maintains that the model it has devised for obtaining users' consent to its ads processing complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) — although, TechCrunch notes, the adtech giant also said that when it was claiming performance of a contract and then legitimate interests for the processing, both of which were subsequently found to be incompatible with the GDPR.

TechCrunch's reading of the incentive: Meta is likely banking on another multi-year round of GDPR complaints, legal challenges and finally a referral to the CJEU, followed by another long wait before a ruling gets handed down, buying it several more years to run with its new legal basis fix and keep feeding its profits by doing what it likes with Europeans' data.



---


# Meta's Proposal: Parental Approval For App Downloads At The App Store

Meta wants to shift the burden of monitoring social media usage among teens back to the app stores — and to parents. In a blog post published November 15, 2023, Meta's global head of Safety, Antigone Davis, argued that parents should be responsible for approving their teens' app downloads, and staked Meta's position in supporting federal legislation that would require parental approval for app downloads for users under the age of 16.

The ground Meta offered is public opinion: it pointed to recent Pew research indicating that 81% of U.S. adults were in favor of requiring parental consent for teens to create social media accounts. TechCrunch's caveat is that while this may speak to popular opinion around parental sentiment, it does not mean that parents have thought through who should be responsible for preventing or allowing teens' access to social media, or how those apps should operate to protect teens.

The warrant tying the proposal to the app stores is one of existing capability: the app stores already have age guidelines, so it would seem to follow that they should also enforce them, if enforcement is to be regulated — or that seems to be Meta's thinking. TechCrunch also notes that a policy position like this is not something that would have been rushed out in a matter of days as a PR response to Bejar's claims, but something Meta has been stewing on for some time.



---


# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# DSA And DMA Oversight Of Meta's Ad Tracking

Meta's subscription plan faces three overlapping regimes, not one. As well as needing to comply with the GDPR, which delineates the qualities necessary for consent to be legal — such as that it is specific, informed and freely given — Meta is now also subject to the pan-EU Digital Services Act (DSA), which also sets conditions on larger platforms when it comes to tracking and profiling people for ads; so it won't just be data protection authorities making a call on whether Meta's subscription-or-tracking offer flies, since the European Commission is responsible for oversight of very large online platforms' DSA compliance.

Meta has also been designated as a so-called gatekeeper under the DSA's sister regulation, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which also puts some limits on use of people's data for ads, and the Commission is the sole enforcer of the DMA. Meta is already in the Commission's sights over its approach to the DSA — the EU's executive has in recent days requested more information from the tech giant about its approach to content threats flowing from the Israel-Hamas war and about election security issues — but it remains to be seen whether the EU will apply the same close scrutiny to Meta's ad tracking offer.



---


# Surveillance As A Restriction On Palestinian Freedom Of Movement

Amnesty International researcher Matthew Mahmoudi argues that the surveillance technologies deployed in the occupied territories are not merely observational but restrictive: "These technologies are deployed to restrict the freedom of movement of Palestinians," he said.

His grounds are the everyday capacities that surveillance curtails: "In particular, your ability to move, to access work, to access education, to access medical facilities is stifled based on the usage of AI-based surveillance like facial recognition."

The warrant joining the technology to political effect is deterrence of dissent. "We see how the technology ends up being used to deter Palestinians in places like Silwan in East Jerusalem from resisting and dissenting the expanding illegal settlements," Mahmoudi said, adding: "Even their family life and the sort of very mundane everyday actions suddenly become acts of resistance in the face of this ubiquitous surveillance apparatus that underpins much of how apartheid is exacted on Palestinians."



---


# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.

qid: Between the report from The Verge on November 7, 2023, portraying Google as the protagonist in the Epic v. Google trial, and the TechCrunch article on December 15, 2023, citing a class action antitrust suit against Google for harming news publishers' bottom lines, has the portrayal of Google's business practices by these news sources remained consistent?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. He called it disconcerting to see the extent of bad-faith efforts inside a company of Google's size, saying you would expect a trillion-dollar company to have developed respectable processes and leadership structures providing checks and balances against wrongdoing. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. # The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. # Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.

# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

# Chinese Government Ban And Crackdown On Falun Gong, 1999

China banned Falun Gong altogether in 1999, after thousands of Li's followers silently protested its repression in Beijing, and the state then set about eradicating the movement.

Labelling it a cult, the Chinese government confiscated Falun Gong books, blocked websites, closed teaching centres and arrested practitioners. Human rights groups reported a brutal crackdown: some adherents were sent to labour camps, while others were tortured and killed.

International human rights organizations condemned China's attempted eradication. In the United States, where Li and some of his practitioners had fled, a new collection of followers organized a campaign to raise awareness and sympathy, using parades, demonstrations and pamphlets that touted the benefits of Falun Gong and the brutality of the Chinese Communist Party.

# Hikvision Video Surveillance Company Profile

Hikvision is one of the world's largest makers of video surveillance equipment, based in Hangzhou, China, and it is among the vendors behind the surveillance cameras deployed in the occupied Palestinian territories.

What distinguishes it from other camera vendors is its record: the company has been accused of aiding what the US has categorized as a genocide. It is already infamous among international human rights groups, has been blacklisted by the US, and has been identified by the UK as a security threat, in both cases for being complicit in China's repression of the Uyghur ethnic minority.

The company's headquarters are in Hangzhou, in eastern China's Zhejiang province.

The SAFE Innovation Framework is Senator Schumer's AI policy program, debuted by his office in June, and the AI Insight Forums are part of it — the forums are the framework's convening mechanism rather than free-standing events.

The framework's defining premise is one of geopolitical standard-setting. There are no signs that USD funds' dealmaking in China will bounce back to its heights in the foreseeable future. The PitchBook report predicts that VC activity with U.S. participation in China during 2023 will hit a nine-year low, followed by a decade low in 2024.

---


# Gen Z: Definition And Formative Events

Gen Z, as characterized in this account, is the cohort aged 11 to 26 as of October 2023 and the first fully digital native generation — the feature that discriminates it from every earlier cohort is not the scale of the history it has lived through but that it has been plugged into the world through the internet from such a young age. Social media posts are its lingua franca, and the "disturbing images" warning is one it is used to encountering there.

The formative events listed are dense. This generation has already lived through a once-per-century pandemic; the Jan. 6 insurrection, an event unseen for centuries in American politics, when armed right-wing extremists stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 following the election defeat of former President Donald Trump; the first major European ground war since World War II, in Ukraine; and market crashes in 2008 and 2020 that recall the Great Depression. Three years before the article, as Gen Z emerged into young adulthood, online videos of the murder of George Floyd shook the country in May 2020, resulting in a summer of violent Black Lives Matter protests and riots. School shootings have only increased in frequency since Columbine in 1999, with more students documenting the terror on their phones and sharing it online — one of them, the Parkland shooting of 2018, tragically created the first spokespeople of the post-millennial generation. Most recently, on Saturday, 2023-10-07, the Islamic militant group Hamas launched an unprecedented attack on Israel, resulting in the worst war the region has seen in 50 years; in three days more than 1,500 people died on both sides, and graphic, difficult-to-watch videos blanketed the internet.

The boundary case the account itself raises is that every generation has lived through era-defining historical events: millennials remember the 9/11 terrorist attacks and the U.S. invasion of Iraq, and baby boomers lived through the civil rights movement and the Vietnam War. What sets Gen Z apart is the medium — experiencing it all through videos, images, and articles online, which is shaping their mental health, workplace attitudes, and financial habits in visible ways.

# Capital Rotation from China into Japanese Assets

One of the most significant changes, according to asset managers quoted by the Financial Times on 1 October 2023, is a fundamental shift in the way global funds now look at China — and the mechanism runs directly to Japan's benefit. The geopolitics of US-China tensions, chip wars, decoupling and "friendshoring" seem in particular to be working significantly in Japan's favour: Asia-focused global investment is rotating out of China and into Tokyo stocks, real estate and other assets, just as large parts of corporate Japan are engaging more actively with shareholders than at any time in the past.

The push side of the model is China's loss of sheen after years of stunning growth and investor attention. Its economy is growing more slowly and the expected post-pandemic rebound is proving elusive. On top of that, Beijing's policymaking — with sudden crackdowns on entire industries such as video games and private tutoring — has generated a series of nasty surprises and the unshakeable fear that others could occur at any time.

"You are seeing more interest in Japan from investors, who were primarily invested in China, as China has slowed and some of its economic policies have been confusing and opaque," says Kirk Neureiter, president of Fidelity Management & Research Japan. "Deployment of capital to China has been a bit more risky in terms of eventual outcome of investment decisions, given that lack of clarity." He qualifies the model's range: interest in Japan has not only come about because of the push away from China.



---


# Why Chinese Apps Rose In The US App Store Rankings

TechCrunch offers two readings of the 2023 download shift. The first is that U.S. tech giants are nearly at a market saturation point, where their apps are not as in demand as they were in previous years because many people already have them installed.

The second is that it points to the growing demand for apps from Chinese firms, like ByteDance, which are attracting younger users' attention along with government scrutiny — with TikTok being banned from a number of government devices over concerns about its China ties.

The scrutiny has not yet translated into a consumer-facing ban: Montana also attempted to ban TikTok in its state, but that ruling was put on hold by the courts for the time being as TikTok's lawsuit progresses.

# China's Data Laws And Government TikTok Device Bans

China's treatment of data as a state resource, backed by national intelligence laws that let the ruling Communist Party pull data on request from companies based in the country, is the reason a string of governments — Australia among them — have banned TikTok from official devices.

The concept has a documented policy history. In 2016 China designated big data a "fundamental strategic resource," and four years later its government designated data as the fifth "factor of production," joining land, labour, capital and technology. China's National Intelligence Law of 2017 requires all organisations and citizens to "support, assist and co-operate with the state intelligence work," which is the legal basis on which the Party can compel disclosure from domestically based companies.

The device bans are the practical consequence: the Australian government this year banned TikTok on government devices over security concerns related to China's intelligence laws, and governments from Britain, Canada, France and New Zealand have also banned the app from official devices. TikTok's own framing of the disputed tool sits alongside this: "Pixel usage, which is voluntary for our advertising clients to adopt, is an industry-wide tool used to improve the effectiveness of advertising services. Our use of this tool is compliant with all current Australian privacy laws and regulations, and we dismiss any suggestion otherwise."

Christian Kirk then broke loose for a 44-yard touchdown after an exchange of punts, retaking the lead for Jacksonville with 3:08 remaining. # Criticism of Thanksgiving as a Celebration of Conquest

The case against Thanksgiving attacks the premise that the holiday commemorates a peaceable shared meal: although many Americans view it as a beloved holiday, it is viewed by many who have abandoned it as an erroneous celebration of what was actually the conquest of Native Americans and Native American lands.

X was facing more competition than ever before at the time it introduced its bot-countering fee, and its own numbers were going the other way: a report published that week by market intelligence firm Similarweb found that X's web traffic and monthly active users on mobile had declined post-acquisition. The warrant is that when advertisers pay, the feed optimizes for them rather than for connection.

Mozilla dates the inflection point: this disconnect between what people want and what today's networks offer hit an inflection point in 2022, when billionaire Elon Musk bought Twitter, leading to a surge of interest in alternatives to centralized social networking including apps like Mastodon and Bluesky. He extended the observation beyond any single platform, to the combined load of professional and amateur sources. "We are also so plugged into all these storylines, whether it's from traditional media, whether it's from user-generated — someone on their phone, you know, posting to a Telegram group. # Microtargeting

## Definition

In the corpus, microtargeting refers to using a platform's ad-targeting tools to aim political or advertising messaging at narrow, algorithmically selected audience segments — including by deliberately excluding groups defined by their interests or political views — rather than at a general audience.

## Context

In the corpus, microtargeting appears in two related EU controversies over data-driven ad targeting on major platforms.
Meta's "pay or consent" model is accused of forcing users to accept being "tracked and profiled" so the company can keep "profiting from microtargeting them," with nearly 20 consumer groups arguing this breaches EU consumer protection law.
Separately, the European Commission itself ran a microtargeted political ad campaign on X to build support for its CSAM-scanning proposal, which became the subject of a DSA-compliance investigation and a European Parliament committee hearing.
Both cases involve platforms designated Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) under the DSA — Facebook and Instagram in the Meta case, X in the Commission's campaign — though only the Commission's campaign was exposed using X's DSA-mandated ad-transparency tools, while the Meta case instead centers on a coordinated consumer-protection complaint.

## Key Characteristics

- **Exclusion-based mechanics** — technologist Danny Mekić's analysis of X's Transparency Report showed the Commission's campaign was configured to exclude specific interest groups (people interested in Julian Assange, in "nexit"/"brexit"/"spanexit," in figures like Viktor Orbán or Nigel Farage, and people interested in Christianity), after which the platform's algorithm found remaining users receptive to the message.
- **Echo-chamber effect** — Mekić described the resulting audience, once critical political and religious groups were filtered out, as "an uncritical echo chamber."
- **Regulatory exposure under the DSA** — the DSA prohibits using sensitive personal data, such as political opinions, to target ads; Mekić argued the Commission's campaign violated X's own advertising policy, the DSA, and the GDPR.
- **Basis for consumer-protection complaints** — separately, Meta's monetization of tracked-and-profiled user data for microtargeted advertising was central to BEUC's complaint that its pay-or-consent model is "unfair" and "illegal" under EU consumer law.
- **Exposed via VLOP transparency obligations** — the Commission's microtargeted campaign became visible only because Mekić used the public ad-transparency tools the DSA requires X, as a VLOP, to provide; Meta's microtargeting practice, by contrast, was already publicly known and became the basis of a separate consumer-protection complaint rather than something uncovered through ad-transparency tools.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, microtargeting is generally defined as the use of online data to tailor advertising or political messaging to individuals or small groups based on their personal characteristics or vulnerabilities, rather than addressing a broad, undifferentiated audience (Wikipedia, "Microtargeting," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microtargeting).

# Zuckerberg On Bringing Threads To The Fediverse

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg seems to earnestly believe that bringing Threads to the fediverse is a good idea, both for Meta's product and for its business, telling The Verge's Alex Heath earlier in the fall: "Not everyone wants to use one product, and I think making it so that they can use an alternative but can still interact with people on the network will make it so that that product also is more valuable."

The Verge's writer treated the remark as striking evidence for the fediverse case — "Mark Zuckerberg! Said that!" — reading it as an acknowledgment that people want to feel like their social connections and content belong to them, not to a company that can disappear or pivot or change its ways. His conclusion from Meta's own stance: if Meta can't build and maintain the One True Social Network For Everybody, nobody can, and it's well past time to try something else.

# Pebble's Moderation-First Market Hypothesis

Pebble's founding hypothesis was that consumers were hungry for a Twitter alternative that prioritized trust, safety and moderation from the start. The company staffed for it: Pebble's founding team included co-founder Sarah Oh, Twitter's former human rights advisor.

What would falsify the proposition is a moderation-first Twitter alternative that consumers decline to adopt — which is the shape of the outcome TechCrunch is reporting on 2023-10-24, in a piece about Pebble shutting down.

# X Found To Have The Worst Disinformation Ratio In EU Analysis

X, formerly Twitter, was called out in the European Union for having the worst ratio of disinformation and misinformation to posts not spreading falsehoods among mainstream social networks.

The finding came in a September 2023 speech by EU commissioner for values and transparency Vera Jourova, discussing the latest updates from platforms signed up to combat disinformation under a beefed-up EU Code of Practice linked to compliance with the bloc's legally binding Digital Services Act. X's poor performance was assessed during a pilot phase of testing of a new methodology developed by Code signatories. "A big novelty under the Code is now the publication of the first set of structural indicators such as how easy it is to find disinformation content, how much engagement such content receives or indicators about sources. These indicators — developed by the signatories — constitute an unprecedented and novel insight into disinformation on online platforms," she said. "Such insight is crucial to understand how effective platforms efforts are to fight this threat even more efficiently. This is a very valuable industry proposal that has great potential while it has to be still further developed. Here, signatories have decided to run a pilot phase in three Member States to evaluate the methodology on two of those indicators. X, former Twitter, who is not under the Code any more is the platform with the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts."

X was contacted for a response to the EU's analysis of the ratio of disinformation it is spreading, and replied with an automated email reading: "Busy now, please check back later." The finding fits a wider pattern: consistent moderation, fact-checking investment and researcher data access are areas where X under new owner Elon Musk has moved out of step with EU expectations on countering disinformation, suggesting that X — designated by the EU as a VLOP under the DSA back in April — continues to put itself squarely in the Commission's crosshairs, including over its priority issue of tackling Kremlin propaganda.

A user posting as Mjoachim said Israel's defence forces have lost their fame, noting that the IDF lost an army base and a general was captured right out of his house: "Invincible 'Merkava MK4 MBT's captured, and destroyed...what is wrong with the Israeli security and defence forces? And (what) MOSSAD did?"

Dr Jaswant Gandhi, a professor of management, drew a lesson for another country: the attack on Israel was a "great Mossad failure", and India had to learn a lot and keep all intelligence agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. "Israel_under_attack Great #Mossad failure. GoI has to learn a lot and keep all Intelligence Agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. BHARAT is not immune to #terrorism and internal enemies," he wrote on X. The warrant common to these comments is that a surveillance and special-forces apparatus of this reputation should have detected preparations on this scale.

# How The Blockade Produces Food Insecurity And Import Dependence In Gaza

About 64% of people in Gaza are considered food insecure, meaning they do not have reliable access to sufficient amounts of food — one of the several practical effects the blockade has for the average Gazan. The dependence has deepened over time: food as a percentage of Gaza's total imports has skyrocketed by 50% since 2005, when Israel first imposed a temporary blockade, while the amount of food the West Bank and Gaza actually produce has tumbled by 30% since then.

The mechanism suppressing local production is partly infrastructural damage. It is hard for Gaza to produce food within its own borders; one factor is that Israeli airstrikes hit Gaza's only power generation plant and main sewage treatment plant in 2008 and again in 2018. Those attacks resulted in the spread of sewage waste on land and in the water, destroying farmlands and food crops and threatening fish stocks in the ocean as well.



---


# Israel-Hamas Conflict: The Limited-Market-Impact Base Case

As of mid-October 2023, the Indian stock market's base case was that the Israel-Hamas hostilities would not escalate, and on that assumption the conflict was expected to have only a limited impact on markets. The grounds are threefold. First, the world can ill-afford another full-fledged war while economies are already battling high inflation and interest rates, an ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and a slowing China, which is precisely why many countries are trying to restrict any escalation; the market movement in the week before 14 October 2023 indicated that non-escalation was the presumed base case. Second, the US treasury secretary stated that the current conflict is not likely to significantly impact the global economic outlook. Third, history supports the same conclusion: a study of past conflicts between Israel and Hamas found that they tend to have limited impact on global financial markets, across crude oil, US 10-year yields, US equities and market volatility.

The warrant joining the evidence to the claim is that market impact tracks escalation, not the mere existence of hostilities: because the incentives of major countries point towards containment and because previous Israel-Hamas episodes transmitted little into the four channels that matter (oil, yields, equities, volatility), the priced-in outcome is a contained conflict. The argument is explicitly conditional on the non-escalation premise holding.



---


# Israel-Hamas War Context, October 2023

As of TechCrunch's 2023-10-14 report, Israel is retaliating militarily against the attacks on its people, on its soil, and the hostages subsequently taken by Hamas — the ruling organization in Gaza that kidnapped at least 150 people and took them into Gaza during brutal attacks on Israel last weekend that killed 1,300 people. That strategy has seen Israel pummeling the "Gaza Strip" with bombs to eradicate it of Hamas and to get its hostages back, and over 1,500 people in Palestine so far have been killed as a result.

The tech industry in Israel — the country's biggest export and its biggest single contributor to GDP — is also taking a big knock, but inevitably the impact on the smaller and more fragile ecosystem in Gaza has been significantly more serious, and the physical, economic and societal destruction resulting from that leaves any future for the tech industry there in doubt: quite simply, there is no escaping the consequences of the war for anyone, let alone tech workers. Israel has now amassed soldiers near the north of Gaza ahead of an expected ground offensive into the densely populated enclave, and about 1.1 million people living in northern areas have been told to leave in the next day. The UN has warned of "devastating humanitarian consequences" from these latest moves, and a total blockade on the territory is being enforced with fuel, food and water running out; Israel says it won't lift the restrictions unless Hamas frees all hostages. TechCrunch notes the piece was later edited to include relevant information about the attacks by Hamas.



---


# Egypt's Role In The Israel-Hamas War And The Leverage It Creates

The war between Israel and Hamas has turned the spotlight on Egypt's role as a regional powerbroker, potentially winning it Western support as it tries to escape a grinding economic crisis. The structure linking the two is that Egypt's two assets in this conflict — long-held ties to Israel and a border with Gaza — make its stance decisive for outcomes the West wants.

Specifically, Egypt's position is shaping up as key to the fate of any refugees and to a sustained flow of aid for the besieged territory's 2 million residents, after Israel cut off crucial supplies in response to Hamas's deadly Oct. 7 assault. That dependence is what converts Egypt's geography and relationships into potential leverage over Western backing for its economy, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-22.



---


# Visual Intelligence Versus Human Sources

Technological sophistication and massive investment in intelligence means have greatly increased the IDF's visual intelligence gathering capabilities, according to former IDF Intelligence Directorate head General (ret.) Aharon Ze'evi-Farkash — but visual collection and human sources play different roles, and only the latter supplies interpretation.

"I'm sure it doesn't come at the expense of human sources, but as time goes by, gathering visual intelligence is easier than human sources and they bring better results," Ze'evi-Farkash said. "It's hard to bring in a Palestinian 'Ashraf Marwan,' the agent who passed the information to Israel before the Egyptian attack in 1973. It's a problem because the human source is essential to provide an interpretation of the rest of the information that's received, and to make decisions. Golda knew who Marwan was and expected to hear what he would say about the Egyptian deployment in the south." Two further gaps sit alongside that structural point: according to "The New York Times," a year before the attack the IDF stopped monitoring Hamas's radio communications, and the US had put stock in Israeli intelligence regarding Hamas in recent years and had not monitored it independently.



---


# Israeli Economy in the First Week of the Gaza War

As the first week of fighting in the war in Israel's south drew to a close, the main index on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the Tel Aviv 35, had fallen 6.4% over the week, with financial markets trying to gauge the damage the Israeli economy would sustain. Globes reported on 12 October 2023 that this was clearly a very significant event, but that the fog of war made it hard to estimate its full consequences.

The assessment came from Prof. Leo Leiderman, chief economic adviser at Bank Hapoalim and a professor of economics at Tel Aviv University, who set out for Globes his proposals for rehabilitating the economy and repairing the damage the war would cause. Asked what had been going through his mind in those first days, Leiderman said: "What most preoccupies me is not the economy but concern for the families of the soldiers, the wounded, and the captives, and solidarity with them. I have four relatives from Kibbutz Nir Oz who are still missing, and we have no information about them. I find it hard to understand how a war like this landed on us in a country as powerful as Israel. But we have no choice but to win."

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# The State Patchwork Of Teen Social Media Laws

Meta's call to bring the app stores into the fight is, if anything, a response to the lack of action in Congress to pass online child safety regulations like the hotly debated KOSA (the Kids Online Safety Act), leaving U.S. states to individually create laws due to a void of federal guidelines.

Utah, for instance, passed a measure that will require social networks to give Utah parents access to their children's posts, messages and comments, and would block social media access during certain hours; the governor also signed a bill to prevent social media companies from adding features designed to addict minors to their platforms. A judge in Arkansas recently blocked a law that would have required parental permission for minors to create social media accounts. Beyond Meta, Montana also became the first state to ban TikTok, claiming the Chinese Communist Party was using TikTok to spy on Americans. Meta's threat, in terms of teen usage, is not one of a foreign power collecting private data on users, but rather risks to teen mental health, body comparison issues and exposure to sexual predators — and TechCrunch notes Montana could easily turn its eyes to Meta next, after the TikTok bill went through.

The overhead of managing apps to meet individual state regulations would be a headache for Meta, but Antigone Davis also argues it would lead to a lack of teen protection in some cases. "U.S. states are passing a patchwork of different laws, many of which require teens (of varying ages) to get their parent's approval to use certain apps, and for everyone to verify their age to access them," she wrote. "Teens move interchangeably between many websites and apps, and social media laws that hold different platforms to different standards in different states will mean teens are inconsistently protected," Davis said.



---


# Discord's Graduated Warning System And Account Standing

Discord is introducing a new warning system for people who violate its policies: outside of incidents involving the most "extreme" violations, the company is moving away from permanent bans, doing so under the belief that most users will choose to be better online citizens given the chance and proper guidance.

In practice the system notifies a person when they have violated one or more of Discord's policies and details the restrictions on their account. It also links out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism. A new "Account Standing" tab within the settings menu lets users see all their current and past policy violations.

Discord frames the design as a model for the industry. "We think we've built the most nuanced and proportionate reporting system," Badalich told Engadget, adding that the company hopes other platforms will look to what Discord has created for inspiration in their own enforcement efforts. "We believe people, especially teens, have the capacity to grow."



---


# Surveillance As A Restriction On Palestinian Freedom Of Movement

Amnesty International researcher Matthew Mahmoudi argues that the surveillance technologies deployed in the occupied territories are not merely observational but restrictive: "These technologies are deployed to restrict the freedom of movement of Palestinians," he said.

His grounds are the everyday capacities that surveillance curtails: "In particular, your ability to move, to access work, to access education, to access medical facilities is stifled based on the usage of AI-based surveillance like facial recognition."

The warrant joining the technology to political effect is deterrence of dissent. "We see how the technology ends up being used to deter Palestinians in places like Silwan in East Jerusalem from resisting and dissenting the expanding illegal settlements," Mahmoudi said, adding: "Even their family life and the sort of very mundane everyday actions suddenly become acts of resistance in the face of this ubiquitous surveillance apparatus that underpins much of how apartheid is exacted on Palestinians."



---


# BEUC's Consumer-Law Case Against Meta's Pay-Or-Consent Model

BEUC's summary of the issues identified with Meta's model under consumer protection law rests on four grounds, each attached to a distinct provision of consumer law.

First, aggression: Meta is partially blocking the use of Facebook and Instagram until users have selected one option or the other, which constitutes an aggressive practice under European consumer law; through persistence and by creating a sense of urgency, Meta pushes consumers into making a choice they might not want to take. Second, a mistaken belief about what the paid tier buys: many consumers likely think that by opting for the paid subscription as it is presented they get a privacy-friendly option involving less tracking and profiling, when in fact users are likely to continue to have their personal data collected and used, but for purposes other than ads.

Third, misleading framing: Meta provides misleading and incomplete information to consumers which does not allow them to make an informed choice, and is misleading them by presenting the choice as between a paying and a "free" option, while the latter option is not "free" because consumers pay Meta through the provision of their data, as past court rulings have already declared. Fourth, and the warrant tying the rest together, the absence of a real choice: given the market power of Meta's Facebook and Instagram services in the EU and the very strong network effects of social media platforms — since all your friends are on Facebook and Instagram — consumers do not have a real choice, because if they quit the services they would lose all their contacts and interactions built over the years; the very high subscription fee for "ad-free" services is also a deterrent, which likewise means consumers do not have a real choice.



---


# The Republican State-Level TikTok Ban Push

Though opposition to TikTok has been bipartisan, the crusade to ban the platform over national security concerns is primarily led by Republicans at the state level, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02. The article treats that position as a likely contributor to the party's social media struggles with young voters.

The observation matters because it sets the party's legislative posture against its outreach problem: the same platform Republicans are campaigning to ban is the one where the youth vote concentrates.

WIRED's Apple Black Friday guide of 25 November 2023 listed six discounted USB-C charging and connectivity products: Anker's 67-watt Prime GaN charger, a four-port desktop charger, Apple's dual USB-C 35-watt adapter, a folding two-port charger, Satechi's four-port hub with an SSD slot, and Anker's compact 30-watt iPad adapter.
