# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Trump Net Worth Valuation Dispute at Trial

Thousands of pages of exhibits detailing the performance of Donald Trump's assets, made available during the New York fraud trial, have provided a deeper look into his fortune. His 2021 statement of financial condition, filed as part of the lawsuit, pegged his net worth at $US4.5 billion. Bloomberg's calculation has consistently been below Trump's figures; at the same time, Bloomberg measured the value of some Trump properties higher than what New York state claims.

Trump took the stand and testified that the properties whose values he is accused of inflating were actually undervalued, based on the premium his "brand" adds. He also said that banks did not rely on his statements of financial condition when weighing loans: "They just weren't a very important element in banks' decision-making process," Trump told the court. "And we'll explain that as this trial goes along."

The Age's 7 November 2023 report set out New York state's valuation of four high-profile Trump properties where the prosecution alleges fraud occurred, alongside Bloomberg's own approach to assessing the assets.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."



---


# George's Claim Of Epstein's Political Influence

Denise George later testified that she thought Epstein was "flexing his political influence over or with the governor" rather than going through the usual channels — her inference from the route by which the waiver request reached her.

Given Epstein's apparent influence in the Virgin Islands, the obvious question was who would want to rock the boat, and George says she was willing to try. Around St. Thomas she has a reputation as a straightshooter, and the former public-corruption attorney stops short of pointing to official wrongdoing; but she makes clear that she, for one, wouldn't tolerate it. "If I have to lose my job to avoid being part of a conspiracy to cover something up, I would do it," George says. "My bar license, my integrity were more important to me. I wasn't going to compromise that."

qid: Does 'The Sydney Morning Herald' suggest that the US economy is slowing down to an optimal level to prevent a recession, while also reporting a prediction by Paul Tudor Jones that the United States economy will enter into a recession early next year?
context:
# Wall Street December 2023 Mixed Session

Most US stocks slipped in the overnight Wall Street session reported on 5 December 2023, though the market stayed near its highest level in 20 months after a mixed set of reports that kept alive questions about whether the world's largest economy can pull off a perfect landing in which it kills high inflation but avoids a recession. The S&P 500 edged down 0.1 per cent for its first back-to-back loss since October, the Dow Jones slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent.

Stocks fell more sharply in Asia amid worries about the health of China's economy, the world's second largest. US stocks and Treasury yields wavered after reports showed that US employers advertised far fewer jobs at the end of October than expected, while growth for services businesses accelerated more in the prior month than expected.

The underlying hope on Wall Street at the time was that the US economy was slowing from its recent hot pace by just the right amount: too much strength would give inflation more fuel, but too little would mean a recession. The Australian market's gains that day came after this mixed US session.



---


# The Wall Street September 2023 Selloff And Bond Yields

September 2023 brought a loss of 5.2 per cent so far for the S&P 500, putting it on track to be the worst month of the year by far, as the realisation set in that the Federal Reserve would indeed keep interest rates high for a long time. That growing understanding sent yields in the bond market to their highest levels in more than a decade, which in turn undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

Treasury yields rose again on Tuesday, 2023-09-26, following a mixed batch of reports on the economy: the yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.55 per cent from 4.54 per cent late on Monday and is near its highest level since 2007, up sharply from about 3.5 per cent in May and from 0.5 per cent about three years ago. One economic report that Tuesday showed confidence among consumers was weaker than economists expected — concerning because strong spending by US households has been a bulwark keeping the economy out of a long-predicted recession.



---


# US Jobs And Services Data In Early October 2023

Wednesday's ADP report suggested private employers added 89,000 jobs last month, a much sharper slowdown in hiring than the 140,000 economists expected. The report does not have a perfect track record in predicting what the more comprehensive jobs report from the US government will say, which was due to arrive on the Friday. Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley Global Investment Office, said that "if Friday's report also shows the labour market is cooling, stock investors may worry a little less about indefinitely higher interest rates".

A second report on the economy said growth in US services industries slowed in September by a touch more than economists expected. The figures were reported by The Age on 4 October 2023 alongside a note that oil prices slumped overnight.



---


# US Equity Sector Moves On 10 October 2023

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.4 per cent to 33,739.30, the S&P 500 gained 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite added 0.6 per cent, with all 11 major S&P 500 sectors advancing — materials and consumer staples led the gains while technology was the slowest gainer, and energy was among the laggards after its more than 3 per cent rally on Monday.

A measure of US-listed Chinese shares added 3 per cent amid reports that the Asian nation is considering new economic stimulus. "Policymakers have begun to acknowledge a lesser need for further policy action given financial conditions have tightened considerably after the recent surge in Treasury yields," said Ben Jeffery at BMO Capital Markets. "This acknowledgment may have reduced angst around the need for additional rate increases." Investors would be watching for any hints in the September Fed meeting minutes, due Wednesday, that would suggest the Fed may not follow through with the last rise indicated in its economic projections, according to Anna Wong at Bloomberg Economics, who noted that two critical coming indicators for the US economy — Thursday's consumer price index and Friday's University of Michigan consumer-sentiment survey — may give a more definitive read.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# Goldman Sachs' Forecast That Home Prices Keep Rising Slowly Through 2024

Goldman Sachs managing director Roger Ashworth predicted that home prices will rise by 1.8% by the end of 2023 and by 3.5% by the end of 2024, and he is not hopeful that prices will drop anytime soon. The proposition is stated with an explicit escape condition: "Absent any negative shocks to the broader economy that would either boost excess supply of homes on the market or fuel an uptick in unemployment, we continue to expect home prices to rise at a slow pace."

That conditional is what would falsify the forecast. A negative shock to the broader economy that pushed excess supply of homes onto the market, or one that fueled an uptick in unemployment, is by his own statement the circumstance under which the expectation of slowly rising prices would no longer hold.



---


# Australian Inflation Data And The RBA's Near-Certain November Rise

GSFM investment strategist Stephen Miller said the inflation data, taken with the October Reserve Bank board meeting minutes — which revealed the board had "low tolerance for a slower return of inflation to target than currently expected" — made the possibility of an interest rate rise from the central bank in November a "near certainty."

Commodity prices nonetheless supported mining companies, as iron ore prices increased 2.9 per cent overnight, bolstering Australia's iron ore giants. This came as Chinese President Xi Jinping stepped up support for the world's second-biggest economy and major commodity trading partner for Australia, issuing additional sovereign debt, raising the budget deficit ratio and even making an unprecedented visit to the central bank. On Wall Street, the benchmark S&P 500 index closed 0.7 per cent higher ahead of tech giants Microsoft and Alphabet reporting results after the close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.6 per cent and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 gained 0.9 per cent. Shares in Microsoft climbed 5 per cent in after-hours trading after the company said its sales jumped 13 per cent to $US56.5 billion ($88.9 billion) and profits climbed 27 per cent to $US22.3 billion in the three months through September.



---


# Prediction: An AI Compliance Industry And Slow Regulation

TechCrunch predicts that big moves like the EU's AI Act will not visibly change the industry in 2024, because such laws tend to be slow to take effect. That slowness is by design, so companies do not have to adjust to new rules overnight, but it also means we will not see the effect of these big laws for a good while except among those willing to make changes preemptively and voluntarily — so expect a lot of "we are beginning the process of…" talk, and a few quiet lawsuits challenging various parts of laws.

The knock-on prediction is a newly flourishing AI compliance industry, as the billions going into the technology prompt matching investments — at a smaller scale, but still considerable — in making sure the tools and processes meet international and local standards.

For the United States, the forecast is negative and dated: unfortunately for anyone hoping for substantive federal regulation, 2024 is not the year to expect movement on that front. Though it will be a year for AI and everyone will be asking for new laws, the U.S. government and electorate will be too busy with the trash fire that will be the 2024 election.

# Why Chinese Apps Rose In The US App Store Rankings

TechCrunch offers two readings of the 2023 download shift. The first is that U.S. tech giants are nearly at a market saturation point, where their apps are not as in demand as they were in previous years because many people already have them installed.

# TikTok's Ad-Free Subscription Tier Test

TikTok is testing an ad-free subscription tier for some users, priced at $4.99 for an ad-free experience with no other strings attached, TechCrunch reported in its Week in Review of October 7, 2023.

# Australian Advertiser Responses To The TikTok Pixel Findings

Of the Australian websites tested, the national mental health organisation Beyond Blue removed the TikTok pixel from its site after being alerted to the tracking issue, while Sportsbet defended its use of advanced matching and Kmart did not respond to requests for comment.

Beyond Blue's spokeswoman said the organisation "takes privacy and security extremely seriously, and we apologise for any concern this has caused," and added: "When The Age and Sydney Morning Herald alerted us to this issue, we immediately commenced a review of our privacy policy and removed the TikTok pixel from our website. A Sportsbet spokesman said: "We use advanced matching, and that's consistent with targeting advertising methods that a lot of companies use. The comparison that gives those responses their force is with other platforms. # The Gaza Information War And The Hamas Narrative

Eylon Levy argues that the conflict is not only a kinetic war in Gaza but also an information war, in which the Hamas narrative is adopted far more easily than Israel's account is accepted. His first ground is a case of a claim that collapsed: the day after what he calls the bluff about the Al-Ahli hospital, which the Palestinians claimed had been hit by an Israeli missile killing 800 civilians but which in the end turned out to have been caused by a splinter group of Islamic Jihad, with no hospital destroyed and certainly not 800 people killed, he explained on Sky News that Hamas lies and makes up numbers, and the reporter asked him, almost speechless with surprise, whether he doubts Hamas' numbers. He describes such moments as intensely frustrating, recounting a BBC interview in which the interviewer told him "Hamas denies what you are saying", to which his answer is that of course Hamas denies this, since Hamas denies that it is even holding hostages, and Hamas massacres, beheads, rapes, burns families and then day and night denies that it did so. Some journalists around the world see that Hamas continues to lie about the biggest things when the whole truth is in front of everyone's eyes, and they continue to echo the lies.

His second ground is a structural claim about where information from Gaza comes from: it comes either directly from Hamas or from independent reporters and photographers who are part of the system in Gaza, and everyone knows that even if they are not affiliated with Hamas they are not free to present the full truth because they are not allowed to. The evidence he offers for the constraint is what is missing: there is not a single photo of a terrorist, not a single photo of a missile being launched from a densely populated area, from a mosque or a school, not even a single photo from the Hamas tunnels under Shifa; the reason is that these reporters, even if not explicitly on Hamas' side, operate under a dictatorial regime and cannot provide the information even if they wanted to, which is why he thinks it very important to keep reminding the world how biased the information reaching them is. Levy qualifies the argument explicitly: he does not want to give the impression that all interviewers are hostile and every question delusional, and he has many interviews with reporters who understand what is happening and simply want information and to hear the Israeli side, which is completely legitimate.

# Hamas Fundraising After October 7

Although it has been almost impossible to transfer money and goods to Gaza since October 7, with hawala shuttered and no trade, Hamas continues to raise funds — chiefly through Judea and Samaria and through online platforms abroad.

"The situation in Gaza is known, and nothing can be brought in, but fundraising activity continues in Judea and Samaria," Ostrovitch-Levi says. "It's also possible to make bank transfers to Judea and Samaria, and the fundraising activity hasn't stopped, because while the fighting is going on, they're continuing to fill their reserves for 'the day after' [the war]. We realize they're raising funds for their continued operations. Hamas is taking advantage of the current sympathy for the Gazans' situation, and is using online platforms, both of organizations whose business is crowdfunding, and also through the creation of fictitious projects to raise funds: throw-pillows, jewelry and whatnot, and more." All of this happens openly in Europe and other places around the world: "Hamas and Islamic Jihad carry out recruitment operations under the guise of humanitarian aid campaigns, and use Telegram, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok to disseminate their announcements. The facade is always supporting humanitarian goals, but in practice it's about channels for funding individuals and entities connected directly to Hamas or Islamic Jihad." IMPA's goal is not only to stop individual fundraising but the entire interrelated chain, from fund-raiser to transferrer to recipient: "We have the ability to build the intelligence scenario, synchronize all the sources of information received, and delineate the money trail from abroad to Hamas. We're interested not only in who is running the campaign, the association or entity, but where the money is coming from, and where it's going. We need to stop all of the elements in this network."

# "Life Partnership" As The Smiths' Own Term For Their Marriage

"Life partnership" is the term Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith use for their relationship in place of a conventional marriage description, and its defining feature is unconditionality rather than cohabitation or romance. Will Smith set out the definition on TIDAL's Rap Radar podcast: he and Jada "refer to ourselves as life partners, where you get into that space where you realise you are literally with somebody for the rest of your life. There's no deal breakers. There's nothing she could do — ever. Nothing that would break our relationship. She has my support till death and it feels so good to get to that space."

Pinkett Smith used the same term as the goal of the couple's repair work. On the Today show on 16 October 2023 she told Hoda Kotb that she and the Suicide Squad actor were "working hard" and "concentrating on healing": "There's no finding another great love, and I think that's the point. It's like we are in a place now that we are in a deep, healing space. And we are really concentrating on healing the relationship between us." She added: "There's no divorce on paper. We really have been working hard. That's the whole thing. We are working very hard at bringing our relationship together. Back to a life partnership." Speaking about the family — the couple's children Jaden, 25, and Willow, 22, plus Will's 30-year-old son Trey with ex-wife Sheree Zampino — she framed the term as what the relationship has become rather than a permanent verdict: "We love our family and we love each other. It's more of a life partnership. Now, 10 years from now, Hoda, who knows?"

# Separation As An Alternative To Divorce: The "LAT" Partnership

New York City-based relationship expert Susan Winter argues that a long separation like Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's is not a failed marriage but a recognised alternative form of one — a "living apart together" partnership — and that it can be the better choice. Speaking to The Independent in October 2023, she drew a sharp line between separation and divorce: divorce, particularly for Hollywood couples, means lengthy legal processes, from dividing financial assets to creating child custody agreements, whereas a separation carries none of that machinery. Although the terms of the Smiths' separation are not public, Winter believes they are showcasing a non-conventional relationship unfamiliar to the public, one whose visible feature is living in separate homes.

Her grounds are that the arrangement's organising purpose is continuity of the partnership rather than its dissolution: "It's an LAT partnership, meaning 'living apart together.' While everybody is at a different point as to why they are doing this, the centre point is the same: the preservation of the partnership is paramount." She attaches a scope condition to the benefit and a limit to what success looks like: "Separations can also be beneficial if both individuals are working on themselves and have the mutual goal of reuniting, or making their relationship better. However, that doesn't necessarily mean that their improved relationship will result in them living together again." The argument arises because the Smiths' seven years apart raise the general question of when couples should give up and when a separation should become a divorce — a question, the article notes, that has no simple answer.

# Britney Spears And David Lucado

Two months after ending her engagement to Jason Trawick, Britney Spears began dating David Lucado, who worked at a legal firm; she announced their split in August 2014 by tweeting "Ahhhh the single life!", and her representative confirmed to People: "Yes, she's single." # Kevin Federline's 2022 Comments And The Spears Camp's Rebuttal

Britney Spears and her camp rejected Kevin Federline's 2022 claim that their teenage sons were distancing themselves from her because of her social media posts, attacking both the causal premise and Federline's standing to make it public. In an August 2022 interview with ITV, Federline said the couple's sons found it "tough" seeing their mother sharing nude photos online — she had been posting such images while embracing her newfound freedom after the end of her 13-year conservatorship — adding: "I can't imagine how it feels to be a teenager having to go to high school." qid: After the Financial Times reported on October 1, 2023, that investors are showing more interest in Japan due to China's economic slowdown, did the investment trend of U.S.-headquartered venture capitalists, as reported by TechCrunch, show agreement or disagreement with this shift in investor interest towards Japan?

# Capital Rotation from China into Japanese Assets

One of the most significant changes, according to asset managers quoted by the Financial Times on 1 October 2023, is a fundamental shift in the way global funds now look at China — and the mechanism runs directly to Japan's benefit. The geopolitics of US-China tensions, chip wars, decoupling and "friendshoring" seem in particular to be working significantly in Japan's favour: Asia-focused global investment is rotating out of China and into Tokyo stocks, real estate and other assets, just as large parts of corporate Japan are engaging more actively with shareholders than at any time in the past.

The push side of the model is China's loss of sheen after years of stunning growth and investor attention. Its economy is growing more slowly and the expected post-pandemic rebound is proving elusive. On top of that, Beijing's policymaking — with sudden crackdowns on entire industries such as video games and private tutoring — has generated a series of nasty surprises and the unshakeable fear that others could occur at any time.

"You are seeing more interest in Japan from investors, who were primarily invested in China, as China has slowed and some of its economic policies have been confusing and opaque," says Kirk Neureiter, president of Fidelity Management & Research Japan. "Deployment of capital to China has been a bit more risky in terms of eventual outcome of investment decisions, given that lack of clarity." He qualifies the model's range: interest in Japan has not only come about because of the push away from China.

# The Outlook For US-China VC Dealmaking

There are no signs that USD funds' dealmaking in China will bounce back to its heights in the foreseeable future. The PitchBook report predicts that VC activity with U.S. participation in China during 2023 will hit a nine-year low, followed by a decade low in 2024.

But the open question is whether Chinese tech firms, now under a new stringent regulatory regime, can deliver the same level of strong growth and returns they experienced in the previous laissez-faire era.

If the U.S. market turns out to be too challenging to penetrate due to competitive and geopolitical factors, there are still other markets to explore. Japan, known for its openness to new technologies, has been particularly popular among China's SaaS startups venturing abroad; sniffing opportunity, China's USD fund managers, still anchored in the Middle Kingdom, will likely follow them to the neighboring country or any other market that will help hedge against uncertainties presented at home and abroad.

qid: Which company, recently involved in an antitrust battle where it provided extensive documentation to the court, was also mentioned by a news publisher in a class action lawsuit for its alleged anticompetitive practices, and is considered by Apple to be the only viable option for search engine services, despite not planning additional measures for its video platform as per reports from TechCrunch and The Verge?
context:
# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.

# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.

# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."

# Patent Litigation

## Definition

In the corpus, patent litigation is the set of formal legal proceedings companies use to fight over patent rights — a patent holder's lawsuit in federal district court and, in parallel, a case before the US International Trade Commission (ITC) — with remedies that can include a monetary verdict or an ITC import ban, and with the accused party able to counter-sue or get the asserted patents ruled invalid or unenforceable.

## Context

The corpus documents two concrete disputes that illustrate the mechanics of patent litigation. Sonos sued Google and won a $32.5 million verdict over patent infringement, but a federal judge later threw out that win after finding Sonos' patents "unenforceable and invalid" — showing that a litigation win is not final until it survives post-trial and appellate review. Separately, Masimo sued Apple in the US District Court for the Central District of California in 2020 for trade-secret theft and infringement of 10 patents related to pulse-oximetry (SpO2) sensing technology, and when that case dragged on, Masimo additionally filed a parallel case with the US International Trade Commission (ITC) in 2021; Apple counter-sued Masimo the following year. The ITC route matters because, unlike a district court, it can issue an import ban that blocks the accused product (the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2) from entering the US market, and any such ban is then subject to a 60-day presidential review period during which the President or US Trade Representative may veto it.

## Key Characteristics

- **Dual venues** — patent disputes can run in federal district court (damages, injunctions) and, in parallel, before the ITC (import bans), as in the Apple-Masimo dispute where Masimo pursued both.
- **Invalidity/unenforceability as a defense** — a defendant can defeat an infringement verdict after the fact by getting the asserted patents ruled unenforceable and invalid, as happened to Sonos' win against Google.
- **Countersuits** — litigation can escalate into cross-litigation, as when Apple sued Masimo back, alleging Masimo's own watch cloned Apple's design.
- **ITC import-ban remedy plus presidential review** — an ITC finding of infringement can trigger a ban on importing the infringing product, but the ban is not final until a 60-day presidential/USTR review period lapses without a veto.
- **Long timelines** — the Apple-Masimo dispute originated roughly a decade before the resulting Apple Watch import ban took effect, illustrating how a single patent dispute can span years across multiple proceedings.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, patent litigation is generally described as the process of enforcing patent rights, and it is decided exclusively by federal (not state) courts in the US.

Remedies available in such litigation typically include a permanent or preliminary injunction ordering the infringing act to stop, and a damages award such as a reasonable royalty.

A defendant can raise defenses including that the patent has expired, that it holds a license, or that the patent is invalid or unenforceable, and disputes may also end in a settlement that includes a licensing agreement.

# PPDA: Passes Allowed Per Defensive Action

PPDA is the number of opposition passes allowed outside of the pressing team's own defensive third, divided by the number of defensive actions by the pressing team outside of their own defensive third, as defined by Sky Sports on 28 October 2023.

The discriminating feature of the metric is the direction in which it reads: a lower figure indicates a higher level of pressing, while a higher figure indicates a lower level of pressing. # Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.



---


# Google One VPN

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

Engadget has not fully tested the Google One VPN yet, but says it will add it to the list if it feels it is warranted.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

qid: After the report by Cnbc | World Business News Leader on October 6, 2023, stating that businesses selling on Amazon might opt to set non-competitive prices, did The Verge report a change or consistency in eBay's approach to pricing competitiveness in their article on October 25, 2023?
context:
# The FTC's Antitrust Lawsuit Against Amazon

The Federal Trade Commission's sweeping 172-page antitrust lawsuit, filed in late September 2023, accuses Amazon of wielding its monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, which the agency alleges has led to artificially inflated prices and a degraded shopping experience for consumers.

The mechanism the FTC describes is an "anti-discounting strategy" backed by a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices" to stifle competition: Amazon punishes third-party sellers who offer cheaper products elsewhere by threatening to disqualify them from appearing in the buy box if it detects a lower price, and losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers' businesses, the complaint alleges. The end result, the FTC argues, is elevated prices across the web — the company steadily hikes the fees it charges sellers and prevents them from discounting on other sites, so sellers often inflate their prices off Amazon, creating an "artificial price floor everywhere." The FTC is seeking to hold Amazon liable for allegedly violating anti-monopoly law but has not yet outlined the specific remedies it believes would best resolve its concerns; in antitrust cases, remedies are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable. Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky responded in a blog post that third-party sellers set their own prices on the marketplace and that the company invests in tools to help sellers offer "competitive prices": "Even with those tools, some of the businesses selling on Amazon might still choose to set prices that aren't competitive. Just like any store owner who wouldn't want to promote a bad deal to their customers, we don't highlight or promote offers that are not competitively priced." Zapolsky argued the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result that would be directly opposed to the goals of antitrust law."



---


# eBay Best Price Guarantee

eBay offers a generous price-matching policy outside the holiday peak: if you find a lower price from a qualifying competitor on an eBay Deal item that you bought within 48 hours — or on another product carrying the "Best Price Guarantee" symbol — you get "110 percent" of the difference. That means eBay gives you an eBay coupon for the difference between what you paid and what the competitor is selling it for, plus an additional 10 percent of that price difference.

The preconditions are that the products must be new, unopened, and identical to the competitor's item. You have to contact eBay Customer Service, and if they verify your claims are legitimate you receive the coupon and can use it toward your next eBay purchase.

Two limits bound the policy, per The Verge's October 25th, 2023 summary: as a general rule eBay does not match the prices of purchases made during the weeks of Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, and the coupons expire within 30 days of being issued.



---


# Discogs Versus eBay And Amazon For Sellers

Even with all of its increasing costs, Discogs is still less expensive than alternatives like eBay or Amazon — albeit now only slightly — but those alternatives, being considerably larger and more mainstream, offer a much broader base of potential buyers as well as a more solid infrastructure and support system. That trade-off has begun to tip against Discogs.

Doug Martin, who sells primarily new vinyl and uses Amazon, Walmart, eBay, and Discogs along with his own website apocalypsevinyl.com, said eBay's fees are usually around 1 percent higher than Discogs': "eBay has much more of a user base, so for the little bit of extra cost it's a no brainer. It's probably double [the business] I do on Discogs, and that's only grown since they raised the fees." With the new fees and the competitiveness of the Discogs market, he said, the platform is becoming less and less useful as a selling channel.

The Connecticut seller, who has been selling on Discogs since 2009, said of the company: "They're under the impression that they're the only game in town. The fees were relatively low, but now that they're higher, there doesn't seem to be a reason to use that anymore." Since the recent changes he has lowered his prices to offset the higher shipping costs and was compelled to institute an order minimum — a major shift for a marketplace that had done considerable business in selling records under $10 and even under $5.



---


# Amazon Q3 2023 Earnings Preview

Ecommerce and cloud giant Amazon was due to release its Q3 earnings on Thursday 26 October 2023 after the market close, with the quarter expected to focus on Amazon's cost-cutting initiatives, supply chain management and AI product deployment as potential positive factors for attracting investment in equities amid current market conditions.

Wall Street analysts held a consensus Strong Buy rating, but Seeking Alpha Quant Ratings assessed the company as a Hold; on a year-to-date basis Amazon shares had expanded by almost 50% in value. SA Investing Group Leader Danie Jones, bullish on the stock, wrote: "AMZN's cost-cutting initiatives and margin improvements make it a solid buying opportunity, despite concerns such as the FTC lawsuit and a weakening economy." Fellow Investing Group Leader Sensor Unlimited expected the stock to continue being range-bound in the near term due to key challenges on operating margins, competition in key growth areas, and valuation risks.

Consensus EPS estimates were $0.60 and consensus revenue estimates $141.621B; Amazon had beaten EPS and revenue expectations in half of the past 8 quarters. Also reporting that day were Kenvue, Intel, Ford, Altria Group, Merck & Co., Bristol-Myers Squibb, Mastercard, Southwest Airlines, Newmont, United Parcel Service, Comcast, Honeywell International, Chipotle Mexican Grill, United States Steel, Royal Caribbean Cruises, Northrop Grumman, International Paper, Boston Scientific, Capital One Financial, L3Harris Technologies, Peabody Energy, Hertz Global Holdings, The Hershey Company, PG&E, Hasbro, FirstEnergy, Harley-Davidson, W.W. Grainger and more.



---


# Holiday Price Matching Policies, 2023

Some major retailers ensured price protection on purchases during the 2023 holiday season, but the terms differ sharply by retailer, so whether you get price matching depends on where and when you shop.

Amazon does not price match, which Polygon calls annoying but tolerable since it often has the lowest prices of all retailers anyway; Amazon only protects the price on pre-orders carrying its "Pre-order Price Guarantee," which ensures you pay the lowest amount a product sells for before it launches. Best Buy not only matches prices from "qualified competitors" but says on its site that most products bought between the article's publication and December 30 can be price-matched through January 13, 2024. Walmart's policy says it will not price match with competitors, nor does it price match for products purchased online that later decrease in price. Target says purchases made between October 22 and December 24 can be price-adjusted if the cost falls within that span and you show proof of purchase; eligibility exists, but the rules for submitting documentation vary depending on whether you shop online or in store.



---


# The EU's Prior Amazon Settlements And Its DMA Gatekeeper Designation

Late in 2022 the EU settled with Amazon over two earlier competition probes: one delving into antitrust concerns about Amazon's use of merchant data to bolster its own retail business, and a second looking at how it operated the "Buy Box" and its Prime loyalty program. In those cases Amazon agreed a series of commitments to end the probes, including saying it would stop using non-public data from its marketplace sellers and boost transparency for merchants, and pledging to treat all sellers equally regardless of whether they pay for its logistics services.

At the time the EU's then competition chief, Margrethe Vestager, trumpeted the outcome as setting what she dubbed "new rules for how Amazon operates its business in Europe," arguing the settlement meant the ecommerce giant could "no longer abuse its dual role" as marketplace operator and own-brand retailer, and further claiming the outcome would ensure "competing independent retailers and carriers as well as consumers will benefit from these changes opening up new opportunities and choice." Given the commitments the EU already extracted from Amazon after those earlier investigations, TechCrunch notes it is interesting to see the bloc remains concerned over levers the ecommerce behemoth still has at its disposal to potentially influence competitive outcomes on its marketplace as between iRobot and rival robot vacs.

Since then Amazon has also been named a gatekeeper under the EU's ex ante competition regulation, the Digital Markets Act, which lists its marketplace as a core platform service. That designation means Amazon must comply with a series of up-front obligations, which include restrictions on self preferencing.



---


# Retailer Sales Competing With Amazon Prime Day

Amazon Prime Day has inspired many imitators, and shoppers will find sales from competitors like Best Buy, Target, and the like.

WIRED's assessment is mixed: some of these sales are great, and it flags them when they are, but others are worth holding off on until Black Friday and Cyber Monday — when, it jokes, WIRED will again be the Internet's only website with deals posts.

qid: Which AI-powered chatbot, covered by both Engadget and TechCrunch, not only celebrated its first anniversary since release but also saw a significant increase in usage during December 2022 and is known for its ability to perform a wide range of tasks including coding, composing music, and emulating a Linux computer?
context:
# ChatGPT's Task Capabilities And Measured Productivity Effects

ChatGPT's skills extend beyond conversation, another likely reason for its staying power. It can complete and debug code, compose music and essays, answer test questions, generate business ideas, write poetry and song lyrics, translate and summarize text, and even emulate a computer running Linux.

The measured effect comes from one study with a specific task set: an MIT study showed that, for tasks like writing cover letters, "delicate" emails and cost-benefit analyses, ChatGPT decreased the amount of time it took workers to complete the tasks by 40% while increasing output quality by 18%, as measured by third-party evaluators.

Ruoxi Shang attributes the breadth to a shift in how such systems are built: "Because [the AI models powering OpenAI] have been trained extensively on vast amounts of data, they [have] shifted focus from training specialized chatbots for specific domains to creating more general-purpose systems that can handle a variety of topics easily through prompting with instructions … [Chatbots like ChatGPT] don't require users to learn any new form of language, as long as they provide a task and some desired output just like how a manager would communicate to an intern."



---


# ChatGPT's Mid-2023 Usage Decline

By June, a little bit of ChatGPT's shine had started to wear off: Congress reportedly limited Capitol Hill staffers from using the application over data handling concerns, and user numbers had declined nearly 10 percent month-over-month.

Even so, ChatGPT was already well on its way to ubiquity, and a March update enabling the AI to comprehend and generate Python code in response to natural language queries only increased its utility.



---


# ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. The fallout was still settling, but it might empower competitors such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, or help other AI startups get attention and funding as the industry watched OpenAI implode and put itself back together. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. GPT-4, which can write more naturally and fluently than previous models, remained largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, although it could be accessed for free through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Safari web browsers. Beyond GPT-4 and the OpenAI DevDay announcements, OpenAI had recently connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users, and with the integration of DALL-E 3, users could generate both text and images right inside ChatGPT.



---


# AI Market Spending Forecasts Reported In October 2023

Total global spending on AI was expected to reach $154 billion by the end of 2023, a 27% increase from 2022, with the following three years also expected to see a compound annual growth rate of 27% — putting annual AI spending in 2026 at over $300 billion. These figures were cited in TechCrunch's 13 October 2023 survey of venture capitalists active in AI investing, as context for how much room startups have in the enterprise market.

Alongside the spending numbers, McKinsey reports that generative AI alone can add up to $4.4 trillion in value across industries through writing code, analyzing consumer trends, personalizing customer service, improving operating efficiencies, and more. Ninety-four percent of business leaders agree AI will be critical to all businesses' success over the next five years, and eighty-two percent of business leaders believe the integration of AI solutions will increase their employee performance and job satisfaction.

A comparative observation accompanies the totals: despite cloud computing remaining critical, AI budgets are now more than double that of cloud computing. The conditions under which these figures were offered matter — they were presented as evidence that startups should expect a high level of desire for and experience with AI solutions in their future customers. Within the enterprise sector there is a clear recognition of the value of AI, but many enterprises lack the internal capabilities to develop AI solutions, and that gap is what is said to present a significant opportunity for startups specializing in AI to engage with enterprise clients. As the business landscape matures, proficiency in leveraging AI is becoming a strategic imperative.



---


# Gemini Pro's Coding Task Failures

Google emphasized Gemini's enhanced coding skills in a briefing in the first week of December 2023, and posts on X suggest it may genuinely have improved in some areas — but it also appears that Gemini Pro struggles with basic coding functions in Python. TechCrunch collected several user reports from 6 and 7 December 2023.

Filip Piekniewski reported that Gemini-based Bard still could not write the intersection of two polygons, calling it one of those rare, relatively simple to express functions that was never implemented in Python and has no Stack Overflow post, and noting that all these models fail on it. Mohsen Azimi found Gemini Pro "pretty disappointing" for his example: he asked it to make an analog clock using HTML like one ChatGPT made, and while it could cite some code from GitHub, it was off by a few milliseconds.

Two head-to-head comparisons went the same way. Edison Ade created a Tic Tac Toe game with both ChatGPT and Bard running on Gemini Pro, and reported that ChatGPT wrote the code on the first try while Bard took three tries, concluding GPT-4 was still greater than Gemini Pro. N Kiran Kumar tested Bard with the Gemini Pro update and got no bugless snake game on the first try; after reporting the bug and asking for a fix, the model could not fix it, whereas the free version of ChatGPT 3.5 returned correct, bug-free code on the first attempt.



---


# Explore With Alexa

"Explore with Alexa" is a feature on Amazon's Echo devices that lets kids have interactive conversations with an AI-powered Alexa. It was first announced in September and, as reported by TechCrunch on 25 October 2023, launched as an addition to the Amazon Kids+ content subscription, allowing children to have kid-friendly conversations with Alexa, powered by generative AI, but in a protected fashion designed to ensure the experience remains safe and appropriate.

The discriminating feature is the combination of generative AI, conversation, and an audience of children under 13. Some AI experiences already cater to younger users — the AI chatbots from Character.ai and other companies, including Meta — but Amazon is among the first to specifically look to generative AI to develop a conversational experience for kids under the age of 13. The two qualifiers that bound the concept are the subscription it lives inside (Amazon Kids+) and the protective framing: this is not an unbounded chatbot but a conversational experience deliberately constructed to stay safe and age-appropriate.



---


# Apple M3 Chip Architecture And GPU Features

The M3 line is the first of Apple's desktop chips to be created using the 3nm process, following the iPhone 15 Pro's lead — Apple had employed the 5nm process since the M1's introduction in 2020 — and the new process brings performance gains with less power consumption, making the Mac the first PC line to employ the technology.

GPU updates were the centerpiece of the M3 announcements, with gaming an important narrative for Apple's silicon journey. The first new feature is Dynamic Caching. Apple writes: "With Dynamic Caching, only the exact amount of memory needed is used for each task. This is an industry first, transparent to developers, and the cornerstone of the new GPU architecture. It dramatically increases the average utilization of the GPU, which significantly increases performance for the most demanding pro apps and games." More simply put, the idea is allocating just the right amount of local memory to a given task, something Apple has been working on for a while.

The other two additions are hardware-accelerated ray tracing and mesh shading. Ray tracing is designed to bring added realism to the gaming experience through more accurate depictions of lighting and reflections; mesh shading, a triangle computer shader, makes processing complex geometrical images more efficient, which in turn allows for higher-quality graphics and more scene detail.



---


# Induced AI's Plain-English Workflow Automation

Sam Altman is among the backers of Induced AI, an AI startup founded by two teenagers that aims to help businesses automate workflows in "previously unexplored" ways.

Manish reported the story in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023. Induced AI was founded that same year, and its product lets businesses type their back-office tasks into it in plain English, converting those instructions into pseudo-code in real time.

qid: Which company is at the center of antitrust allegations involving monopolistic behavior in the search engine, app distribution, and news publishing markets, as reported by both The Verge and TechCrunch?
context:
# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# US Tech Giants' 2023 App Download Rankings

Meta and Google both lost ground in Apple's 2023 U.S. iPhone download rankings. Meta, which last year held the No. 3, No. 4 and No. 9 spots with WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook respectively, showed up in the top 10 this year with a slightly different mix: Facebook is gone from the charts, while Meta's new app Instagram Threads was the No. 3 app by U.S. downloads, with Instagram and WhatsApp following at No. 6 and No. 9, both slipping from their ranking last year.

Google had dominated last year's list with the No. 2 app YouTube, just behind TikTok, as well as No. 5 Google Maps, No. 6 Google Search and No. 7 Gmail. In 2023, however, Google's only two apps in the top 10 by downloads were No. 7 Google Search and No. 8 YouTube, both also slipping in ranking from last year.

The only other top app in the list not from Meta, Google or a Chinese firm was Max, formerly HBO Max, which showed up as the No. 3 app by downloads in the U.S.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Lawsuit Redactions As Signal: The Amazon Precedent

TechCrunch reads heavy redaction as itself informative: you know it is bad news for the company when they request pages and pages of redactions.

The precedent it cites is recent. This recently happened with Amazon as well, and it turned out they were trying to hide the existence of a price-hiking algorithm that skimmed billions from consumers.

The comparison is used to rank severity rather than to equate the two: it is much worse, TechCrunch writes, when you are redacting COPPA complaints.

# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Thirty years on from Istanbul, United headed to Turkey knowing they had rarely been convincing in the Champions League in recent years, The Guardian reported on Nov. 27, 2023: a 3-1 away win against Paris Saint-Germain in the 2018-19 round of 16, after losing the home leg 2-0, was the last time they won a crunch match.

In 2020-21 they lost their final two group games and were eliminated, while back in 2015-16 Wolfsburg won the deciding group match to knock them out. United had done little learning in recent times, repeating the same failures in Europe's elite competition. Manchester United were out of Europe altogether after a limp display against Bayern at Old Trafford, where Kingsley Coman sealed a 1-0 win for Thomas Tuchel's side on the final day of Champions League group-stage play, per Sporting News on Dec. 12 and Dec. 13, 2023.

# Manchester United's 2023 Champions League Group Stage Exit

Ten Hag's United compiled arguably the worst performance by any English team in a Champions League group stage in 2023, finishing bottom of their group and shipping 15 goals — more than any other English team ever.

# Manchester United's Defensive Imbalance: Ferdinand's Critique

Rio Ferdinand argued that Manchester United's European problems stem from a lack of balance in the team — they can score at will but make defensive mistakes that undo the game plan — and that the fix has to be applied over a period of games, not one or two, talkSPORT reported on 29 November 2023.

"I think they've got to look at themselves," said Ferdinand, a 2007/08 Champions League winner with United. "You can't go into a Champions League campaign and score nine goals in three away games and have one point at the end of it. The warrant is that the tactical work was sound and the errors, not the plan, cost the points — and that repeated collapses leave a psychological residue. "I think the manager will be scratching his head and thinking, 'The game plan first-half worked perfectly,' and then all of a sudden they score a goal, it changes the dynamic of the game.
