So I think there's a lot of question marks in the performances and the way they're going about things at the moment but balance for me is one of the key aspects that they've got to really find." He continued: "We mentioned in commentary, scars from throwing away leads, those are hard to get away, you've got to really manage games and he mentioned that himself Bruno, you've got to go out managing games correctly. They've got to do that not over one or two or three games, they've got to do that over a period of games now so they can erase those scars that they've created and they'e grown through bad results and throwing away leads, especially in Europe."

# Jean-Claude Blanc and the United Chief Executive Challenge

The question The Guardian posed on 25 December 2023 is whether any chief executive can make Manchester United a best-in-class elite club again — and the candidate in frame is Jean-Claude Blanc, billed as the "Lionel Messi of business" by Nice's chief executive, Fabrice Bocquet.

# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Ramaswamy's TikTok National Security Contradiction

The objection TechCrunch raises on 2023-10-02 attacks the premise that Ramaswamy's TikTok presence is a coherent outreach strategy: his presence on the platform conflicts with his own stated stances on social media and on young voters. His strategy is puzzling because he appears to be trying to replicate the success of previous candidates who became social media stars over the course of their campaigns, while holding positions that undercut the very audience and platform he is courting.

Two of his own positions supply the contradiction. Like many of his Republican colleagues, Ramaswamy has accused TikTok of being a threat to national security, and during a town hall days before he launched his account he described the platform as "digital fentanyl" from China. He has also proposed barring anyone under 25 from voting, unless they serve in the military or pass a civics exam. His communications director, Tricia McLaughlin, did not immediately respond to TechCrunch's request for comment.

# Cohen's Cross-Examination Of Caroline Ellison

Mark Cohen's cross-examination of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 aimed at the premise that her direct testimony was reliable — she had recounted many conversations held in person or on auto-deleting messaging platforms, and she had an incentive to flip on Bankman-Fried in the form of possible leniency at sentencing — but The Verge's reporter judged that the defense absolutely biffed it. In Cohen's disorganized cross-examination he mostly bored the jury; at one point two different jurors appeared to be asleep, and midway through the morning the reporter began wondering whether there was a mercy rule for cross-examinations.

The lines of attack were opened and dropped. Cohen established that Bankman-Fried had a much larger appetite for risk than Ellison, that the two reacted differently to stress, and that they took different approaches to media — Ellison avoided it while Bankman-Fried sought it out — without building on any of it. He drew out that Alameda had one accountant in 2021 and hired two more junior accountants in 2022, and had a problem retaining accountants, then dropped that too. He appeared to be trying to suggest the government had coerced Ellison's testimony by getting her to plead guilty to defrauding investors, conduct she could not have been involved in since she did not prepare materials for them; unfortunately she said she had had conversations with investors as part of their due diligence, and Alameda was in any case taking on losses from FTX to keep FTX's balance sheet pristine. Cohen also pressed the hedge he had blamed her for not taking out in his opening — hedging being long crypto by selling Nasdaq futures — which raised the question of whether the defense was that she should have taken more customer funds, or taken them sooner.

Small failures accumulated. Cohen asked Ellison to define what "buy on the way down" meant as though it were a term of art, which seemed to puzzle her, and at other times he seemed to forget what she had testified to and brought up things she had not said; like FTX employee Adam Yedidia before her, Ellison was fastidious about making sure a question was clear and her answer precise. She appeared at one point to be toying with him: having testified on direct about the token Luna, she noted when Cohen asked about Terra/Luna that she had only spoken about Luna, leaving him to fumble the relationship between the two. There were many sidebars, enough that several jurors looked entertained when one occurred, and in one the day before the prosecution complained that Bankman-Fried was visibly scoffing at Ellison's answers, per the court transcript. What Cohen was up against was strong direct evidence: fake balance sheets, one sent to crypto lender Genesis, after which a Genesis representative texted Ellison to say he had spoken to Bankman-Fried — strongly suggesting Bankman-Fried knew the contents of the fake balance sheet. Afterwards, the defendant's mother Barbara Fried engaged Christian Everdell in an animated conversation, gesticulating and clearly holding a strong opinion; Everdell walked off and Cohen talked to her for a bit.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Elizabeth Warren's Criticism Of Apple Blocking Beeper

U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) rejected Apple's security rationale for cutting off Beeper Mini, attacking it as pretextual while the Beeper team scrambled for a fix. In a post on X, formerly Twitter, she wrote: "Green bubble texts are less secure. So why would Apple block a new app allowing Android users to chat with iPhone users on iMessage? Big Tech executives are protecting profits by squashing competitors. Chatting between different platforms should be easy and secure."

Her argument turns Apple's own premise against it: if the alternative to iMessage — green bubble texts — is less secure, then blocking an app that extends iMessage to Android cannot be explained by user security, leaving competitive self-interest as the explanation.

qid: Who is the individual under 30, previously reported by TechCrunch as the richest in the world, who is alleged by the prosecution to have committed fraud for wealth and influence, discussed governance structures with Paradigm for a company, and is connected to a $14 billion customer fund misuse as reported by Cnbc | World Business News Leader and TechCrunch?
context:
# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.



---


# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."

qid: Has the focus on the impact of sleep on the immune system decreased in the reports from 'The Independent - Life and Style' after the article discussing the lives of insomniacs published on October 1, 2023, compared to the article about the clock change published on October 24, 2023?
context:
# The Clock Change, Circadian Disruption And Immunity

The health case against the clock change runs through sleep: moving off daylight saving time interferes with the natural circadian rhythm, the 24-hour biological cycle influenced by morning light and evening darkness, and research shows that even a small reduction in sleep affects the immune system — which matters because a good night's sleep during the winter months is essential protection against the seasonal increase in colds and flu.

Giulia Guerrini, lead pharmacist of the digital pharmacy Medino, sets out the grounds and the practical implication. "It's hard to understate the importance of a good night's sleep," she says. "Having too much or too little sleep can have adverse side effects, so you should aim to get between seven and eight hours of sleep as consistently as possible." She names the clock change as a leading disruptor: "One of the biggest disruptors to our sleep is when UK clocks go forward one hour at 1am on the last Sunday in March and go back one hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October, which is rapidly approaching on 30 October." Her advice follows from the premise that consistency matters most: "One of the most important aspects of a healthy sleep schedule is waking up around the same time each morning, so try to limit yourself to a one-hour window if you need to adjust when you get up in the morning and when you go to sleep at night. One hour sounds like an insignificant amount of time, but it can completely throw our circadian rhythm, or more simply known as internal clock, off balance."



---


# The DIY Sleep Hacks Insomniacs Report Trying

The Independent's October 2023 report on insomniacs catalogues the remedies people actually use: lavender oil, eating kiwis, masturbation — the days of counting sheep long gone. Jennifer Aniston's top tip for battling insomnia is to "sleep with my phone at least five feet away from me," while Martha Stewart recommends focusing on your breathing; in her 1973 feminist novel Fear of Flying, Erica Jong wrote that sometimes the only way to overcome sleeplessness is to pretend you don't care about nodding off, after which "sleep became piqued, like a rejected lover, and crept up to try to seduce you." The article notes that the internet is littered with tips promising sound sleep, that not all of them are effective and none are foolproof, and that kiwis contain serotonin and antioxidants, which is why they are thought to have sleep-promoting benefits.

Two case histories illustrate the trial-and-error. Social media consultant and mother of two Amy Fieldhouse-Downes began suffering from insomnia after the birth of her second son in 2019 and believes it was rooted in anxiety: "If you Google how to go to sleep, I've probably tried everything on there. Going to bed earlier, going to bed later, meditations that would get cut off by an advert, lavender products, sleep cream, eye masks, Sominex sleep tablets. And I even used it as an excuse to have a few glasses of wine." Only specialised earplugs finally let her rest. Long-time insomniac and video producer Preshita has tried "from drinking chamomile tea to counting backwards from 1,000," and found that showering before bed and keeping her bedroom clutter-free were most effective: "Someone recommended masturbating, and that was another thing that worked."



---


# Realigning The Circadian Clock Through Meal Timing

The goal of the restricted eating is to restore the circadian rhythm, the researchers said, which could help counteract the numerous disruptions that Alzheimer's patients face when it comes to sleep and schedule-related confusion.

Feeding timing is the lever on the clock. "Our study emphasizes the power of feeding timing in aligning the circadian clock and its impact on the brain," said senior study author Paula Desplats, PhD, professor in the Department of Neurosciences at UC San Diego School of Medicine, in a statement to Fox News Digital.

The researchers hope that the public recognizes the importance of the circadian clock in regulating many aspects of health. "Sustaining healthy sleep and eating habits that are more synchronized with the natural environment are vital in a society that is constantly exposed to food, light and shift work," said Desplats.



---


# Sleepagotchi, NFT-Powered Sleep Game

Sleepagotchi is a seed-stage mobile app game founded by Anton Kraminkin that aims to help people develop healthy sleep habits by gamifying sleep with NFTs; it appeared in Alliance DAO's All11 cohort at the 2023-10-18 demo day. The application is currently available on Apple's App Store, and its game rewards users daily for hitting sleep goals while also letting them collect items as motivation to sleep better.

Kraminkin reported during demo day that the game has 14,000 monthly active users and a 41% one-year retention rate, and according to its website 60.2% of users reported improved sleep since using the game. In January it raised $3.5 million from investors including 6th Man Ventures, Sfermion, 1kx and Shima Capital, and it is currently raising from strategic investors.



---


# Siesta Napping and Mortality Uncertainty

The siesta, a brief afternoon nap and a traditional habit in Mediterranean countries, is the component scientists remain undecided about: in the current study, specific napping habits were found to be associated with higher risk of mortality and cardiovascular disease, cutting against the presumption that every element of the Mediterranean lifestyle is protective.

The researchers themselves qualify that finding. Similar to the case of olive oil consumption, they say they did not have detailed information on frequency and duration of naps or sleep structure — how often and for how long — which weakens their conclusion. "Moreover, reverse causation is also possible, with people napping because of subclinical conditions or other chronic diseases (for instance, if they had more prevalence of sleep apnea), especially since napping faces a stigma in Anglo-Saxon countries," said Sotos-Prieto. She also points to a different shape of relationship in earlier work: "Previous studies have found a J-shaped relationship — a smile-like curve — between napping and cardiovascular diseases," a chart type in which low values of one variable (short nap duration) lead to a decrease in the second variable (incidence of cardiovascular events), while the trend reverses at higher values. "Short naps, which range from 0 to 30 minutes, were associated with lower incident cardiovascular disease," she said. "An inverse association between short naps and mortality and cardiovascular diseases was found in our previous publications." Asked for a definitive answer as to whether napping is beneficial, Sotos-Prieto indicated that more research is needed.



---


# Solar Cycle Maximum Forecast Revision

The major news about the sun in 2023 was that the solar maximum is arriving faster and will be more explosive than initially forecast: the peak would likely arrive by 2024 and be more active than the original prediction, and in October space weather scientists released an updated forecast for the current solar cycle that is more in line with what experts told Live Science.

When the current solar cycle began in 2019, forecasts from space weather scientists suggested that the solar maximum would arrive sometime from 2025 onward and be relatively weak compared with past solar cycles. Numerous warning signs early in the year — rising sunspot numbers, powerful X-class solar flares and changes in Earth's upper atmosphere — hinted that the solar cycle was not progressing as expected, and in June Live Science published an exclusive, in-depth feature on the upcoming solar maximum that laid out the revised picture. During the solar maximum the sun is much more chaotic than during the solar minimum. When the maximum does arrive, Earth can expect to be bombarded with more solar storms, resulting in frequent auroral displays, radio blackouts, potential satellite problems and disruptions to the migration patterns of some animals.



---


# American Public Climate Worry Polling

A 2022 poll found that almost two-thirds of Americans say they have been affected by extreme weather they believe was at least partially due to climate change, and about 27% of Americans say they are "very worried" about climate change while another 27% just avoid the subject as best they can.

One in 10 Americans reported feeling symptoms of anxiety or depression over climate change. The article introduces these figures to make the point that climate change is weighing not only on scientists but also on everyday Americans.



---


# An Australian Pandemic Account By Aisha Dow And Melissa Cunningham

Aisha Dow and Melissa Cunningham's account of how the pandemic affected Australia, published by Scribe at $35 on 3 October, is a timely publication coming only a few days after Daniel Andrews — "the man who approved probably the world's longest cumulative lockdown" — left office, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its defining feature is the treatment: while many people may not want to revisit those stressful years, the two journalists with Nine newspapers "manage to make this a riveting story of discovery, dismay, and recovery".

The reviewer places it against what was still to come: "Ahead of the government's impending inquiry, you might find some answers here."

Amazon's fall Prime Day event was underway on October 10th, 2023, and The Verge published a roundup of the best gaming deals it could scrounge up during Prime Big Deal Days, spanning PlayStation 5, PS4, Xbox Series X / S, Nintendo Switch, and PC, and extending to hardware deals on things like controllers, streaming peripherals, and the consoles themselves. A truckload of PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and Nintendo Switch games dropped in price for Black Friday 2023: both Sony and Microsoft rolled out holiday sales on their respective digital storefronts, while a number of physical games fell to new lows at Amazon, Best Buy and others.

# Roblox's PlayStation And Cross-Platform Expansion

At Roblox's annual developer conference in San Francisco two weeks before the Code Conference interview published on October 12th, 2023, the biggest crowd reaction in the opening keynote was for PlayStation support. # Mario Kart 8 Deluxe

Polygon says no multiplayer Nintendo Switch list would be complete without mentioning the most recent edition of the 20-year Mario Kart series; it appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Though the game came out in 2017, it still reigns supreme as far as kart racing goes.

It also still gets new courses, such as the recent addition of Mario Kart 7's Rainbow Road.

# Lil Gator Game

Lil Gator Game, developed by MegaWobble for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X, is ranked 35 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31.

Critic Chris Grant acknowledges that in an unprecedented year for game releases, readers may be surprised to see it this high on the list — and says he was just as surprised to find, in a moment of introspection, that it was one of his own favorite games of 2023.

At the risk of diminishing its accomplishments, he offers a comparison that should cut to the quick for interested parties: this is the most A Short Hike-alike he has discovered yet, a singular high he has been chasing for years. # Amazon Prime Free Games And DLC

Amazon offers freebies for Prime members round the calendar year, not just during the holiday months, and Polygon reports that Amazon's suite of giveaways has improved over time.

As a sample of what was up for grabs as of the article's November 2023 publication, Polygon named Rage 2, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and Doom 3, and said it collects the latest free games and DLC on an ongoing page.

# Console Subscription And Store Gift Cards For Gamers

If you're not sure which type of games your giftee prefers, The Verge suggests an Xbox, PlayStation, or Nintendo subscription: these memberships grant access to free digital titles and come with perks such as online multiplayer and cloud-based saves.

# Classic Nintendo Franchise Picks For The Switch

Polygon's advice for a first-time Switch owner is to start with the modern-day Zelda, Mario, and Animal Crossing games, on the grounds that Nintendo is home to some of the most iconic gaming franchises.

# Scope and Update Policy of Polygon's Best New Streaming Series Roundup

qid: Between the report from The Verge on the Epic v. Google case and the subsequent report from TechCrunch on the same case, was there disagreement on the nature of Epic Games' arguments against Google?
context:
# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Epic's Post-Verdict Remedy Strategy And Global Cases

Told that Google has said it will challenge the verdict, Tim Sweeney said Epic is not going to wait: it will do absolutely everything it can as quickly as it can to start changing the world, rather than pausing for the appeal.

His reasoning for the reach of the win is the market Epic established at trial — a market worldwide excluding China — so this is, in his framing, a worldwide verdict, and Epic presumes any remedies would be worldwide too. Beyond the US case, he pointed to the European DMA, to Epic v. Apple and Epic v. Google cases coming up in Australia, and to another in the UK. He also stressed that the push no longer depends on Epic alone: a lot of legislators, a lot of regulators, and other litigation are all pushing in the direction of openness. On whether the Google verdict helps Epic's Apple appeal, Sweeney said there is no linkage between the cases in law and no legal connection between the two, so it would come down only to whether the court is in any way following current events — to the decisions of the humans involved, the justices and support teams considering the appeal.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

Trump's lawyers asked the judge to throw out the case, and he denied the request. Their arguments attacked the attorney general's standing and the timing of the claims: they contend that James was not legally allowed to file the lawsuit because there is no evidence that the public was harmed by Trump's actions, and they also argued that many of the allegations in the lawsuit were barred by the statute of limitations.

Engoron, noting that he had "emphatically rejected" those arguments earlier in the case, equated them to the "time-loop in the film 'Groundhog Day.'"

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. # The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Simulcasting

## Definition

Simulcasting, as the corpus uses the term, is airing or streaming the same live content on two or more channels or platforms at the same time.

## Context

In the corpus the term spans two different media businesses: linear sports broadcasting and livestreaming.
For sports, simulcasting means a single live event airs at the same time on multiple TV and streaming outlets — the Seahawks-Giants "Monday Night Football" game was simulcast on both ABC and ESPN, and under NASCAR's new $7.7 billion media-rights deal with Fox Sports, NBC, Amazon, and Warner Bros. Discovery, races will be simulcast on Warner Bros. Discovery's MAX streaming service and on TNT cable simultaneously.
For livestreaming, Twitch's 2023 policy reversal reframed simulcasting as a creator freedom: streamers were newly permitted to stream to Twitch and other livestreaming platforms at the same time, reversing a long-standing exclusivity requirement.

## Key Characteristics

- **Simultaneity across outlets** — the defining feature is that the same content airs at the same time on more than one channel or platform, not that it is merely repeated later.
- **Can mix distribution types** — a simulcast can pair a free-to-air or cable channel with a streaming service, as in NASCAR's races airing on both TNT (cable) and MAX (streaming).
- **Reach vs. audience fragmentation** — Sports Business Journal's Adam Stern noted that simulcasting NASCAR races onto cable-gated TNT (rather than keeping them on a free-to-air network) risks lower ratings because cable requires a paid subscription, even though the deal nominally broadens distribution.
- **A policy lever in livestreaming** — Twitch's decision to allow simulcasting to other platforms, announced at TwitchCon 2023, reversed a prior ban on simultaneous multi-platform streaming.
- **Framed as community-driven, not competitive** — Twitch's Chief Monetization Officer Mike Minton said the simulcasting change (along with Partner Plus and ad-embed features discussed in the keynote) was an acknowledgment of community feedback, explicitly saying "I wouldn't call it out of competitive pressures" from rivals like Kick.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Wikipedia describes "simulcast" as a portmanteau of "simultaneous broadcast," meaning the broadcasting of a program or event across multiple mediums, resolutions, or bitrates, or across several services on one medium, at the same time (Wikipedia, "Simulcast," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simulcast).
