X's poor performance was assessed during a pilot phase of testing of a new methodology developed by Code signatories. "A big novelty under the Code is now the publication of the first set of structural indicators such as how easy it is to find disinformation content, how much engagement such content receives or indicators about sources. These indicators — developed by the signatories — constitute an unprecedented and novel insight into disinformation on online platforms," she said. "Such insight is crucial to understand how effective platforms efforts are to fight this threat even more efficiently. This is a very valuable industry proposal that has great potential while it has to be still further developed. Here, signatories have decided to run a pilot phase in three Member States to evaluate the methodology on two of those indicators. X, former Twitter, who is not under the Code any more is the platform with the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts."

X was contacted for a response to the EU's analysis of the ratio of disinformation it is spreading, and replied with an automated email reading: "Busy now, please check back later." The finding fits a wider pattern: consistent moderation, fact-checking investment and researcher data access are areas where X under new owner Elon Musk has moved out of step with EU expectations on countering disinformation, suggesting that X — designated by the EU as a VLOP under the DSA back in April — continues to put itself squarely in the Commission's crosshairs, including over its priority issue of tackling Kremlin propaganda.



---


# The Evolution Of Meltwater's Media Monitoring Business

Meltwater's business has evolved through three stages, each driven by a change in where the media lives: manual press clipping, digitized monitoring of print decline, and then social-media-era sentiment analysis over unstructured data.

The company's roots are in businesses where humans physically sifted through piles of newspapers daily to clip mentions of a company's name, collate those and send them to clients to help them track how they are being covered in the media. The decline of print media digitized that effort, and then the rise of social media turned it into a wider game — sentiment analysis — as words became structured and, more usually, unstructured data. The influx of a whole new set of tools to glean insight out of that data turned a media challenge into a technical one.

Meltwater's response was to build AI in-house and to acquire a stream of businesses in an analytics consolidation play. The most high-profile of these acquisitions was undoubtedly DataSift, the groundbreaking firm that was an early friend of Twitter's in monetizing its firehose, only for that relationship to turn sour. Companies like Meltwater are at a crossroads these days in technology terms.



---


# Thesis That Music Labels Are Headed for Irrelevance

The argument, common among music business observers from the world of tech, is that record labels could in the long term be headed for irrelevance. Its grounds are the arrival of digital platforms, including open ones like YouTube and SoundCloud, together with the proliferation of indie music distribution platforms such as DistroKid and TikTok's SoundOn.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is a claim about what labels are for: in a world where anyone can record music using a desktop audio workstation (DAW) and upload it directly to YouTube, or to Spotify via a distribution platform, labels have little left to do. Recording and distribution — the functions the label historically supplied — are available to any artist directly, so on this reasoning the label's remaining role shrinks toward nothing. Music Business Worldwide presented this as the speculation that tech-world observers "like to" make, and as the position Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl was answering at the Code Conference in September 2023.



---


# Public Policy Objectives: Efficiency, Equity And Stability

Public policies attempt to fulfill one or more of three objectives: efficiency, equity, and stability. The discriminating roles are stated as a division of labour between them: efficiency and stability are necessary conditions for sustainable growth, while equity is what helps make development inclusive.

The framing appears in the second article of a Business World series following the 2nd SGV Tax Symposium, which focused on how a sustainable and effective tax ecosystem can advance the sustainability agenda for both the public and private sectors, published on 5 November 2023.



---


# Azarus CEO on Curated Versus Grassroots Sports Streaming

Alex Casassovici, founder and CEO of Azarus — a company that works with online creators to enhance the streaming experience — told Polygon for its 2023-10-20 story that livestreaming sports and sports-related content on platforms like Twitch creates a more intimate experience for streamers and fans alike.

He frames the landscape as a split between two models.

"I think what we're looking at is either a very curated kind of managed channel, and more grassroots-like, creator-led experiences," Casassovici says. "That's clearly something that can be differentiated when it comes to streaming."

qid: After Wired reported on October 10, 2023, that Best Buy also had deals on Apple products, did The Verge's article on October 26, 2023, about the availability of deals on current Macs with M1, M2, or M3 chips indicate a consistent or inconsistent trend in the availability of Apple deals at retailers?
context:
# MacBook Pricing And Discount Landscape

Apple sells MacBooks equipped with its own M-series chips in a wide range of sizes and price points, starting with the 13-inch MacBook Air from 2020 at $999 and going up to the latest 16-inch MacBook Pro starting at $2,499 — and, as The Verge put it on October 26th, 2023, finding a deal on a current Mac with an M1, M2, or even the new M3 chip, as well as the higher-end M3 Pro and M3 Max, is actually not that difficult.

The discriminating feature of Mac discounting is that it is episodic rather than continuous: Macs may not experience perpetual discounts, but it is not uncommon to see various current models discounted by as much as $400. The alternative route to savings is buying refurbished directly from Apple, which avoids waiting for the changing winds of deals; Apple's refurbished store provides a one-year warranty on all products and generally offers discounts of up to 15 to 20 percent off the price of a new unit.

One boundary case is explicitly excluded. The Verge does not recommend buying any older Intel-based Macs: retailers may try to tempt buyers with very low prices on leftover new or refurbished stock, but there is a reason nobody wants them anymore — they are completely outclassed by all the newer models, unless you have some super-niche Windows Boot Camp needs, and even then you should consider which Windows apps you really need and whether they work with Parallels.



---


# Supply Signals Pointing To A MacBook Pro M3 Refresh

There is a very good chance Apple will have at least one MacBook Pro refresh to show off at the event: both Kuo and Gurman have indicated that will be the case.

The supply-side evidence is specific. Gurman pointed out that the 13-inch, 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro all currently have extended shipping times on Apple's web store, which is often an indicator that the company is winding down the supply of existing products.

Gurman also reported that Apple has been testing M3 Max and M3 Pro MacBook Pro models, which could now be ready for prime time.



---


# WIRED's Prime Day 2023 Apple Roundup Scope

WIRED's Apple-specific Prime Day roundup exists because discounts on Apple products are few and far between: with Amazon's second big sale event of the year, officially called Prime Big Deal Days, it found a variety of Apple deals covering iPads, Apple Watches, iPhone cases, and MagSafe accessories.

Its scope is not limited to one store — the deals aren't just at Amazon, and WIRED links to other retailers like Best Buy when available — and the list is maintained as the event runs: an October 11 update added new deals on the Apple Magic Keyboard, Apple Studio Display, ESR HaloLock 3-in-1 Travel Wireless Charging Set, Monoprice Extra Wide Microfiber Desk Mat, and Apple AirTags.



---


# Mac Mini M2 Holiday Deal

The base model of Apple's diminutive desktop computer, the Mac mini, was on sale for $100 off at Amazon, B&H Photo and Best Buy for both Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2023; the wider Black Friday roundup lists the 256GB model at $500 at Best Buy and the 512GB model at $690 at Amazon with a clippable coupon, while the Apple roundups put a 512GB SSD version at $699 at B&H Photo.

It earned an 86 in Engadget's review because it packs a lot of processing power, using the same M2 chip as the two current-model MacBook Airs while being much cheaper than either laptop. Though Engadget expects an upgrade to the new M3 chip at some point over the next year, the current model is still a great option for a speedy desktop that runs macOS, and it has a headphone jack, a Gigabit Ethernet port, two USB-A connectors, two Thunderbolt 4 USB-Cs and an HDMI 2.0 port.



---


# WIRED Black Friday 2023 MacBook Air And Mac Mini Deals

WIRED's Apple Black Friday guide of 25 November 2023 covered four discounted consumer Macs: the 13-inch M2 MacBook Air, the 15-inch M2 MacBook Air, the M1 MacBook Air and the Mac Mini.

The M2 MacBook Air (7/10, WIRED Recommends) has a modern design with a MagSafe connector so the laptop will not fly off if you trip on the cable, and the M2 chip delivers plenty of power for everyday tasks, solid battery life and a 1080p webcam. WIRED is careful about the price history: it has dipped lower, to $899, in the past and it hits this price often, but WIRED still calls it a solid deal, while noting Apple is rumoured to launch M3-powered 13-inch and 15-inch MacBook Airs next year. The 15-inch MacBook Air (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is the first large-screen option in the Air lineup and packs the same features as the 13-inch version including the redesigned chassis and 1080p webcam, with the M2 delivering excellent performance and about 10 hours of battery life; WIRED recommends opting for 16 gigabytes of RAM if it fits your budget, and notes it is also on sale for $1,449 ($250 off).

The M1-powered MacBook Air (9/10, WIRED Recommends) came out in 2020 but remains one of the most powerful laptops you can buy at this price and WIRED's favourite budget MacBook, offering great performance, battery life that easily lasts a full workday, an improved keyboard and a lightweight chassis good for travel — with the caveat that it frequently goes on sale for this price. The Mac Mini (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a powerful, compact desktop that only needs a monitor, keyboard and mouse; it does not pack as many ports as the M2 Pro version, but still offers two Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, two USB-A, HDMI, a 10-gigabit Ethernet connection and a 3.5-mm headphone jack, and WIRED notes it has dipped this low a few times before but is still a great deal.



---


# Retailer Sales Competing With Amazon Prime Day

Amazon Prime Day has inspired many imitators, and shoppers will find sales from competitors like Best Buy, Target, and the like.

WIRED's assessment is mixed: some of these sales are great, and it flags them when they are, but others are worth holding off on until Black Friday and Cyber Monday — when, it jokes, WIRED will again be the Internet's only website with deals posts.



---


# Retailer Price-Matching Overview

To avoid overpaying, check the price-matching policy of the retailer you bought from: many retailers promise to match a lower price you have found elsewhere in order to keep customers happy and prevent them from going elsewhere, which The Verge noted on October 25th, 2023 was information that could come in handy with Black Friday and Cyber Monday just around the corner. The frustration it addresses is buying a new pair of headphones, an OLED TV, or a backpack only to find out you could have got it for a lot cheaper somewhere else.

Three cautions apply before using any of these policies. First, all price-matching policies have a number of rules attached to them: The Verge summarised some of them but advised readers to follow the links it provided and read each policy carefully. Second, and logically enough, retailers that serve as marketplaces for other sellers, such as Costco, do not have price-matching policies. Third, there are always exceptions to the rules — if you are looking for a deal on a product and you know it is available for a lower price elsewhere, or was previously offered at the same retailer, it never hurts to call or chat with a customer service rep and ask if they will match the price.

The illustration The Verge used: if Best Buy offers a better discount than Target on the latest Kindle Paperwhite, Target will refund you the difference.



---


# WIRED's Pre-Black Friday 2023 Deal Window

WIRED's October 19, 2023 roundup covers the lull between sales events: with the latest Amazon-created Prime-themed sale day behind us and Black Friday slowly approaching, the deals world feels a bit like Pippin waiting on the edge of battle.

The point of the list is that the lull is not empty — there are still sales to score while waiting for winter to come — and its scope is the best deals right now on TVs, gaming gear, and other electronics.



---


# Anti-Prime Big Deal Day Competing Sales

Despite what the name might suggest, Amazon's fall Prime Day event is not just a day filled with deals for Prime members: thanks to competing sales from retailers like Best Buy and Walmart, everybody can take advantage of steep discounts without needing to pay a monthly premium to join in.

In some cases retailers are matching Amazon's pricing, meaning shoppers can score the same discounts available to Prime members on items like the Kindle Paperwhite and Echo Pop. There are also terrific deals available on other gadgets, including noise-canceling headphones, tablets and smartwatches, which The Verge rounded up to make deal hunting easier.

qid: Does the article from 'The Independent - Life and Style' suggest that 'Taylor Swift' is open about her relationship with a specific individual, while the article from 'The Age' only confirms her presence at a sporting event without mentioning her openness about personal relationships?
context:
# Taylor Swift's Stated Approach To Public Scrutiny

Taylor Swift told Time in December 2023 that she has nothing to hide in her relationship with Travis Kelce, and defined what she means by a public relationship: "When you say a relationship is public, that means I'm going to see him do what he loves, we're showing up for each other, other people are there and we don't care. The opposite of that is you have to go to an extreme amount of effort to make sure no one knows that you're seeing someone. And we're just proud of each other." Although her love life makes headlines with every Kansas City Chiefs game she attends, the "Blank Space" singer said she is focused on being there for her partner rather than on concealing the relationship.

On scrutiny more broadly, the "Anti-Hero" singer said she tries not to let the paparazzi get to her even though so many of her outings with friends become headlines: "Over the years, I've learned I don't have the time or bandwidth to get pressed about things that don't matter. Yes, if I go out to dinner, there's going to be a whole chaotic situation outside the restaurant. But I still want to go to dinner with my friends." She described the change in her perspective over time: "Life is short. Have adventures. Me locking myself away in my house for a lot of years — I'll never get that time back. I'm more trusting now than I was six years ago."



---


# Travis Kelce's WSJ Magazine Interview on Swift

In an interview with WSJ Magazine published on 20 November 2023, Travis Kelce described how much he admires Taylor Swift's skills as a musician and said he was not letting media attention affect the relationship.

"I've never been a man of words. Being around her, seeing how smart Taylor is, has been f***ing mind-blowing. I'm learning every day," he explained. Kelce acknowledged the public attention his personal life had received because he has "never dated anyone with that kind of aura around them", but specified that he was not letting the media affect his relationship.

"But at the same time, I'm not running away from any of it," he said. "The scrutiny she gets, how much she has a magnifying glass on her, every single day, paparazzi outside her house, outside every restaurant she goes to, after every flight she gets off, and she's just living, enjoying life. When she acts like that I better not be the one acting all strange."



---


# Style: Named For Harry Styles, Explained As A Song About Fashion

Style is an epic aural painting of windswept coastlines and propulsive wanderlust, supposedly named for Harry Styles, with whom Taylor Swift had a brief relationship in 2012 — many of 1989's songs were supposedly inspired by that relationship. Swift's own account differs: she says the song was inspired by fashion, and how certain items like a black dress or red lipstick will "never go out of style", which prompted her to write about the people who'll always be part of your life even after the flame of romantic love wanes. The BBC notes that this all sounds like a classic piece of deflection to a probing journalist.

Whichever interpretation you prefer, the song marks a shift in Swift's psychology, as she briefly admits to having been unfaithful — the discriminating feature that separates it from her earlier writing. "I would never have said anything like that on a previous album," she told Ryan Seacrest. "My previous albums have always been, 'I was right, you were wrong'. What happens when you grow up is you realise that the rules in a relationship are very blurred. It gets very complicated, very quickly."



---


# Travis Kelce's Comments On Relationship Privacy

Travis Kelce broke his silence on Taylor Swift's Chiefs game attendance on his podcast on 27 September 2023, while saying he would not speak much more about the relationship, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

On the game itself, Kelce said: "To see the slow-motion chest bumps, to see the high-fives with Mom, to see how Chiefs Kingdom was all excited that she was there -- that s--- was absolutely hysterical. It's definitely a game I'll remember, that's for damn sure."

He then set the limit, noting that he wants "to respect both of our lives," and drew a distinction between his own exposure and Swift's: "Yeah, my personal life -- that's not so personal. I did this to myself Jason, I know this. What's real is that you know it is my personal life. ... She's not in the media as much as I am doing this show every single week."



---


# Taylor Swift's Arrowhead Appearance And Its Easter Eggs

At Arrowhead Stadium, the 12-time Grammy winner appeared to shout "let's f—ing go" after Travis Kelce scored a touchdown before chest-bumping other Chiefs fans, and fans then found a string of apparent Easter eggs around the visit, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

Because Swift is known for being an Eagles fan — she is originally from Pennsylvania and even references the team in Gold Rush — her outward support for Kelce's team seemed extra telling. Swifties were immediately on high alert, with some capturing Swift and Kelce leaving the stadium together. Extra observant fans noted that Kelce's blue and white post-game outfit was supposedly labelled the "1989 bedroom painting set", perhaps an intentional reference to Swift's 2014 album, which she was due to re-release in October; the paper suggests Swift's penchant for Easter eggs must be rubbing off on the tight end. They were also spotted in a "getaway car" together outside the stadium, potentially a nod to her 2017 track.

None of this actually confirms Swift and Kelce are dating, the piece notes. But regardless of whether it is a friendship or a romantic relationship, it has sent shockwaves through two massive cultural franchises, expanding the NFL's audience into uncharted territory — a cultural pairing on par with, and perhaps even bigger than, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West.



---


# Britney Spears' Unconfirmed Romances With Wade Robson And Colin Farrell

Two of the romances attributed to Britney Spears in the early 2000s were never confirmed by either party. Shortly after her breakup from Justin Timberlake, Spears was rumoured to be dating Wade Robson, a dancer and choreographer who appeared in the music video for her 2009 song "(You Drive Me) Crazy"; neither Spears nor Robson confirmed the rumours.

In 2003, Spears and Colin Farrell made headlines when they were spotted holding hands at the premiere of The Recruit, sparking speculation that they were dating. Farrell explicitly denied it in an interview with Entertainment Tonight at the time, saying the two were just friends: "She's just a mate. Seriously, we just met a week ago, [we're] having a laugh." The quote was reported by People in 2003.



---


# Young Swifties Struggle To Open The 1989 (Taylor's Version) CD

A group of 11- and 12-year-old "Swifties" went viral after a TikTok video captured their attempts to open a "1989 (Taylor's Version)" compact disc, FOX News Lifestyle reported on 11 November 2023.

The girls came together to give their friend Annika the newly released Taylor Swift CD in hopes of cheering her up after she broke her wrist during soccer practice, mom Shannon Schmidt told Fox News Digital. "The girls knew what a CD was, but we had to borrow Grandma and Grandpa's CD player to let them fully experience it," Schmidt shared. The video captures the comical moment the three sixth and seventh graders attempted to open the CD: the girls — Lilly, Henslee and Annika — can be heard struggling to figure out how to get the CD out without breaking it, or looking for a button to press to release it from the case.

Watching their efforts, Schmidt said, "You guys are making me laugh because this is how we used to listen to music." Seconds later Lilly can be seen pressing the middle of the CD, releasing it from the case, and the girls were amazed when they finally got their hands on the soundtrack. They usually can be found listening to Swift while making her popular friendship bracelets or playing soccer with one another.



---


# The NFL's Statement Defending Its Taylor Swift Coverage

Following criticism that the league was focusing too much on Taylor Swift, the NFL rejected the premise that its coverage had become disproportionate, in an official statement handed to People on 4 October 2023. It first defended the practice as routine: "We frequently change our bios and profile imagery based on what's happening in and around our games, as well as culturally. The Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce news has been a pop cultural moment we've leaned into in real time, as it's an intersection of sport and entertainment, and we've seen an incredible amount of positivity around the sport."

The league then attacked the proportionality claim directly, arguing that the Swift material was a small share of its output: "The vast majority of our content has remained focused on the game, our players and variety of other initiatives, including our Toy Story Funday Football alt-cast, the international games and more."

qid: Which NFL quarterback, featured in articles from Sporting News, Sportskeeda, and CBSSports.com, threw four touchdowns against the Cowboys, has accumulated significant fantasy points over recent games, boasts an undefeated start to the season, but struggles with a decreased completion rate and yards per attempt when under pressure?
context:
# Week 13 Seahawks-Cowboys: Start Dallas, Fade The Seattle Passing Game

CBS Sports argues that in the Week 13 Seahawks-Cowboys game the Dallas side of the ball should be started and the Seattle passing game faded, because the Cowboys defense should keep pressure on Geno Smith and a Seattle offense that has struggled to gain consistency over the last month. The grounds: Smith did OK completing passes when pressured last week (a 60% completion rate) but not at an efficient level (5.4 yards per attempt); only two quarterbacks have exceeded 250 yards against Dallas this year and only four have thrown multiple touchdowns against them. The warrant joining these is that the author does not like Smith's chances to do either, which hurts any upside case for any Seahawks receiver — if the quarterback cannot reach volume or touchdown thresholds, the pass-catchers downstream of him cannot either. A supporting data point on how hard Dallas is to beat through the air: Curtis Samuel was the first receiver to get 100 yards on the Cowboys this year, and it took him 12 targets and 9 catches to get there; no one else has had more than 86.

One scope condition is stated up front: both teams had a week of rest, so this should not be treated like a typical Thursday game. The resulting verdicts are STARTS — Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, Tony Pollard, DK Metcalf (as a low-end WR2), Jake Ferguson and the Cowboys DST; SITS — Tyler Lockett (flex at best), Geno Smith, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Zach Charbonnet, Michael Gallup and the Seahawks DST; SLEEPERS — Brandin Cooks.



---


# Russell Wilson As A Week 5 2023 Sit Against The Jets

CBS Sports listed Russell Wilson under "Sit Him" for Week 5 of the 2023 season: the claim is that this should be one of his toughest matchups of the season, and the warrant is that Wilson's fantasy value depends on outside receivers and the deep ball, exactly the two things the Jets take away, behind a pass rush Denver's line cannot hold.

The grounds are matchup-specific. The Jets have given up over 16 fantasy points to a quarterback only once all season — Dak Prescott in Week 2 — with Josh Allen in Week 1 and Patrick Mahomes in Week 4 both held under 16. They get to the quarterback without blitzing: a 19.5% blitz rate is bottom-five while their 41.6% pressure rate is third-best in the league and consistent, their only low game coming at Dallas where they still bothered Prescott 32.5% of the time. Denver's front five allows the sixth-highest pressure rate in the league at 39.5%, and the Bears pressured Wilson on 32.3% of dropbacks the previous week, their second-highest rate of the season, albeit with heavy blitzing. Wilson's own pressure numbers do not look bad over the season, but they are weighted by Week 1 against the Raiders; across his past three high-volume games, against Washington, Miami and Chicago, he completed 56.4% under pressure for 8.0 yards per attempt with a better-than-most 5.1% touchdown rate and a strong 2.6% off-target rate — and of those, only the off-target rate is better under pressure than without it. He shouldn't have much time this week.

The deep-ball and alignment evidence closes the argument. The Jets are good against throws of 15-plus air yards, allowing a 40.7% completion rate with four interceptions and an in-context low 23.1 yards per grab, seventh-best. Wilson ranks top-10 among quarterbacks in completion rate (50%) and yards per attempt (17.2) with the second-lowest off-target rate (12.5%) on those long throws but is below league average in attempts, and his numbers are inflated by the Commanders game and the Hail Mary he hit. Against outside receivers the Jets allow the second-highest catch rate to perimeter players at 79.4% but are top-five in yards per catch (10.7), average depth of target (10.38) and completions allowed of 20-plus yards (three, best in the NFL), and outside players have seen the third-fewest targets because teams know not to attack there — a problem for Wilson, who has sent 50 of his 132 passes, 38%, to outside receivers, along with seven of his nine touchdowns. His recent scoring is also flattered by soft conditions: his 28-plus fantasy-point game the previous week came against a bad Bears defense with a beat-up secondary, and his other high score, Week 2 against the Commanders, included 92 yards and a Hail Mary touchdown in the final 0:48 worth an extra 9.7 points, though he still had 22.2 without it. The forecast is a much more subdued and boring version of Wilson's game, possibly resembling Mahomes' line against the Jets; the author would rather start Jared Goff, Trevor Lawrence, Joshua Dobbs and C.J. Stroud.



---


# Week 14's Top Fantasy Quarterback Starts

Sporting News made Josh Allen its QB1 for Week 14 of the 2023 season, ahead of Tua Tagovailoa, Dak Prescott, Jalen Hurts, Patrick Mahomes, Lamar Jackson, Jared Goff and C.J. Stroud.

Despite Buffalo being on the outside looking in for a playoff berth, Allen (at the Chiefs) had come through in fantasy; the Chiefs' defense had done its part in keeping quarterbacks in check that season, entering Week 13 allowing the fifth-fewest fantasy points per game to the position, but Allen had performed well against Steve Spagnuolo's defense in the past, averaging 276.4 passing yards per game with a strong 14:2 touchdown-to-interception ratio over five career games against Kansas City. Not far behind sat Tagovailoa (vs. Titans), who had shredded the Commanders' defense for 280 yards and two touchdowns in Sunday's blowout, with another juicy matchup awaiting against a lackluster Tennessee coverage unit. Prescott (vs. Eagles) remained a top-three play in the rematch against a team he had torched for 374 yards and three touchdowns in a narrow 28-23 loss in Week 9. Hurts (at Cowboys) and the Eagles looked to get back on track in a pivotal NFC East clash in Dallas, facing a Cowboys defense that had let Geno Smith post top-end QB1 numbers the previous week. Mahomes (vs. Bills) was in line for strong numbers in a potential shootout, and although his receiving corps had issues, the reigning MVP was still a top-five play. Jackson (vs. Rams) faced an exploitable Los Angeles secondary, while Goff (at Bears) looked to build off a dominant Week 13 effort against an ascending Chicago stop unit. Stroud (at Jets) saw a slight dip in his Week 14 ranking in a tough road test, but the Rookie of the Year frontrunner still profiled as a set-it-and-forget-it QB1.



---


# DraftKings Week 14 DFS Quarterback And Running Back Picks

Sporting News built its Week 14 DraftKings DFS lineup around quarterback Justin Fields of the Bears ($6,800) and running backs Christian McCaffrey ($9,200) and Alvin Kamara ($8,200), publishing on Dec. 7, 2023.

The framing was that most season-long fantasy leagues were entering their final week of the regular season, and if a team was not going to qualify, DFS was where every week is a new season: managers do not have to sweat injury reports, make difficult trades, or concern themselves with bad matchups, and instead get to enjoy each week as a new opportunity.

Fields (Bears vs. Lions) was picked because the Lions might have control over the NFC North but their defense was losing steam as the season progressed — Detroit appeared well on their way to a dominant victory over New Orleans until they let the 2023 Saints march back into it, alarming with that version of Derek Carr leading the charge — and Fields recently had success against the divisional foe, rushing for 104 yards and tossing a touchdown in Week 11, so the dual-threat quarterback should be in line for a great day at home.

McCaffrey (49ers vs. Seahawks) was the splurge: fantasy's best running back had been a little rich all season, but the 49ers were coming off an emotional win over the Eagles after stomping the Seahawks on Thanksgiving and were trying to track down the top spot in the NFC while leaning on their stars; McCaffrey had just rushed for over 100 yards and two touchdowns against that same defense two weeks earlier, and his floor remained at the penthouse with a ceiling stretching to the moon. Kamara (Saints vs. Panthers) was backed despite the Saints' quarterback problem and an offense stuck in quicksand: Derek Carr would likely be out with a concussion, leaving Jameis Winston to start, and Kamara remained a fixture as arguably the team's top runner and receiver thanks to his work as a security blanket for whichever quarterback was under center; with the Panthers remaining terrible at defending running backs, Sporting News penciled him in for at least 100 total yards and a touchdown.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on OpenAI's launch of GPT-3 without vision and the TechCrunch report on OpenAI's push for an "app store for AI" as the primary platform for obtaining AI tools, was there a change in OpenAI's strategic focus as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# OpenAI DevDay 2023 Announcements

On November 6, 2023 — prior to the leadership chaos — OpenAI held its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, and announced a slew of updates to GPT, including GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API, and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT.

GPT-4 Turbo, unveiled at the conference, is a super-charged version of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model, and comes in two versions: one that is strictly text-analyzing and another that understands the context of both text and images. The GPT Store was announced alongside it: users and developers would soon be able to make their own GPT with no coding experience required, list it on OpenAI's marketplace, and monetize it in the future. OpenAI also announced the Assistants API to help developers build "agent-like experiences" within their apps, with use cases ranging from a natural language-based data analysis app to a coding assistant or even an AI-powered vacation planner.

The GPT store slipped. According to a memo seen by Axios, OpenAI planned to delay the launch of its highly anticipated GPT store to early 2024; custom GPTs and the accompanying store had been a major DevDay announcement, with the store expected to open the previous month.



---


# OpenAI Chip Rumors And Nvidia's Position

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-13 that rumors were swirling that OpenAI may be considering developing its own AI chips, and set that against Nvidia's position: Nvidia's ongoing stock market rally is likely driven by the current boom in AI, so an in-house OpenAI chip would make things interesting.

Two further figures anchor the week. ChatGPT's mobile app hit a record $4.6 million in revenue in the previous month, but growth is slowing. And the newsletter argues there is no need to shed tears for Nvidia quite yet, pointing to Brian's piece breaking down how Nvidia became a major player in robotics — that is, Nvidia's exposure is not confined to supplying the AI boom.

The surrounding context that week was AI coverage generally. TechCrunch's most-read stories consistently continue to be about AI, the AI hype cycle continues apace, and that week brought a batch of stories about what the newsletter calls the seedy underbelly of AI, including how humans are part of the problem, continuing to trick AI systems into generating boobs and 9/11 memes. TechCrunch spoke with investors to figure out whether the future of AI has hope beyond daft memes, and reports that it does. The OpenAI chip item is explicitly a rumor as of that date, not a confirmed plan.



---


# The OpenAI Crisis As A Case Against Centralized AI Control

The claim is that the OpenAI debacle exposes a structural risk in depending on a centralized proprietary AI player. The situation remained fluid as of November 21, 2023, with any number of potential outcomes still on the table, but the whole debacle has shone a spotlight on the forces that control the burgeoning AI revolution, leading many to question what happens if you go all-in on a centralized proprietary player and things then go belly-up.

Mark Surman, president and executive director at the Mozilla Foundation, put the ground this way to TechCrunch: "The OpenAI / Microsoft drama underlines one of the big near-term risks with AI — that this next wave of technology is controlled by the same tiny set of players who have shaped that last era of the internet. We might have a chance of avoiding this if GPT-X were responsibly open sourced, giving researchers and startups a shot at making this technology safer, more useful and more trustworthy for people everywhere." The warrant is that concentration of control is itself the hazard, and open sourcing distributes it.

TechCrunch qualifies the claim: it is still too early to make any surefire claims on what impact the OpenAI fallout will have on LLM development and uptake in the future, and Altman and Brockman are undoubtedly steady hands for a commercial AI startup who may even return to steward OpenAI. But some might argue it is unhealthy that so much focus lies on just a handful of people — and it is telling that their departure has created such widespread havoc.



---


# ChatGPT's Launch And Its First Year Of Evolution

ChatGPT, OpenAI's viral AI chatbot, turned one on November 30, 2023. A year earlier OpenAI released it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with AI startup Anthropic. The goal, OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time, was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models.

Initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5, ChatGPT would go on to become the company's most popular product ever — and the fastest-growing consumer app in history. Sam Altman marked the anniversary on X: "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…"

In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating capabilities via DALL-E 3. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions.



---


# OpenAI's Updated Preparedness Framework

OpenAI's "Preparedness Framework," described in a new document and blog post covered on 18 December 2023, is the company's internal process for identifying, analyzing, and deciding what to do about "catastrophic" risks inherent to the models it is developing. The update is part of an expansion of OpenAI's internal safety processes to fend off the threat of harmful AI: a new "safety advisory group" will sit above the technical teams and make recommendations to leadership, and the board has been granted veto power — though whether it will actually use that power is another question entirely.

TechCrunch's framing is that policies like these normally do not warrant coverage, since in practice they amount to closed-door meetings with obscure functions and responsibility flows that outsiders will seldom be privy to. What makes this one worth examining is the recent leadership fracas at OpenAI and the evolving AI risk discussion, given that OpenAI is the world's leading AI development company.

The report notes that the framework appears to have been retooled after November's shake-up, which removed the board's two most "decelerationist" members: Ilya Sutskever, who remained at the company in a somewhat changed role, and Helen Toner, who left entirely.



---


# Theory: A Long-Term Strategy Disagreement Over OpenAI's Economics

The proposition is that Altman and the board fell out over when OpenAI's money-losing growth strategy has to end. Despite being the hottest tech company in the world and everyone talking about ChatGPT, OpenAI is not exactly a sound business: it is shoveling money into the furnace as fast as it can by serving, by all accounts, a fantastically expensive product at bargain-bin prices. That is all well and good for a year or two, but at some point that strategy changes from a growth hack to an existential liability — so could Altman and the board have had irreconcilable differences on where that point lies?

TechCrunch judges this unlikely, and gives the disconfirming evidence: the company has been very deliberately pursuing this very publicly, confidently and on a long-term basis. Altman and the board seem to be in sync on this, at least for the present.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.



---


# Robert Menendez's Bribery Indictment

In September 2023 the Justice Department charged Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.) and his wife Nadine with accepting bribes and allegedly using his Senate seat to improperly aid the Egyptian government; Menendez pleaded not guilty.

A raid of Menendez's house turned up $100,000 in gold bars and bundles of cash stuffed into jacket pockets. The charges were pending in December 2023 when Menendez, as Fortune reported on 2023-12-06, gave Wall Street bank executives a pop quiz about their own corporate misbehavior that they all failed — an irony the reporting made explicit, since Menendez's own adherence to the law happened to also be in question.

# Trade and Free Agency

## Definition

Trade and free agency are the two channels by which professional sports rosters change hands outside the amateur draft: a trade moves a player between clubs in exchange for other players, picks, or salary-cap considerations while he is still under contract, and free agency is the period in which a player whose contract (or club control) has ended is free to negotiate and sign with any team, including his current one.

## Context

The corpus documents both mechanisms operating in parallel across MLB, NFL, NHL, and AFL. In baseball, the trade market and free-agent market are explicitly linked: Juan Soto is framed as a top trade candidate precisely because he is "entering his final year of club control" and the price to acquire him will only rise "now that he's a year and a half closer to free agency," and he was ultimately traded from the Padres to the Yankees at the 2023 Winter Meetings rather than reaching the open market at all. The Winter Meetings tracker shows signings (Eduardo Rodriguez to the Diamondbacks, Craig Kimbrel to the Orioles) and trades (Soto to the Yankees) being reported side by side as the offseason's two parallel transaction tracks. In the NFL, the corpus ties trades to a fixed calendar event — the "2023 trade deadline," before which the 49ers acquired Chase Young — while pending free agency (Kirk Cousins "approaching free agency," Michael Pittman Jr. "scheduled to be a free agent at season's end") is treated as a separate, later-arriving roster risk that mock-draft analysts weigh when projecting a team's draft needs. The NHL and AFL passages show the same free-agent path playing out for individual players: Patrick Kane was "traded last year at the deadline" and then, once his contract with the Rangers ended, "hit free agency for the first time in his career"; Adams and McStay are each described as having "arrived... as an unrestricted free agent."

## Key Characteristics

- **Contract-status distinction** — a trade moves a player who is still under contract to his current club; free agency begins only once that contract or club-control period has lapsed, as with Soto's approaching free agency versus his active trade candidacy.
- **Fixed deadlines govern trades** — leagues set a cutoff (the NFL's 2023 trade deadline, before which the 49ers acquired Chase Young; MLB's "summer deadline," which the Soto piece contrasts with the harder-to-project offseason) after which in-season trades are no longer permitted.
- **Compensation differs by channel** — trades exchange players, draft picks, or cap-related pieces between clubs (the 49ers sent a 2024 third-round pick for Chase Young), while free-agent moves are direct contract signings between a player and a new or returning club (Eduardo Rodriguez's four-year, ~$20M/year deal with Arizona).
- **A single player can pass through both channels sequentially** — Patrick Kane was traded away from Chicago at last year's deadline, then, once his Rangers tenure ended with a playoff exit, reached unrestricted free agency, illustrating that trade and free agency are sequential stages of the same player-movement pipeline rather than mutually exclusive categories.
- **Roster-planning implications extend beyond the transaction itself** — pending free agency (Cousins, Pittman) is treated by draft analysts as a signal of future roster need, just as trade acquisitions (Young) raise downstream questions about whether the move is a short-term "rental" or requires salary-cap restructuring to retain the player long-term.

# Amazon Echo Buds (2023) Deal Prices

The 2023 Amazon Echo Buds were $35 — a $15 drop and an all-time low — for both October Prime Day and Black Friday 2023, Engadget reported, recommending them in its budget wireless earbuds guide for people who hate the feeling of traditional in-ear headphones.

# EU Sends Amazon A Statement Of Objections Over The iRobot Deal

European Union regulators sent Amazon a formal statement of objections setting out competition concerns over its proposed acquisition of robot vacuum maker iRobot, TechCrunch reported on November 27, 2023. The step does not confirm the EU will seek to block the deal, but it shows antitrust regulators do remain concerned, and it could push Amazon to offer remedies to EU authorities to settle the investigation and avoid the risk of the acquisition being blocked.

The deal's price had already moved. Amazon lowered its acquisition price for iRobot — originally an all-cash offer of $1.7 billion back in August 2022 — by 15%, owing to increased debt taken on by its target while regulatory snags delayed closing the deal at the original purchase price.

The bloc had been closely scrutinizing the Amazon-iRobot deal since July, when the EU announced its in-depth probe; the Commission said at the time it was worried the transaction would allow Amazon to restrict competition in the market for robot vacuum cleaners (RVCs) and strengthen its position as online marketplace provider in a number of ways. The November announcement, following several months of in-depth examination, lays out formal concerns for Amazon to respond to, focused on foreclosure risks. The EU reached this pass after conducting what it describes as a "wide-ranging investigation to understand the market and the potential impact of the deal," which it says included analysing internal documents provided by Amazon and iRobot and gathering views from market participants such as suppliers of RVCs and other smart home devices, as well as from providers of online sales channels. It also says it closely cooperated with other competition authorities during both the initial and the in-depth investigation and will continue to do so during the remainder of the in-depth investigation — although the U.K.'s competition authority had already cleared the deal back in June.

Some major retailers ensured price protection on purchases during the 2023 holiday season, but the terms differ sharply by retailer, so whether you get price matching depends on where and when you shop.

Walmart's policy says it will not price match with competitors, nor does it price match for products purchased online that later decrease in price. # Amazon Echo Dot And Echo Show 5

Amazon knocked the price of the latest Echo Dot down to $23 for October Prime Day. # Scott Hurff Recommends "Getting Real"

Scott Hurff recommends "Getting Real: The Smarter, Faster, Easier Way to Build a Successful Web Application," by Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson and Matthew Linderman, calling it an absolute treasure from 2006 that is still teaching him things. As a writer, Hurff does not always write about product design, but when he does he is able to share his perspective as someone who is also a product maker and designer — an intersection that nurtured his own book, "Designing Products People Love: How Great Designers Create Successful Products."

His grounds are the book's originality and its voice. It was the first time anyone building in modern tech put together a practical, straightforward, all-encompassing guide for conceiving, building, shipping and marketing web apps, and Fried and Heinemeier Hansson's words are efficient when they need to be, detailed when it matters, and packed full of nuance that is both unique and endearing. Hurff suspects the book feels like it started as an internal series of posts or a handbook to help scale 37signals beyond the core team, recalling that Basecamp launched in 2004 and had quickly found success.

The warrant he leans on is that the method was proven on its authors' own product: whatever the format, what lends "Getting Real" authenticity is the fact that 37signals used these exact techniques to ship Basecamp and find its customer base. To this day he has never read anything like it — one of those books you can finish in an afternoon but that stays with you far longer, morphing into a reference book for the times when you need some extra perspective.

# Product Design In The AI And Spatial Computing Era

Product design is in a moment of profound change and redefinition as technologies like artificial intelligence and spatial computing dramatically affect computing experiences. The two technologies act on different layers: AI, especially, may have only minor impacts on interface design but will significantly impact the holistic product or ecosystem experience, whereas spatial computing will change human-computer interactions and unmoor our understanding of what a computer is.

The premise is the year just ending: 2023 was a banger for AI as the technology went from niche to mainstream about as fast as anything ever has. How do we think about curation and all the things, all the capabilities and tools that we've created over the years? How does that work in a world that's federated, and from a user experience point of view? That is a great question."

# Ohanian's Critique of Social Media and the Creator Economy

Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, speaking at an event at the University of Virginia in an interview with Kara Swisher published 31 October 2023, argued that social media as currently built brings out the "worst parts of our nature in many ways" — and that the creator economy is a large part of why. His grounds are behavioural: everyone has "been so trained and conditioned now to just get the likes and retweets, get the upvotes…I wish I could be more optimistic about it, but we're seeing it play out before our eyes." He added a second ground, the race for primacy, worrying about the desire for people to be first and win on whatever leaderboard a platform features, which then leads to a situation where misinformation is able to spread. The warrant joining the two is that platform scoring mechanics are not incidental decoration but the thing shaping what users do, so the resulting misinformation is a product of the design rather than a failure of individual users.

Ohanian paired that critique with a supporting claim about human wiring, posted the same day: "Humans evolved trusting the faces & voices we knew around the campfire. The idea of believing something bc of experts/institutions you've never met is actually new to our species. I visited @UVADemocracy + chatted with @karaswisher + @dkroy about what's next for social media."

Despite the negative reading, Ohanian — also the founder of venture fund Seven Seven Six — ultimately described himself as a "techno-optimist," an apparent nod to a16z General Partner Marc Andreessen's recent diatribe where he claimed technology could solve all our problems. "Guilty as charged," Ohanian said. "I do think that pendulum will swing back. I think even swifter than we realize." He theorised that the war in the Middle East may even be the tipping point, as it is now "abundantly clear" that we need something better to figure out the world than the platforms we have today.

His own record is offered as partial evidence that the pendulum can move. He notably resigned from Reddit's board in 2020 over differences of opinion on moderation and wanting to crack down on communities about violence and hate, a moment where he seemed to be reckoning with what his platform had wrought; at the time he asked for his board seat to be replaced by a Black board member, and the company agreed, appointing its first Black board member with Y Combinator partner Michael Seibel. Reddit also later banned several toxic communities, including r/donaldtrup following violence at the U.S. Capitol, and Ohanian says the site has "gotten demonstrably better" since, as well as better as a business.

# Amazon's Offline Guardrail Pipeline For Alexa Kids Generative AI

Amazon does not hook kids up to a large language model at runtime; instead it runs the LLM offline to generate content in bulk, puts that content through a review process using both humans and AI, and only then loads the reviewed material into the "Explore with Alexa" experience. "We want to go slow and be intentional and be measured with how we're introducing this new tech, as well as any new tech for kids, which is why we're not just hooking the experience up to an LLM at runtime and kind of letting kids go at it," explains Arjun Venkataswamy, senior product manager for Alexa Kids, in an interview with TechCrunch. "The way that we've integrated an LLM here is we use it to generate content at scale offline, and then go through a review process that includes both humans, as well as AI, and then take that reviewed content and then put it into our experience," he says.

The preconditions that motivate the pipeline are the two failure modes of the technology and the audience: generative AI can be led astray or "hallucinate" answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions. Amazon's answer is a sequence of constraints applied before any child hears an answer. First, the Alexa Kids science team narrowed the new experience, which leverages Alexa's LLM technology, to include only kid-friendly fun facts and trivia questions. Second, the source material is restricted: initially, the content comes from just two partners, the World Wildlife Fund and A-Z animals. Third, the LLM generates content at scale offline rather than on the device in real time. Fourth, that generated content goes through review by humans and by AI — AI is enlisted here because the model can generate tens of thousands of potential responses, so not every answer can be reviewed by a human before being added to the experience. Fifth, only the reviewed content is put into the experience, so kids are not using generative AI on the fly when conversing with Alexa, and what they hear is pre-reviewed and drawn from a small dataset of just animal facts and sources.

The procedure is scoped to the current, offline arrangement and explicitly does not yet extend to runtime generation for kids. Amazon has no date for that step: "I can't give you a timeline, because we don't have a concrete answer for what exactly we're going to be doing yet, although we do have plans and experiments we're planning to look into," Venkataswamy says. The gating criterion is external validation rather than an internal milestone — "I will say that in terms of our criteria for when we're going to get there, we're working closely with the Family Trust team at Amazon that's connected to a variety of research institutions in the U.S…we want to be able to get some confidence from external partners that our approach is right," he adds. The narrow content scope is likewise provisional: in time the team would like to expand the AI to include other areas of interest to kids, like space, music, video games and sports.



---


# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

# UMG's USCO Filing Rejecting Fair Use For AI Training

Universal Music Group's response to the US Copyright Office rejected the notion that using copyrighted material to train large language models is "fair use" — a position MBW called unsurprising and the starkest possible contrast to Google's assertion that prohibiting or limiting the use of copyrighted materials for AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the opportunities of the technology.

# Layering Comparisons Against Growth And A Stock's Own History

To avoid pitfalls while using relative valuation, add layers of comparison after the initial peer screen. The first step is the ordinary one, comparing stocks based on relative valuation. The second step is to assess how their valuation fares relative to growth prospects, since many other factors can justify different valuations. The worked illustration is that TCS has always commanded a valuation premium to peer stocks like Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech because of its superior margins and much more consistent growth, so just because the other stocks are cheaper on a PE basis does not mean they are cheap compared to TCS.

The third layer is to assess each company's valuation against its own long-term, that is 5-10 year, mean and median valuations, and to judge how the stocks fare relative to their own history. The precondition for the procedure is that a peer comparison has already been made; its purpose is to stop a cheaper headline multiple being read as a cheaper stock when growth quality or a company's own valuation history explains the gap.

# Broadcom Q4 Earnings Preview and VMware Integration

Broadcom (AVGO) was set to announce its Q4 results after Thursday's closing bell in the week following Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 preview, going in with shares up more than 67% for the year on the AI wave, a Buy consensus among sell-side analysts, and a Seeking Alpha Quant Rating that had transitioned to Strong Buy from Hold in mid-November.

# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. # Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.
