# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. ---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Since 1991, when Michael Lynagh's late try handed Australia victory, Ireland had not come close to ending their last-eight hoodoo; never mind winning one, they had not led a World Cup quarter-final since the first half of the 1995 defeat to France, a mammoth 10,353 days earlier.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.



---


# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.



---


# Alphabet Q3 2023 Earnings Preview

Alphabet was set to announce its Q3 results during Tuesday 24 October 2023's post-market session, with the search-engine giant having outperformed the broader market index at a 55% growth rate that year, surpassing the S&P 500's 12%.

Following the company's upbeat Q2 results, investment firm Bank of America said it was expecting "favorable" headlines, due in part to strength in YouTube, search and artificial intelligence. Just a few days before the earnings report, Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating system changed its view from Strong Buy to Hold, while Wall Street analysts maintained a bullish view with a Strong Buy rating.

Consensus EPS estimates were $1.45 and consensus revenue estimates $75.73B. On the earnings insight, Google had topped EPS expectations in 4 of the past 8 quarters, beating revenue estimates in 5 of those reports.

# How The Aurora Works And Where In The UK It Can Be Seen

The Northern Lights are produced when electronically charged particles enter the Earth's atmosphere from space, producing dazzling displays of green, yellow, purple and even red lights. At certain periods during the year the lights regularly illuminate the skies of northern countries that sit in the "aurora zone" of the Arctic Circle.

The geographic relation holds most strongly at high latitudes: the phenomenon is visible every year in some areas of European countries like Finland, Iceland, Sweden and Norway, with regular sightings in parts of Canada and Greenland too. But the range extends further south than that suggests — sightings have become more frequent in the UK, with the lights seen as far south as Wiltshire in February 2023, so Brits don't necessarily need to trek to those countries to see the aurora borealis.

The limits of the model are its own unpredictability. Although numerous UK locations have reported sightings in recent years, these do tend to be in northern areas of the British Isles, and it is tough to predict exactly when and where the spectacle will make an appearance — which is why The Independent's 21 December 2023 guide rounds up the best places where you might be lucky enough to see it.



---


# The Solar Cycle Peak and Stronger Auroras

The Northern Lights, or Aurora Borealis, were expected to be even stronger and brighter in the winter of 2023-24 than they have been in the past because of the sun's recent activity.

The evidence cited is sunspot observation. "Recent observations of sunspots, a measure of how active the sun is, show a dramatic increase from this time last year, and we are approaching the expected peak of the 11-year solar cycle in 2024 or 2025," New Scientist reported. "This means that over the next few months in the Northern Hemisphere, the Northern Lights will probably be stronger than they have been for at least a decade."

The practical implication drawn in this October 2023 account is a travel one: head north with a warm hat and mittens to watch the display vividly light up the sky, and now may be the time to pack your bags and get a close look at the dancing waves of light — the remaining question being where to go to capture the magic.



---


# Aurora Displays Over Britain and Ireland, November 2023

Observers across Scotland, England, Wales and Northern Ireland photographed exceptional aurora displays on the night of Nov. 5, 2023, with several describing them as among the best they had ever seen.

Debby Thorne captured a vibrant pink display from Cullen on the Moray Firth in Scotland, looking towards Bow Fiddle Rock, using an iPhone 14 Pro in night mode on Nov. 5. "I am lucky to have seen the Aurora many times as used to live on the west coast of Scotland — and lucky to still see them on the Moray Firth where we live now," Thorne told Space.com. "But I have to say the display last night was incredible." She added: "I've never seen such bright pinks — usually greens with faint pink. I never tire of seeing them and often feel overwhelmed by this amazing thing going on in the sky and we are but a dot. I often wonder what our ancestors must have made when they saw the sky dancing, I just feel incredibly lucky to be able to experience it from my back door in Scotland." Astrophotographer Josh Dury saw red auroras from the Mendip Hills in Somerset, UK: "On the night of this shoot, I was scouting a number of locations where clear skies would permit," he told Space.com. "With most of the South-West under cloud, clear skies persisted on The Mendips. Making it possible to view a window to the aurora and capture the beautiful red pillars low on the north horizon." Astrophotographer Gareth Mon Jones caught red and green aurora above Penmon Lighthouse, Anglesey — "A whopper of a display on Anglesey tonight," he wrote on X, adding that "my girlfriend was happy to see one of the best displays of the northern lights in a long time." Philip McErlean witnessed pink and green aurora borealis above the southern shores of Lough Neagh, Northern Ireland: "It was an exceptional night of aurora here in Northern Ireland and one of the best displays I have seen/photographed," he told Space.com. Landscape photographer Alistair Hamill captured his first sub-auroral arc of solar cycle 25 at Glenarm, posting on X: "I had to try for a pano to fit it all in. This arc was right above my head at the time!"



---


# Solar Auroras Above Sunspots

A study from November 2023 revealed that the sun itself has auroras — a phenomenon previously thought to occur only on some planets and moons within the solar system — although they are a little different from the ones seen on Earth.

Astronomers detected radio bursts crackling above a sunspot after pointing a radio telescope at the dark patch, and the frequencies of the radio waves were very similar to the wavelengths given off by auroras on Earth, which strongly suggests a similar process is occurring on the sun. The mechanisms differ, however. On Earth, auroras are born when solar storms and solar wind bash into the planet and temporarily weaken its magnetic shield, allowing radiation from the sun to excite gas molecules in the upper atmosphere. Researchers think solar auroras are instead created by electrons that are accelerated to incredibly high speeds along the sun's magnetic field lines.

# The Lineage Of English-Language Vampire Fiction

Vampire fiction has a long and distinguished pedigree in English, dating from the moment Robert Southey introduced the British Isles to the concept of the coffin-sleeping undead at the turn of the 19th century.

Polygon's organising claim about that lineage is that it tracks its readership: from that starting point onward, the authors of vampiric stories have mirrored the changing face of the society that reads them.

# Why Communicating Deep-Sea Science Matters

Jon Copley argues that communicating deep sea science matters because the deep sea is not somewhere people think about every day: we can go out at night and look at the sky and wonder what is going on up there, but you cannot glance into the deep sea in the same way, so it has become a realm of myth and darkness.

Even the names of the deepest parts — the abyssal plains and the hadal zone — evoke that kind of underworld, he says. The conclusion he draws is that it is nice to be able to shine a light on that for people and to highlight how our lives are connected to it.



---


# The Model Versus Observation Climate Sensitivity Discrepancy

Early in the 2010s, a substantial discrepancy was noted between estimates of climate sensitivity derived from climate models and estimates based on the observed warming record and radiative balance, with the observation-based estimates pointing to much lower values than the model-derived ones.

Radiative balance here means the balance between incoming and reflected solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation. A key breakthrough toward solving this conundrum has been the recognition of the pattern effect, the process whereby climate sensitivity depends on the geographic pattern of surface warming. This advance was rated as one of the most promising avenues for further constraining climate sensitivity in the future by Forster et al. (2021).

# NIO November 2023 Vehicle Deliveries

NIO delivered 15,959 vehicles in November 2023 — up 12.6% year over year but down roughly 1% month over month — an announcement the EV maker made on the Friday before Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 week-ahead preview.

The two comparisons point in opposite directions and are the whole substance of the datapoint: measured against November 2022 the figure is growth, while measured against the immediately preceding month it is a slight decline. The month-on-month dip is small, at about one percent, so the number reads as flat sequentially rather than as a fall.

# The North American Box Office Forecast For 2023

Paul Dergarabedian believes the two concert films — Taylor Swift's and Beyoncé's — should help lift the North American box office to more than $9 billion in 2023.

The proposition is anchored by two comparison points that would show whether it holds: the $7.4 billion taken in 2022, which the forecast would have to exceed, and the $11.4 billion of 2019, which it would edge closer to without reaching.

# Thanksgiving Observance Outside the United States

Thanksgiving is not observed only in America: while it is one of the most important cultural holidays in the United States, Canada also has its own Thanksgiving Day, held on the second Monday in October, and Liberia celebrates Thanksgiving on the first Thursday of November.

The distinguishing feature between these observances is therefore the date rather than the existence of the holiday — the American fourth-Thursday-in-November timing is one national convention among several.

# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. # Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."

# The Rogers Family Boardroom Battle Of 2021

The bad blood inside the Rogers family spilled into full view in October 2021, when Edward Rogers publicly battled his sisters and his mother for control of the board and won in court. The result was that five Rogers Communications directors were fired and replaced by five allies of Edward Rogers. Soon after, then-CEO Joe Natale was sacked and replaced by Tony Staffieri, the former chief financial officer; Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers had opposed the CEO change.

This was not an isolated episode. The children of late founder Ted Rogers have frequently fought one another — sometimes driving down Rogers' stock price as investors grew worried about the company's governance.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Code Evidence Outweighs Deleted Signal Messages

The Verge's reporter argued after Gary Wang's October 6th, 2023 testimony that Bankman-Fried's vanishing Signal messages might not help him as much as he had hoped, because the durable evidence was the code — and the code implicates him even without the messages. The grounds: Wang's account was the first full account of Alameda's and FTX's entanglements heard in the trial, and it came from a co-owner of both companies; while there was evidence of the computer code that gave Alameda special privileges, there was no evidence of the conversations Wang recounted.

The warrant is that the code constrains who could have made the decisions. Wang was a dev; the money was not his area. And while Bankman-Fried can try to blame Ellison for some of the decisions, the code shows she could not have made all the calls — after all, she was not FTX's CEO, and in 2019 she was not Alameda's CEO either. Bankman-Fried also said too many things in public to too many people, so even without the smoking gun of Signal messages, it is hard to see how he was not involved.

The same logic explains Wang's own behaviour: of course he turned himself in quickly, because sooner or later someone would find his code — and Singh's, too.

# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# Embedded Finance

## Definition

In the corpus, embedded finance is the practice a software platform adopts when it integrates financial services and payments directly into its own product surface — exemplified by Rainforest, which "works with software companies to help them embed financial services and payments into their platforms."

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces through Rainforest, an Atlanta-based startup that "works with software companies to help them embed financial services and payments into their platforms," positioning itself against incumbent processors Fiserv and FIS as well as fintech rival Stripe and its Connect product.
The concept is framed against a counter-claim from a16z general partner Angela Strange, who argued in 2019 that every company would eventually become a fintech; Rainforest's CEO Joshua Silver disagreed, arguing that most software companies do not want to become fintechs and absorb the associated regulatory and compliance burden — they simply want to accept payments and capture the associated revenue.
That disagreement marks the boundary of the concept in the corpus: embedded finance is presented as a narrow slice of financial functionality a software platform adopts, not a full transformation of that platform into a financial institution.

## Key Characteristics

- **Embedding, not becoming** — the software platform integrates financial services and payments into its own product surface; it does not itself become a bank or a fintech.
- **Processor-agnostic competitive layer** — providers enabling embedded finance (Rainforest, Stripe Connect) compete against both legacy processors (Fiserv, FIS) and each other for the same underlying volume.
- **Revenue motive over financial-identity motive** — per the corpus's framing, platforms adopt embedded finance to accept payments and generate revenue, not to take on the regulatory and compliance profile of a fintech.
- **Distinct from the platform's core compliance burden** — because the platform is embedding rather than becoming a financial company, it can avoid the "regulatory and compliance issues" Silver describes as the cost of the alternative "everyone is a fintech" path.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, embedded finance is a recognized industry term: Plaid defines it as "the integration of financial services, like payments, lending, or banking services, into non-financial offerings," letting users access financial tools within products they already use (Plaid, "What Is Embedded Finance?", https://plaid.com/resources/fintech/what-is-embedded-finance/, accessed 2026-09-02).

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.



---


# Gary Wang's Cross-Examination By Everdell

Defense attorney Christian Everdell's cross-examination of Gary Wang on October 10th, 2023 attacked the premise that Alameda's ability to run a negative balance was unique to Alameda. Wang had testified the week before that Alameda got access to a special credit line and an option to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation, something he alleged no other FTX account received; Everdell countered by pointing to FTX's spot margin program, which let users lend each other assets for margin trading and in which it was possible to have a negative balance in a specific coin.

The Verge's reporter judged the counter incomplete rather than false: in spot margin cases it was not possible for those accounts to avoid liquidation, as Wang testified Alameda could, or to have an overall negative balance. Her read was that the defense was betting jurors would throw up their hands in confusion — Everdell could not undo the damage of the previous week's code review, but he shook the rust off long enough to make Wang sound less reliable by drowning the jury in confusing technicalities.

A second line of attack went to Wang's consistency. What Wang said in court apparently contradicted something he had told the government in earlier interviews about market making — "apparently," because Everdell was probably handing him his previous testimony to refresh his recollection while Wang insisted he did not remember, and whatever Wang was shown was not submitted as evidence or shown to the court. The reporter got the gist and bet the jury did too, calling it probably the strongest work the defense had done so far.

# Black Friday 2023 Dates And Retailer Schedules

Black Friday 2023 lands on November 24, with Cyber Monday 2023 following a few days later on November 27 — but the early deals have already begun, and Engadget says the entire month of November might as well be renamed Holiday Shopping Month, as that's when companies really start to get serious with their discounts.

---


# Mozilla's Rationale For Investing In The Fediverse

Mozilla believes there is a better way forward for social networking and, more importantly, that now is exactly the right time to invest in that path. Its structural claim about why it can pursue that path: as a wholly owned subsidiary of a nonprofit, the company says it is not motivated by generating earnings for shareholders or returning a VC investment, allowing it to progress with a collaborative approach where it takes in input from a lot of different voices.

The grounds, per Mozilla Senior Director of Content Carolyn O'Hara, are a decade of observed behavior by incumbents: Mozilla's involvement came about because the company looked at the history of social media over the past decade and did not like what it saw. "I think that it's a pretty poor track record by existing companies that are only model motivated by profit and just insane user growth, and are willing to tolerate and amplify really toxic content because it looks like engagement," she says. "[They] aren't just putting forward the kind of standards that are good for people, but are just good for their bottom lines." The timing claim rests on a change in consumers: they are now becoming aware of this, which is new. "Consumers feel that the vibes are off a little bit…these platforms aren't necessarily working in their best interests, or satisfying them," O'Hara points out.

For Mozilla, that discontent presented an opportunity to enter the social networking space and compete for consumers' attention — but with a broader goal of helping the fediverse itself gain traction, not just its own Mastodon server. "We're not seeking to get, like 2 billion users on our instance. We want people to have choice and agency," says O'Hara, adding that choice is in line with Mozilla's values. Building directly on the fediverse is not the only way the company is prompting new forms of social networking: it has also financially backed a startup, Mammoth, the makers of a third-party app for Mastodon.

# Samsung Smart Monitor M8

The Samsung Smart Monitor M8 was down to just $500, which is $200 off its starting price — though it regularly sells for $600 — and the lowest price Engadget had seen thus far.

This 32-inch display has built-in apps and lets you access streaming services just as you would on a smart TV. It can also act as a smart home hub, showing your smart camera feeds and more.

The discounted model is the updated 2023 version of the monitor that launched at CES 2022.



---


# Pebble's Moderation-First Market Hypothesis

Pebble's founding hypothesis was that consumers were hungry for a Twitter alternative that prioritized trust, safety and moderation from the start. The company staffed for it: Pebble's founding team included co-founder Sarah Oh, Twitter's former human rights advisor.

What would falsify the proposition is a moderation-first Twitter alternative that consumers decline to adopt — which is the shape of the outcome TechCrunch is reporting on 2023-10-24, in a piece about Pebble shutting down.



---


# TikTok's Ad-Free Subscription Tier Test

TikTok is testing an ad-free subscription tier for some users, priced at $4.99 for an ad-free experience with no other strings attached, TechCrunch reported in its Week in Review of October 7, 2023.

The test is narrow, and TechCrunch cautioned readers not to expect the option to arrive anytime soon: TikTok said it was piloting the plan in a single, English-speaking market outside the United States for now.

A week later, in the issue of October 13, 2023, TechCrunch noted a parallel experiment at a different platform: X, formerly Twitter, appeared to be testing three tiers of its Premium service according to its CEO, and code in the app showed that one of those tiers may be ad-free.



---


# Meta's EU Pay-Or-Consent Ad-Free Subscription

Meta's pay-or-consent model, rolled out in November 2023, is a binary offer to EU users of its social networks Facebook and Instagram: agree to being tracked and profiled by the behavioral ads business in order to continue or get free access to its products, or else pay a monthly subscription of at least €9.99 per month for an ad-free version of its mainstream social networks.

The defining feature is that the two branches trade off against each other in different currencies. As TechCrunch characterizes it, Meta's updated offer to EU users is either hand over your privacy or hand over your hard earned cash. What is presented to the user as a "choice" — TechCrunch puts the word in scare quotes — is a choice between being profiled and paying.



---


# Holiday Discounting As The Driver Of 2023 Online Spend

Adobe's account of Thanksgiving 2023 spending is that growth was led by discounts rather than by consumers buying more expensive products: inflation is making an impact, but not as much as the worry around consumer spending, and spending is being led by more discounts to encourage buying rather than less buying of pricier goods.

The mechanism shows up in the discount data. Both Adobe and Salesforce said U.S. discounts were up by about 28%. Categories that saw dramatic markdowns included toys, electronics and computers per Adobe's figures; toys and electronics respectively saw sales up by 182% and 113% over the previous month. That relation between deeper discounts and higher unit volume leads one to wonder what kind of impact it is having on retailers' margins.

"Cyber Week is off to a strong start with Thanksgiving driving a record $5.6 billion in online spend as consumers took advantage of strong discounts and continued their shopping plans, virtually," said Vivek Pandya, lead analyst, Adobe Digital Insights, in a statement. "Mobile shopping hit an all-time high, as shoppers took to their smartphones to get the best deals during holiday gatherings, further solidifying mobile's growing importance in e-commerce."

Black Friday is often a boon for deals on headphones and earbuds, and 2023 was no different, Engadget reported on 2023-11-24: the shopping holiday brought a plethora of deals on all kinds of headphones, including several top picks from its guides to the best wireless headphones, wireless earbuds, budget wireless earbuds and gaming headsets.
