Sporting News said it would be updating the rankings all week.



---


# Cooper Kupp Rams Hot Seat

Yardbarker's Nov. 30, 2023 NFC hot-seat roundup named wide receiver Cooper Kupp as the Los Angeles Rams' hottest seat: at his peak he was one of the best offensive players in the league, but age (30) and injuries — appearing in 16 of a possible 28 games the past two seasons — had hurt his production.

The immediate grounds are recent form and replacement: he had been a non-factor over the past five games, with 12 catches for 127 yards, while young receivers Puka Nacua and Tutu Atwell stepped up. The warrant is that when a declining, injury-prone veteran's snaps are already being absorbed productively by cheaper younger players, his standing on the roster is what comes into question.



---


# Week 13 Wide Receiver Injury Report

Entering Week 12, Tee Higgins (hamstring), Noah Brown (knee), Treylon Burks (concussion) and Kadarius Toney (ankle, hip) all failed to suit up due to nagging injuries. For Week 13, published Nov. 29, 2023, Sporting News placed Higgins and Brown in its rankings list and omitted Burks and Toney. It was also watching the Chargers' Josh Palmer (knee), eligible to come off IR that week but probably not suiting up against New England.

Four more receivers left their games hurt the previous week: Chris Olave (concussion), Amari Cooper (ribs), Demario Douglas (concussion) and Rashid Shaheed (thigh). All four were left out of the initial Week 13 list, with their teams' injury reports to be monitored closely to gauge their playing prospects.

qid: Does the 'Business Line' article on investment options for high networth investors suggest evaluating the same criteria, specifically historical performance and management team, before making decisions as the 'Business Line' article recommends for investors considering Reliance Industries stock?
context:
# Reliance Industries Share Price and Growth Catalysts

The stock of India's most valued company, Reliance Industries (RIL), has trebled over the last six years after a decade-long underperformance from 2007 to 2017. On a three-year basis, however, RIL has delivered 11 per cent CAGR returns including the value of demerged Jio Financial Services, underperforming the Nifty 50's CAGR of a little over 14 per cent over the same period.

Business Line argued on 9 December 2023 that this is nothing to fret about, because the stock has typically tended to underperform whenever the company has been in a heavy investment phase — something it has embarked on in its green energy ventures.

The catalysts behind the six-year outperformance were the launch of Jio's data services in 2016, the maturation of the retail business, and the subsequent stake sales in FY21. Although the markets have already assigned a significant re-rating in valuation to both businesses, the article holds that scope for further outperformance from them remains, given the opportunity ahead.



---


# Portfolio Management Services In India

Portfolio Management Services are a managed-account alternative available alongside AIFs to Indian HNIs, governed by guidelines that date back to 1993 but that have grown in popularity with HNIs only recently. The growing financialisation of savings, the formalisation of the economy and the growing prosperity of tier 2 and 3 cities have raised PMS AUM, excluding EPFO and PF money, to ₹5.28 lakh crore as of July 2023. Because the minimum investment is ₹50 lakh, this option too is available only to HNIs.

The discriminating features are drawn against mutual funds. Both PMS and mutual funds provide expert guidance in navigating volatile markets and seizing wealth-creating opportunities, but because mutual funds cater to retail investors their guidelines are relatively stringent and compliance is rigorous, whereas PMS investment guidelines are somewhat more flexible, allowing portfolio managers to outperform mutual funds. A second appeal to HNIs is ownership: in PMS the beneficial ownership of securities belongs to the investors, as opposed to mutual funds where ownership belongs to the fund. PMS comes in two variants, discretionary and non-discretionary; in the former the portfolio managers make all decisions, in the latter the investor does.



---


# Why Investors Can Continue To Accumulate NTPC

Business Line maintained a positive stance on NTPC on 11 November 2023 and advised investors to continue accumulating the stock, on account of growth plans in place along with strong revenue and earnings visibility due to the assured return model, plus a decent dividend yield of around 3 per cent. The grounds are the track record since the previous call and the reasons behind the re-rating. Since the accumulate rating on NTPC in bl.portfolio dated 13 August 2023, the stock has gained around 48 per cent, majorly on account of growth in earnings as well as a re-rating in the stock from a trailing P/E of around 10 times then to 12 times now.

The earnings evidence is that during FY23 the company's revenue increased by around 32 per cent, and while there was flattish growth in PAT during that period on account of an increase in fuel cost, PAT grew nearly 30 per cent year-on-year in H1FY24. NTPC is now trading at a one-year forward P/E of around 11 times, which is around 35 per cent higher than its historical five-year average P/E of around 8.2 times. The warrant that turns an already re-rated stock into a continued buy is that the re-rating happened mainly due to company-specific and industry-level structural positives, which justify the current premium to the historical average, and due to the company's aggressive capacity addition plans; the premium is therefore treated as earned rather than as stretched valuation.



---


# Layering Comparisons Against Growth And A Stock's Own History

To avoid pitfalls while using relative valuation, add layers of comparison after the initial peer screen. The first step is the ordinary one, comparing stocks based on relative valuation. The second step is to assess how their valuation fares relative to growth prospects, since many other factors can justify different valuations. The worked illustration is that TCS has always commanded a valuation premium to peer stocks like Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech because of its superior margins and much more consistent growth, so just because the other stocks are cheaper on a PE basis does not mean they are cheap compared to TCS.

The third layer is to assess each company's valuation against its own long-term, that is 5-10 year, mean and median valuations, and to judge how the stocks fare relative to their own history. The precondition for the procedure is that a peer comparison has already been made; its purpose is to stop a cheaper headline multiple being read as a cheaper stock when growth quality or a company's own valuation history explains the gap.



---


# Individual Trader's Hello Group Bottom-Formation Thesis

Individual Trader, a Seeking Alpha author, argued in the December 3, 2023 week-ahead that MOMO's recent downtrend may be concluding, pointing to signs of a bottom forming, and that the stock is an appealing investment option.

The argument runs on two distinct kinds of ground. The first is technical: signs of a bottom forming, offered as evidence that the recent downtrend may be ending rather than continuing. The second is valuation and income: the analyst added that the combination of cheap earnings and a high dividend yield makes MOMO appealing. The warrant joining them is that a stock trading on cheap earnings with a high yield is worth owning once the price trend stops working against it — the technical read supplies the timing, the valuation read supplies the reason to hold.

Scope conditions: this is one Seeking Alpha author's view as relayed on December 3, 2023, and it is hedged in the original — the downtrend "may" be concluding, with signs of a bottom rather than a confirmed one.



---


# Why Indian Investors Should Look To US Big Pharma

For cutting-edge tech and pharmaceutical exposure, the US is the place for Indian investors to look to, because Indian markets already give them access to growth in manufacturing, banking, commodity, services and IT, but not to that frontier. The grounds are structural: the US is the largest pharmaceutical market in the world, and by virtue of its size, its ideal IP protection laws and its deep-pocketed insurers, most of the cutting-edge innovation in pharma tends to be concentrated there. The warrant is that for investors and general readers alike one should be abreast of the latest pharmaceutical innovation taking place overseas, since the open questions of the field, whether a weight loss pill will be a reality, when HIV will be cured, and what the future of cancer treatments is, are being answered in that market.

The article's scope is set out with the argument: it highlights the largest unmet needs in medicine currently being addressed by US Big Pharma such as Merck, Gilead and Eli Lilly, and also by big players based in Europe, namely Novo Nordisk and Roche, and it lays down the basic framework for investing in or assessing US pharma and the stocks currently in focus.



---


# Family Offices and the "This Time Is Different" Test for Japan

Large global funds are not the only investors whose interest in Japan has been piqued, says Keith Truelove, head of global markets at UBS Securities Japan: "There is still a lot of dry powder on the sidelines. There is a lot of interest in Japan from family offices and from high net worth individual investors, who value wealth preservation more highly than institutional investors — it's really taking off now."

The condition those investors applied before committing was sustainability rather than short-term return. "They took their time to decide if it was safe to invest in Japan again, because they need to get confidence in the idea that the Japan story will be more sustainable this time," Truelove adds. He notes that Japan has offered investors a number of false dawns over the years, and that the bar for deciding that 'this time is different' remains high.



---


# What Really Matters Is The Underlying Catalogue Performance

MBW argues that amongst all the noise around Hipgnosis Songs Fund, what will most likely interest its investors, including the likes of Investec Wealth & Investment, Aviva Investors and BlackRock, is the ongoing underlying commercial performance of the firm's copyrights. The noise is substantial: the article notes plenty of drama surrounding HSF, from the discontinuation vote seen at the company in October through to a recent lawsuit launched against Hipgnosis Songs Fund by a former business partner of Merck Mercuriadis.

The questions that matter are posed as three: how are HSF's assets performing versus the market; how is the company's "premium-only" acquisition strategy holding up against its promise of growth "uncorrelated" to other industries; and what does all of this suggest about the ongoing growth potential of the HSF portfolio versus the multiples that Merck Mercuriadis paid to acquire it. The warrant for prioritising these over the governance drama is that such questions will only be answered when HSF's board elects to release the six-monthly financial results to 30 September, which makes the delayed results the decisive document. MBW names the most important KPI within those results, in its view: the company's Pro-Forma Revenue, and how it compares like-for-like against the previous year's equivalent period.

qid: Which company, according to multiple reports by TechCrunch, is facing allegations of anticompetitive behavior for paying billions to remain the default search engine across devices, influencing app distribution and payment processing on Android, and harming news publishers' revenue and content distribution?
context:
# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Lawsuit Redactions As Signal: The Amazon Precedent

TechCrunch reads heavy redaction as itself informative: you know it is bad news for the company when they request pages and pages of redactions.

The precedent it cites is recent. This recently happened with Amazon as well, and it turned out they were trying to hide the existence of a price-hiking algorithm that skimmed billions from consumers.

The comparison is used to rank severity rather than to equate the two: it is much worse, TechCrunch writes, when you are redacting COPPA complaints.



---


# Google One VPN

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

Engadget has not fully tested the Google One VPN yet, but says it will add it to the list if it feels it is warranted.

qid: Which AI-powered chatbot, reported by both TechCrunch and Engadget, not only saw a meteoric rise in usage during December 2022 but also has diverse capabilities such as completing and debugging code, composing music, and emulating a computer running Linux?
context:
# ChatGPT's Task Capabilities And Measured Productivity Effects

ChatGPT's skills extend beyond conversation, another likely reason for its staying power. It can complete and debug code, compose music and essays, answer test questions, generate business ideas, write poetry and song lyrics, translate and summarize text, and even emulate a computer running Linux.

The measured effect comes from one study with a specific task set: an MIT study showed that, for tasks like writing cover letters, "delicate" emails and cost-benefit analyses, ChatGPT decreased the amount of time it took workers to complete the tasks by 40% while increasing output quality by 18%, as measured by third-party evaluators.

Ruoxi Shang attributes the breadth to a shift in how such systems are built: "Because [the AI models powering OpenAI] have been trained extensively on vast amounts of data, they [have] shifted focus from training specialized chatbots for specific domains to creating more general-purpose systems that can handle a variety of topics easily through prompting with instructions … [Chatbots like ChatGPT] don't require users to learn any new form of language, as long as they provide a task and some desired output just like how a manager would communicate to an intern."



---


# ChatGPT FAQ: Basics And Definitions

ChatGPT is a general-purpose chatbot developed by tech startup OpenAI that uses artificial intelligence to generate text after a user enters a prompt; it runs on GPT-4, a large language model that uses deep learning to produce human-like text. GPT stands for Generative Pre-Trained Transformer.

The boundary against the wider category matters: a chatbot can be any software or system that holds dialogue with a person and does not necessarily have to be AI-powered — there are rules-based chatbots that give canned responses to questions — whereas ChatGPT is AI-powered and uses LLM technology to generate text after a prompt. ChatGPT was released for public use on November 30, 2022. Both the free version of ChatGPT and the paid ChatGPT Plus are regularly updated with new GPT models, and the most recent model is GPT-4; the free version requires only a sign-in. There is a free ChatGPT app, at launch limited to U.S. iOS users, with OpenAI saying an Android version is "coming soon," and there is an API, released March 1, 2023.

Anyone can use ChatGPT, and more and more tech companies and search engines are using the chatbot to automate text or quickly answer user questions and concerns. Multiple enterprises use it, although others limit use of the tool. Microsoft announced at its 2023 Build conference that it is integrating its ChatGPT-based Bing experience into Windows 11; the Brooklyn-based 3D display startup Looking Glass uses ChatGPT to produce holograms you can communicate with; and the nonprofit organization Solana integrated the chatbot into its network with a ChatGPT plug-in geared toward end users to help onboard into the web3 space.



---


# ChatGPT's Mid-2023 Usage Decline

By June, a little bit of ChatGPT's shine had started to wear off: Congress reportedly limited Capitol Hill staffers from using the application over data handling concerns, and user numbers had declined nearly 10 percent month-over-month.

Even so, ChatGPT was already well on its way to ubiquity, and a March update enabling the AI to comprehend and generate Python code in response to natural language queries only increased its utility.



---


# Gemini Pro's Coding Task Failures

Google emphasized Gemini's enhanced coding skills in a briefing in the first week of December 2023, and posts on X suggest it may genuinely have improved in some areas — but it also appears that Gemini Pro struggles with basic coding functions in Python. TechCrunch collected several user reports from 6 and 7 December 2023.

Filip Piekniewski reported that Gemini-based Bard still could not write the intersection of two polygons, calling it one of those rare, relatively simple to express functions that was never implemented in Python and has no Stack Overflow post, and noting that all these models fail on it. Mohsen Azimi found Gemini Pro "pretty disappointing" for his example: he asked it to make an analog clock using HTML like one ChatGPT made, and while it could cite some code from GitHub, it was off by a few milliseconds.

Two head-to-head comparisons went the same way. Edison Ade created a Tic Tac Toe game with both ChatGPT and Bard running on Gemini Pro, and reported that ChatGPT wrote the code on the first try while Bard took three tries, concluding GPT-4 was still greater than Gemini Pro. N Kiran Kumar tested Bard with the Gemini Pro update and got no bugless snake game on the first try; after reporting the bug and asking for a fix, the model could not fix it, whereas the free version of ChatGPT 3.5 returned correct, bug-free code on the first attempt.



---


# AI Market Spending Forecasts Reported In October 2023

Total global spending on AI was expected to reach $154 billion by the end of 2023, a 27% increase from 2022, with the following three years also expected to see a compound annual growth rate of 27% — putting annual AI spending in 2026 at over $300 billion. These figures were cited in TechCrunch's 13 October 2023 survey of venture capitalists active in AI investing, as context for how much room startups have in the enterprise market.

Alongside the spending numbers, McKinsey reports that generative AI alone can add up to $4.4 trillion in value across industries through writing code, analyzing consumer trends, personalizing customer service, improving operating efficiencies, and more. Ninety-four percent of business leaders agree AI will be critical to all businesses' success over the next five years, and eighty-two percent of business leaders believe the integration of AI solutions will increase their employee performance and job satisfaction.

A comparative observation accompanies the totals: despite cloud computing remaining critical, AI budgets are now more than double that of cloud computing. The conditions under which these figures were offered matter — they were presented as evidence that startups should expect a high level of desire for and experience with AI solutions in their future customers. Within the enterprise sector there is a clear recognition of the value of AI, but many enterprises lack the internal capabilities to develop AI solutions, and that gap is what is said to present a significant opportunity for startups specializing in AI to engage with enterprise clients. As the business landscape matures, proficiency in leveraging AI is becoming a strategic imperative.



---


# Explore With Alexa

"Explore with Alexa" is a feature on Amazon's Echo devices that lets kids have interactive conversations with an AI-powered Alexa. It was first announced in September and, as reported by TechCrunch on 25 October 2023, launched as an addition to the Amazon Kids+ content subscription, allowing children to have kid-friendly conversations with Alexa, powered by generative AI, but in a protected fashion designed to ensure the experience remains safe and appropriate.

The discriminating feature is the combination of generative AI, conversation, and an audience of children under 13. Some AI experiences already cater to younger users — the AI chatbots from Character.ai and other companies, including Meta — but Amazon is among the first to specifically look to generative AI to develop a conversational experience for kids under the age of 13. The two qualifiers that bound the concept are the subscription it lives inside (Amazon Kids+) and the protective framing: this is not an unbounded chatbot but a conversational experience deliberately constructed to stay safe and age-appropriate.



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."

qid: Which company has been reported by both TechCrunch and The Verge to have influenced the internet by paying billions to remain the default search engine on various platforms and altering the web's appearance, while also being accused of harming news publishers' business through anticompetitive practices?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Google Warps The Web It Observes

The article's central claim is that Google, not the SEOs, defined the shape of the modern internet: you cannot be the most powerful observer in the world for two decades and not deeply warp what you are looking at.

The grounds are the structural impossibility built into Google's founding goal. The company started with a noble cause — trying to make the internet easier to navigate at scale — and did accomplish that, but in doing so it inadvertently and profoundly changed how the internet looked. The problem lay in Google trying to be an objective and neutral arbiter of an information landscape that was meant to pretend it did not exist: you cannot design a free, automated system to help people find information without some people trying to game that system.

The warrant that shifts responsibility away from practitioners is a comparison of scale and agency. For the past 25 years the internet as we know it has been almost entirely defined and controlled by Google; what the SEOs do matters for all of us on a daily basis, distorting how we perceive the world in ways we can hardly begin to imagine or understand, yet any money any SEO has made is a fraction of a crumb compared to Google's 10-layer cake. The company brings in hundreds of billions of dollars a year, profits that skew Google's choices and priorities — as Google's founders themselves wrote back in 1997, "we expect that advertising funded search engines will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers."

The writer reaches this position by way of Lily Ray, who seemed the most reasonable person she had spoken to — even granting that Ray calls herself a "thought leader" and changed her last name to improve her personal branding by more closely associating herself with her grandmother's uncle, the artist Man Ray. Maybe some people would say that is the kind of absurd behavior that merits being attacked by an alligator, but the writer was beginning to come down on the side of the SEOs, who seemed to have a lot less agency than she had first imagined.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. # Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." # Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. On October 28th, 2023, before the cross-examination had even begun, Judge Lewis Kaplan had already instructed Sam Bankman-Fried to answer the question he was being asked by his own lawyer — which The Verge's reporter called honestly kind of incredible, a man torpedoing his own credibility on direct testimony. Much of the morning went on vocabulary — explaining "Amazon Web Services" and "database" was a bit too detail-oriented — and when Bankman-Fried tried to define "market manipulation," Kaplan told the jury that he, the judge, was the final authority on that.

In fairness, the reporter added, he was clearer and much easier to understand than at the evidentiary hearing the day before, with a minimum of word salad; she could not tell whether he was more relaxed or simply more rehearsed, and said she would be watching to see whether he became much less coherent once Sassoon got him on cross. # Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. # The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."



---


# Cohen's Cross-Examination Of Caroline Ellison

Mark Cohen's cross-examination of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 aimed at the premise that her direct testimony was reliable — she had recounted many conversations held in person or on auto-deleting messaging platforms, and she had an incentive to flip on Bankman-Fried in the form of possible leniency at sentencing — but The Verge's reporter judged that the defense absolutely biffed it. In Cohen's disorganized cross-examination he mostly bored the jury; at one point two different jurors appeared to be asleep, and midway through the morning the reporter began wondering whether there was a mercy rule for cross-examinations.

The lines of attack were opened and dropped. Cohen established that Bankman-Fried had a much larger appetite for risk than Ellison, that the two reacted differently to stress, and that they took different approaches to media — Ellison avoided it while Bankman-Fried sought it out — without building on any of it. He drew out that Alameda had one accountant in 2021 and hired two more junior accountants in 2022, and had a problem retaining accountants, then dropped that too. He appeared to be trying to suggest the government had coerced Ellison's testimony by getting her to plead guilty to defrauding investors, conduct she could not have been involved in since she did not prepare materials for them; unfortunately she said she had had conversations with investors as part of their due diligence, and Alameda was in any case taking on losses from FTX to keep FTX's balance sheet pristine. Cohen also pressed the hedge he had blamed her for not taking out in his opening — hedging being long crypto by selling Nasdaq futures — which raised the question of whether the defense was that she should have taken more customer funds, or taken them sooner.

Small failures accumulated. Cohen asked Ellison to define what "buy on the way down" meant as though it were a term of art, which seemed to puzzle her, and at other times he seemed to forget what she had testified to and brought up things she had not said; like FTX employee Adam Yedidia before her, Ellison was fastidious about making sure a question was clear and her answer precise. She appeared at one point to be toying with him: having testified on direct about the token Luna, she noted when Cohen asked about Terra/Luna that she had only spoken about Luna, leaving him to fumble the relationship between the two. There were many sidebars, enough that several jurors looked entertained when one occurred, and in one the day before the prosecution complained that Bankman-Fried was visibly scoffing at Ellison's answers, per the court transcript. What Cohen was up against was strong direct evidence: fake balance sheets, one sent to crypto lender Genesis, after which a Genesis representative texted Ellison to say he had spoken to Bankman-Fried — strongly suggesting Bankman-Fried knew the contents of the fake balance sheet. Afterwards, the defendant's mother Barbara Fried engaged Christian Everdell in an animated conversation, gesticulating and clearly holding a strong opinion; Everdell walked off and Cohen talked to her for a bit.



---


# Tim Sweeney's Role As Epic's Controlling Shareholder

Tim Sweeney is Epic's CEO, co-founder, and — importantly — its controlling shareholder, which is what makes him the person behind Epic's lawsuits: challenging these companies in court was his idea, and it has been his fight from the very beginning.

That personal ownership of the fight extended to the courtroom itself. Sweeney watched almost the entire trial in person from the best seat in the house, with a clear view of the jury, the judge, each witness, and the faces of Google's lawyers.



---


# Dismissed Theories: A Murati Coup And A Personal Matter

TechCrunch pushes back on two explanations circulating for Altman's removal. The first is that interim CEO Mira Murati engineered the ouster: probably not — she seems cool, and anyway what CTO wants to be CEO?

The second is that the trigger was personal or legal rather than professional. When someone is kicked out in a hurry, it is not uncommon that there was some kind of unprofessional behavior in the workplace; some CEOs get a pass on things like having kids with direct reports, but not all. Altman also has three siblings, and his younger sister Annie has publicly accused him of abuse — allegations TechCrunch says it has no way of evaluating, and which involve private matters.

The premise both theories rest on is that the board's action had a personal or legal cause. TechCrunch's read on the board's language in dismissing Altman is that it was not a legal or personal problem that provoked the action, but a professional or business one.



---


# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.

qid: Who is the individual facing a criminal trial on fraud and conspiracy charges, who was once considered a trustworthy figure in the cryptocurrency industry before the collapse of a major exchange, and is accused of using customer funds to buy out a competitor, according to articles from both TechCrunch and The Verge?
context:
# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.
