# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# OpenAI DevDay 2023 Announcements

On November 6, 2023 — prior to the leadership chaos — OpenAI held its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, and announced a slew of updates to GPT, including GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API, and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT.

GPT-4 Turbo, unveiled at the conference, is a super-charged version of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model, and comes in two versions: one that is strictly text-analyzing and another that understands the context of both text and images. The GPT Store was announced alongside it: users and developers would soon be able to make their own GPT with no coding experience required, list it on OpenAI's marketplace, and monetize it in the future. OpenAI also announced the Assistants API to help developers build "agent-like experiences" within their apps, with use cases ranging from a natural language-based data analysis app to a coding assistant or even an AI-powered vacation planner.

The GPT store slipped. According to a memo seen by Axios, OpenAI planned to delay the launch of its highly anticipated GPT store to early 2024; custom GPTs and the accompanying store had been a major DevDay announcement, with the store expected to open the previous month.



---


# OpenAI Chip Rumors And Nvidia's Position

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-13 that rumors were swirling that OpenAI may be considering developing its own AI chips, and set that against Nvidia's position: Nvidia's ongoing stock market rally is likely driven by the current boom in AI, so an in-house OpenAI chip would make things interesting.

Two further figures anchor the week. ChatGPT's mobile app hit a record $4.6 million in revenue in the previous month, but growth is slowing. And the newsletter argues there is no need to shed tears for Nvidia quite yet, pointing to Brian's piece breaking down how Nvidia became a major player in robotics — that is, Nvidia's exposure is not confined to supplying the AI boom.

The surrounding context that week was AI coverage generally. TechCrunch's most-read stories consistently continue to be about AI, the AI hype cycle continues apace, and that week brought a batch of stories about what the newsletter calls the seedy underbelly of AI, including how humans are part of the problem, continuing to trick AI systems into generating boobs and 9/11 memes. TechCrunch spoke with investors to figure out whether the future of AI has hope beyond daft memes, and reports that it does. The OpenAI chip item is explicitly a rumor as of that date, not a confirmed plan.



---


# OpenAI's Q4 2023 Product Launches

The fourth quarter of 2023 has been a hell of a decade for OpenAI, Engadget writes. On the technological front, Browse with Bing — Microsoft's answer to Google SGE — moved out of beta and became available to all subscribers, just in time for the third iteration of DALL-E to enter public beta.

Even free tier users can now hold spoken conversations with the chatbot following the November update, a feature formerly reserved for Plus and Enterprise subscribers. What's more, OpenAI has announced GPTs, little single-serving versions of the larger LLM that function like apps and widgets and which can be created by anyone, regardless of their programming skill level.



---


# ChatGPT's Launch And Its First Year Of Evolution

ChatGPT, OpenAI's viral AI chatbot, turned one on November 30, 2023. A year earlier OpenAI released it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with AI startup Anthropic. The goal, OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time, was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models.

Initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5, ChatGPT would go on to become the company's most popular product ever — and the fastest-growing consumer app in history. Sam Altman marked the anniversary on X: "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…"

In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating capabilities via DALL-E 3. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions.



---


# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.



---


# The OpenAI Crisis As A Case Against Centralized AI Control

The claim is that the OpenAI debacle exposes a structural risk in depending on a centralized proprietary AI player. The situation remained fluid as of November 21, 2023, with any number of potential outcomes still on the table, but the whole debacle has shone a spotlight on the forces that control the burgeoning AI revolution, leading many to question what happens if you go all-in on a centralized proprietary player and things then go belly-up.

Mark Surman, president and executive director at the Mozilla Foundation, put the ground this way to TechCrunch: "The OpenAI / Microsoft drama underlines one of the big near-term risks with AI — that this next wave of technology is controlled by the same tiny set of players who have shaped that last era of the internet. We might have a chance of avoiding this if GPT-X were responsibly open sourced, giving researchers and startups a shot at making this technology safer, more useful and more trustworthy for people everywhere." The warrant is that concentration of control is itself the hazard, and open sourcing distributes it.

TechCrunch qualifies the claim: it is still too early to make any surefire claims on what impact the OpenAI fallout will have on LLM development and uptake in the future, and Altman and Brockman are undoubtedly steady hands for a commercial AI startup who may even return to steward OpenAI. But some might argue it is unhealthy that so much focus lies on just a handful of people — and it is telling that their departure has created such widespread havoc.



---


# Balderton's Investment Thesis On Scalable Capital

Balderton general partner Rana Yared is joining Scalable Capital's board with the December 2023 round. In a statement she said: "Scalable's one-stop, digital-first, wealth building and generating platform brings a suite of top-class financial products to individuals across Europe, and is unparalleled in the market. We've been impressed by Erik, Florian and team's vision and execution to date and are delighted to be supporting them in this next chapter."

TechCrunch noted at publication that it hoped to hear from Yared directly later that day and would update the piece afterwards.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article discussing Meta's moderation bias problem suggest a different impact on users compared to the TechCrunch article on Meta's proposed legislation for teen app downloads, with the former affecting Palestinian voices and the latter concerning parental oversight of teen social media usage?
context:
# Meta's Proposal: Parental Approval For App Downloads At The App Store

Meta wants to shift the burden of monitoring social media usage among teens back to the app stores — and to parents. In a blog post published November 15, 2023, Meta's global head of Safety, Antigone Davis, argued that parents should be responsible for approving their teens' app downloads, and staked Meta's position in supporting federal legislation that would require parental approval for app downloads for users under the age of 16.

The ground Meta offered is public opinion: it pointed to recent Pew research indicating that 81% of U.S. adults were in favor of requiring parental consent for teens to create social media accounts. TechCrunch's caveat is that while this may speak to popular opinion around parental sentiment, it does not mean that parents have thought through who should be responsible for preventing or allowing teens' access to social media, or how those apps should operate to protect teens.

The warrant tying the proposal to the app stores is one of existing capability: the app stores already have age guidelines, so it would seem to follow that they should also enforce them, if enforcement is to be regulated — or that seems to be Meta's thinking. TechCrunch also notes that a policy position like this is not something that would have been rushed out in a matter of days as a PR response to Bejar's claims, but something Meta has been stewing on for some time.



---


# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Meta's Under-13 Policy Versus Its Internal Growth Goals

An internal presentation called "2017 Teens Strategic Focus" appears to specifically target kids under 13, noting that children use tablets as early as 3 or 4, and that "Social identity is an Unmet need Ages 5-11." One stated goal, according to the lawsuit, was specifically to "grow [Monthly Active People], [Daily Active People] and time spent among U13 kids" — a growth objective aimed at the age group Meta's own account rules exclude.

TechCrunch flags an important boundary on what this does and does not show. While Meta does not permit accounts to be run by people under 13, there are plenty of ways it can lawfully and safely engage with that demographic: some kids just want to watch videos from SpongeBob Official, and that is fine. What the law requires is that Meta must verify parental consent, and the ways it can collect and use their data are limited. So targeting under-13s as an audience is not by itself unlawful; the legal question is consent and data use.



---


# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# Meta's Subscription Age Restriction And Teens

The subscription is only being offered to people aged 18 and up, which raises questions over how it will comply with requirements in the DSA and DMA not to process children's data for ad targeting, TechCrunch noted on 2023-10-30.

Meta's stated position on that gap: "We're continuing to explore how to provide teens with a useful and responsible ad experience given this evolving regulatory landscape."



---


# Common Sense Media's Teen Smartphone Study: Design And Scope

A study from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit group in San Francisco, California, researched phone usage among a diverse group of 203 kids aged 11 to 17, and the results were startling, experts say. The researchers found that smartphones have become a "constant companion" for young people, according to a news release, although results varied.

The method combined passive measurement with youth interpretation. In its report, Common Sense Media said it used "software to collect data from the smartphones of a diverse group of about 11- to 17-year-olds. We then interpreted this data with assistance from an advisory council of young people to understand the nuanced relationships that young people develop with their smartphones."

The study carries an explicit platform limitation: it was done with "Android phone users only, because Apple device tracking does not share with the research community the names of specific non-Apple apps that young people commonly use."



---


# The Republican State-Level TikTok Ban Push

Though opposition to TikTok has been bipartisan, the crusade to ban the platform over national security concerns is primarily led by Republicans at the state level, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02. The article treats that position as a likely contributor to the party's social media struggles with young voters.

The observation matters because it sets the party's legislative posture against its outreach problem: the same platform Republicans are campaigning to ban is the one where the youth vote concentrates.



---


# Discord's Graduated Warning System And Account Standing

Discord is introducing a new warning system for people who violate its policies: outside of incidents involving the most "extreme" violations, the company is moving away from permanent bans, doing so under the belief that most users will choose to be better online citizens given the chance and proper guidance.

In practice the system notifies a person when they have violated one or more of Discord's policies and details the restrictions on their account. It also links out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism. A new "Account Standing" tab within the settings menu lets users see all their current and past policy violations.

Discord frames the design as a model for the industry. "We think we've built the most nuanced and proportionate reporting system," Badalich told Engadget, adding that the company hopes other platforms will look to what Discord has created for inspiration in their own enforcement efforts. "We believe people, especially teens, have the capacity to grow."



---


# Pebble's Moderation-First Market Hypothesis

Pebble's founding hypothesis was that consumers were hungry for a Twitter alternative that prioritized trust, safety and moderation from the start. The company staffed for it: Pebble's founding team included co-founder Sarah Oh, Twitter's former human rights advisor.

What would falsify the proposition is a moderation-first Twitter alternative that consumers decline to adopt — which is the shape of the outcome TechCrunch is reporting on 2023-10-24, in a piece about Pebble shutting down.

# Messi's Fitness And Inter Miami's Offseason, October 2023

Lionel Messi's club Inter Miami were eliminated from MLS playoff contention by a 1-0 loss to FC Cincinnati the weekend before Argentina's Oct. 12, 2023 qualifier against Paraguay — and that elimination changed the calculus around his minutes for Argentina.

Messi had missed the previous four matches, including Argentina's fixture against Bolivia, but returned for the final 30 minutes against Cincinnati and was powerless to turn the tide after Inter Miami missed so many gilt-edged chances in the first half. # Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.

# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.

# Cohen's Cross-Examination Of Caroline Ellison

Mark Cohen's cross-examination of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 aimed at the premise that her direct testimony was reliable — she had recounted many conversations held in person or on auto-deleting messaging platforms, and she had an incentive to flip on Bankman-Fried in the form of possible leniency at sentencing — but The Verge's reporter judged that the defense absolutely biffed it. In Cohen's disorganized cross-examination he mostly bored the jury; at one point two different jurors appeared to be asleep, and midway through the morning the reporter began wondering whether there was a mercy rule for cross-examinations.

The lines of attack were opened and dropped. Cohen established that Bankman-Fried had a much larger appetite for risk than Ellison, that the two reacted differently to stress, and that they took different approaches to media — Ellison avoided it while Bankman-Fried sought it out — without building on any of it. He drew out that Alameda had one accountant in 2021 and hired two more junior accountants in 2022, and had a problem retaining accountants, then dropped that too. He appeared to be trying to suggest the government had coerced Ellison's testimony by getting her to plead guilty to defrauding investors, conduct she could not have been involved in since she did not prepare materials for them; unfortunately she said she had had conversations with investors as part of their due diligence, and Alameda was in any case taking on losses from FTX to keep FTX's balance sheet pristine. Cohen also pressed the hedge he had blamed her for not taking out in his opening — hedging being long crypto by selling Nasdaq futures — which raised the question of whether the defense was that she should have taken more customer funds, or taken them sooner.

Small failures accumulated. Cohen asked Ellison to define what "buy on the way down" meant as though it were a term of art, which seemed to puzzle her, and at other times he seemed to forget what she had testified to and brought up things she had not said; like FTX employee Adam Yedidia before her, Ellison was fastidious about making sure a question was clear and her answer precise. She appeared at one point to be toying with him: having testified on direct about the token Luna, she noted when Cohen asked about Terra/Luna that she had only spoken about Luna, leaving him to fumble the relationship between the two. There were many sidebars, enough that several jurors looked entertained when one occurred, and in one the day before the prosecution complained that Bankman-Fried was visibly scoffing at Ellison's answers, per the court transcript. What Cohen was up against was strong direct evidence: fake balance sheets, one sent to crypto lender Genesis, after which a Genesis representative texted Ellison to say he had spoken to Bankman-Fried — strongly suggesting Bankman-Fried knew the contents of the fake balance sheet. Afterwards, the defendant's mother Barbara Fried engaged Christian Everdell in an animated conversation, gesticulating and clearly holding a strong opinion; Everdell walked off and Cohen talked to her for a bit.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.

# The Bankman-Fried And Zhao Convictions And Binance's Aftermath

Sam Bankman-Fried, who faces potential life behind bars, was scheduled to be sentenced in March, and Changpeng Zhao's sentencing was set for February; while guidelines suggest a sentence of 12 to 18 months, the Justice Department could push for a lengthier punishment for the Binance founder. Unlike FTX, which filed for bankruptcy in late 2022, Binance is still standing, though now without Zhao, who agreed to step down as CEO as part of the plea deal. Even before that the company was seeing a plunge in trading, with volume down by two-thirds between the first and third quarters of the year according to crypto analyst site CoinGecko. With assets of more than $65 billion on the platform Binance remains the world's largest crypto exchange globally, but its market share fell from over 60% in February to under 50% in September, which CoinGecko called "an indication that the exchange may be losing its grip on the industry as regulators continue to pressure it". In the first 24 hours after the Justice Department announced its $4.3 billion settlement with Binance, customers pulled more than $1 billion from the exchange, and liquidity dropped 25% in the immediate aftermath as market makers pulled back their positions, according to data provider Kaiko. A Binance spokesperson told CNBC that Zhao appeared in court "to protect our users and to ensure the longevity of our company", that "Binance's resilience has been tested unlike any other exchange around today", and that it continues to operate the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by volume and currently sees a climbing percentage of institutional user transactions.

Coinbase is the fourth-biggest global exchange by daily volume according to CoinGecko, the only one publicly traded in the U.S., with a market cap of close to $30 billion. In a report to clients on the Wednesday, analysts at Mizuho noted that Coinbase shares are up about 20% since Zhao's settlement, a rally likely "in anticipation of potential share gains for COIN in wake of outflows from Binance, the industry's largest exchange". Coinbase shares fell 2.4% to $124.72 on the Thursday, wiping out some recent gains, and Mizuho raised its price target on the stock to $35 from $31 while keeping the underperform rating it has maintained since December.

# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. Burrow dodged a sack, rolled left and flipped 18 yards to Tee Higgins at the Bills' 21, Mixon ran three up the middle and Burrow found Smith for 11 to the 7 and first-and-goal; at 8:30 p.m. Smith made a leaping grab over Jordan Poyer for a seven-yard touchdown, his first of the year, for 7-0.

Buffalo answered immediately. Ty Johnson returned the kickoff to the Bills' 15, Allen found Dalton Kincaid for five out of an RPO, then hit Stefon Diggs for nine on third-and-5 and again for a 34-yard strike, Diggs carving down the left sideline to the Bengals' 37. Allen scrambled and flipped a pass to Khalil Shakir that went 22 yards to the Bengals' 15, then connected with Kincaid for 13 to the Cincinnati 2, and at 8:39 p.m. rushed in for a two-yard touchdown — drawing a taunting flag as he ran through the right side — to tie it 7-7 with 6:03 left in the quarter.

Cincinnati retook the lead on a long drive. Williams returned to the Cincinnati 31; Burrow's throw to Ja'Marr Chase was broken up but he was roughed on the play for 15 yards; Andrei Iosivas, involved after back-to-back weeks with a touchdown, caught nine on a rollout and Mixon ran three for the first down at the Bills' 42. Facing their longest third down of the day at third-and-10 after a Mixon no-gain and a missed connection with Smith, the Bengals stayed perfect on third downs as Tyler Boyd caught 15 in front of the sideline to the Bills' 27, and Hudson's second catch went 13 to the 14. Burrow escaped the pocket and got the ball to Higgins, who dove for the pylon but was ruled out at the 2; Cincinnati then twice tried Chase, who was tackled at the 2 on a screen and could not hold a leaping grab in the end zone. At 8:52 p.m. Mixon bulldozed up the middle for a two-yard touchdown and a 14-7 lead. Buffalo took the ball at the 25 after a fair catch at the 2 with 35 seconds left, and James Cook's first rush of the game gained two to end the quarter.

# ChatGPT Competitors And Alternatives

There are multiple AI-powered chatbot competitors to ChatGPT — Together, Google's Bard and Anthropic's Claude among them — and developers are creating open source alternatives, though the latter are harder, if not impossible, to run today.

Bard is the closest comparison. Much like ChatGPT, Bard is a chatbot that answers questions in natural language; Google announced at its 2023 I/O event that it would soon add multimodal content to Bard, meaning it can deliver answers in more than just text, with rich visuals — pictures for now, and later possibly maps, charts and other items. The discriminating advantage claimed for ChatGPT is time in the field: its generative AI has had a longer lifespan and thus has been "learning" for a longer period than Bard.

Two further challengers were in development. The Google-owned research lab DeepMind claimed that its next LLM would rival, or even best, ChatGPT; DeepMind is using techniques from AlphaGo — its AI system that was the first to defeat a professional human player at the board game Go — to make a ChatGPT-rivaling chatbot called Gemini. Apple is developing AI tools to challenge OpenAI, Google and others, and has created a chatbot that some engineers internally refer to as "Apple GPT," although Apple has yet to determine a strategy for releasing the AI to consumers.



---


# ChatGPT's Launch And Its First Year Of Evolution

ChatGPT, OpenAI's viral AI chatbot, turned one on November 30, 2023. A year earlier OpenAI released it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with AI startup Anthropic. The goal, OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time, was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models.

Initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5, ChatGPT would go on to become the company's most popular product ever — and the fastest-growing consumer app in history. Sam Altman marked the anniversary on X: "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…"

In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating capabilities via DALL-E 3. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# AI Hallucination

## Definition

AI hallucination, in the corpus, is the tendency of a generative AI system — a large language model — to produce fabricated content: ChatGPT's "tendency to hallucinate facts and figures," illustrated by a fabricated legal-citation incident, and Alexa's capacity, per Amazon, to "be led astray or 'hallucinate' answers."

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in two very different settings that share the same underlying risk.

The first is ChatGPT's real-world track record: its "tendency to hallucinate facts and figures" produced a documented incident in which a New York lawyer used the chatbot for "legal research" and was given "a number of entirely made-up, nonexistent cases to cite in his argument," which he then filed without independently verifying them.

The second is a product-design setting: Amazon, in building the "Explore with Alexa" conversational AI feature for children, explicitly names hallucination as one of the two core risks the product has to design around, noting that "generative AI can be led astray or 'hallucinate' answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions."

Across both cases hallucination is treated not as an occasional glitch but as an inherent property of generative AI systems that any deployment — whether a general-purpose chatbot or a child-safety-scoped assistant — must account for.

## Key Characteristics

- **Fabrication, not error-correction failure** — the model does not merely get a fact wrong; it invents content (fake case citations, made-up figures) that did not exist.
- **Plausibility is the danger** — the fabricated case citations were credible enough that the lawyer who received them filed them "without bothering to independently validate any of them."
- **Treated as a known, recurring property of generative AI** — both docs frame hallucination with a definite article ("its tendency to hallucinate," "generative AI can be led astray or 'hallucinate'"), not as a one-off bug.
- **Drives downstream mitigation design** — in the Alexa Kids case, hallucination is named alongside kids asking inappropriate questions as one of the risks Amazon built guardrails around, generating content offline and running it through a human-and-AI review process rather than hooking kids up to an LLM at runtime.

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), AI hallucinations are cases where an AI system generates outputs that seem believable but are actually incorrect, unrelated, or completely made up — such as fake facts, invented studies, or nonexistent sources presented as if true (IBM, "What Are AI Hallucinations?", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/ai-hallucinations).



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

qid: Which platform is at the center of discussions about the ethical use of AI-driven voice replication for artists, the debate over "reaction" content monetization, the investment in AI technology to combat copyright and trademark abuse, and is also the most used app by kids overnight according to a study reported by sources including Music Business Worldwide, Polygon, and FOX News - Health?
context:
# YouTube's AI Music Incubator And Its Rightsholder Pledges

During its period of discussions with the majors, YouTube made a series of announcements aimed at the biggest issue for any rightsholder regarding AI-driven voice replication of artists: their ability to police it.

In August, YouTube and Universal Music Group jointly announced that the video platform was launching an "AI Music Incubator" — a program by which new tools and innovations would be developed at YouTube in close conjunction with artists and the music business; to progress the incubator, YouTube said it was working behind the scenes with a number of UMG-affiliated artists. Also in August, YouTube publicly committed to three principles or pledges behind its development of music-based generative AI tools. These pledges promised "appropriate protections… for music partners who decide to participate" in such tools, and promised "invest[ment] in the AI-powered technology" that, among other things, would help YouTube "protect our community of viewers, creators, artists and songwriters… [from] trademark and copyright abuse" — all of which seemed to hint at a desire to build a "Content ID"-style system on YouTube to control and police content made by cloning artists' voices. Then, earlier in November, YouTube announced it was developing a specific system for music partners allowing them to request the removal of content on its platform that "mimics an artist's unique singing or rapping voice."



---


# Sony Music's Pipeline Of AI Startup Partnerships

Kooker said Sony Music has "roughly 200 active conversations taking place with startups and established players" right now about building new AI-related products and tools, and that some of these conversations "also include potential equity investments which would accelerate the development of these companies."

He framed this as the optimistic counterweight to the harms: despite the negative impacts of AI, including unauthorized clones and low-quality AI music, there are still "many positive and optimistic developments to highlight," and he highlighted legitimate AI startups and established firms "with music ideas that want to partner with the industry." The products under discussion range from tools for "creative or marketing assistance," to tools that "potentially give us the ability to better protect artist content or find it when used in an unauthorized fashion," as well as "brand new products that have never been launched before."



---


# The US Copyright Office's 2023 Study Of AI And Copyright

The US Copyright Office is spearheading one of the key US efforts to address AI and copyright: in the summer of 2023 it issued a call for submissions on the issue of AI and copyright, with the goal of putting together a study to "help assess whether legislative or regulatory steps in this area are warranted."

The call for submissions came as legislators and regulators around the world grappled with the many issues that had emerged since AI technology "went mainstream" about a year earlier. Numerous businesses involved in AI, and those with substantial copyright holdings, submitted their thoughts on the issue — including Universal Music Group and AI developer Anthropic.



---


# YouTube Content ID as Blueprint for AI Rights Management

Robert Kyncl's model treats the solutions built for user-generated content as a "blueprint" that can be applied to AI-generated content on platforms. The analogy has three parts: the explosion of AI use among the public maps onto the explosion of user-generated content (UGC) a decade or two ago; just as UGC often infringed copyright, AI threatens the rights of artists and music rights holders; and therefore the same class of remedy should apply.

The remedy he describes is YouTube's Content ID. "When YouTube was formed… people started to upload content, including copyrighted material, which, obviously, put YouTube into hot water with lots of different copyright holders. And I had the privilege of working through a lot of that and fix it up. But we made a very important decision, which was to go above and beyond the law, and build a fingerprinting software that allowed us to track the copyright on our platform, and then have commercial relationship[s] with copyright holders to send them the money. Out of that we built a multi-billion-dollar business, which now is a multi-billion-dollar business per year. And it was an incredible new revenue stream for everyone. AI is that with new super tools." Content ID scours uploaded videos for copyrighted content, video and audio, then offers the copyright owner the option to monetise that video or to request that it be taken down — a system that has essentially allowed YouTube users to upload content without paying much attention to copyright while ensuring copyright owners are paid.

Two conditions bound the model. First, the same thoughtfulness must be applied to AI as was applied to UGC, and "we have to make sure that artists have a choice" — detection alone is not the point; owner election between monetisation and takedown is. Second, refusal is not available as a strategy: "You have to embrace technology, because it's not like you can put technology in a bottle. The genie is not going back."



---


# AI Day Of Action Campaign

In the week of 2023-10-06, digital rights organization Fight for the Future partnered with music industry labor group United Musicians and Allied Workers to launch #AIdayofaction, a campaign that calls on Congress to block corporations from obtaining copyrights on music and other art made with AI.

The mechanism the campaign is betting on is indirect. The idea is that by preventing industry behemoths like major record labels, for example, from copyrighting music made with the assistance of AI, those companies will be forced to keep looping humans into the creative process. Those same concerns — and the same potential strategies for pushing back against the onslaught of AI — exist across creative industries, which is why the launch was pitched beyond music.

The launch landed in a moment when creative industries were grappling with AI's explosion into every artistic medium at once, and separate calls from artists warning the world to take action before it's too late were starting to converge. From fake Drake songs to stylized Instagram profile pictures, art conjured with newly sophisticated AI tools was suddenly ubiquitous — and so were conversations about how to rein in the technology before it does irrevocable harm to creative communities.

By the following week, on 2023-10-13, TechCrunch characterized the effort as a campaign that targets potential corporate abuse of AI technology while remaining realistic about the ways that musicians and some other creatives could benefit on an individual level from automating parts of their work. The stated goal is that AI tools "become ways for individual humans to make more money, work less, and compete with the corporations that exploit them."



---


# TikTok Users' Music Discovery And Sharing Rates

The Luminate study found that the TikTok audience can be an effective marketing tool for artists, because TikTok users in particular are considerably more likely to discover and share music than overall social media and short video platform users.

In the UK, TikTok users were 108% more likely to discover and share music than other social media users; in Germany they were 100% more likely; and US TikTok users were 71% more likely. "In doing so, TikTok users help both emerging and established artists to reach new audiences," the Luminate report stated.



---


# Under-13 Access To Age-Inappropriate Apps

Of the 85 participants under age 13, 68% used social media and had at least one app rated "teen" or higher, allowing access to "age-inappropriate experiences," the study suggested.

TikTok was the most popular app used by kids aged 11 and 12, while nearly half -- 45% -- of participants used apps with mature or adult-only ratings, such as porn sites, fantasy sports and betting apps, according to the study findings.



---


# Meta's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

Facebook and Instagram parent Meta's report to the EU disinformation Code includes a recognition that "widespread availability and adoption of generative AI tools may have implications for how we identify, and address disinformation on our platforms."

Meta's stated approach is collaborative rather than unilateral: "We want to work with partners in government, industry, civil society and academia to ensure that we can develop robust, sustainable solutions to tackling AI-generated misinformation." It notes it has signed up to the Partnership on AI's Responsible Practices for Synthetic Media, and professes the company to be "committed to cross-industry collaboration to help to maintain the integrity of the online information environment for our users." Meta adds: "Besides, to bring more people into this process, we are launching a Community Forum on Generative AI aimed at producing feedback on the principles people want to see reflected in new AI technologies. It will be held in consultation with Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioural Insights Team, and is consistent with our open collaboration approach to sharing AI models. We look forward to expanding this effort as a member of the Code's Task Force Working Group on Generative AI, and look forward to working together with its other members."

Over the next six months, Meta says it wants to "work with partners in government, industry, civil society and academia in Europe and around the world, to ensure that we can develop robust, sustainable solutions to tackling AI-generated misinformation," adding: "We will participate in the newly formed working group on AI-generated disinformation under the EU Code of Practice."

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried's actions were motivated by personal gain, while The Verge article focuses on the specific use of FTX customer funds by Sam Bankman-Fried?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" # Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. # The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. Asked how he himself would find a reliable attorney — lawyers, accountants and contractors being particularly lucrative SEO customers because they are eager for attention from people going online for local recommendations — he answered: "I don't know if you can trust anything you read online. A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

# Epic's Post-Verdict Remedy Strategy And Global Cases

Told that Google has said it will challenge the verdict, Tim Sweeney said Epic is not going to wait: it will do absolutely everything it can as quickly as it can to start changing the world, rather than pausing for the appeal.

His reasoning for the reach of the win is the market Epic established at trial — a market worldwide excluding China — so this is, in his framing, a worldwide verdict, and Epic presumes any remedies would be worldwide too. Beyond the US case, he pointed to the European DMA, to Epic v. Apple and Epic v. Google cases coming up in Australia, and to another in the UK. He also stressed that the push no longer depends on Epic alone: a lot of legislators, a lot of regulators, and other litigation are all pushing in the direction of openness. On whether the Google verdict helps Epic's Apple appeal, Sweeney said there is no linkage between the cases in law and no legal connection between the two, so it would come down only to whether the court is in any way following current events — to the decisions of the humans involved, the justices and support teams considering the appeal.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.



---


# Fortnite's Battle Royale Live-Service Model

Fortnite is a battle royale-style third-person shooter where 100 players swarm a massive but shrinking virtual island with the goal of being the last man standing. In the process they generally engage in myriad well-animated virtual antics as the game has become wackier and more elaborate over time, all while dressed in custom skins you earn by playing or purchase in Epic's lucrative virtual swag shop.

What makes it a live-service game is its release cadence: like other live service online games, Fortnite releases new content every three-ish months, refreshing the destinations scattered across its cartoony island locale, changing the rules of physics and generally adding additional mayhem, often in the form of weapons. Epic's hit game has both imported and exported popular culture since its launch in 2017, and those seasons are punctuated by flashy concerts and pop culture tie-ins, like a psychedelic Ariana Grande show, an in-game lightsaber fight with Darth Vader or the appearance of Dragon Ball Z's Goku as an in-game skin. The massive online shop for skins and other character customizations betrays Epic's loftier aspirations of building an interconnected virtual online world — a kind of metaverse, if you will.



---


# Fortnite's Live-Service Content Treadmill

Polygon's model, published 2023-10-19, is that around 2018 Twitch and its personalities turned Fortnite into a juggernaut so powerful that much of the gaming industry started molding itself in its image — and that what kept Fortnite from being a mere fad was not its approachable aesthetic and surprising gameplay but its model: where content expansions and adjustments previously took months or years and often cost money, Fortnite set a more cutthroat standard of free weekly content updates.

The conditions that made this possible were unique to Epic. It could swing ceaseless delivery because the bulk of its profits at the time came from its engine, which many games — including Fortnite's competitors — license; those deep pockets made Fortnite possible in the first place, since the bubbly shooter was initially a flop before Epic perfected the formula. The cadence also let Epic quickly adapt Fortnite to whatever was trending or novel, whether Among Us or Splatoon, and much like Roblox it became a game that could give you anything — and if Epic did not emulate it, the players would. "You can't replicate Fortnite's growth from, like, the [content creator] standpoint and also definitely from the developer standpoint," says a Twitch streamer turned game developer who requested anonymity because he is not authorized to discuss the popular AAA live-service shooter he works on.

Those conditions were immaterial to publishers who could only imagine profits: suddenly "live service" was everywhere, and games like Overwatch, which could not achieve a similar pace, were posed as disappointments by content creators.

The limit of the model is the audience it assumes. Developers say getting half their players to actually finish games is unusual and worth celebrating, because most people will never finish a game they start, and 22% of purchased games on Steam are unplayed outright — affected by factors like sales or Game Pass, but still telling. Per Statista, a reported 25% of players between 18 and 34 enjoy games between three and six hours a week, 28% play two hours or less, and 19% play between 13 to 24 hours or more; as fans get older they apparently spend less time in games, and in the most engaged age group half of all players only log a couple of hours or so per week in their favorite games.

# Synapse Laid Off 86 People, About 40% Of The Company

Banking-as-a-service startup Synapse confirmed on Friday that it had laid off 86 people, or about 40% of the company.

The San Francisco–based company operates a platform enabling banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services, and it has been open about past layoffs. In June, CEO Sankaet Pathak wrote in a blog post that the company had let go of 18% of its workforce, because "the current macroeconomic conditions" had begun to impact its clients and platforms, affecting its anticipated growth.
