Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

# The Competitive Response To ChatGPT Across The AI Industry

ChatGPT became priority number one at OpenAI — not simply a one-off product but a development platform to build upon — and, as often happens in a competition-driven marketplace, it shifted the focus at other AI firms and research labs too.

Google scrambled to launch a response to ChatGPT, eventually releasing Bard, a more or less comparable AI chatbot, in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives have arrived to market since, most recently Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. And DeepMind, Google's premier AI research lab, is expected to debut a next-gen chatbot, Gemini, before the end of 2023.

# The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. # Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

# The 2023 Cybersecurity Consolidation Wave

Cybersecurity remains a moving target, and that dynamic drives a repeating acquisition cycle: malicious hackers are turning to technologies like AI to break into networks, so as smaller startups come up with new cyber techniques themselves, they become acquisition targets for larger companies looking to stay ahead of the curve.

The pattern shows up in a chain of reactive deals. CrowdStrike acquired the security startup Bionic for $350 million, and IBM bought Polar for $60 million — a deal IBM made, TechCrunch understands, partly in response to Palo Alto buying Cider Security in 2022. There are mega deals in the same trend, such as Cisco's plan to buy Splunk for $28 billion.

The competitive relation runs in two directions at once: for security companies it becomes a question of competitive edge both against malicious hackers and against other security companies. "Palo Alto is buying partly in reaction to these deals," one source said, and some Palo Alto competitors like Wiz, now valued at $10 billion, are also part of that competitive threat.

qid: After TechCrunch reported on Biden's AI Executive Order as broad but lacking depth without corresponding legislation on October 31, 2023, and Music Business Worldwide shared concerns from the National Music Publishers Association about generative AI being a significant risk to the human creative class on November 30, 2023, is the stance of these two news sources on the need for regulatory measures for AI consistent or inconsistent?
context:
# Reaction To Biden's AI Order

Respondents to Biden's AI executive order attacked the premise that an executive order alone is a sufficient regulatory response, arguing that its breadth is real but its depth is not, and that the substantive work still requires Congress. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia said he was "impressed by the breadth" of the order, though, he implies, not the depth: "I am also happy to see a number of sections that closely align with my efforts around AI safety and security and federal government's use of AI," he said in a statement. "At the same time, many of these just scratch the surface – particularly in areas like health care and competition policy. While this is a good step forward, we need additional legislative measures, and I will continue to work diligently…" TechCrunch's own reading is that given the state of the legislature and the fact that an incredibly contentious election period is upcoming, it will be a miracle if any substantive law whatsoever is passed in the near future, let alone a potentially divisive and complex bill like AI rules.

Paul Barrett, deputy director of the NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights, acknowledged both sides of the issue and attacked the inference that direction of travel equals capacity to act. "President Biden is sending a valuable message that certain AI systems create immediate risks that demand immediate attention. The administration is moving in the right direction," he wrote. "But today is just the beginning of a regulatory process that will be long and arduous–and ultimately must require that the companies profiting from AI bear the burden of proving that their products are safe and effective, just as the manufacturers of pharmaceuticals or industrial chemicals or airplanes must demonstrate that their products are safe and effective. Without fresh resources provided by Congress, it's not clear that the federal government has the resources to assess the vastly complicated training process or the adequacy of red-teaming and other necessary testing."

A more favorable reading came from Sheila Gulati, co-founder of Tola Capital, who said the EO showed a "clear intention to walk the line of promoting innovation while protecting citizens." "It is most essential that we don't prevent agile innovation by startups. Putting AI explainability at the forefront, taking a risk-based approach with more focus on areas where harm or bias could be at play, and bringing security and privacy to the center of focus are all sensible steps," she told TechCrunch. "With this executive order and the standards implications through NIST, we would anticipate leadership from standards bodies versus legislators in the near term." It is worth mentioning as well that the federal government is a major customer of today's AI and tech products, and any company that intends to keep them as a customer will want to color inside the lines for the immediate future. Bob Cattanach, partner at legal mega-firm Dorsey and Whitney, added that the timing feels slightly off.



---


# Sony Music's Generative AI Principles For Congress

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, asked Congress at the November 29, 2023 AI Insight Forum to embrace a set of five principles around generative AI, on the argument that "if copyrights are protected and enforced appropriately, we are at the beginning of a multi-decade marathon that will change the creative and commercial landscape for music."

The framing condition Kooker set is that "Music is a tremendous driver for AI technology, and AI technology presents a tremendous opportunity for the creative development of music. But these opportunities must be grounded by the human creators' vision with the machine assisting, not with the machine replacing the human creator." The principles are: Assure Consent, Compensation, and Credit — "New products and businesses built with music must be developed with the consent of the owner and appropriate compensation and credit. It is essential to understand why the training of AI models is being done, what products will be developed as a result, and what the business model is that will monetize the use of the artist's work. Congress and the agencies should assure that creators' rights are recognized and respected." Confirm That Copying Music to Train AI Models is Not Fair Use — "Even worse are those that argue that copyrighted content should automatically be considered fair use so that protected works are never compensated for usage and creators have no say in the products or business models that are developed around them and their work. Congress should assure and agencies should presume that reproducing music to train AI models, in itself, is not a fair use." Prevent the Cloning of Artists' Voices and Likenesses Without Express Permission — "We cannot allow an artist's voice or likeness to be cloned for use without the express permission of the artist. This is a very personal decision for the artist. Congress should pass into law effective federal protections for name, image, and likeness." Incentivize Accurate Recordkeeping — "Correct attribution will be a critical element to artists being paid fairly and correctly for new works that are created. In addition, rights can only be enforced around the training of AI when there are accurate records about what is being copied. Otherwise, the inability to enforce rights in the AI marketplace equates to a lack of rights at all, producing a dangerous imbalance that prevents a thriving ecosystem. This requires strong and accurate record keeping by the generative AI platforms, a requirement that urgently needs legislative support to ensure incentives are in place so that it happens consistently and correctly." And Assure Transparency for Consumers and Artists — "Transparency is necessary to clearly distinguish human-created works from AI-created works. The public should know, when they are listening to music, whether that music was created by a human being or a machine." MBW summarised the intended effect: "The principles will ensure that intellectual property businesses can succeed in this new world alongside tech partners, further advancing investment and expanding economic opportunities."



---


# The NMPA Submission Calling Generative AI The Greatest Risk To The Creative Class

The National Music Publishers Association's submission to the US Copyright Office, dated October 30, 2023, argues that generative AI may be the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed — and therefore that the Office should adopt proactive protections for human creators and, where uncertain, err on their side.

The argument is deliberately framed as pro-technology at its base. The submission starts by stressing that the NMPA's membership — US music publishers major and independent — are "not opposed" to AI: "There is widespread belief in the music industry that great benefits could come from generative AI systems that can assist human creators." It then goes for the jugular: "However, the development of the generative AI marketplace is marked by breathtaking speed, size and complexity. Hindsight may well prove that there is no hyperbole in saying that generative AI is the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed." The warrant for urgency is temporal: "Even more alarming is that we do not know how long the window is to act before it is too late. We therefore implore the [US Copyright] Office to support proactive protections for human creators and, where there is uncertainty, to err on the side of protecting human creators." MBW notes the position is not a surprise from an organisation that earlier in 2023 joined the fledgling Human Artistry Campaign, whose goal in broadest terms is to ensure AI does not replace or "erode" human culture — yet the submission is hardly a Luddite diatribe against high tech; it advocates regulations and principles it sees as the right way to keep the interests of musical artists and rights holders from being subjugated in the frenzy to build an AI-powered world.



---


# FTC Generative AI Roundtable

At the FTC's conversation on generative AI and the creative industries, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-06, chair Lina Khan set out the agency's framing: "I know that generative AI in particular poses a unique set of opportunities and challenges to creative industries. We've already heard significant concerns about how these technologies could virtually overnight significantly disempower creators and artists who may watch their life's creation be appropriated into models over which they have no control."

The concerns raised by participants clustered on two points. In the comments, representatives from myriad creative communities expressed concerns around opt-out requirements that by default train AI models on artists' original work, and around how existing copyright law could be a useful if not comprehensive tool for setting out regulatory guardrails.

A representative with the WGA used the conversation to say the fight was not finished by collective bargaining: while striking writers obtained their own protections in a newly won agreement, the fight for artists' livelihoods "doesn't stop at the bargaining table."

Whether Congress mobilizes in time to address mounting concerns around AI and creative industries or not, for its part the FTC does appear to be very tuned into the technology's risks — and the power of bringing voices together across industries. FTC commissioner Rebecca Slaughter put the agency's position in categorical terms: "Art is fundamentally human. Humans may use technology to assist in creating art, but something cannot be art without human input. Technology is, by definition, not human . . . humans may endeavor to make generative AI that is ever more intelligent, [but] it cannot and will not replace human creativity."

# Discogs' Database Completeness At Risk

# Messi's Four-Game Injury Absence And His 35-Minute Return

Lionel Messi missed four straight Inter Miami games with injury before returning off the bench for 35 minutes against FC Cincinnati on Oct. 7, 2023. He was left out entirely for the Oct. 4 trip to the Chicago Fire: 35 minutes before kickoff the lineups showed him not part of the squad, with Josef Martinez up front as Leonardo Campana was out with a knock. An hour before kickoff, Michelle Kaufman of the Miami Herald reported Messi "did not arrive with the team" to Soldier Field — a strong indication rather than outright confirmation that he would not play. Meanwhile Chicago was still feeling Messi fever, with Messi shirt vendors outside Soldier Field and the Fire media team joking that they had "the GOAT in the building."

Against FC Cincinnati he was available. Two hours before kickoff, well-connected Argentine journalist Gaston Edul had reported the night before that Inter Miami were likely to have Messi back in some capacity — "the idea is for Leo Messi to get minutes when Inter Miami plays FC Cincinnati" — which sounded like bench availability, alongside reporting that Messi was battling "fatigue" and a "scar tissue issue." He entered in the 55th minute, replacing Tomas Aviles in a very attacking change with around 35 minutes to save Inter Miami's season, alongside Jean Mota for David Ruiz. By the time he stepped on the pitch, Inter Miami's early dominance had come and gone; Messi played a part but was unable to fully change the tide of the game.

Lionel Messi's club Inter Miami were eliminated from MLS playoff contention by a 1-0 loss to FC Cincinnati the weekend before Argentina's Oct. 12, 2023 qualifier against Paraguay — and that elimination changed the calculus around his minutes for Argentina.

Reports on the day said Messi would not start but was likely to play much or all of the second half, with Lautaro Martinez and Julian Alvarez both starting a national team match together for the first time — something World Cup hero Mario Kempes was a big fan of. # The FTC's Antitrust Lawsuit Against Amazon

The Federal Trade Commission's sweeping 172-page antitrust lawsuit, filed in late September 2023, accuses Amazon of wielding its monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, which the agency alleges has led to artificially inflated prices and a degraded shopping experience for consumers.

The mechanism the FTC describes is an "anti-discounting strategy" backed by a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices" to stifle competition: Amazon punishes third-party sellers who offer cheaper products elsewhere by threatening to disqualify them from appearing in the buy box if it detects a lower price, and losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers' businesses, the complaint alleges. The end result, the FTC argues, is elevated prices across the web — the company steadily hikes the fees it charges sellers and prevents them from discounting on other sites, so sellers often inflate their prices off Amazon, creating an "artificial price floor everywhere." The FTC is seeking to hold Amazon liable for allegedly violating anti-monopoly law but has not yet outlined the specific remedies it believes would best resolve its concerns; in antitrust cases, remedies are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable. Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky responded in a blog post that third-party sellers set their own prices on the marketplace and that the company invests in tools to help sellers offer "competitive prices": "Even with those tools, some of the businesses selling on Amazon might still choose to set prices that aren't competitive. Just like any store owner who wouldn't want to promote a bad deal to their customers, we don't highlight or promote offers that are not competitively priced." Zapolsky argued the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result that would be directly opposed to the goals of antitrust law."

# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.

# GPT Model Lineage And The ChatGPT Launch

GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is the large language model that ChatGPT runs on, and OpenAI had been developing it since 2016 — unveiling GPT-1 in 2018 and iterating it to GPT-3 by June 2020. With the November 30, 2022 release of GPT-3.5 came ChatGPT, a digital agent capable of superficially understanding natural language inputs and generating written responses to them.

The first iteration's limits were plain: it was rather slow to answer and couldn't speak to questions about anything that happened after September 2021, not to mention its issues answering queries with misinformation during bouts of "hallucinations." Even so, that kludgy first iteration demonstrated capabilities far beyond what other state-of-the-art digital assistants like Siri and Alexa could provide — the discriminating feature that set it apart from what came before.

# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# The "General Purpose AI" Terminology Choice In The EU AI Act

The EU AI Act refers to the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools as "general purpose" AI models and systems rather than using the industry's preferred terms such as "foundational" or "frontier" models, and per the Commission that choice was made with an eye on futureproofing the incoming law.

The reasoning is that a generic term avoids a classification that could be chained to the use of a specific technology — that is, transformer-based machine learning. "In the future, we may have different technical approaches. And so we were looking for a more generic term," a Commission official said. The category is deliberately broader than the industry term it replaces: "Foundation models, of course, are part of the general purpose AI models. These are models that can be used for a very large variety of tasks, they can also be integrated in systems."

The official also drew the model/system boundary with a worked example: "To give you a concrete example, the general purpose AI model would be GPT-4 and the general purpose AI system would be ChatGPT — where GPT-4 is integrated in ChatGPT."

# June 2022: Alameda's Reckoning And Lender Repayment

By 2022 Alameda's negative balance on FTX had become a cause for concern for Caroline Ellison, Nishad Singh, and Gary Wang, who built a spreadsheet to work out how negative Alameda actually was; the version shown in court ran to several pages of attempts to reconcile, and Wang figured Alameda owed FTX about $11 billion at a time when FTX's revenue was about $1.5 billion. Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried then met in the Bahamas office, where Alameda's lenders wanted their money back and Bankman-Fried directed the group to pay the lenders back using FTX customer funds.

Bankman-Fried considered shutting Alameda down and even wrote a long memo about it, but Wang testified that in a now-deleted Signal discussion of that memo he told Bankman-Fried and Singh they could not shut Alameda down because they could not repay its debt. Another empty Signal chat, with its setting to delete messages after a week, was shown to the court; its members were Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried.

Bankman-Fried's own account from the stand ran differently. He testified that in June 2022 he heard about the account called "fiat@ftx" tracking how much money Alameda owed to FTX, that he did not know what it was and did not bother to find out because he was busy, and that this was when he directed Ellison to repay Alameda's lenders because he thought Alameda was good for it. Cole Palmer, who left Manchester City for Chelsea in a deal worth around $A82 million in September, showed supreme composure to fire past Ederson in the dying stages of the 4-4 draw at Stamford Bridge, scoring from the spot in the 95th minute, The Roar reported on Nov. 12, 2023.

In his post-match interview he said of penalties: "I'm not going to say I work on them, because I don't. I just trust in my natural abilities."

# Cole Palmer's Penalty-Taking Role And Record

Cole Palmer has, in effect, anointed himself as the spot-kick taker for Chelsea, the £1bn team, taking the ball at Turf Moor to open his Chelsea account. "It was just an in-game thing, really," he said, with a matter-of-fact stance. "Once I scored at Burnley, I just thought: 'I'll take them'." If penalties have been the English disease, Palmer has no hesitation when asked if he would be willing to come off the bench as a specialist from 12 yards for a shootout: "Yeah, I would be," he said.

He is not daunted by the last penalty he missed, as a substitute in the shootout when City lost the 2019 FA Youth Cup final to Liverpool. He can only remember failing from 12 yards on one other occasion, "when I was dead, dead young versus [Manchester] United," and a willingness to take responsibility is similarly apparent in open play. "I think I am a player who always wants the ball, anywhere, to try and help the team get out of a difficult situation or create a chance," he said.

One such penalty came at Tottenham in November 2023. Palmer stepped up in the 35th minute and Vicario got a touch on the Englishman's penalty, yet could only deflect it onto the right post, from where the ball ricocheted into the bottom-right corner to pull the West London visitors level.

# Belgium-England: The Second Half And Wullaert's Penalty

Belgium won the game on 31 October 2023 through Tessa Wullaert's 85th-minute penalty, awarded by referee Esther Staubli after Georgia Stanway handballed Yana Daniels' 83rd-minute effort; Wullaert fired it into the bottom-left corner despite Mary Earps diving the correct way, Sport Grill reported.

England had the better of the half without converting. On the restart Fran Kirby quickly drew a foul from Kassandra Missipo, but Alessia Russo fumbled control from Chloe Kelly's free-kick and her shot was blocked; Nicky Evrard then saved Kirby's shot from Lucy Bronze's pullback pass in the 52nd minute as England continued to test the Red Flames' defence. Just past the hour mark England were given an almighty scare as Wullaert pounced on a through ball and side-stepped both Jess Carter and Millie Bright, only for Earps to block her shot with a stunning save.

Belgium were forced to defend for much of the last half-hour as Russo and Stanway saw shots denied, while substitute Rachel Daly nodded wide in the 80th minute from Keira Walsh's deep corner towards the left post. Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses were eventually made to pay for their wasted chances.



---


# Romero's Red Card And Palmer's Penalty Equaliser

The defining moment of Tottenham vs. Chelsea on Nov. 6, 2023 came in the 31st minute, when a wild passage of play ended with Moises Caicedo's goal ruled out, Cristian Romero sent off on VAR review, and Cole Palmer converting the resulting penalty to level the scoreline at 1-1.

The sequence began with the ball pinging around the Tottenham penalty area, Spurs unable to clear after blocking multiple efforts, until Caicedo finally buried a long-distance effort with a low finish inside the left post. Despite initially appearing to count, the offside flag was raised extremely late, with the assistant referee determining, after a moment to think, that Nicolas Jackson was interfering with play from an offside position.

That was only the beginning of the saga. With the goal disallowed, a VAR review began for a penalty, as Romero had swung wildly into the shins of Raheem Sterling: while he got the ball with his tackle, he followed through with extreme force straight onto both of Sterling's legs, and referee Michael Oliver was sent to the monitor. After a few looks, Oliver produced a straight red card for Romero's tackle and awarded Chelsea a penalty, which Palmer dispatched. NBC Sports Soccer's account of the passage described Romero's red card as following a challenge on Enzo Fernandez, with Chelsea given a penalty and Tottenham down to 10 men.

# Chelsea 2-0 Blackburn Carabao Cup Last 16

Chelsea beat Blackburn 2-0 at Stamford Bridge to secure a Carabao Cup last-eight spot, with goals from Benoît Badiashile and a rejuvenated Raheem Sterling, The Guardian reported on Nov. 1, 2023.

Even 2-0 up and cruising, Mauricio Pochettino was a bundle of nerves throughout what turned out to be a comfortable victory in the end — no wonder he spends most of his time watching Chelsea on the edge of the touchline with his hands clasped tightly in his pockets and a tense expression. Blackburn certainly caused problems even after the hosts made their intentions clear from the kick-off, when Nicolas Jackson forced a corner with a blocked shot. Travis was very lucky not to concede a penalty when he slid in against Sterling after 10 minutes, with no VAR to overrule what looked like a clear and obvious error from referee Tim Robinson. It took a good save from Leopold Wahlstedt to deny James, but Blackburn then enjoyed a good period of possession in their opponents' half; James was inches away midway through the first half but his shot just eluded the far post, before Enzo Fernández forced Wahlstedt to palm away his effort. The Swedish goalkeeper was at fault when Chelsea finally scored, palming Gallagher's cross — after he had combined with Palmer — straight to the feet of Badiashile, who calmly sidefooted home. Blackburn's supporters then felt aggrieved when a Callum Brittain cross struck Gallagher's trailing arm, but once again Robinson waved away strong appeals for a penalty.

The visitors showed no intention of surrendering when Harry Leonard caught Axel Disasi napping and raced onto a long ball at the start of the second half, only to curl his shot wide; not for the first time, Robert Sánchez was then far too casual as the Chelsea goalkeeper's pass was almost intercepted. Almost 15 minutes passed before Fernández had Chelsea's first effort of the second half, and Palmer came closer from a tight angle; having cleared the ensuing corner, Blackburn shot themselves in the foot trying to play out, as Brittain's pass was intercepted by Palmer and Sterling curled home from the edge of the area to give Pochettino welcome breathing space. Jackson should have made it more comfortable but blazed over from close range, before the post denied the outstanding Palmer a deflected goal. Sterling could and probably should have added to his tally after finding space in behind more than once late on. But it was Palmer who was afforded a standing ovation when withdrawn at the end, as Chelsea's supporters celebrated only their fourth home win of the season — three of them in this competition.

Rebecca Welch became the first female referee to take charge of an English Premier League match on 23 December 2023, officiating Fulham's home game against Burnley, as reported by The Roar that day.

England made two changes for the Dec. 5, 2023 Nations League finale at Hampden: Beth Mead returned to the starting lineup and Esme Morgan replaced Jess Carter.

The UN's decision to hold the summit in the United Arab Emirates, a major oil and gas producer, wound up giving the fossil fuel industry unprecedented access: there were more fossil fuel lobbyists in Dubai than at any climate conference in the 28 years the United Nations has convened it.

# Accessibility Localisation

Accessibility localisation is the work of adapting a digital product or platform's language coverage — dialects, translation, and rollout scope — to serve users outside the default language, and the gap that opens when that work is incomplete. In the corpus it shows up in two forms: a company's own roadmap for extending a feature beyond one language, and the moderation failures that surface when a platform's language resources are thin relative to the languages and dialects it actually serves.

## Context

Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" generative-AI feature for kids launched on 25 October 2023 available in English only, with internationalization described as "further down the road" — an explicit statement that localisation is a staged rollout, not a launch-day requirement. On the other end of the spectrum, TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 reporting on Meta describes localisation as an unmet obligation rather than a future roadmap item: Meta "struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic, a language with over 25 dialects, and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources," and a third-party report commissioned by Meta after the May 2021 conflict found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, attributing the gap partly to Hebrew being a "more standardized language" and to reviewers lacking competence in less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic. Meta's response to the October 2023 Israel-Hamas war — a special operations center staffed with Hebrew and Arabic speakers that removed or flagged over 795,000 pieces of content in those two languages in three days — is itself evidence of how much moderation capacity a platform must mobilize once it takes multilingual coverage seriously.

## Key Characteristics

- **Staged rollout vs. structural gap** — a company can frame incomplete localisation as a temporary phase (Amazon's "English only… internationalization further down the road") or it can be a longstanding structural deficit that draws external criticism (Meta's under-resourced Arabic-language moderation).
- **Dialect granularity matters** — Arabic's 25+ dialects mean that broad-language coverage is not the same as coverage of a specific dialect (e.g., Palestinian Arabic), and a platform can claim "Arabic support" while still failing specific dialect communities.
- **Localisation gaps have asymmetric enforcement effects** — Meta's own commissioned report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content for the same underlying conduct, tying uneven language resourcing directly to uneven moderation outcomes.
- **Crisis response can expand localisation capacity rapidly** — Meta stood up a dedicated Hebrew/Arabic special operations center and processed hundreds of thousands of pieces of content in those languages within days once the Israel-Hamas war escalated, showing localisation investment is elastic to urgency, not fixed.

# Egypt's Refusal To Host Palestinian Refugees

President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi has rejected any suggestion that Egypt host Gazan refugees, even as the same Western governments now court him for help in alleviating the pressure on Gaza, suggesting instead that Israel take in Palestinians in its Negev desert: "They can transport Palestinians there until Israel implements its announced plan to destroy Hamas," he said on Wednesday, 2023-10-18. The core political ground is that "there is little to no constituency for going against decades of policy on not allowing Palestinian displacement," said Mirette Mabrouk of the Middle East Institute, while the inducements offered "might wind up becoming a political liability, especially in an election year."

Three further grounds support the refusal. Egypt already hosts some 9 million refugees and other migrants from countries including Syria, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Opening a route for Palestinians may also present a new security risk in the Sinai peninsula, where the army has only just managed to get a handle on its fight with Islamist militants. And Jordan has also refused to accept more Palestinians, making it unlikely Egypt would become a regional exception and take in refugees many suspect may never be let back into Gaza — which would risk being seen in the Arab world as facilitating another mass displacement and betraying the Palestinian cause all Arab countries vocally espouse.

The warrant tying these grounds to the policy is that the domestic political cost outranks the economic one. While Egypt could absorb a certain number of people, the domestic political consequences would be "huge," said the Washington Institute's Robert Satloff: "The political leadership considers this a red line not to be crossed and would prefer to face worsening financial distress than accept a significant number of refugees."

Bill Kenwright spent 19 seasons as Everton chairman, having been on the board since 1989 and taking over as chairman at Goodison Park in 2004. Liverpool beat Brentford 3-0 with Mohamed Salah continuing his remarkable Anfield scoring record with two more goals to bring up his 200th in English football, The Roar reported on Nov. 12, 2023, leaving them second, just a point behind City, with Tottenham fourth and two points adrift.

# Ten Hag's Defence Of Manchester United's Performance

Erik ten Hag tried to put a positive spin on the defeat to West Ham on 23 December 2023 by claiming to the BBC that his side were the better team before the first goal: the claim is that the loss came from a single lapse rather than a systemic failure, and the warrant is that United created the better chances and had recently matched the top of the league.

His grounds for the first part are the shape of the match: "I think it was a decent 72 minutes where we didn't take our chances. We should've gone in the lead but we didn't and then it was one moment of switching off."

His grounds for the second part are the previous fixture, which he uses to set the standard he says the team must reproduce: "At this moment we are not top, but we have seen last week against the top of this league we were head-to-head. # Everton Under Sean Dyche As A Derby Threat

The Guardian argued on 20 October 2023 that Sean Dyche's Everton posed a genuine threat in the Merseyside derby, because Liverpool's defensive concerns were matched against a visiting side whose overall performance had improved even if its scoring had not.

The grounds run both ways. Liverpool's defensive concerns were heightened by the loss of Andy Robertson for up to three months with a shoulder injury, but were offset by the visitors' troubles in front of goal: a 3-0 defeat of Bournemouth last time out was only the eighth time Everton had scored more than once in a Premier League match in the past 12 months. Against that, the overall improvement in Everton's performance, coupled with three wins in the past four games, raised Dyche's hopes of capitalising on any post-international fatigue in the opposition ranks.

Klopp's compliments towards Dyche and his local rivals were of the back-handed nature, and they supply the warrant — the threat is stylistic, not a matter of form alone. "Everton are in a good moment," he said. "Burnley in their best moments [under Dyche] were a super-difficult team to play against and you can see that again; it's similar with different players. We have to be ready for second ball fights, runs in behind, a compact defence. It will be a tough one. Burnley games were always tough. We have to have football understanding, patience, put a proper shift in and take the fight."

# Ten Hag's Rebuttal Of Carragher's "Going Backwards" Claim

Erik ten Hag disagreed with Jamie Carragher's claim that Manchester United are going backwards this season, attacking the premise directly by saying the statistics show his team has actually improved, Sky Sports reported on 28 October 2023.

Carragher's argument, made in his column in The Daily Telegraph, was that United's summer signings have led to the club becoming "stale" and that Ten Hag should now be questioned about whether he can get the best out of his squad. Ten Hag hit back at those claims in his pre-match press conference before the Manchester City derby. "In possession we have to do better, but there are reasons and I don't go into them, but everyone is seeing why. But there are also facts so I disagree [with Carragher], we are much better," he said. The premise he denies is the factual one about performance level, and the evidence he offers is pressing data: "In high ball regains, we are a top of the Premier League. In the middle [of the pitch] ball regains, we are top. The pressing is very good. So that's not the truth, what he [Carragher] is telling."

Ten Hag conceded ground on consistency without conceding the direction of travel. In a fortnight in which United had picked up three straight wins against Brentford, Sheffield United and FC Copenhagen, albeit via far from convincing performances, Christian Eriksen said United still need to find their "balance and routines" this season. Asked about those comments, Ten Hag said: "We are in the right direction. We have a way to go. I see positives but I see negatives. What Christian is referring to is we are not consistently in possession on the level where we can be. Like Arsenal away, the first 30 minutes in Bayern Munich away. We should do this on a consistent basis. We don't take the benefit in the attacking transition moments, we should be because the ability in the team can take benefit from it. We pay attention to it, we need to grow. Then games will become easier." United hosted Manchester City in a Super Sunday derby that weekend, live on Sky Sports with a 3.30pm kick-off, billed as the latest acid test of how far the side had improved from last season.

# Liverpool Beat Toulouse In The Europa League Group Stage

Liverpool beat Toulouse at Anfield on 26 October 2023 to make it three wins from three Europa League group games, each with something to spare, leaving qualification for the knockout phase already close at hand — and making Jürgen Klopp's prediction that Liverpool would not "fly" through the group stage their only mis-step so far.

Klopp was able to ring the changes before Nottingham Forest's Premier League visit on the Sunday, give a full debut to 19-year-old left-back Luke Chambers and first Liverpool outings to Calum Scanlon and James McConnell, and still enjoy a fluent, dominant display. It was polished by goals from Diogo Jota, Wataru Endo, Darwin Núñez, the highly impressive Ryan Gravenberch and Mohamed Salah, whose strike with the final kick of the game was his 43rd European goal for Liverpool and took him above Thierry Henry as the most prolific goalscorer for an English club in European competition.

"I think I said it before — it is really easy to fall in love with this team, there is so much excitement," Klopp said after a seventh win in seven home matches that season. "We have to make massive steps, we have to grow, but a lot of signs are really positive and how the team interacts with each other is really nice." The Guardian judged that the three wins underlined why Liverpool were favourites for the competition, and that the visit of French Cup winners Toulouse proved the most entertaining contest so far — Toulouse's terrible defending a contributory factor, but so too the marauding midfield play of Gravenberch and Liverpool's quality in front of goal.

# FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.

# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. # Theory: Altman Circumvented The Board On A Deal

The prevailing theory floating around on November 18, 2023, based on the board's language and the way these giant tech companies work, is that Altman went around the board on a deal. "Not consistently candid" is a very diplomatic way of saying Altman lied.

The proposition: Altman — and potentially OpenAI President Greg Brockman, who stepped down as chairman simultaneously, then resigned — wanted to make a bold move that he knew the board would not like. It is not uncommon for these deals to be hammered out quietly in smoke- or vape-filled rooms and then presented as a fait accompli, but if it was controversial enough and the board found out about these maneuvers, it could be fuel for an ouster. The open question TechCrunch poses is what kind of deal would be big and dangerous enough for a summary dismissal of the CEO and famous face of the company, given the man was onstage two weeks earlier.

Microsoft is the natural candidate: few would be shocked if Microsoft, which is deeply embedded in OpenAI as an investor and customer, is a factor. Could Altman have been working with — or against — OpenAI's patron in secret? If Altman wanted to kill the golden goose by going independent, that might have activated the board's fiduciary or otherwise statutory duty; if he was negotiating some other deal, like an acquisition or deeper and more exclusive integration, it could also have caused the board to bristle, either at the idea itself or at being excluded. # Coupled Models Fail to Reproduce Observed Warming Patterns

Coupled climate models seem unable to simulate observed surface warming patterns across some key regions in which surface sensitivity modulates clouds: most importantly, models do not re-create observed cooling in the equatorial and subtropical eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean, and it is concerning that all models have the same sign of error in the trend patterns (Wills et al., 2022).

Coupled climate models simulate a freely evolving ocean surface and hence have their own expression of internal variability — one would not expect a coupled model to simulate El Niño events at the same time as they happened in nature, except by chance — which complicates comparisons between models and observations, especially on decadal timescales and beyond, for which little is known about the spectrum of internal variability in the real world. Even accounting for internal variability, the pattern failure persists, and models strongly disagree about the timescales over which future warming may occur in these regions. Limited knowledge of the drivers of surface warming pattern biases hampers the ability to evaluate them: it is not known whether the models' inability to reproduce observed trends is due to biases in how they represent the spectrum of internal variability, aerosol forcing, ocean-atmosphere interactions, deep and shallow atmospheric convection, Southern Ocean cloud-radiative properties, ocean thermocline depth, and ocean circulation, or something else entirely.



---


# Gen Z Mental Health And Climate Anxiety

Gen Z has the worst reported mental health of any generation: 45% of young people report having "excellent" or "very good" mental health, according to a 2018 report by the American Psychological Association. One of the major sources of that distress is climate change — nearly seven in 10 Gen Zers say they experience anxiety when viewing climate change content on social media, according to a 2021 Pew Research report.

They are not only reading about the effects of human-caused global warming but living through the consequences. The summer of 2023 reached record-breaking temperatures, with July the hottest month the planet has seen in over 100,000 years; Arizona experienced a monthlong heat wave with temperatures at or above 110 degrees every day; deadly fires broke out across the Mediterranean; suffocating smoke from Canadian wildfires blanketed New York City and the Northeast for days; and ice melt in the Arctic accelerated. Extreme heat is likely here to stay — and get worse — unless countries can rapidly reduce their carbon emissions, which is why Gen Z is more concerned with sustainability than any generation before them.

Greta Thunberg is the emblem the article offers: the 20-year-old has become one of the best-known environmental activists, famously speaking at the United Nations in 2019 with scathing words for world leaders. "You have stolen my dreams and my childhood with your empty words. And yet I'm one of the lucky ones," Thunberg said. "People are suffering. People are dying. Entire ecosystems are collapsing. We are in the beginning of a mass extinction, and all you can talk about is money and fairy tales of eternal economic growth. How dare you!"

# "No Place Is Safe": Climate Impacts on Kalmus's Life

Kalmus concluded that "no place was safe" after a 2020 heat wave — considered nearly impossible if not for the influence of climate change — seared the Pacific Northwest for three days, killing hundreds of people, buckling roadways and sending overheated baby birds jumping from their nests to their deaths, in the very region where he had dreamed of making a life he thought might be buffered from the worst of climate change.

"It feels like it's worse than I thought it would be in 2023," Kalmus said, pointing to record-low Antarctic sea ice and record-high sea surface and land temperatures as signs that Earth systems could be shifting more quickly than the scientific community can grasp. In recent years climate change has begun to sting his personal life: in summer 2020 he sickened himself hiking in a California heat wave, then watched a wildfire burn a few miles from his California home, spewing smoke that left his voice raspy and his head aching, while the searing temperatures killed a dogwood tree in his front yard and his productivity slowed so that he could not focus on science. His family relocated to North Carolina for his wife Sharon's work, but the Pacific Northwest experience planted a seed: if he could not stop climate change and could not avoid it, could he at least find a better way to survive it? He knew what would not work — "I very quickly eliminated the idea of being a prepper — you know, hoarding beans and ammunition," he said — but he found himself daydreaming of a simpler life where he could keep bees, grow vegetables and press cider to drink on a Friday night, living closer to the land.

# Why Communicating Deep-Sea Science Matters

Jon Copley argues that communicating deep sea science matters because the deep sea is not somewhere people think about every day: we can go out at night and look at the sky and wonder what is going on up there, but you cannot glance into the deep sea in the same way, so it has become a realm of myth and darkness.

Even the names of the deepest parts — the abyssal plains and the hadal zone — evoke that kind of underworld, he says. The conclusion he draws is that it is nice to be able to shine a light on that for people and to highlight how our lives are connected to it.

# Global Water Scarcity Under Climate Change

More than one in every four people across the planet live in places without enough clean water, and climate change is making this worse: Earth's freshwater supply is falling, and by 2050 more than five billion people are expected to lack water at least one month per year.

Some shortages are due to warmer temperatures and less snow to feed into rivers, which puts stress on supplies of water for drinking and for growing crops. Whatever the cause, better water-slurping gels could make it easier to grow food in such water-stressed places, including those plagued by drought — and scientists have now created a new salty gel that sucks record-breaking amounts of moisture out of the air to make fresh drinking water, even in dry climates.

# Protecting Populations Most Exposed to Extreme Heat

Public health measures and mitigation strategies are needed to protect the citizens at greatest risk from heat, especially as rising temperatures become more common — and studies of existing exposure disparities are the way to identify who those citizens are.

"Studies like this, which seek to understand more deeply the existing disparities in heat exposure, are important for identifying which communities are at greatest risk of suffering environmental changes related to climate change, such as extreme heat that keeps getting worse," said Neelima Tummala. Lara Whitely Binder, climate preparedness programme manager for King County, Washington, who was not involved in the research, located the cause: "Areas with fewer street trees, less access to green spaces — that is where you start to see the legacy of disinvestment and institutional racism that has come into play." Because the climate is changing and advancing, cities must from now on prepare for hotter summers and more frequent deadly heat waves by various means, both indoors and outdoors. "We not only need to better understand where it is hot, but also what the socioeconomic factors are for the inhabitants of those areas," Whitely Binder said. "We can begin to analyse what is in the heat islands and use that to start informing the policy decisions we are going to make."



---


# The Great Dying as an Analogue for Modern Climate Extinction

Michael Mann argues that the Great Dying — arguably the greatest extinction event of all time, which appears to have resulted at least in part from a massive heat-inducing release of carbon into the atmosphere 250 million years ago — poses the question of whether it is a possible analogue for a sixth, human-caused, climate-change-driven mass extinction today.

The ground for taking the analogy seriously is mechanistic: the mechanisms that can freeze the planet, as was the case with Snowball Earth, can also lead to inhospitably hot climates when enough carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere. Mann's stated payoff in working through the details of the science is that readers will see not just that scientists are able to unravel such mysteries, but how they do it. The passage is excerpted from "Our Fragile Moment: How Lessons from Earth's Past Can Help Us Survive the Climate Crisis" (Hachette Book Group, 2023) by Michael E. Mann, copyright 2023, available from PublicAffairs, an imprint of Hachette Book Group, Inc.; it looks at how climate change following the Cambrian explosion caused the biggest mass extinction on Earth, dooming the creatures set to dominate and setting the stage for dinosaurs to rule.



---


# Global Warming Of 1.2 Degrees And Its Impacts

The world, on average, is about 1.2 degrees Celsius hotter than it was before the industrial revolution — the scientific fact underpinning the COP28 negotiations.

The Verge notes that this might not sound like much, but it is enough to drive more devastating hurricane and wildfire seasons, and to suck drought-vulnerable places dry while displacing other communities faced with rising tides.
