# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# US Treasury Yields And Fed Rate Expectations In October 2023

The mechanism linking data to yields to stocks ran in both directions during October 2023. On 4 October, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, the centrepiece of the bond market, pulled back from its highest level since 2007, down to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late on the Tuesday, with shorter- and longer-term yields also easing to allow more oxygen for the stock market. Yields fell following reports indicating a slowing US economy, the first suggesting that hiring by employers outside the government was much weaker than expected; on Wall Street that is currently good news because a cooling job market could mean less upward pressure on inflation, which in turn could convince the Federal Reserve to take it easier on interest rates. After already raising its main interest rate to the highest level since 2001, the Fed had indicated it may keep its overnight rate higher next year than earlier expected, and Treasury yields had correspondingly snapped higher as traders accept a new normal of high rates for longer; the Fed pays particular attention to the job market because too much strength there could drive wages much higher, which it fears could keep inflation well above its target of 2 per cent.

By 12 October the same mechanism was running the other way. The stock market has largely been taking its cue from the bond market recently, and weak results announced in the afternoon for an auction of 30-year Treasury bonds sent yields of all kinds higher; higher yields can knock down prices for stocks and slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive. Yields had already been rising in the morning after a report showing consumer-level inflation a touch higher than economists expected, raising worries about the Fed keeping its main interest rate high for a long time as it tries to undercut inflation by knocking down investment prices and slowing the economy. The report also had encouraging nuggets: after ignoring prices for food and fuel, which Fed officials see as a better predictor of where inflation is heading, prices consumers paid were in line with expectations and continued to decelerate from earlier months. A second report said slightly fewer US workers than expected applied for unemployment benefits, indicating a job market with few lay-offs and therefore strength for the overall economy, though it could also add fuel to upward pressure on inflation. After the reports the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.7 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Wednesday, and the two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks expectations for the Fed, climbed to 5.06 per cent from 4.99 per cent, with yields still down slightly for the week after regressing from more-than-decade highs following speeches that investors saw as hints the Fed may not raise its main overnight rate further. The big jump for the 10-year yield since the summer has pulled mortgage rates to their highest levels since the turn of the millennium, and such moves could slow the economy without requiring more Fed hikes; Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said nothing in Thursday's inflation report should sway the Fed one way or the other on what it will do on 1 November, calling the data "reassuringly uneventful".



---


# Australian Market Resilience And The Range-Bound Reading

Novus Capital senior client adviser Gary Glover argued that the Australian sharemarket was surprisingly resilient following a negative lead from Wall Street and the latest inflation data, with markets starting to wake up to the fact that interest rates could stay higher for longer. His ground was the mismatch between the overseas move and the local one: "Considering the damage overnight in the US, Australian markets held on pretty well. I thought it would be a bigger down day across the board."

Glover characterised the market as volatile but quite range-bound, drawing an analogy to previous periods of high inflation in the 1940s and 1970s. The Wall Street lead he referred to was severe: Wall Street's ugly September got even worse on Tuesday as a sharp drop for stocks brought them back to where they were in June, with the S&P 500 tumbling 1.5 per cent for its fifth loss in the last six days, the Dow Jones dropping 1.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite losing 1.6 per cent.

qid: After The Independent - Life and Style reported on 2023-10-01 that internet sleep tips and tricks are not guaranteed to work, did FOX News - Health suggest on 2023-12-06 that Time-restricted eating, as a specific approach, could improve the quality of sleep, indicating a potential agreement or disagreement with the effectiveness of internet-advised sleep interventions?
context:
# The DIY Sleep Hacks Insomniacs Report Trying

The Independent's October 2023 report on insomniacs catalogues the remedies people actually use: lavender oil, eating kiwis, masturbation — the days of counting sheep long gone. Jennifer Aniston's top tip for battling insomnia is to "sleep with my phone at least five feet away from me," while Martha Stewart recommends focusing on your breathing; in her 1973 feminist novel Fear of Flying, Erica Jong wrote that sometimes the only way to overcome sleeplessness is to pretend you don't care about nodding off, after which "sleep became piqued, like a rejected lover, and crept up to try to seduce you." The article notes that the internet is littered with tips promising sound sleep, that not all of them are effective and none are foolproof, and that kiwis contain serotonin and antioxidants, which is why they are thought to have sleep-promoting benefits.

Two case histories illustrate the trial-and-error. Social media consultant and mother of two Amy Fieldhouse-Downes began suffering from insomnia after the birth of her second son in 2019 and believes it was rooted in anxiety: "If you Google how to go to sleep, I've probably tried everything on there. Going to bed earlier, going to bed later, meditations that would get cut off by an advert, lavender products, sleep cream, eye masks, Sominex sleep tablets. And I even used it as an excuse to have a few glasses of wine." Only specialised earplugs finally let her rest. Long-time insomniac and video producer Preshita has tried "from drinking chamomile tea to counting backwards from 1,000," and found that showering before bed and keeping her bedroom clutter-free were most effective: "Someone recommended masturbating, and that was another thing that worked."



---


# Realigning The Circadian Clock Through Meal Timing

The goal of the restricted eating is to restore the circadian rhythm, the researchers said, which could help counteract the numerous disruptions that Alzheimer's patients face when it comes to sleep and schedule-related confusion.

Feeding timing is the lever on the clock. "Our study emphasizes the power of feeding timing in aligning the circadian clock and its impact on the brain," said senior study author Paula Desplats, PhD, professor in the Department of Neurosciences at UC San Diego School of Medicine, in a statement to Fox News Digital.

The researchers hope that the public recognizes the importance of the circadian clock in regulating many aspects of health. "Sustaining healthy sleep and eating habits that are more synchronized with the natural environment are vital in a society that is constantly exposed to food, light and shift work," said Desplats.



---


# Sleep School's Impartial Position On The Clock Change's Impact

Against the claim that the clock change is a major disruptor of sleep, a spokesperson for Sleep School — a science-based sleep education and therapy service — told The Independent that the organisation is "impartial" on the extent to which the clocks changing impacts sleep.

The premise it declines to grant is that the timing of the shift is what matters: Sleep School argues instead that the important factors are the duration of time asleep and a consistent schedule.



---


# Sleepagotchi, NFT-Powered Sleep Game

Sleepagotchi is a seed-stage mobile app game founded by Anton Kraminkin that aims to help people develop healthy sleep habits by gamifying sleep with NFTs; it appeared in Alliance DAO's All11 cohort at the 2023-10-18 demo day. The application is currently available on Apple's App Store, and its game rewards users daily for hitting sleep goals while also letting them collect items as motivation to sleep better.

Kraminkin reported during demo day that the game has 14,000 monthly active users and a 41% one-year retention rate, and according to its website 60.2% of users reported improved sleep since using the game. In January it raised $3.5 million from investors including 6th Man Ventures, Sfermion, 1kx and Shima Capital, and it is currently raising from strategic investors.



---


# The MEDLIFE Mediterranean Lifestyle Index

MEDLIFE is a Mediterranean lifestyle index designed and developed by Mercedes Sotos-Prieto and her team, using a questionnaire that calculates an individual's adherence to a Mediterranean way of life across three primary components: food consumption, dietary habits, and physical activity — the last including rest, social habits, and conviviality.

The index exists because of a specific analytic gap. Scientists stress that the Mediterranean diet should be understood more as a way of life than a mere dietary pattern, with scientific evidence acquired over the last four decades establishing its benefits on life expectancy, quality of life, and the prevention of several chronic diseases; the challenge lies in deciphering which elements contribute most significantly to improved health. This type of analysis allowed the researchers to dissect the impact of each of the three components, even drilling down to specific items like "hours of sleep" or "socializing with friends," and the MEDLIFE index could also help capture synergistic effects of multiple components that may not be apparent when examining individual components in isolation.



---


# Kristen Bell's Household Screen-Time Rules

Kristen Bell's screen-time rule is that her daughters are not allowed phones or screens at all during the week, with TV permitted on weekends on fairly liberal terms, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

The rule as she states it: "They're not allowed to play with our phones or have any screens really. They are allowed to watch TV on the weekends, and we're pretty liberal with it, which I've been considering paying more attention to." The weekday ban has a predictable weekend consequence: "But since they're not allowed at all during the week, they will wake up at 6:30 on a Saturday morning, and they will watch TV until noon. I will also sleep until 9:45, which is really nice, and then get stuff done."

The limit Bell herself flags is the handover at the end: "But I will say, I notice how hard it is to pull them away from the TV at noon." She also admits the weekend rules get a little lax.



---


# Skepticism That Food Is Addictive The Way Drugs Are

Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based dietitian with a focus on diabetes and nutrition who was not involved in the study, is skeptical that foods can be as addictive as drugs -- and the premise she attacks is the equation of a habit-forming reward response with true addiction.

"Although foods rich in added sugar may stimulate the feel-good chemicals in the brain and become habit-forming, sugar itself is not addictive in the way cocaine or another drug may be," she told Fox News Digital. Her test is withdrawal: "Consuming sugar and then reducing or eliminating it from the diet will not result in withdrawal symptoms or side effects as would happen from a true addiction," she continued.

In place of an addiction model she offers a multi-causal account of cravings. "Food cravings are complex and tied into not just the nutrition profile of a food, but also the emotions and learned behaviors around eating," she said. Emotions, stress, overall metabolic health, sleep habits and learned feeding behaviors all shape people's food choices, behaviors and responses, Palinski-Wade said. "A food craving or binge-eating is almost always tied to an emotional response," she said. "Chronic dieting, food shame, food accessibility and even early childhood feeding experiences can all be tied back to food choices and disordered eating habits."



---


# Origin of the Cavefish Ketogenic Diet Collaboration

Believing that cavefish might be useful for the study of autism, Masato Yoshizawa approached his colleague Ryan Lee, a physician working with autism patients at Shriners Hospital for Children Honolulu: "When I showed him the video of the cavefish he immediately said, 'yes, that is very similar to what I observe in my patients'," Yoshizawa recounted.

Lee, who has experimented with ketogenic diets to improve autism symptoms with some success, suggested they try it with the fish. In humans, not all patients receiving the ketogenic diet improve, but some do; if it worked with the fish, the researchers might then be able to figure out how the diet affects behaviour and improve the effectiveness of the treatment for humans. Yoshizawa was again sceptical: "I doubted it at first," he said. "I didn't think it was going to work, but it did." The article carries a correction dated November 2, 2023: Ryan Lee was originally described as working at the University of Hawai'i Mānoa, which was incorrect and has been corrected to Shriners Hospital for Children Honolulu.



---


# Teens' Own Reports Of Difficulty Managing Phone Use

More than two-thirds of all participants admitted they sometimes or often find managing their use of technology difficult -- or that they use it to escape "sorrow" or "negative feelings."

They also said they've missed sleep due to being on their phones at night.

qid: Was there inconsistency in the TechCrunch report on the Google antitrust case published after November 5, 2023, or in the TechCrunch report on the class action antitrust suit against Google in reporting Google's anticompetitive behavior?
context:
# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Google One VPN

As of early 2023, Google One subscriptions include access to the company's VPN, which works similarly to other VPNs on the list, hiding your online activity from network operators.

Google One subscribers can access the VPN in 22 countries on Android, iOS, Windows and Mac devices, and they can share VPN access with up to five people who are on their One plans.

Engadget has not fully tested the Google One VPN yet, but says it will add it to the list if it feels it is warranted.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---


# A Federal Judge Throws Out Sonos' $32.5 Million Win Against Google

In the week reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-13, a federal judge threw out the $32.5 million win that the audio company Sonos had scored against Google a while back, after Sonos' patents were deemed unenforceable and invalid.

The sequence matters: the award came first and stood for some time, and the reversal followed from a ruling on the patents themselves rather than on the size of the damages. With the patents held unenforceable and invalid, the judgment they supported did not survive.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Google's Black Summit Offensive Notebook Incident

People who attended Google's K&I Black Summit in August 2023 were given third-party notebooks containing highly insensitive language, in what TechCrunch called another Google PR blunder. Reporter Dominic-Madori wrote that the inside of the notebooks was printed with the phrase "I was just cotton the moment, but I came back to take your notes."

It goes without saying that this would not have been well received by the mostly Black audience in attendance. Google pledged to "avoid similar situations as [it engages] with [merchandise] vendors going forward."

qid: After TechCrunch reported on the U.K. Judicial Office issuing guidance for judges on the responsible use of AI tools like ChatGPT on September 28, 2023, and Music Business Worldwide discussed YouTube's investment in AI-powered technology to protect its community from trademark and copyright abuse on November 23, 2023, is the stance on the use of AI for regulatory or protective purposes within these reports consistent or inconsistent?
context:
# YouTube's AI Music Incubator And Its Rightsholder Pledges

During its period of discussions with the majors, YouTube made a series of announcements aimed at the biggest issue for any rightsholder regarding AI-driven voice replication of artists: their ability to police it.

In August, YouTube and Universal Music Group jointly announced that the video platform was launching an "AI Music Incubator" — a program by which new tools and innovations would be developed at YouTube in close conjunction with artists and the music business; to progress the incubator, YouTube said it was working behind the scenes with a number of UMG-affiliated artists. Also in August, YouTube publicly committed to three principles or pledges behind its development of music-based generative AI tools. These pledges promised "appropriate protections… for music partners who decide to participate" in such tools, and promised "invest[ment] in the AI-powered technology" that, among other things, would help YouTube "protect our community of viewers, creators, artists and songwriters… [from] trademark and copyright abuse" — all of which seemed to hint at a desire to build a "Content ID"-style system on YouTube to control and police content made by cloning artists' voices. Then, earlier in November, YouTube announced it was developing a specific system for music partners allowing them to request the removal of content on its platform that "mimics an artist's unique singing or rapping voice."



---


# The US Copyright Office's 2023 Study Of AI And Copyright

The US Copyright Office is spearheading one of the key US efforts to address AI and copyright: in the summer of 2023 it issued a call for submissions on the issue of AI and copyright, with the goal of putting together a study to "help assess whether legislative or regulatory steps in this area are warranted."

The call for submissions came as legislators and regulators around the world grappled with the many issues that had emerged since AI technology "went mainstream" about a year earlier. Numerous businesses involved in AI, and those with substantial copyright holdings, submitted their thoughts on the issue — including Universal Music Group and AI developer Anthropic.



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."



---


# YouTube Content ID as Blueprint for AI Rights Management

Robert Kyncl's model treats the solutions built for user-generated content as a "blueprint" that can be applied to AI-generated content on platforms. The analogy has three parts: the explosion of AI use among the public maps onto the explosion of user-generated content (UGC) a decade or two ago; just as UGC often infringed copyright, AI threatens the rights of artists and music rights holders; and therefore the same class of remedy should apply.

The remedy he describes is YouTube's Content ID. "When YouTube was formed… people started to upload content, including copyrighted material, which, obviously, put YouTube into hot water with lots of different copyright holders. And I had the privilege of working through a lot of that and fix it up. But we made a very important decision, which was to go above and beyond the law, and build a fingerprinting software that allowed us to track the copyright on our platform, and then have commercial relationship[s] with copyright holders to send them the money. Out of that we built a multi-billion-dollar business, which now is a multi-billion-dollar business per year. And it was an incredible new revenue stream for everyone. AI is that with new super tools." # The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. # CSAM Scanning

## Definition

CSAM scanning is the practice of using detection technology — hash matching, or broader content-scanning systems — to find child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on a platform so it can be removed and, where required, reported.
CSAM itself is treated across the corpus as a category of illegal content, alongside terrorism content and fraud, that platforms and regulators single out from ordinary "harmful" content because hosting or transmitting it is against the law.

## Context

The corpus shows CSAM scanning arising in three distinct regulatory and platform contexts.
In the EU, the European Commission's home affairs commissioner Ylva Johansson is spearheading a CSAM-scanning proposal that would require in-scope platforms to deploy prevention measures first and, only if those are insufficient, detection measures after a court decision; she notes that companies today already scan non-encrypted communications for CSAM under a temporary ePrivacy derogation, and that her proposal is meant to be "technology neutral" rather than naming a specific vendor's tool.
In the UK, Ofcom's first Online Safety Act guidelines recommend that platforms use "hash matching" to detect and remove CSAM, and reserve a separate "accredited technology" power that could require services — including encrypted messaging apps — to scan for CSAM, which critics say would require breaking end-to-end encryption.
At the platform level, Discord's scrutiny over CSAM followed an NBC News investigation that identified 35 cases over six years of adults allegedly using the platform to kidnap, groom, or sexually assault minors, plus 165 cases of prosecutions for sharing CSAM or using Discord to extort sexual images from young users; Discord responded by banning teen dating servers, banning sharing of AI-generated CSAM, and rolling out Teen Safety Assist content filters, rather than describing a scanning system of its own.
Mozilla's planned fediverse instance separately lists CSAM as illegal content its trust-and-safety policies will act against, alongside hate speech and harassment.

## Key Characteristics

- **Detection technique, not one product** — the corpus describes hash matching as the recommended baseline technique (per Ofcom), while the EU proposal is explicitly framed as "technology neutral," naming no specific vendor's scanning tool.
- **Ordered obligation, not a first resort** — in the EU proposal, platforms must attempt prevention before detection/scanning is permitted, and only after a court decision.
- **Encryption tension** — both the EU proposal and the UK's "accredited technology" power are described as potentially requiring scanning of end-to-end encrypted messages, which critics argue is incompatible with maintaining that encryption.
- **Legal basis already exists for some scanning** — Johansson notes companies currently scan non-encrypted content for CSAM under an ePrivacy derogation, which her proposal would replace.
- **Distinct from policy/moderation responses** — Discord's post-scrutiny response (bans, content filters, Teen Safety Assist) is a moderation and policy response to CSAM risk rather than a scanning system per se, illustrating that "addressing CSAM" and "CSAM scanning" are not synonymous.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Portfolio Management Services In India

Portfolio Management Services are a managed-account alternative available alongside AIFs to Indian HNIs, governed by guidelines that date back to 1993 but that have grown in popularity with HNIs only recently. The growing financialisation of savings, the formalisation of the economy and the growing prosperity of tier 2 and 3 cities have raised PMS AUM, excluding EPFO and PF money, to ₹5.28 lakh crore as of July 2023. Because the minimum investment is ₹50 lakh, this option too is available only to HNIs.

The discriminating features are drawn against mutual funds. Both PMS and mutual funds provide expert guidance in navigating volatile markets and seizing wealth-creating opportunities, but because mutual funds cater to retail investors their guidelines are relatively stringent and compliance is rigorous, whereas PMS investment guidelines are somewhat more flexible, allowing portfolio managers to outperform mutual funds. A second appeal to HNIs is ownership: in PMS the beneficial ownership of securities belongs to the investors, as opposed to mutual funds where ownership belongs to the fund. PMS comes in two variants, discretionary and non-discretionary; in the former the portfolio managers make all decisions, in the latter the investor does.

# Web Summit and the Paddy Cosgrave Controversy

Web Summit, the big tech conference brand that runs events in several cities and whose 70,000-person flagship event in Lisbon was taking place the month after 16 October 2023, was running into a wall — a wall of outrage. Founders, investors and others from the technology community in Israel had gone ballistic over comments made by the founder and figurehead of Web Summit, Paddy Cosgrave, related to the fighting underway across Israel and Gaza, specifically his criticism of Israel's retaliatory actions. The anger with Cosgrave had gone viral, and on the day of reporting it looked like it was about to overrun promotion efforts for Web Summit. The situation also highlighted how Israel's tech industry, the country's most valuable and arguably best-known export, built on business development and relationships, has been willing to cut those ties in the battle of public opinion in this most polarizing of conflicts. "Here in Israel, we're basically now in rage mode after the first week of shock and awe," one tech source told TechCrunch. "We ain't got time to f_ck around with anyone remotely suggesting Israel needs to sit it out and not put an end to Hamas."

The trigger was the opening day of the war. It all started the day that Hamas busted through Israel's walls and rampaged through villages and a music festival on a murdering and pillaging spree, killing 1,400 people, mostly civilians; Hamas, the ruling party in the Palestinian territory, is considered a terrorist organization by the U.K., U.S. and other countries, and they also took 199 hostages back into Gaza. On that day, Cosgrave was in Doha, Qatar — the city where Web Summit would be holding its newest event in four months' time.

What Cosgrave posted, and what he left out, is the specific grievance. As some were taking to social media to express shock, or sympathy, or in some cases advocating for restraint, some took more critical stances; Cosgrave, for his part, posted data on X of the human cost of the Israel-Palestine conflict between 2008 and 2023, and it omitted the events and casualties of that weekend. That stirred debate, but Cosgrave did not acknowledge that the numbers were out of date or comment about the attacks in Israel. He instead proceeded, over the next several days — between posts about Qatar, political comments related to Ireland, and rugby reactions — to put out several more posts, all highlighting the opinion that Israel was taking an unjust approach.

As the posts racked up a range of alarming and extreme responses on both sides of the argument, Cosgrave doubled down. On the Friday he noted he was "shocked by the rhetoric and actions of so many Western leaders" in supporting Israel. But as attention mounted, the rejections to Web Summit started, too.

# The Gaza Information War And The Hamas Narrative

Eylon Levy argues that the conflict is not only a kinetic war in Gaza but also an information war, in which the Hamas narrative is adopted far more easily than Israel's account is accepted. His first ground is a case of a claim that collapsed: the day after what he calls the bluff about the Al-Ahli hospital, which the Palestinians claimed had been hit by an Israeli missile killing 800 civilians but which in the end turned out to have been caused by a splinter group of Islamic Jihad, with no hospital destroyed and certainly not 800 people killed, he explained on Sky News that Hamas lies and makes up numbers, and the reporter asked him, almost speechless with surprise, whether he doubts Hamas' numbers. He describes such moments as intensely frustrating, recounting a BBC interview in which the interviewer told him "Hamas denies what you are saying", to which his answer is that of course Hamas denies this, since Hamas denies that it is even holding hostages, and Hamas massacres, beheads, rapes, burns families and then day and night denies that it did so. Some journalists around the world see that Hamas continues to lie about the biggest things when the whole truth is in front of everyone's eyes, and they continue to echo the lies.

His second ground is a structural claim about where information from Gaza comes from: it comes either directly from Hamas or from independent reporters and photographers who are part of the system in Gaza, and everyone knows that even if they are not affiliated with Hamas they are not free to present the full truth because they are not allowed to. The evidence he offers for the constraint is what is missing: there is not a single photo of a terrorist, not a single photo of a missile being launched from a densely populated area, from a mosque or a school, not even a single photo from the Hamas tunnels under Shifa; the reason is that these reporters, even if not explicitly on Hamas' side, operate under a dictatorial regime and cannot provide the information even if they wanted to, which is why he thinks it very important to keep reminding the world how biased the information reaching them is. Levy qualifies the argument explicitly: he does not want to give the impression that all interviewers are hostile and every question delusional, and he has many interviews with reporters who understand what is happening and simply want information and to hear the Israeli side, which is completely legitimate.

While price stability and fiscal sustainability are important macroeconomic issues, environmental sustainability is increasingly gaining importance: climate change uncertainties and challenges need to be managed, and both the Philippine government and the private sector are hard-pressed to deliver on their commitments. # Criticism Of The Wilma Mankiller Barbie's Inaccuracies

Critics attacked the premise that Mattel's Wilma Mankiller doll faithfully represents Cherokee culture, pointing to specific errors in the product and its packaging. Chuck Hoskin Jr, Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, told The New York Times that the doll's basket was not authentically Cherokee, and that the wrong sets of symbols for the Cherokee language were used on the packaging — with the result that the symbols read "Chicken Nation" rather than "Cherokee Nation." "To someone who doesn't read Cherokee syllabary, they're not going to notice it," he said. "To the Cherokee people for whom Wilma is of such enduring significance and we have such enduring love for her, to see our seal incorrect, it's very disappointing because it would not have taken much effort or thought to avoid that." Hoskin said he learned of the doll's creation six months earlier and that Mattel did not work directly with the Cherokee Nation, though he added the company has been understanding of the criticism. The tribe's own statement said: "Regrettably, the Mattel company did not work directly with the tribal government's design and communications team to secure the official Seal or verify it."

Cherokee women raised a second objection — that Mattel overlooked the problematic details on both the doll and the packaging. "Mixed emotions shared by me and many other Cherokee women who have now purchased the product revolve around whether a Wilma Barbie captures her legacy, her physical features and the importance of centering Cherokee women in decision making," Stacy Leeds, the law school dean at Arizona State University and a former Cherokee Nation Supreme Court justice, told The Associated Press in an email. Regina Thompson, a Cherokee basket weaver who grew up near Tahlequah, does not think the doll looks like Mankiller, and said Mattel should have used traditional pucker toe moccasins instead of black shoes and included symbols on the basket that Cherokees use to tell a story. # The Monetary And Fiscal Policy Coordination Debate

# Judicial Reform (Israel, 2023)

## Definition

Judicial reform, in the corpus, is the Israeli government's contested 2023 "bid for judicial reform" — a domestic political fight the corpus treats as a settled point of reference (a fault line the country was already living through before the Hamas attacks of October 7) rather than something it explains from first principles. What the reform actually proposed is set out only in the Background (external) section below, not in the cited corpus documents.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the reform twice, each time as backdrop to a different story rather than as its subject. In the Eylon Levy profile, the reform is the fault line of Levy's own pre-war life: he "was also active in the protests against the government's judicial reform," and Globes pressed him on the shift — "one day you are at a demonstration against the government and the next day you are its spokesperson" (doc_0413). In the TechCrunch piece on Israel's startup ecosystem, the reform is the fault line of the tech sector's pre-war life: "the tech industry led opposition to the government's bid for judicial reform," with companies and investors "already refusing to do business in the country with the prospect of the reforms getting pushed through," a boycott effort that "has been brought to a halt" once the war made the two sides of that debate "stand together for what they see as the significantly bigger fight and threat" (doc_0448).

## Key Characteristics

- **Government-initiated, not judiciary-initiated** — doc_0448 describes it as the government's "bid" for reform; both docs frame it as opposed from outside government (doc_0413, doc_0448).
- **Provoked street protests** — Levy is identified by his participation in "the protests against the reform," which he describes as "no secret" (doc_0413).
- **Provoked tech-sector opposition** — the tech industry "led opposition" to the reform bid, with some companies and investors already refusing to do business in the country over it, before the war began (doc_0448).
- **Superseded, not resolved, by the war** — doc_0448 frames the reform fight as merely "brought to a halt" by October 7, with opposing sides now "standing together" against what they see as a bigger threat, not as a dispute that was settled; doc_0413 echoes this, with Levy describing pre-war disputes as something Israeli society "pulled our hair out over" that now look small against the war.

## Background (external)

The corpus names the "judicial reform" and its protest and boycott fallout but does not describe what the reform itself proposed. Per Wikipedia, the reform package introduced by Justice Minister Yariv Levin and MK Simcha Rothman in January 2023 proposed giving the government majority control over the committee that selects judges, curbing the Supreme Court's power to strike down legislation (including Basic Laws), letting the Knesset override certain court rulings with a 61-seat majority, making government legal advisors' opinions non-binding, and eliminating "unreasonableness" as a ground for judicial review of administrative decisions — changes aimed at reducing judicial checks on the government and the Knesset (Wikipedia, *2023 Israeli judicial reform*, accessed 2026-09-02). Mass protests began almost immediately after the plan's introduction in January 2023, well before the events covered in the corpus.

# Sputnik: A Russian Sci-Fi Horror Built On A Twisted Trolley Problem

Sputnik is Egor Abramenko's 2020 directorial debut, starring Oksana Akinshina, Fedor Bondarchuk and Pyotr Fyodorov, and available on Hulu — Polygon's pick if you are hungry for a great piece of contemporary Russian sci-fi horror not directed by Andrei Tarkovsky or Yakov Protazanov. Set in 1983 at the height of Cold War tensions, the film (whose title is Russian for "fellow traveler") centres on Tatyana, an uncompromising young psychiatrist with a staunch attitude regarding the ends justifying the means, who is recruited by the Soviet military to treat Konstantin, a wounded cosmonaut and the lone survivor of a mysterious satellite crash. Only on arriving at the remote hospital facility and interacting with him does Tatyana realise the horrifying truth: Konstantin did not return from space alone — his body has become the unwitting host to an organism unlike anything seen on Earth. Caught between her duty to study the creature and her desire to save Konstantin from further harm, she must make a hard decision on which the survival of all humanity may rest.

What makes the debut compelling is how it takes the basic premise of the "trolley problem" thought experiment and twists it repeatedly, and successfully, to dramatic emotional effect. Akinshina (The Bourne Supremacy) delivers a convincing performance as a woman forced to confront and overcome the uncompromising attitude that had once assured her success but now threatens another man's life, potentially everyone on the planet, and her own soul; Fyodorov delivers a sympathetically complex and on occasion implicitly sinister performance as a Russian "hero" torn between his perceived duty to his country and his emotional obligation to a loved one he all but abandoned before his most recent mission. The creature design is terrific, as are the cinematography and the score.

Its distribution history is part of why Polygon spotlights it: having previously been slated for a world premiere at the 2020 Tribeca Film Festival and subsequently dumped on video-on-demand in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, Sputnik is exactly the kind of rare gem of intellectually and viscerally stimulating horror that otherwise goes unappreciated if not given the opportunity to shine.

His second ground extends his fiscal reasoning to monetary policy: as with fiscal policy, a country at war is allowed to deviate temporarily from the set inflation target. At the LIBE committee hearing the journalist Apostolis Fotiadis testified that documents he and his colleagues obtained showed email threads granting a CSAM-scanning "key stakeholder" privileged access inside Johansson's department, and, under pressure from MEPs, the commissioner read out a list of her meetings with technology companies and child safety organizations. TechCrunch reported the session on 25 October 2023.

Fotiadis, one of the journalists involved in the investigation the committee was examining, had also been invited by the committee to participate in the exchange of views, and he took the opportunity to defend their reporting from direct public attacks by Johansson. In a blog post ahead of the hearing — which deploys a crisis-PR-esque headline claim of "setting the record straight" — she criticized the article as "a series of insinuations looking for a home", claiming it paired an outline of "a selection of meetings I had, of events I attended, or conferences I addressed" with "a conspiratorial tone" in an attempt "to create the impression of financial influence where there is none".

Asked by the LIBE committee about the accusation that the journalists had, essentially, been spreading disinformation — and specifically whether he believed Johansson and the Commission's response to it amounted to a restriction on media freedom — Fotiadis responded by saying he did not think that was the case. He went on to express surprise at how the Commission had reacted to the scrutiny, and at its instinct to deploy "spin-doctor" tactics to try to discredit the article rather than engaging with the substance of the concerns being raised. The Commission risks straying close to making attacks on journalists by using such tactics, Fotiadis warned, adding: "You cannot just dismiss everything by calling fake news" — before also noting that Johansson's office had declined multiple interview requests ahead of publication of the article.

On the substance of the reporting, Fotiadis said documents obtained by the journalists included email threads between Commission officials in Johansson's department, DG-Home, and a "key stakeholder" advocating for the use of technology for CSAM-scanning, which indicated what he described as "privileged access" that "speaks directly to cooperation" and goes "way beyond" mere consultation or exchange of views on the proposal.

He gave the committee the shape of that access. "It's an official chain discussing invitation, how the stakeholder would be able to allocate experts that would speak in workshops — first attended by representatives of the Member States, and then afterwards actually by ministers in the Council in a meeting chaired by commissioner Johansson. So when we say facilitate, it's obvious that the EU officials discuss what kind of experts will be available from this particular stakeholder to attend these meetings and to present the point of view, which seems to be a privileged access," he explained. "Also in the same email thread there's mention of EU officials being allocated to specifically attend the cooperation between the stakeholder and DG-Home on the proposal, which to our understanding is something that goes way beyond the level of consultations or exchange of views or exchange of opinions on the proposal and speaks directly to cooperation."

The committee then pressed Johansson about her contacts with companies and other lobbyists during the drafting of the CSAM proposal, with MEPs saying they wanted clear answers to the allegations of commercial interest and heavy lobbying when the Commission was setting up and drafting the proposal. In the event MEPs got some bare bones detail. Asked for a list of these contacts, the commissioner responded that she had met with Google six times; Microsoft, Meta and TikTok three times each; twice with Twitter (X); and once apiece with Apple and Amazon. She also said she had met with the child safety organizations Thorn (twice) and Brave Movement (twice), and with Tech Alliance and ICANN once apiece.

# Passkeys As The Default Google Sign-In Method

A passkey is a phishing-resistant alternative to a password that lets users sign in to accounts using the same biometrics or PINs they already use to unlock their devices, or with a physical security key. As TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-13, Google is now making passkeys the default sign-in method for all users.

Two features discriminate a passkey from a password. First, resistance to phishing is the property the definition leads with — it is what the mechanism is for, not an incidental benefit. Second, the credential is not something the user types and remembers: authentication reuses the device unlock factors, biometrics or a PIN, or else a separate physical security key. That gives three admissible forms of the same method, one of which is hardware the user carries rather than anything stored on the signing-in device.

The scope of the Google change as reported is the default, applied to all users — the default sign-in method, rather than the only one available.

# Foundation Model

## Definition

A foundation model is a large AI model — trained by a small set of well-resourced providers — that sits at the base of the generative-AI stack and is adapted or built upon by other tools and applications, rather than being the end product itself.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in two distinct settings: market structure and government regulation. In a TechCrunch survey of venture capitalists on the emerging LLM stack, Glasswing Ventures' Rick Grinnell divides the generative-AI landscape into four layers — foundation model providers, middle-tier companies, end-market/top-layer applications, and full-stack vertical companies — with foundation models sitting at the base layer that middle-layer tooling and top-layer applications are built on top of. He names Alphabet/Google's Bard, Microsoft/OpenAI's GPT-4, and Anthropic's Claude as examples of this foundational layer. Separately, in coverage of the Biden Administration's AI executive order, "foundation model" is the regulatory unit the order targets: it directs new reporting standards specifically for developers whose foundation models might affect national or economic security.

## Key Characteristics

- **Base-layer position** — foundation models sit beneath the middle tier (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, orchestration) and the application layer in the GenAI tech stack; other companies build and compete on top of them rather than replacing them.
- **Concentrated provider set** — the layer is dominated by a small number of large players (Alphabet/Google, Microsoft/OpenAI, Anthropic), whose advantages in data access, talent, and compute are expected to push this layer toward an oligopolistic structure akin to the cloud-provider market, tempered by open-source alternatives.
- **Reused across applications** — applications "blend" foundation models with in-house middle-layer tooling to build specialized, defensible products, rather than starting from scratch.
- **Trigger for regulatory reporting** — under the White House AI executive order, a company training any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, economic security, or public health/safety must notify the federal government when training the model and share red-team safety test results before public release.
- **High-capability threshold for regulation** — the EO's reporting duty is scoped to a computational threshold (10^26 petaflops) beyond the capacity of existing models at the time, so it targets only the next generation of the largest foundation models, not models currently on the market or built by small/independent developers.

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. # Wearable Fitness Tracker

## Definition

A wearable fitness tracker is a wrist-worn device — spanning dedicated fitness bands such as the Fitbit Charge 6 and general-purpose smartwatches such as the Apple Watch and Google Pixel Watch — that uses onboard sensors to track a person's activity and health signals, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and wrist-motion data, and displays the results on-device (doc_0222, doc_0241, doc_0491).

## Context

In the corpus, the category shows up almost entirely through product coverage of the two dominant lines: Apple Watch (Series 9, Ultra 2, SE) and Fitbit/Google's Pixel Watch, alongside Samsung's Galaxy Watch and dedicated bands like the Fitbit Charge 6.
Reviewers repeatedly frame the Apple Watch as "an excellent fitness companion, offering comprehensive health and activity data," and describe the Apple Watch SE's "fitness features and tracking data" as "well-rounded" even though it omits pricier sensors like blood oxygen (doc_0104, doc_0091).
The Fitbit Charge 6 is described as a dedicated fitness tracker distinct from a smartwatch, with an AMOLED touchscreen for activity stats, built-in GPS for outdoor workouts, and week-long battery life (doc_0222).
The first-generation Google Pixel Watch is presented as a smartwatch whose fitness-tracking capability comes from native Fitbit integration, including FDA-cleared EKGs; the same article notes the first-gen model omits the Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and nightly SpO2 features that arrived with the second-generation Pixel Watch (doc_0069).
A separate corpus thread ties the category's sensor hardware directly to a patent fight: Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 use an SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation) sensor that Masimo successfully argued infringed its pulse-oximetry patents, leading the ITC to order an import ban on those two watches (doc_0241).
The corpus also documents how newer silicon expands what a wrist-worn tracker can sense and act on: the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip adds four neural engines that process wrist accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate sensor data to recognize the Double Tap gesture, a feature unavailable on older Apple Watches that lack that chip (doc_0491).

## Key Characteristics

- **Wrist-worn form factor** — the category covers both single-purpose bands (Fitbit Charge 6) and multi-purpose smartwatches (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Galaxy Watch) that add fitness tracking to broader smart functionality (doc_0222, doc_0069).
- **Core sensed metrics** — step count, heart rate, and activity/workout data are baseline across models; higher-end devices add blood oxygen (SpO2) sensing and GPS for mapping outdoor workouts (doc_0104, doc_0222).
- **Tiered sensor availability** — cheaper models in a lineup (e.g., Apple Watch SE) drop specialized sensors like the blood oxygen app while keeping core step/activity tracking, distinguishing entry-level from flagship tiers (doc_0091, doc_0104).
- **On-wrist signal processing is noisy** — detecting subtle wrist gestures and vitals requires filtering accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data against motion artifacts from the arm, muscles, and individual differences in wrist size (doc_0491).
- **Sensor IP is contested territory** — the SpO2 sensor at the center of the Apple–Masimo dispute shows that the sensing hardware inside these devices can itself be the subject of patent litigation with real market consequences (an import ban) (doc_0241).
- **Ecosystem integration matters** — fitness data on a smartwatch is often powered by a partner platform (Fitbit integration on the Pixel Watch) rather than being built entirely in-house (doc_0069).

# Usage-Based Pricing

## Definition

In the corpus, usage-based pricing (also called consumption pricing) is the charging model that VCs discuss as the one whose "trajectory... has organically aligned with the needs of large language models," with OpenAI's per-token API pricing cited as the motivating example, in contrast to conventional periodic SaaS pricing.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in a TechCrunch roundup of venture capitalists discussing how AI startups should charge for AI-powered tooling, prompted directly by "the OpenAI pricing schema based on tokens and usage."
Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures frames usage-based pricing as the model whose "trajectory... has organically aligned with the needs of large language models," because prompt/output sizes and per-user resource consumption vary significantly from one request to the next.
Lisa Calhoun of Valor VC makes the mechanism concrete: companies like OpenAI charge largely "by the token," which she calls "a very different metric than most cloud computing," and notes cost monitoring may be a key aspect of tracking that metric.
The same discussion frames usage-based pricing as one leg of a three-way choice facing AI startups, alongside conventional periodic SaaS pricing and hybrid structures that blend the two.

## Key Characteristics

- **Cost tracks consumption, not time** — charges scale with resource use (e.g., tokens processed) rather than a fixed subscription period.
- **Aligned with LLM cost structure** — the model fits large language models well because compute cost per request varies with prompt/output size and per-user resource utilization; OpenAI itself reportedly spends upward of $700,000 per day on compute, making usage-based allocation a way to recover those variable costs.
- **Unpopular for budgeting** — tying all costs to volume is "generally unpopular with end users," who prefer the predictability of a fixed periodic fee.
- **Not universal across AI products** — applications that don't rely on an LLM as a backbone, and that make no direct token calls to a model provider, tend to gravitate toward conventional periodic SaaS pricing instead.
- **Persists via hybrid structures** — as LLM adoption widens, vendors are expected to combine tiered periodic payments and usage limits for smaller customers with uncapped usage-based tiers for larger enterprises, rather than replacing usage-based pricing outright.
- **Tied to data dependency** — because large language technology remains heavily dependent on continuous data inflow, the source article argues usage-based pricing is unlikely to disappear even as the market matures.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, usage-based pricing (also called pay-per-usage) is a general software/SaaS revenue model: charges are calculated from measured consumption — "the number of users, transactions, amount of storage space used, or other metrics" — rather than a flat recurring fee, and Wikipedia notes many buyers favor it because they see themselves as "relatively light users of the software," while it can create revenue uncertainty and added billing overhead for the seller. (Wikipedia, "Software as a service," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_as_a_service)
