# Barbie (Greta Gerwig)

Barbie is Greta Gerwig's film starring Margot Robbie, Ryan Gosling, and Will Ferrell, ranked 9 on Polygon's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and available for digital rental/purchase before streaming on Max.

Polygon concedes that any description of the film's big themes — toxic masculinity, how Barbie branding affects young girls, women as playthings, the commodification of girl power — makes it sound preachy and stilted, but says Gerwig and co-writer Noah Baumbach never hold still long enough for viewers to feel they are sitting through a Gender Studies 101 class. They package these ideas into a giddy satire full of bright and winning performances, pointed jokes aimed at Mattel and the corporate world, terrific casting with Issa Rae as President Barbie, Simu Liu as one of many Kens, and Kate McKinnon as Weird Barbie as standouts, and endless cultural gags, plus bright poppy meta-humor musical numbers including Ryan Gosling turning "I'm Just Ken" into 2023's top movie anthem.

Critic Tasha Robinson calls it perky, playful, and deceptively caustic, one of just a few films — like 1995's The Brady Bunch Movie and 2007's Enchanted — that gleefully satirize a cultural staple while also treating it with real affection. Margot Robbie makes a perfect Barbie, whether in perky-and-plastic mode or slowly revealing her underlying humanity as fears of death and dying leak into the endless party of Barbieland. There is so much going on in this patter-filled, joke-a-second comedy that it feels like 2023's Everything Everywhere All at Once, right down to the big life messages smuggled into all the goofery — a high-speed joke-fest that does not take Barbie any more seriously than she deserves but does pay solemn homage to all the ways, positive and negative, that Barbie fandom makes people feel.

Since 2021 Petersen had been seeking a successor for then-operating chief Sanne Manders, in part to address what several ex-employees described as lingering issues with the company's troubled billing processes; fixing that was Clark's job. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." While price stability and fiscal sustainability are important macroeconomic issues, environmental sustainability is increasingly gaining importance: climate change uncertainties and challenges need to be managed, and both the Philippine government and the private sector are hard-pressed to deliver on their commitments. ## Definition

In the corpus, the Nobel Prize is the award administered by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for the physics, chemistry, and economics categories, exemplified by the 2023 chemistry prize given to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus, and Alexei Ekimov for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots.

## Key Characteristics

- **Administered by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences** for the physics, chemistry, and economics categories, with nominations solicited a year in advance from thousands of university professors and scholars worldwide, and nominee deliberations kept confidential for 50 years.
- **Committee-driven selection** — a committee for each prize discusses candidates over a series of meetings before presenting proposals to the full academy for a vote.

- **Multi-category, staggered announcements** — physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace, and economics prizes are announced on separate weekdays within the same week.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the Nobel Prizes are a set of six international awards — physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, peace, and economic sciences — managed by the Nobel Foundation and funded from Alfred Nobel's bequest, first awarded in 1901 and given annually (with rare exceptions, such as wartime gaps in 1940-1942); the economics prize was added later, in 1968, by Sweden's central bank in Nobel's memory. In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. # The US Sound Recording Public Performance Right Gap

The US "is the only significant music economy in the world that does not have these full rights in their domestic legislation," the artists' groups said — the gap being a public performance right in sound recordings for terrestrial broadcast.

The legislative history explains the shape of the gap. The US Congress extended copyright protections to sound recordings in 1971, but those protections did not include a public performance right that would have ensured royalty payments to artists, producers and labels. In 1995, Congress passed the Digital Performance Right in Sound Recordings Act, which did include performance rights, but limited those rights to performances made "by means of a digital audio transmission," which does not include terrestrial radio.

He attached a date to it: asked when that sea change would occur, he said "I would say within the next year you will see lots of evolution around AI… What you will likely see is increasing quality at a very fast pace."

His reasoning is structural rather than accidental. "Music – because it's so broadly distributed and it's so well aligned with the internet, because it's short format, it lends itself to recommendations, it's on all platforms – is generally first in most transformations and most innovations. So it digitizes first." He generalises from the previous cycle: "Whatever happened to the music industry 20 years ago is starting to happen in the movies and TV shows now. In the meantime, music emerged out of [digitization] better and stronger and more resilient. So, I would imagine the same will happen here, which is we'll likely be first."

The hypothesis is falsifiable on two fronts as stated. It fails if other industries, rather than music, lead on both exploiting and regulating AI; and it fails on its own timetable if the year following September 2023 does not bring the predicted rapid evolution and fast-rising quality in AI. # Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# Apple's Privacy Stance Versus Google's Default Payments

Meagan Bellshaw's privacy line of questioning attacked the premise that Apple chose Google because Google had the best product: if Apple genuinely regards Google as bad on privacy, then something other than product quality must explain why Apple gives Google a central place on its platform.

Bellshaw asked Cue whether Apple believes user privacy is important, to which he said, "Absolutely." She then showed a series of emails and slides in which Cue and Apple railed against Google's privacy policies, and Cue readily agreed with them: "We've always thought we had better privacy than Google." He said one provision of the ISA was that Google had to allow people to search without logging in, and that Apple has done things in Safari and around its platforms to make it harder for Google or anyone else to track users. Bellshaw never quite said it, but The Verge read the DOJ's implication as this: Google is a privacy menace anathema to everything Apple believes is important to its users, yet Apple gives it that central place because Google pays so handsomely. She then asked Cue to review some of Apple's financial filings and whether it is true that the ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits. Cue's rebuttal was that this is not how Apple looks at it, because the framing doesn't account for all the work Apple did to make its platform so appealing that an agreement like this could work as well as it does.



---


# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# Alphabet's Q3 2023 Results And Cloud Miss

Shares in Alphabet fell 6 per cent after hours after the Google parent delivered a mixed result: revenue climbed 11 per cent to $US76.7 billion with net income of $US19.7 billion thanks to a recovery in digital advertising revenue, but its closely watched cloud division — which houses its data storage business and many of its AI efforts — missed Wall Street expectations.

"Investors were disappointed by the relatively weak performance at its Google cloud platform, which is at risk of falling further behind" competitors' offerings, Jesse Cohen, a senior analyst at Investing.com, wrote in an email. During trading hours the S&P 500 slipped off session highs, led by losses in energy shares as oil slid below $US84 a barrel, but once again the index found support above the key 4200 mark; Verizon Communications, 3M and General Electric climbed on bullish forecasts, while Facebook and Instagram owner Meta dropped after being sued by California and dozens of other US states over harmful youth marketing claims. Bitcoin briefly topped $US35,000, and Treasury 10-year yields edged lower following Monday's intense volatility. Investors looking to the earnings season for a dose of good news were hanging their hopes on big tech: the five biggest companies in the S&P 500 — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and AI chipmaker Nvidia — account for about a quarter of the benchmark's market capitalisation, and their earnings were projected to jump 34 per cent from a year earlier on average, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

# ASPI's Analysis Of TikTok Pixel Data Aggregation Risk

Researchers at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute argue that the danger of TikTok's tracking pixel lies less in the type of data collected — which resembles what US tech giants gather — than in how that data can be aggregated and in who can ultimately reach it.

Jocelinn Kang, a technical specialist at the institute, said data from a tracking pixel could be aggregated across websites, apps and social media platforms, and that pixel tracking could identify users through their "browser fingerprint," a combination of their IP address, browser and system details. The linking gets sharper as identifiers accumulate: "However, when more identifying data such as email and phone number is associated with a user, their web activity can be better linked," Kang said.

Strategic Policy Institute researcher Samantha Hoffman said the data collected by TikTok's pixel was similar to that of US-based tech giants Google and Meta, but that the difference was "the intent." Advertising data had "incredible propaganda value," she said, and the warrant joining that to the risk is state access: "If you think about that, plus the access that TikTok is required to give the Chinese government, that's the problem." She notes TikTok itself made that access explicit — in November 2022 the company changed its privacy policy to state clearly that user data can be accessed by some employees from across the world, including China. "They talk about how even data collected overseas can be used by the company and its partners, and would be kept private unless security organisations make demands of it," Hoffman said. China's national intelligence laws allow the government to pull data upon request from companies based there.



---


# Expedia's Testimony On Google Ad Costs And Organic Listings

On November 1, 2023, Barry Diller, chair of Expedia and IAC, testified about his concerns that the increasing number of ads in search results was having an impact on organic listings. Quoting a letter he had written to Google back in 2019, per Bloomberg: "I must say I'm on the edge of revolt now that Google's actions are so punitive, not just for Expedia but also for IAC and all the players that depend upon something of a level playing field." Google CEO Sundar Pichai fired back that Google's travel listings was one of the most popular experiences the company built.

Expedia executives also testified about the cost of ads and how increases had no impact on search results. On October 19, 2023, Expedia's former chief operating officer, Jeff Hurst, told the court that the company's ad fees increased tenfold, from $21 million in 2015 to $290 million in 2019, and yet Expedia's traffic from Google did not increase. The implication was that this was due to direct competition from Google itself; Hurst pointed out that Google began sharing its own flight and hotel data in search results in that period, according to The Seattle Times.

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# Creator Economy Sustainability And Creator Venture Capital

Writing in TechCrunch's 2023-10-13 startups roundup, the newsletter's author argues that creators getting together to work out how to make the job sustainable makes sense, but that creators raising venture capital does not.

The grounds are the two events reported that week. Amanda reported that VidCon is still kicking, and that for the first time the conference hosted an industry leadership summit where creator economy experts and creators could hash out their grievances with the state of the business and share ideas to make the job of a creator more sustainable. Lauren reported that a former TikTok employee is building a social app for content creators to network and "spill the tea," so creators can help each other out making better, more engaging content. Both are creators pooling knowledge rather than capital.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is an economics argument about returns: it is, in the author's words, "so eye-wateringly hard to make money as a creator" that he would love to see the pitch that convinces a VC to cut a check to a creator with a realistic expectation of a venture-scale return. Venture capital requires venture-scale outcomes, and individual creator economics are held not to reach that scale — which is why the peer-support route is endorsed and the VC route is not. The claim is scoped to creators raising venture capital as individuals; it is stated as the author's own view in a newsletter, not as a survey finding.

# Government's Role In Technology Innovation

The claim is that for entrepreneurs, innovators and businesses to thrive and unlock the economic potential that comes from creating new industries, a consistent approach from the government is required. The author states his standpoint: as Americans who chose to build a biocatalyst engineering company in the U.K., they are acutely aware of the impact such a reversal of policy has on every stage of their sector's existence.

The grounds are historical: all major technological innovation ultimately comes from government support at the very beginning — we wouldn't have affordable solar panels, microchips, mobile phones or the internet without government funding, government subsidies, government encouragement and government infrastructure. The warrant is a capital constraint: you can't scale technology that is going to make a considerable impact without upfront capital to match.

# Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio's Collaboration

Polygon models it as a symbiotic exchange that elevated both men: the industry outsider who needed a safe box-office bet to finally get his epic, expensive dream projects financed, and the teen heartthrob who needed an auteur with arthouse gravitas to take him seriously so the industry would.

To date the project has been wildly successful, producing six films over 21 years, and the first five — Gangs of New York, The Aviator, The Departed, Shutter Island, and The Wolf of Wall Street — are Scorsese's top five highest-grossing films, with the box office for Killers incoming.

The relationship extends beyond casting. Polygon presents this as evidence DiCaprio has not "just" been a muse and a face on the posters: he has had a say in deciding which projects Scorsese takes on and has made significant decisions shaping Scorsese's stories — Scorsese entirely reimagined Killers of the Flower Moon after DiCaprio offered notes on an early draft of the script, including shifting focus to a different main character and moving DiCaprio into that role.

# What SEO Is, And Why People Hate It

Search engine optimization is the practice of telling the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results, leveraging Google's supposed objectivity to lure people in and then, usually, show them some kind of advertising — a business model. It is less straightforward than buying the advertising space labeled "Sponsored" above organic search results; it is more like the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority.

The discriminating feature is that SEO borrows credibility from a system users believe is neutral. Over time SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up "sneaker" in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike ("footwear that allows you to just do it!"). Perhaps this is why nearly everyone hates SEO and the people who do it for a living: the practice seems to have successfully destroyed the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff.

The reputational context in 2023 is a broad unhappiness with finding information online, which for almost everyone means the quality of Google Search results. Users call the links that come back "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Some blame Google itself, asserting that an all-powerful, all-seeing, trillion-dollar corporation with a 90 percent market share for online search is corrupting our access to the truth; others blame the SEO practitioners.

The stereotype of the practitioner is a hustler: a content goblin willing to eschew rules, morals, and good taste in exchange for eyeballs and mountains of cash — a nihilist in it for the thrills, a prankster gleeful about getting away with something. "This is modern-day pirate shit, as close as you can get," explained Cade Lee, who has over a decade working in SEO. What Lee said he has noticed most at SEO conferences and networking events is a certain arrogance: "There's definitely an ego among all of them. You succeed, and now you're a genius. Now you've outdone Google." The writer's own admitted starting position was that a bunch of megalomaniacal jerks were degrading our collective sense of reality because they wanted to buy Lamborghinis and prove they could vanquish the almighty algorithm — which, technically, constitutes many algorithms, but we think of as a single force.

# The 2023 Chemistry Nobel for Quantum Dots

The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry honours three scientists who discovered and created quantum dots: Moungi Bawendi, a chemist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Louis Brus, a chemist based at Columbia University in New York City; and Alexei Ekimov, a physicist now working at Nanocrystals Technology, Inc., in Briarcliff Manor, N.Y.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the honour on October 4, and the trio will split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor, or about $1 million. The award recognises a peculiar class of matter: typically, matter made of the same kinds of atoms arranged in the same way has the same properties, but tiny specks called quantum dots can contain the same molecules yet have different colours and other qualities depending on their size. The ability to make a whole rainbow of quantum dots simply by tweaking their size makes them highly useful — they light up TV screens and help doctors see inside the body.

# Rate My Professors Harassment Of Janani Umamaheswar

In the winter of 2019, Janani Umamaheswar, then an assistant professor in sociology at Southern Connecticut State University, began noticing strange remarks on her Rate My Professors profile, where most comments had previously been positive or at least constructive. One review, rated "awful" with a score of one out of five, read: "Textbook only discusses crimes of the poor. I get discriminated against all semester. I felt like I was in Germany in the 1930s with my grandparents." More followed into early 2020, including "This is the worst professor I've ever had," a claim she had been dishonest about going to school in Canada (she completed her bachelor's and master's at the University of Toronto), an allegation that she had a "tyrannical authoritarian ideology" and practised "discrimination against students with prior substance abuse histories," and one reading: "Emailed me a bribe offering a grade boost if I did her a favor of attending a meeting she was hosting. I did not respond because accepting a bribe is illegal." She had never bribed any students; someone was inventing specific defamatory accusations about her behavior.

Because Rate My Professors users post anonymously, there is no surefire way to verify or screen the people who write reviews, and Umamaheswar and her husband Alex Sinha — then a law professor at Quinnipiac University — could not work out who was posting. He suggested she contact the site to remove the comments, and they assumed the company complied, but a short time later comments in the same tone resurfaced under a new class code; she reached out again, weeks passed, and more posts emerged. A separate signal then appeared: a report from her web hosting company logging IP addresses that visited her lightly trafficked professional website showed one local address appearing repeatedly at all hours, sometimes more than two dozen hits an hour. Sinha checked his own site and found the same IP address visiting frequently, lingering on his résumé and published writing.

In December, Southern Connecticut State University police contacted Umamaheswar's department: a student — referred to here as S. — had filed a police report against her and two other sociology professors, claiming "a possible hacking of her personal laptop computer" perpetrated by the three faculty members and accusing them of using students in the class to follow her around and look at her papers. S. had also emailed accusations to school officials, reaching the president and the Title IX office; in one message to administration on February 9th, 2020, S. wrote, "I genuinely believe Dr. Umamaheswar is a danger to other students as she was to me," and called her "a pathological liar and capable of twisting words to get what she wants." The other two accused professors filed police reports against S. for harassment; Umamaheswar, who studies law, social inequality, and incarceration, decided not to, believing S. was probably someone struggling with mental health issues and knowing how the legal system might treat her. Administrators from four separate university offices and the police department investigated, and after two trying months dismissed S.'s claims as "factually incorrect, disparaging" and "legally actionable." The school sent S. a cease and desist letter and banned her from the university, warning on February 9th, 2020 that violating either directive would subject her to arrest and prosecution; shortly after, law enforcement arrested S. for harassment and later released her to await a court date. Police issued alerts about S., offered to relocate professors to a more secure area of the school, and at one point offered to install a panic button in Umamaheswar's office; Sinha installed a security camera at home. A month later the pandemic shut down campuses, S. seemed to quiet, and a year passed: Umamaheswar took a job at George Mason University and the family moved to Virginia, Sinha teaching remotely and later commuting to Hofstra University. Then, one afternoon in March 2022, a former colleague now teaching sociology at Vassar College texted about a strange, hidden comment on her Twitter account bearing a name she had heard two years earlier. S. was back.

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. # The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." # Philippine National Government Budget Definition

Its constitutional basis is Section 22, Article VII: "The President shall submit to the Congress within 30 days from the opening of every regular session, as the basis of the general appropriation bill, a budget of expenditures and sources of financing including receipts from existing and proposed revenue measures."

The National Government budget is the totality of the budgets of all government entities: the National Government itself, the non-financial government-owned and -controlled corporations (usually only the 14 major GOCCs), government financial institutions, local government units, the social security institutions (GSIS, SSS, military pensions, PhilHealth and others), the Oil Price Stabilization Fund, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the Central Bank-Board of Liquidators. # Spider-Man 2 and the Canon Events Critique

Polygon's claim on 2023-10-16 is that while Marvel's Spider-Man 2 does not push against established Spider-Man story as hard as the critic wanted, where it does go is still satisfyingly slant — and that this matters, because if we are going to retell a story we ought to retell it anew: canons were made to be broken, and Spider-Man 2 swings in that direction.

The standard the critic sets is high, and named: they were hungry for the game to treat the established story like Angela Carter repurposing "Little Red Riding Hood" to her whims, like Michael Cunningham plumbing "Rumpelstiltskin" for a story about the desire to have a child, or like Helen Oyeyemi and her body of work — or, in mass media terms, like Star Wars: Visions, which gives creative leeway to a variety of animators and storytellers to play with the very basics of what makes Star Wars Star Wars.

The grounds for the qualified verdict are that wrinkles to critical characters and plot points keep even seasoned Spider-fans on their toes, and that the game plays like a dream: smart additions to combat enhance the power fantasy, with each Spider-Man having a full arsenal of special moves and gadgets that complement one another, making even the most basic encounter feel like a choreographed ballet of kicks, thwips, and zaps. It is beautifully rendered, taking full advantage of the newest PlayStation, with textures on each unlockable suit so detailed you would swear they were real and ray-traced window after ray-traced window in a loving rendition of New York — if you can get past the Frankenstein-ification of the boroughs.

The critic also registers what the game gestures at but cannot develop: hints of greater thematic aspirations appear, including questions about mass incarceration, recidivism, and reintegration into society for formerly incarcerated people, and worries about the surveillance state and what we give up when we engage with modern technology. These appear only fleetingly, because there is not enough time to elaborate on any single one in the unrelenting march of set-piece after glorious set-piece — but the critic is glad they are there, and with a sequel teed up by the game's final act is eager to see where Insomniac goes next.

Andor, created by Tony Gilroy and starring Diego Luna, Kyle Soller, and Adria Arjona, is called one of the best Star Wars shows to date in Polygon's 2023-10-25 roundup of the best new TV series on every streaming service — and it also holds the No. 1 spot on the outlet's list of the best shows of 2022, which together make its inclusion feel all but mandatory.

Gilroy, of Michael Clayton, returns to Star Wars after co-writing 2016's Rogue One, diving into an origin story of the eponymous Rebel captain that also functions as an origin story of the Rebel Alliance itself. The series meticulously moves away from the rote, Easter egg-laden iconography many fans associate with the franchise and substitutes a down-to-earth aesthetic and tone that treats the stakes of its universe as seriously as the underdogs who occupy it.

Critic Toussaint Egan writes that Diego Luna, much like his character Cassian Andor, is the perfect leading man for the job, while Stellan Skarsgård's supporting performance as the cunning rebellion ringleader Luthen Rael has quickly asserted itself as one of the best characters to come out of Star Wars since Disney acquired the property in 2012. The game improves upon Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order in every conceivable way, with a more entertaining, action-oriented start and a ton of aerial movements and lightsaber stances that make you feel even more like a seasoned Jedi Knight. Quality-of-life improvements like fast travel make it less frustrating to play, while new locales packed with hidden collectibles and upgrades make exploration more rewarding.

Critic CA argues that what makes it truly special is not this crude matter but its luminous heart: the memorable characters you meet on your galactic journey, whether the people you help or the friendships you forge and reconcile with; the classic, crowded cantina where you actually want to check in with the barkeep; the tactile, reverent way you craft your lightsaber; and the kinetic set-pieces that recall the serials Star Wars was originally inspired by.

# Disney's Remake And Franchise Oversaturation

Polygon argues that even with much higher budgets and flashier visuals, the live-action remake fad Disney has ridden for the past decade contributes to a feeling of nostalgia oversaturation, and that the studio's many spinoffs and reboots do not help — some legacy projects have been good, but the sheer volume of them does not seem built to last.

The sharpest case is timing. One of the most recent Disney live-action projects announced is a rendition of 2016's animated hit Moana, a great movie that has not even really had a chance to build its own legacy: the kids who watched it when it first came out are mostly still kids. Disney, the argument goes, is assuming anything it makes will have an instant legacy without letting the nostalgia naturally brew. The second case is breadth. Disney's brand management of Star Wars, Marvel, Fox, the Muppets, and a host of other properties emphasizes the oversaturation, with characters like Baby Yoda and Tony Stark sitting alongside Mickey Mouse and Cinderella in theme parks, on Disney Plus promotional material, and on Bob Iger's X header. # Mary Jane's Mission Pacing And The Verdict On Spider-Man 2

Essentially Sports argued on 1 November 2023 that the best thing about Mary Jane's quests in Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is that they never try to overpower the ongoing story: the claim is that restraint improves them, and the warrant is that keeping her sequences within limits lets each character shine without her missions overlapping Peter's or Miles' stories.

The grounds are about proportion. The game's narrative remains intact no matter what, and there never occurs a feeling of the developers trying too hard to make her missions stretch beyond their boundaries; although they are designed well this time, the article commends Insomniac's team for keeping a limit on not making MJ's gameplay moments seem forced or going beyond a certain point. At times it may feel like her playable sequences should have been extended, but the article treats the decision not to as correct — sometimes less is more and fine. Despite Spider-Man 2 being more of Peter's story in its entirety, MJ's role has been given equal significance, with visible growth in her arc especially considering her profession as a journalist; she is Peter's love interest, but that's not everything she's there for, and players can easily see it happening throughout the game's duration.

The verdict concedes a limit on the claim before stating it. It's obvious to expect that a lot of fans who didn't like MJ's missions in the first installment won't like her this time either, but considering how she was before and how she is in Spider-Man 2, the overall change is quite praiseworthy. Her missions now have actual meaning attached to them rather than acting like fillers; players who want a few interesting moments aside from the main quests featuring Miles and Peter can get a sense of finishing well-designed stealth quests, and Mary's gameplay missions end up increasing the overall quality of Spider-Man 2 — so it is great to see Insomniac improving on this aspect instead of removing it completely.

# Wearable Device

## Definition

In this corpus, "wearable device" (or "wearable") is the umbrella term outlets use for a body-worn consumer or health-tech gadget — a smartwatch, fitness ring, fitness band, or medical-sensing device — interchangeably with specific products like the Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air, and Acurable's respiratory monitors.

## Context

The corpus uses "wearable" as the umbrella term spanning consumer smartwatches (Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch), fitness rings (Ultrahuman Ring Air), fitness bands (Whoop 4), and specialized medical-sensing gadgets (Acurable's respiratory monitors, the Willow Go wearable breast pump). Some wearables are purely consumer-facing fitness/lifestyle products sold through holiday deals coverage, while others sit at the boundary of consumer electronics and regulated medical devices — the Apple Watch's SpO2 blood-oxygen sensor and EKG feature are the clearest example, since they triggered patent litigation with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor over the underlying sensing technology. Acurable is described explicitly as "a medical device company that makes patient-friendly wearable devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions at home," showing wearables also serving a clinical diagnostic role outside the smartwatch category.

## Key Characteristics

- **Body-worn form factor** — worn on the wrist (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Galaxy Watch), finger (Ultrahuman Ring Air), or elsewhere on the body (Acurable's respiratory monitors, Willow Go breast pump).
- **On-board sensing** — wearables carry sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, optical heart-rate sensors, and SpO2 (blood-oxygen) sensors; the Apple Watch Series 9's double-tap gesture, for instance, is detected from accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data collected at the wrist.
- **Companion-app dependence** — many wearables (Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air) have no display of their own and instead offload data to a smartphone app for analysis and coaching.
- **Health/medical crossover** — some wearables function as, or overlap with, regulated medical devices: the Apple Watch's SpO2 and EKG features became the subject of ITC patent disputes with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor, and Acurable markets its wearables as home-use medical devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions such as sleep apnea.
- **Rapid feature iteration** — newer models add capabilities like Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and gesture controls (double tap), often gated behind newer chips (the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip with four neural engines).

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general definition is broader than any single corpus device: wearable technology comprises small electronic and mobile devices, worn on the body or built into clothing or accessories, that commonly detect and transmit information such as vital signs, sometimes with immediate biofeedback to the wearer (Wikipedia, "Wearable technology," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearable_technology).

# The Clinical Benefits Of AI In Health Care

Patel views AI as a "powerful instrument" that helps magnify physicians' capabilities rather than replacing them, and he groups its clinical benefits into pattern recognition, volume handling, automation, early risk detection and personalized medicine.

Pattern recognition comes first. "One of AI's primary strengths is its ability to recognize patterns that might escape the human eye," he said. The technology also helps providers by sifting through and analyzing vast volumes of information, far more than what would be humanly possible, Patel said, and it automates mundane and routine tasks, allowing health care professionals to redirect their focus to the patient.

Early risk detection is another key benefit. "AI tools can predict potential health risks by analyzing a combination of genetic, behavioral and environmental factors, facilitating early interventions and potentially saving lives," Patel said.

AI can also help enable the delivery of personalized medicine and proactive preventative care. Fortnite is a battle royale-style third-person shooter where 100 players swarm a massive but shrinking virtual island with the goal of being the last man standing. # Fortnite's Live-Service Content Treadmill

Polygon's model, published 2023-10-19, is that around 2018 Twitch and its personalities turned Fortnite into a juggernaut so powerful that much of the gaming industry started molding itself in its image — and that what kept Fortnite from being a mere fad was not its approachable aesthetic and surprising gameplay but its model: where content expansions and adjustments previously took months or years and often cost money, Fortnite set a more cutthroat standard of free weekly content updates.

The conditions that made this possible were unique to Epic. It could swing ceaseless delivery because the bulk of its profits at the time came from its engine, which many games — including Fortnite's competitors — license; those deep pockets made Fortnite possible in the first place, since the bubbly shooter was initially a flop before Epic perfected the formula. The cadence also let Epic quickly adapt Fortnite to whatever was trending or novel, whether Among Us or Splatoon, and much like Roblox it became a game that could give you anything — and if Epic did not emulate it, the players would. "You can't replicate Fortnite's growth from, like, the [content creator] standpoint and also definitely from the developer standpoint," says a Twitch streamer turned game developer who requested anonymity because he is not authorized to discuss the popular AAA live-service shooter he works on.

# Melissa Lucashenko: Family History, Late-Discovered Ancestry And A Writing Career

Melissa Lucashenko is a novelist preoccupied with survival who knows a lot about it personally. Born to an Aboriginal mother, Cecile, and a Russian-speaking Ukrainian father — Vladimir Lucashenko, known as Wally Lucas, whose family fled the Russian Revolution via China — she and her six older brothers grew up on the outskirts of Logan, south of Brisbane, in circumstances where the chances of becoming an author, let alone a celebrated one, were remote. "My father was a meatworker and a cane cutter … Mum worked at a fish and chip shop and sold plants at the local markets," she says. "Mum left school in about grade three or four. She was a domestic from a very young age, as her mother and grandmother were. At one point as a young mother she was working three jobs. Dad went to high school but I'm not sure how far he got. As a child, he was in an orphanage in Brisbane at one point with his brothers, after his father was violent, and his mother needed to escape."

She did not know she was of Aboriginal descent until she was 15, when someone she knew "picked it" and told her, "You're Aboriginal … go home and ask your parents." Around that time a photo appeared on her mother's dresser of "this very black woman"; when she asked who it was, her mother said, "Oh, that's my grandmother. That's why we've all got olive skin and dark hair." Lucashenko was shocked and felt "momentary disquiet", something she attributes to internalised racism, but says it "instantly made sense". "For the 40 years since then, I've been learning the culture and I've had different teachers from different mobs and I've taught other people what I know." She later learnt that her grandmother Eleanor had defeated an attempt by authorities to remove her as a child in about 1907 or 1908, in Wolvi in Queensland's Gympie region, and that her great-grandmother Christina Copson had worked as a domestic servant from the age of eight: "She was a slave, she had no rights." The family came under extra scrutiny after Copson shot and injured a man who tried to rape her; she was arrested and jailed for a week, told the judge she had acted in self-defence, and was found not guilty, with her perpetrator jailed for six months instead. The would-be rapist was an Aboriginal man — "No way she would have gotten away with shooting a white assailant," Lucashenko says.

Her career path ran through work and education before writing. On leaving school in 1983 at the end of year 12 she worked as a barmaid, a delivery truck driver and a support worker for women out of prison; she used to be obsessed with karate and has a black belt in it. In 1990 she graduated from Griffith University with an honours degree in public policy, the first in her immediate family to go to university — "My mother had no education and was determined that her daughter would have the chances she didn't. There was no skipping school in my household. I was always in the library if I wasn't on the back of a horse ... I was taken up to the headmaster's office in grade one and made to read aloud and they all oohed and ahhed." She published her first book, Steam Pigs, in 1997; it won the Dobbie Literary Award for women's fiction and she was away, publishing three more books over the next 15 or so years. In 2018 she told The Sydney Morning Herald that "Australia is a profoundly racist country and that is why I write more than anything else". She married Bill, a foreign aid specialist for AusAID, had a son and a daughter, and the family moved around for his job, living in Canberra and on overseas postings including Tonga, eventually settling on her ancestral land, Bundjalung, in the northern coastal area of NSW, buying a property and raising horses. That idyll ended in 2007 with divorce: she could not afford to stay on the land and worried about becoming a "bag lady", and around that time her 16-year-old daughter was hospitalised with mental health difficulties and the two moved back to Logan City, poor again. As she said in a 2013 Melbourne Writers' Festival address: "I knew what life was like in a suburb where the majority of people were ordinary, decent Australians, but a significant minority were prepared to sell their children's Ritalin in order to fund a heroin habit. Like some kind of weirdly reverse Charles Ryder coming upon Brideshead, I'd been there before. I knew all about it." When she won the Miles Franklin in 2019 for Too Much Lip — a novel the judges called "a novel of celebratory defiance" — her first reaction was "Bugger me dead!", which the profile says neatly sums her up: unpretentious, frank and on easy terms with vernacular.

# Clean: The Imogen Heap Collaboration That Closed 1989

# Philippine Debt And The Case For Fiscal Consolidation

The argument for fiscal consolidation is that although the current 61% debt-to-GDP ratio may be manageable for an emerging economy like the Philippines for some time, the country may not have the fiscal space to respond to another potential domestic or external shock. The grounds are historical: the National Government's debt was less than 40% before the pandemic struck, and it expended much of its fiscal space combatting the pandemic, incurring debt and large budget deficits. The warrant is a crowding-out mechanism: if the debt continues to rise more than the economy, risks will increase and the government may crowd out private investment as it competes with the private sector for funds to service its debt.

The planned consolidation entails harmonizing revenue needs with the promotion of investment through the structure and administration of the reformed incentive system. The National Government plans to raise more revenue to finance the country's socio-economic needs, largely through a progressive and simplified tax system and more efficient and effective tax collection measures through digitalization, and to some extent from policy measures such as value-added tax on digital service providers and excise tax on sweetened beverages and junk food. The conclusion is stated as a conditional pair: achieving fiscal stability presupposes the sustainability of fiscal policy, and fiscal stability helps crowd in private investment.

# Public Health Guidance

## Definition

Public health guidance, in the corpus, is the population-level recommendations and standards that named authorities — the CDC and the WHO — issue on vaccination, disease-eradication targets, dietary/consumer advice, and antibiotic-resistance standards, as distinct from a clinician's advice to an individual patient.

## Context

In the corpus this guidance takes several concrete forms. The CDC recommends that everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine every season, an estimate it grounds in a documented burden of nine million illnesses, four million medical visits, 10,000 hospitalizations, and 5,000 deaths in the 2021-2022 season alone.
The WHO similarly issues disease-eradication targets, such as its aim to eradicate Hepatitis C by 2030, and consumer-facing advice, such as advising against sugar substitutes for weight loss or disease prevention.
On antibiotic resistance, the CDC tracks 18 concerning bacteria for rising drug resistance and the WHO defines a "priority" list of bacteria that new antibiotics should target, and both agencies' guidance underpins hospital-level antibiotic stewardship efforts such as auditing prescriptions and requiring special clearance for the broadest-spectrum drugs.

## Key Characteristics

- **Issued by named authorities** — the corpus attributes guidance specifically to the CDC and the WHO, not to unnamed "experts" or generic health advice.
- **Population-level rationale** — guidance is justified by aggregate burden data (illnesses, hospitalizations, deaths, or bacterial deaths worldwide) rather than any single patient's case.
- **Spans prevention and treatment-adjacent domains** — the corpus shows guidance covering vaccination recommendations, dietary/consumer advice, and antibiotic-prescribing standards.
- **Operationalized locally** — guidance translates into concrete institutional practice, such as hospital antibiotic stewardship programs auditing individual prescriptions to lower "overall population-level risk."
- **Distinct from individual clinical advice** — Dr. Gregg Sylvester's public comments urging flu vaccination echo the CDC's population-level recommendation, but they are expert commentary given to the press rather than a treating clinician's advice to a specific patient.

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), public health is "the science of protecting and improving the health of people and their communities," concerned with protecting the health of entire populations — from a neighborhood to a country or region — through prevention, policy recommendations, and health communication, distinct from healthcare professionals like doctors and nurses, who "provide care to individuals and meet their individual needs" (CDC Foundation, "What is Public Health?", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.cdcfoundation.org/what-public-health).

# Balanced Versus Deficit Budget in Philippine Fiscal Practice

The DBM calls a budget balanced when revenues match expenditures or disbursements. When expenditures exceed revenues, the government incurs a deficit, which may lead to three situations: the government borrows money either from foreign sources or from the domestic capital market, which increases the debt stock of the National Government and its debt servicing requirements; the government borrows money from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas; or the government withdraws funds from its cash balances in the Treasury.

The historical case is one of persistent deficits. National Government expenditures have always exceeded total revenues, resulting in annual budget deficits, the DBM declared, and "the National Government had to resort to borrowing to cover said deficits which resulted in the ballooning of foreign and domestic debts," the budget office admitted.

The boundary case is 1994: "in 1994, the government broke the deficit trend by posting a budget surplus of P16 billion through an aggressive privatization and revenue generation program and a prudent expenditure program. Since then, the government has been exerting efforts to maintain the surplus budget policy. The surplus budget policy is important to encourage economic growth," the DBM said.

# Meta Bias Mechanisms

Meta's disproportionate suppression of Palestinian and Arabic content is produced by a stack of interacting mechanisms rather than any single fault: thin Arabic language resources, categorical policies that cannot handle nuance, a blanket prohibition on support for terrorist organizations, government partnerships that shape policy decisions, automated enforcement backed by "minimally trained humans," and an allocation of moderation resources that tracks regulatory pressure rather than need. TechCrunch set out this account on 19 October 2023, drawing chiefly on the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

The linguistic layer comes first. Meta struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic, a language with over 25 dialects, and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources. On top of that, the company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic — content that discusses violence without condoning it is the example given.

The policy layer compounds it. Meta forbids support of terrorist organizations, as most U.S.-based social media companies do, but struggles to moderate content around that prohibition, from user discourse to journalistic updates. Combined with the company's partnership with Israel to monitor posts that incite violence, the rule complicates matters for Palestinians living under Hamas' governance: as EFF points out, something as simple as Hamas' flag in the background of an image can result in a strike. Advocacy groups have separately raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions.

The enforcement layer supplies the inconsistency. Jillian York, EFF's director for international freedom of expression, blames automation and decisions made by "minimally trained humans," and says Meta's zero tolerance policy and imprecise enforcement often suppress content from or about conflict zones. The range of the effect is wider than Palestine: the site's moderation issues have negatively affected multiple non-English speaking regions, including Libya, Syria and Ukraine. "These rules can prevent people from sharing documentation of human rights violations, documentation of war crimes, even just news about what's happening on the ground," York said. "And so I think that is what is the most problematic right now about that particular rule, and the way that it's enforced."

The resourcing layer explains why the effect is unevenly distributed across languages. York says Meta has made more contact with regional Palestinian organizations since 2021 but has been slow to implement recommendations from EFF and other advocacy groups, and that it is "very clear" Meta is not putting the same resources behind Arabic and other non-English languages compared with the attention it gives countries that exert the most regulatory pressure. Moderation of English and other European languages tends to be more comprehensive, for example, because the EU enforces the Digital Services Act.

Meta contests the picture. In its response to the report, human rights director Miranda Sissons said the company was "assessing the feasibility" of reviewing Arabic content by dialect and that it has "large and diverse teams" who understand "local cultural context across the region," including in Palestine; responding to the escalating violence earlier that month, Meta said it had established a "special operations center" staffed with fluent Hebrew and Arabic speakers to monitor and respond to violating content. # ASPI's Analysis Of TikTok Pixel Data Aggregation Risk

Strategic Policy Institute researcher Samantha Hoffman said the data collected by TikTok's pixel was similar to that of US-based tech giants Google and Meta, but that the difference was "the intent." Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. # The USD Fund Copycat Playbook In China

USD-denominated funds in China have long operated on a benchmark model: draw inspiration from Silicon Valley startups and use them as templates for investment targets back home. # Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# Urban Heat Islands and Chronic Heat Health Effects

Urban heat islands — hot zones of a city where asphalt, high building density and infrastructure push temperatures higher than in surrounding areas — house millions of people who cannot escape the effects of relentless summer heat, and chronic exposure to that excess heat affects cardiovascular, respiratory and mental health.

The exposure pathway runs through daily life outdoors. "People who live in urban areas usually walk to do their daily errands. One of the advantages of living in a city is that things are close and you can use public transport, but that also means you have to spend more time outdoors," said Neelima Tummala, a physician and co-director of the Institute for Environmental Health at George Washington University, who was not involved in the study. In neighbourhoods without parks or large trees, where asphalt and buildings absorb and radiate summer heat, residents can find it hard to escape extreme temperatures either indoors or outdoors, and this kind of continuous exposure can be very dangerous because the body becomes unable to cool itself adequately by sweating. # Mozilla's Open Letter On AI Openness

The letter's claim is that openness makes AI safer, against the counter-position that proprietary control does. # DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.
